Ordered, That the Book written by *Robert Hooke*, Master of Arts and Fellow of this Society, Entitled, *Micrographia: or some Physiological <note>In this context, "physiological" refers to the physical properties and internal workings of natural objects, rather than just biology.</note> Descriptions of Minute Bodies made by Magnifying Glasses, with Observations and Inquiries thereupon*, Be printed by *John Martyn*, and *James Allestry*, Printers to the said Society.

# The PREFACE.

*...many details are much surpassed by those of other creatures, and even at their best, they fall far short of the perfection they seem capable of. These infirmities of the senses arise from a double cause: either from the disproportion of the object to the organ—whereby an infinite number of things can never enter them—or else from error in the perception, so that many things which come within their reach are not received in a correct manner.*

*Similar frailties are to be found in the memory; we often let many things slip away from us that deserve to be retained, and of those which we treasure up, a great part is either frivolous or false. Even if they are good and substantial, they are either obliterated over the course of time or, at best, so overwhelmed and buried under more trivial notions that when there is need of them, they are sought for in vain.*

*Since the two main foundations are so deceptive, it is no wonder that all the succeeding works we build upon them—arguing, concluding, defining, judging, and all the other degrees of reason—are liable to the same imperfection, being, at best, either vain or uncertain. So it is that the errors of the understanding correspond to the other two, being defective both in the quantity and the quality of its knowledge; for the limits to which our thoughts are confined are small compared to the vast extent of Nature itself. Some parts of it are too large to be comprehended, and some too small to be perceived. And from this it must follow that, not having a full sensation of the object, we must be very inadequate and imperfect in our conceptions about it, and in all the propositions which we build upon it. Hence, we often take the shadow of things for the substance, small appearances for good similarities, and similarities for definitions; even many of those which we think to be the most solid definitions are expressions of our own misguided apprehensions rather than of the true nature of the things themselves.*

*The effects of these imperfections are manifested in different ways, according to the temper and disposition of the various minds of men: some they incline toward gross ignorance and stupidity, and others toward a presumptuous imposing of their opinions on other men, and a confident dogmatizing on matters about which no assurance can be given.*

<meta>catchword: Thus</meta>

<summary>Hooke discusses the inherent fallibility of human senses, memory, and reason, arguing that these limitations lead to imperfect knowledge of the natural world. He notes that these flaws result in either ignorance or the confident assertion of false opinions.</summary>
<keywords>senses, memory, reason, nature, human fallibility, perception, epistemology, Robert Hooke</keywords>

# The PREFACE.

*Thus all the uncertainty and mistakes of human actions proceed either from the narrowness and wandering of our senses, from the slipperiness or delusion of our memory, or from the confinement or rashness of our understanding; so that it is no wonder that our power over natural causes and effects is so slowly improved, seeing that we must not only contend with the obscurity and difficulty of the things upon which we work and think, but even the forces of our own minds conspire to betray us.*

Since these are the dangers in the process of human *Reason*, the remedies for them all can only proceed from real, mechanical, and experimental *Philosophy*. This has an advantage over the *Philosophy* of discourse and disputation: for while that chiefly aims at the subtlety of its *Deductions* and *Conclusions* without much regard for the first groundwork—which ought to be well laid in the *Sense* and *Memory*—this experimental approach intends the right ordering of them all and making them serviceable to each other.

The first thing to be undertaken in this weighty work is a watchfulness over the failings, and an enlargement of the dominion, of the *Senses*.

To that end, it is requisite, first, that there should be a scrupulous choice and a strict examination of the reality, constancy, and certainty of the *Particulars* that we admit. This is the first step upon which truth is to begin, and here the most severe and most impartial diligence must be employed; the storing up of everything, without any regard for evidence or use, will only lead to darkness and confusion. We must not, therefore, estimate the riches of our *Philosophical* treasure by the number alone, but chiefly by the weight; the most common *Instances* are not to be neglected, but above all, the most instructive are to be embraced. The footsteps of *Nature* are to be traced, not only in her ordinary course, but also when she seems to be put to her shifts, forced to make many doublings and turnings, and to use some kind of art in endeavoring to avoid our discovery.

The next care to be taken, in respect of the *Senses*, is the supplying of their infirmities with *Instruments* and, as it were, the adding of artificial *Organs* to the natural ones; this, in one of them, has been in recent years

# THE PREFACE.
<meta>catchword: And</meta>

*accomplished with prodigious benefit to all sorts of useful knowledge by the invention of* Optical Glasses. *By means of* Telescopes, *nothing is so far distant that it cannot be represented to our view; and by the help of* Microscopes, *nothing is so small that it escapes our inquiry; hence, a new visible* World *is discovered to the understanding. By this means the* Heavens *are opened, and a vast number of new* Stars, *new* Motions, *and new* Productions *appear in them, to which all the ancient* Astronomers *were utter* Strangers. *By this the* Earth *itself, which lies so near us under our feet, shows itself to be quite a new thing to us; and in every little particle of its matter, we now behold almost as great a variety of* Creatures *as we were able before to count in the whole* Universe *itself.*

*It seems not improbable that by these aids the subtlety of the composition of* Bodies, *the structure of their parts, the various texture of their matter, the instruments and manner of their inward motions, and all the other possible appearances of things may come to be more fully discovered. All of these the ancient* Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle's philosophy.</note> *were content to encompass in two general and (unless further explained) useless words: "Matter" and "Form." From this, many admirable advantages may arise toward the increase of* Operative *and* Mechanical Knowledge, *to which this* Age *seems so much inclined; because we may perhaps be enabled to discern all the secret workings of* Nature *almost in the same manner as we do those that are the productions of* Art, *and are managed by* Wheels, *Engines, and* Springs *that were devised by human* Wit.

*In this regard, I here present to the* World *my imperfect* Endeavors; *though they shall prove significant in no other way, yet I hope they may be in some measure useful to the main* Design *of a reformation in* Philosophy, *even if only by showing that what is required for it is not so much any strength of* Imagination, *exactness of* Method, *or depth of* Contemplation (*though the addition of these, where they can be had, must surely produce a much more perfect composition*) *as a sincere* Hand *and a faithful* Eye *to examine and record things as they appear.*

# THE PREFACE.
<meta>catchword: And</meta>

And I beg my *Reader* to allow me the boldness to assure him that in this current state of knowledge, a man so qualified as I have endeavored to be—with only resolution, integrity, and plain intentions of employing his *Senses* correctly—may venture to compare the reality and the usefulness of his services toward true *Philosophy* with those of other men who possess much stronger and more acute speculations, but who shall not make use of the same method by the *Senses*.

The truth is, the *Science of Nature* has already been for too long made only a work of the *Brain* and the *Imagination*. It is now high time that it should return to the plainness and soundness of *Observations* on material and obvious things. It is said of great *Empires* that the best way to preserve them from decay is to bring them back to the first principles and arts upon which they began. The same is undoubtedly true in *Philosophy*, which, by wandering far away into invisible *Notions*, has almost completely destroyed itself; it can never be recovered or continued except by returning to the same sensible paths in which it first proceeded.

If, therefore, the *Reader* expects from me any infallible *Deductions* or certainty of *Axioms*, I must say for myself that those stronger *Works of Intellect and Imagination* are above my weak *Abilities*; or, if they had not been so, I would not have made use of them in this present *Subject* before me. Wherever he finds that I have ventured any small *Conjectures* at the causes of the things that I have observed, I beseech him to look upon them only as doubtful *Problems* and uncertain guesses, and not as unquestionable *Conclusions* or matters of irrefutable *Science*. I have produced nothing here with the intent to bind his understanding to an implicit consent; I am so far from that, that I desire him not to rely absolutely upon these *Observations* of my eyes if he finds them contradicted by the future *Ocular Experiments* of sober and impartial *Discoverers*.

As for my part, I have achieved my goal if these small *Labors* of mine shall be thought fit to take some place in the large stock of natural *Observations* which so many hands are busy providing. If I have contributed the most humble foundations whereon others may raise nobler

# THE PREFACE.
<meta>catchword: shyness</meta>

Superstructures, I am abundantly satisfied; and all my ambition is that I may serve the great *Philosophers* of this *Age* as the makers and the grinders of my *Glasses* did for me: that I may prepare and furnish them with some *Materials* which they may afterwards order and manage with better skill and to far greater advantage.

The next remedies in this universal cure of the *Mind* are to be applied to the *Memory*, and they are to consist of such *Directions* as may inform us what things are best to be stored up for our purpose, and which is the best way of so disposing them that they may not only be kept in safety, but ready and convenient to be at any time produced for use, as occasion shall require. But I will not here anticipate what I may say in another *Discourse*, wherein I shall make an attempt to propose some *Considerations* on the manner of compiling a *Natural* and *Artificial History*, and of so ranging and registering its *Particulars* into *Philosophical Tables* as may make them most useful for the raising of *Axioms* and *Theories*.

The last indeed is the most hazardous *Enterprise*, and yet the most necessary; and that is, to take such care that the *Judgment* and the *Reason* of *Man* (which is the third *Faculty* to be repaired and improved) should receive such assistance as to avoid the dangers to which it is by nature most subject. The *Imperfections* which I have already mentioned, to which it is liable, either belong to the *extent* or the *goodness* of its *knowledge*; and here the difficulty is greater, lest that which may be thought a remedy for the one should prove destructive to the other; lest by seeking to enlarge our *Knowledge*, we should render it weak and uncertain; and lest by being too scrupulous and exact about every *Circumstance* of it, we should confine and restrict it too much.

In both these, the middle ways are to be taken: nothing is to be omitted, and yet everything must undergo mature deliberation. No *Intelligence* from *Men* of all *Professions* and quarters of the *World* is to be slighted, and yet all must be so severely examined that there remains no room for doubt or instability: much rigor in admitting, much strictness in comparing, and above all, much slowness in debating, and

# THE PREFACE.
<meta>catchword: by</meta>

caution in determining is to be practiced. The *Understanding* is to order all the inferior services of the *lower Faculties*; but yet it is to do this only as a lawful Master, and not as a *Tyrant*. It must not encroach upon their offices, nor take upon itself the employments which belong to either of them. It must watch the irregularities of the *Senses*, but it must not go before them or prevent their information. It must examine, range, and dispose of the bank which is laid up in the *Memory*; but it must be sure to make a distinction between the sober and well-collected heap, and the extravagant *ideas* and mistaken *images* which it may sometimes light upon there. So many are the links upon which the true *Philosophy* depends, of which, if any one be loose or weak, the whole chain is in danger of being dissolved; it is to begin with the Hands and Eyes, and to proceed through the Memory, to be continued by the *Reason*; nor is it to stop there, but to come back to the Hands and Eyes again. Thus, by a continual passage round from one faculty to another, it is to be maintained in life and strength, as much as the body of man is by the circulation of the blood through the several parts of the body—the Arms, the Feet, the Lungs, the Heart, and the Head.

If once this method were followed with diligence and attention, there is nothing that lies within the power of human *wit* (or which is far more effectual, of human *industry*) which we might not compass; we might not only hope for *inventions* to equal those of *Copernicus*, *Galileo*, *Gilbert*, *Harvey*, and of others whose names are almost lost—those who were the *inventors* of *gunpowder*, the *seaman's compass*, *printing*, *etching*, *engraving*, *microscopes*, and so on—but multitudes that may far exceed them. For even those discoveries seem to have been the products of some such method, though but imperfectly applied; what, therefore, may not be expected from it if thoroughly prosecuted? Talking and contention of *arguments* would soon be turned into labors; all the *fine dreams of opinions* and universal metaphysical natures, which the luxury of subtle brains has devised, would quickly vanish and give place to solid *histories*, *experiments*, and *works*. And as at first, mankind fell by tasting of the *forbidden Tree of Knowledge*, so we, their *posterity*, may be in part restored by

# THE PREFACE.
<meta>catchword: gated</meta>

*in the same way, not only by beholding and contemplating, but by tasting too those fruits of* Natural knowledge *that were never yet forbidden. From here the* World *may be assisted with a variety of* Inventions; *new matter for* Sciences *may be collected, the old improved, and their rust rubbed away; and as it is by the benefit of the* Senses *that we receive all our skill in the works of* Nature, *so they also may be wonderfully benefited by it, and may be guided to an easier and more exact performance of their* offices; *it is not unlikely that we may find out wherein our* Senses *are deficient, and just as easily find ways of repairing them.*

*The endeavors of skillful men have been most focused on the assistance of the* Eye, *and many noble productions have followed from it; and from here we may conclude that there is a way opened for advancing the operations, not only of all the other* Senses, *but even of the* Eye *itself; that which has been already done ought not to content us, but rather to encourage us to proceed further, and to attempt greater things in both similar and different ways.*

*It is not unlikely that there may yet be invented several other helps for the eye, exceeding those already found as much as those do the bare eye, such as those by which we may perhaps be able to discover living creatures in the* Moon, *or other* Planets, *the shapes of the compounding particles of matter, and the particular* <term>Schematisms</term> *and* <term>Textures</term> *of* Bodies.

*And as* glasses *have highly promoted our seeing, so it is not improbable that there may be found many* mechanical inventions *to improve our other* senses—*of hearing, smelling, tasting, and touching. Nor are the other three senses so perfect that diligence, attention, and many mechanical contrivances might not also highly improve them. For since the sense of smelling seems to be produced by the swift passage of the air (impregnated with the vapors and effluvia of several odorous bodies) through the gristly meanders of the nose, whose surfaces are covered with a very sensitive nerve and moistened by a transudation from the <term>processus mamillares</term> of the brain and some adjoining glands, as well as by the moist vapor of the lungs with a fluid suitable for the reception of those effluvia; and by the adhesion and mixing of those vapors with that fluid, thereby affecting the nerve—or perhaps by working their way into the juices of the brain in the same manner as I have suggested in the following observations regarding how particles of salt pass through the skins of <term>efts</term> and frogs—since, I say, smelling seems to be produced in some such way, it is not improbable that some contrivance for making a large quantity of air pass quickly through the nose might promote the sense of smelling as much as any way of hindering that passage dulls and destroys it. I have conducted several trials, both of hindering and promoting this sense, and have succeeded in some according to expectation; and indeed, it seems to me capable of being improved for judging the constitutions of many bodies. Perhaps we may thereby also judge (as other creatures seem to do) what is wholesome and what is poison; and in a word, what the specific properties of bodies are.

There may also be other mechanical ways found to perceive the effluvia of bodies sensibly. I could give several instances of this regarding mineral vapors and exhalations, were it appropriate here; and it seems not impossible that, through such improved methods, it may be discovered what minerals lie buried under the earth without the trouble of digging for them. Some things to confirm this conjecture may be found in <term>Agricola</term> and other writers on minerals, who speak of the plants that are apt to thrive or wither in those vapors.

If a physician is therefore accounted more able in his faculty because he has had long experience and practice—the remembrance of which, though perhaps very imperfect, regulates all his later actions—what ought to be thought of that man who has not only a perfect register of his own experience, but has grown old with the experience of many hundreds of years and many thousands of men?

And though of late, men, beginning to be sensible of this convenience, have here and there registered and printed some few centuries <note>Collections of 100 observations or experiments.</note>, yet for the most part they are set down very weakly and imperfectly; and, I fear, many times not so truly, as several of them seem to be designed more for ostentation than public use. Notwithstanding all this, these kinds of histories are generally esteemed useful, even to the ablest physician.

What may not be expected from the rational or deductive faculty that is furnished with such materials, and those so readily adapted and arranged for use, that in a moment, as it were, thousands of instances serving for the illustration, determination, or invention of almost any inquiry may be represented even to the sight? How near the nature of axioms must all those propositions be which are examined before so many witnesses? And how difficult will it be for any error in philosophy, no matter how subtle, to escape from being discovered after it has endured the touchstone and so many other trials?

*What kind of mechanical method, and physical invention as well, is required that might not be discovered in this way? The success of all these great men, and many others, and the now seemingly great obviousness of most of their and various other inventions—which from the beginning of the world have been, as it were, trodden on and yet not noticed until these last inquisitive ages (an argument that there may yet be many more remaining)—reminds me to recommend such studies, and the pursuit of them by such methods, to the gentlemen of our nation, whose leisure makes them suitable to undertake, and the abundance of their fortunes to accomplish, extraordinary things in this way. And I do not only propose this kind of *experimental philosophy* as a matter of high rapture and delight of the mind, but even as a tangible and sensory pleasure. So vast is the variety of objects which will come under their *inspections*, so many different ways there are of handling them, and so great is the satisfaction of finding out new things, that I dare compare the contentment which they will enjoy not only to that of contemplation, but even to that which most men prefer from the very *senses* themselves.

And if they will please to take any encouragement from such humble and imperfect endeavors as mine, I can assure them from my own experience, without arrogance, that there has not been any inquiry or problem in *mechanics* that I have hitherto proposed to myself, but by a certain method (which I may explain on some other opportunity) I have been able immediately to examine the possibility of it; and if it is possible, as easily to devise various ways of performing it. And indeed, it is possible to do as much by this method in *mechanics* as can be performed by *algebra* in *geometry*. Nor can I at all doubt that the same method is as applicable to *physical inquiries*, and as likely to find and reap from them as plentiful a crop of *inventions*; and indeed, there seems to be no subject so barren that it may not be highly improved with this diligent cultivation.

Toward the pursuit of this method in *physical inquiries*, I have here and there gathered a handful of *observations*, in the collection of most of which I made use of *microscopes* and some other *lenses* and *instruments* that improve the sense. Every significant improvement of *telescopes* or *microscopes* produces new worlds and *unknown lands* (Terra Incognita) for our view.

The glasses I used were of *English* make, but though very good for their kind, they were far short of what might be expected if we could once find a way of making glasses *elliptical*, or of some more perfect shape. For though both *microscopes* and *telescopes*, as they currently exist, will magnify an *object* about a million times larger than it appears to the *naked eye*, the apertures of the *objective lenses* are so very small that very few *rays* are admitted. Even among those few, there are so many distorted rays that the *object* appears dark and indistinct. Indeed, these inconveniences seem inseparable from *spherical glasses*, even when most precisely made; but the method we have used so far for that purpose is so imperfect that perhaps ten might be crafted before one is made tolerably well, and of those ten, every one perhaps differs in quality from the others—which is an *argument* that the method used until now is, at least, very uncertain. So, these glasses have a double defect: the first is that very few of them are crafted with exact precision; the second is that even among the best of them, none will admit enough *rays* to magnify the *object* beyond a certain size. I have found only these remedies for these inconveniences:

First, for *microscopes* (where the *object* we view is nearby and within our control), the best way to make it appear bright in the glass is to cast a large amount of light on it by means of *convex glasses*. By doing so, even though the aperture is very small, such a multitude of rays will crowd through it that an *object* will, by this means, sustain being magnified twice as much as it would be without it. The method for doing this is as follows: I choose a room that has only one window facing south, and at about three or four feet from this window, I place my *microscope* on a table. Then I position either a round globe of water or a very deep, clear *plano-convex glass* (with its convex side turned toward the window) so that a large quantity of *rays* is collected and thrown upon the *object*. Or, if the *sun* is shining, I place a small piece of *oiled paper* very near the *object*, between it and the light; then, with a large, high-quality *burning glass*, I collect and focus the *rays* onto the paper so that a very large amount of light passes through it to the *object*. If the heat is applied gradually, this plate will endure a much higher temperature and, consequently, greatly increase the useful light. By all these means, the light of the sun or from a window may be directed onto an object so as to make it twice as bright as it would otherwise be, and without the inconvenience of glare, which direct sunlight is very likely to create in most objects. By this method, the light is so equally diffused that all parts are illuminated alike; but when direct sunlight falls on an object, the reflections from a few parts are so vivid that they drown out the appearance of all the others and are themselves indistinct because of the unequal light, appearing only as radiant spots.

But because the light of the sun and the light from a window vary continually, many objects cannot be viewed long enough to be thoroughly examined. Besides, the weather is often so dark and cloudy that for many days together nothing can be viewed. Furthermore, because there are many objects encountered at night that perhaps cannot be conveniently kept until the day, I thought of and often used this expedient to produce and direct a sufficient quantity of light onto an object at night.

I obtained a small pedestal, such as is described in the fifth figure of the first scheme. On the lower arm, I placed a fairly large glass globe, G, filled with exceedingly clear brine, stoppered, inverted, and fixed as shown in the figure. By means of this instrument, properly placed as shown in the figure, the small flame of a lamp can direct as much useful light onto the object as it can reasonably endure. Since this light is always constant and available at any time, I found it most suitable for drawing representations of those small objects I had occasion to observe.

None of these methods (though far better than any others used so far by anyone I know) provide sufficient help; after a certain degree of magnifying, they leave us at a disadvantage again. *means, the longer the glass is, the larger the aperture it will bear, if the glasses are of equal quality for their kind. Therefore, a six-foot glass will endure a much larger aperture than a three-foot glass; and a sixty-foot glass will proportionally bear a greater aperture than a thirty-foot one, and will excel it as much as a six-foot does a three-foot, as I have experimentally observed in one of that length made by Mr. Richard Reives here in London, which will bear an aperture above three inches wide, and yet make the object proportionally large and distinct; whereas there are very few thirty-foot glasses that will endure an aperture of more than two inches wide. So that for telescopes, supposing we had a very ready way of making their object-glasses with exactly spherical surfaces, we might, by increasing the length of the glass, magnify the object to any assignable size. And for performing both these, I cannot imagine any way more easy and more exact than by this following engine, by means of which any glasses, of whatever length, may be speedily made. It seems the easiest because with one and the same tool, an object-glass of any necessary length or breadth may be ground with care, and that with very little or no trouble in fitting the engine, and without much skill in the grinder. It seems to be the most exact because, to the very last stroke, the glass regulates and rectifies the tool to its exact figure; and the longer or more the tool and glass are worked together, the more exact both of them will be to the desired figure. Furthermore, the motions of the glass and tool cross each other so much that there is not one point on either surface that does not have thousands of cross-motions thwarting it, so that no kind of rings or gutters can be made in either the tool or the glass.*

The contrivance of the engine is only to make the ends of two large *mandrels* <note>The spindles or shafts of a lathe</note> move so that their centers may be at any convenient distance apart, and so that the axes of the *mandrels*, lying both in the same plane when extended, may meet each other at any assignable angle. *By means of this instrument I can with little trouble, and a very small quantity of any liquor, examine, most accurately, its refraction, not only for one inclination, but for all; and thereby am enabled to make very accurate tables; several of which I have also experimentally made, and find that oil of turpentine has a much greater refraction than spirit of wine, though it is lighter; and that spirit of wine has a greater refraction than water, though it is lighter also; but that salt water also has a greater refraction than fresh, though it is heavier: but alum water has a less refraction than common water, though heavier also. By this I have also found, that whatever proportion the *Sine* of the *Angle* of one *Inclination* has to the *Sine* of the *Angle* of *Refraction* corresponding to it, the same proportion exists between all the *Sines* of other *Inclinations* and the *Sines* of their appropriate *Refractions*.

My method for measuring how much a glass magnifies an object, placed at a convenient distance from my eye, is this. Having adjusted the *Microscope* to see the desired object through it very distinctly, at the same time that I look at the object through the glass with one eye, I look at other objects at the same distance with my other bare eye. By this means I am able, by the help of a *Ruler* divided into inches and small parts and laid on the pedestal of the *Microscope*, to project, as it were, the magnified appearance of the object onto the ruler, and thereby exactly measure the diameter it appears to have through the glass. This, being compared with the diameter it appears to have to the naked eye, will easily provide the amount of its magnification.

The *Microscope* which I used for the most part was shaped much like that in the sixth figure of the first *scheme*; the tube was usually no more than six or seven inches long, though, because it had four drawers, it could be lengthened significantly as occasion required. This was designed with three glasses: a small *Object Glass* at A, a thinner *Eye Glass* around B, and a very deep one around C. I used this only when I had occasion to see much of an *Object* at once; the middle glass collects a very great number of *radiating pencils* <note>bundles of light rays</note>, which would otherwise go another way, and throws them upon the deep *Eye Glass*. But whenever I had occasion to examine the small parts of a body more accurately, I took out the middle glass and only used one eye glass with the object glass; for the fewer the *refractions* are, the more bright and clear the object appears. And therefore it is not to be doubted that if we could make a *Microscope* that had only one *refraction*, it would, *ceteris paribus* <note>all other things being equal</note>, far excel any other that had a greater number. And hence it is that if you take a very clear piece of broken *Venice glass* and in a lamp draw it out into very small hairs or threads, then holding the ends of these threads in the flame until they melt and run into a small round *globule* or drop which will hang at the end of the thread; and if further you stick several of these upon the end of a stick with a little sealing wax so that the threads stand upwards, and then on a whetstone first grind off a good part of them, and afterward on a smooth metal plate with a little *Tripoli* <note>a fine-grained silica used for polishing</note>, rub them until they become very smooth; if one of these is fixed with a little soft wax against a small needle hole pricked through a thin plate of brass, lead, pewter, or any other metal, and an object placed very near is looked at through it, it will both magnify and make some objects more distinct than any of the large *microscopes*. But because these, though exceedingly easy to make, are yet very troublesome to use because of their smallness and the closeness of the object; therefore to prevent both of these issues, and yet have only two *refractions*, I provided myself with a tube of brass, shaped much like that in the fourth figure of the first *scheme*; into the smaller end of this I fixed with wax a good *plano-con-*

*Now though this was the* Instrument *I used most, I have nevertheless made several other* trials *with other kinds of* Microscopes, *which both in material and form were very different from common spherical* Glasses. *I have made a* Microscope *with one piece of* Glass *where both surfaces were* planes. *I have made another only with a* plano-concave *lens, without any kind of reflection, and several others by means of reflection. # THE PREFACE.

The things I observed will be revealed by the following descriptions; in brief, they were either exceedingly small bodies, exceedingly small pores, or exceedingly small motions. The reader will find some of each of these in the following notes, and I presume many of them at least will be new, and perhaps no less strange. The reader will find some specimen of each of these categories in the subsequent illustrations—indeed, more than I initially intended, which was caused by my first intentions to print a much greater number than I have since found time to complete. Of those I had, therefore, I selected only a few from every category which seemed most noteworthy for certain details, rejecting the rest as unnecessary for the current design.

*The following descriptions annexed to each will inform what each of the illustrated subjects are. I shall only add here, once and for all, that in various instances the engravers followed my directions and drawings quite well; and that in making them, I endeavored (as far as I was able) first to discover the true appearance, and next to make a plain representation of it. I mention this particularly because there is much more difficulty in discovering the true shape of these kinds of objects than of those visible to the naked eye; the same object seems quite different in one position relative to the light than what it really is or what may be discovered in another position. Therefore, I never began to make any drawing until, through many examinations in various lights and in several positions relative to those lights, I had discovered the true form. For it is exceedingly difficult in some objects to distinguish between a prominence and a depression, between a shadow and a black stain, or between a reflection and a whiteness in the color. Besides, the transparency of most objects renders them much more difficult to depict than if they were opaque. In one kind of light, the eyes of a fly appear almost like a lattice, drilled through with an abundance of small holes; which is probably the reason why the ingenious* Dr. Power *seems to suppose them to be such. In the sunshine, they look like a surface covered with golden nails; in another position, like a surface covered with pyramids; in another with cones; and in other positions with quite other shapes. However, that which exhibits them best is the light collected on the object by those means I have already described.*

# THE PREFACE.

And this was undertaken in pursuit of the *Design* which the **ROYAL SOCIETY** has proposed for itself. For the *Members* of the *Assembly*, having before their eyes so many fatal *instances* of the errors and falsehoods in which the greatest part of *mankind* has so long wandered because they relied upon the strength of *human Reason* alone, have begun anew to correct all *hypotheses* by *sense*, just as *seamen* do their *dead reckonings* by *celestial observations*; and for this purpose, it has been their principal endeavor to enlarge and strengthen the *senses* by *medicine*, and by such outward *instruments* as are appropriate for their particular tasks. By this means, they find some reason to suspect that those effects of *bodies*, which have been commonly attributed to *qualities*—including those confessed to be *occult*—are performed by the small *machines* of *nature*, which cannot be discerned without these helps, appearing to be the mere products of *motion*, *figure*, and *magnitude*; and that the *natural textures*, which some call the *plastic faculty*, may be made in *looms* that a greater perfection of *optics* may make discernible through these *glasses*: so that they are now no more puzzled by them than common people are to understand how *tapestry* or *flowered fabrics* are woven. And they intend the ends of all these inquiries to be the pleasure of *contemplative minds*, but above all, the ease and speed of the labors of men's hands. They indeed neglect no opportunity to bring all the rare things of *remote countries* within the scope of their knowledge and practice. But they still acknowledge their most useful information to arise from common things, and from diversifying their most ordinary operations upon them. They do not wholly reject experiments of mere light and theory; but they principally aim at those whose applications will improve and facilitate the current methods of *manual arts*. And though some men, who are perhaps occupied with less honorable employments, are pleased to criticize their proceedings, yet they can show more fruits from their first three years of assembly than any other society in *Europe* can for a much longer span of time. It is true that such undertakings as theirs commonly meet with little encouragement, because men are generally more taken with the plausible and discursive rather than the real and solid part of *philosophy*; yet by the good fortune of their institution, in an age more inquisitive than all others, they have been assisted by the contribution and presence of many of the chief *nobility* and *gentry*,

But to return to my subject from a digression, for which I hope my reader will pardon me, seeing the example is so rare that I can make no more such digressions. If these first labors of mine shall be in any way useful to inquiring men, I must attribute the encouragement and promotion of them to a very Reverend and Learned Person, of whom this ought in justice to be said: that there is scarce any one invention which this nation has produced in our age that has not in some way or other been set forward by his assistance. My reader, I believe, will quickly guess that it is *Dr. Wilkins* whom I mean. He is indeed a man born for the good of mankind and for the honor of his country. In the sweetness of his behavior, in the calmness of his mind, and in the unbounded goodness of his heart, we have an evident instance of what the true and the primitive dispassionate religion was, before it was soured by particular factions. In a word, his zeal has been so constant and effectual in advancing all good and profitable arts that, as one of the ancient Romans said of *Scipio*—that he thanked God that he was a *Roman*, because wherever *Scipio* had been born, there would have been the seat of the empire of the world—so may I thank God that *Dr. Wilkins* was an *Englishman*, for wherever he had lived, there would have been the chief seat of generous knowledge and true philosophy. To the truth of this, there are so many worthy men living who will subscribe to it, that I am confident what I have said here will not be looked upon by any ingenious reader as a <term>panegyric</term> <note>a formal speech or text of high praise</note>, but only as a real testimony.

By the advice of this excellent man I first began this enterprise, yet I still came to it with much reluctance, because I was to follow the footsteps of so eminent a person as *Dr. Wren*, who was the first who attempted anything of this nature; whose original drawings now make one of the ornaments of that great collection of rarities in the King's Closet. This honor, which his first beginnings of this kind have received—to be admitted into the most famous place of the world—did not encourage me so much as the risk of following after *Dr. Wren* frightened me; for of him I must affirm that, since the time of *Archimedes*, there have scarcely ever met in one man, in so...

He also admits to feeling intimidated by the high standard of scientific drawings previously established by Dr. Christopher Wren.</summary>

<header>### The PREFACE.</header>

...great a perfection, such a mechanical hand, and so philosophical a mind.

But at last, being assured both by *Dr. Wilkins* and *Dr. Wren* himself that he had given up his intentions of pursuing it, and not finding that there was anyone else who intended to follow it, I set upon this undertaking. I was not a little encouraged to proceed in it by the honor the Royal Society was pleased to favor me with, in approving of those drafts (which I presented to them from time to time as I had an opportunity of describing them). I was particularly encouraged by the urgings of various noble and excellent persons in it, who were my closer friends and were no less urgent for me to publish them than they were for me to pursue them.

After I had almost completed these *Pictures* and *Observations* (having had several of them engraved and being ready to send them to the press), I was informed that the ingenious physician *Dr. Henry Power* had made several *Microscopical Observations*. If I had not afterwards found—upon our interchangeably viewing each other's papers—that they were for the most part different from mine, either in the subject itself or in the details noted, and that his design was only to print observations without pictures, I would have even then suppressed what I had so far produced. But being further encouraged by several of my friends, in compliance with their opinions that it would not be unwelcome to various inquisitive men, and also hoping that I should thereby discover something new to the world, I have at length contributed my mite to the vast treasury of *A Philosophical History*. And it is my hope, as well as my belief, that these labors of mine will be no more comparable to the productions of many other natural philosophers, who are now everywhere busy with greater things, than my little objects are to be compared to the greater and more beautiful works of nature: *a flea, a mite, a gnat, to a horse, an elephant, or a lion.*

<summary>Hooke explains that he began his microscopic studies after Christopher Wren abandoned the subject, encouraged by the Royal Society and his friends. He notes that he chose to publish his work despite Henry Power's similar research because their findings and methods differed.</summary>

### Observation I. *Of the Point of a sharp small Needle.*

<margin>Scheme 2, Figure 1.</margin>
<image-desc>Large decorative woodcut drop cap 'A' featuring a bird and floral motifs.</image-desc>
Just as in *Geometry*, the most natural way to begin is from a mathematical *point*; so too in *observations* and *natural history*, this same method is the most genuine, simple, and instructive. We must first endeavor to form letters and draw single strokes accurately before we venture to write whole *sentences* or draw large *pictures*. And in *physical inquiries*, we must endeavor to follow Nature in the plainer and easier paths she treads in the most simple and uncomplicated bodies—to trace her steps and become acquainted with her manner of walking there—before we venture into the multitude of *meanders* she has in bodies of a more complicated nature; lest, being unable to distinguish and judge our way, we quickly lose both *Nature*, our guide, and ourselves too, and are left to wander in the labyrinth of groundless opinions, lacking both judgment (that light) and experience (that thread) which should direct our proceedings.

We will therefore begin these inquiries of ours with the observations of bodies of the most *simple* nature first, and then gradually proceed to those of a more complex nature. In following this method, we shall begin with a *physical point*; the *point of a needle* is commonly considered to be one of this kind, and is indeed, for the most part, made so sharp that the naked eye cannot distinguish any of its parts. It very easily pierces and makes its way through all kinds of bodies softer than itself. But if viewed with a very good *microscope*, we may find that the *tip* of a needle (though as to the

<summary>Robert Hooke introduces his microscopic observations by arguing that scientific inquiry should begin with the simplest possible forms, starting with the point of a needle as a physical representation of a mathematical point.</summary>

<header>MICROGRAPHIA.</header>
<sig>B</sig>
<meta>catchword: so</meta>

sense very *sharp*) appears a broad, blunt, and very irregular end; not resembling a cone, as is imagined, but only a piece of a tapering body, with a great part of the top removed, or deficient. The points of pins are even more blunt, and the points of the most curious mathematical instruments very seldom arrive at such a great sharpness; how much, therefore, can be built upon demonstrations made only by the productions of the ruler and compasses, he will be better able to consider who shall but view those points and lines with a *microscope*.

Now, though this point is commonly accounted the sharpest (whence, when we would express the sharpness of a point most superlatively, we say, "As sharp as a needle"), yet the *microscope* can afford us hundreds of instances of points many thousand times sharper: such as those of the *hairs*, and *bristles*, and *claws* of multitudes of *insects*; the *thorns*, or *hooks*, or *hairs* of *leaves*, and other small vegetables; nay, the ends of the *striae* <note>small rod-like filaments</note> or small parallelepipeds of *amianthus* <note>asbestos</note>, and *alumen plumosum* <note>feather alum, a mineral similar to asbestos</note>; of many of which, though the points are so sharp as not to be visible even when viewed with a *microscope* (which magnifies the object, in bulk, above a million times), yet I do not doubt that if we were able practically to make *microscopes* according to the *theory* of them, we might find hills, and dales, and pores, and a sufficient breadth or expansion to give all those parts elbow room, even in the blunt top of the very point of any of these so very sharp bodies. For certainly the *quantity* or extension of any body may be *divisible to infinity*, though perhaps not the *matter*.

<margin>Scheme 1, Figure 1.</margin>
But to proceed: the image we have exhibited here in the first figure was the top of a small and very sharp needle, whose point nevertheless appeared through the *microscope* above a quarter of an inch broad, not round nor flat, but *irregular* and *uneven*; so that it seemed to have been big enough to have afforded a hundred armed mites room enough to be ranged by each other without endangering the breaking of one another's necks by being thrust off on either side. The surface of this, though appearing very smooth to the naked eye, could not nevertheless hide a multitude of holes, scratches, and ruggedness from being discovered by the *microscope* to cover it; several of which inequalities (as A, B, and C seemed to be holes made by some small specks of *rust*; and D some external body that stuck very close to it) were *accidental*. All the rest that roughen the surface were only so many marks of the rudeness and bungling of *Art*. So inaccurate is it in all its productions, even in those which seem most neat, that if examined with an organ more acute than that by which they were made, the more we see of their shape, the less appearance will there be of their *beauty*; whereas in the works of *Nature*, the deepest discoveries show us the greatest excellencies. It is an evident argument that He who was the Author of all these things was no other than *Omnipotent*, being able to include as great a variety of parts and contrivances in the smallest discernible point as in those vaster bodies (which comparatively are also called points), such as the *Earth*, *Sun*, or *Planets*. Nor need it seem strange that the Earth itself may be, by an analogy, called a *physical point*; for as its body, though now

### Observ. II. *Of the Edge of a Razor.*

<margin>
Scheme 2.
Fig. 2.
</margin>
The sharpest edge has the same kind of affinity to the sharpest point in physics as a line has to a point in mathematics; and therefore the discussion concerning this may very properly be attached to the former. A razor does appear to be a body of a very neat and curious aspect, until more closely viewed by the *microscope*, and there we may observe its very edge to be of all kinds of shapes, except what it should be. For examining that of a very sharp one, I could not find that any part of it had anything of sharpness in it; instead, it appeared as a rough surface of a very considerable breadth from side to side, the narrowest part not seeming thinner than the back of a fairly thick knife. Nor is it likely that it should appear any otherwise, since as we just now showed that a *point* appeared as a *circle*, it is rational that a *line* should be a *parallelogram*.

Now, for the drawing of this second figure (which represents a part of the edge, about one-eighth of an inch long, of a well-sharpened razor), I so placed it between the <term>objective lens</term> and the light that there appeared a reflection from the very edge, represented by the white line *a b c d e f*. In this, you may perceive it to be somewhat sharper than elsewhere around *d*, to be indented or pitted around *b*, to be broader and thicker around *c*, and unequal and rugged around *e*, and fairly even between *a b* and *e f*. Nor was that part of the edge *g h i k* as smooth as one would imagine smooth bodies such as a hone and oil should leave it; for besides those multitudes of scratches which appear to have scarred the surface *g h i k* and to cross each other in every direction—not even half of which are expressed in the figure—there were several great and deep scratches, or furrows, such as *g h* and *i k*, which made the surface even more rugged, caused perhaps by some small dust accidentally falling on the hone, or some harder or more flinty part of the hone itself. The other part of the razor *l l*, which is polished on a grinding stone, appeared much rougher than the other, looking almost like a plowed field with many parallels, ridges, and furrows, and a cloddy or uneven surface. Nor shall we wonder at the roughness of those surfaces, since even in the most carefully wrought lenses for *microscopes* and other optical uses, I have, when the sun has shone well on them, discovered their surfaces to be variously scarred or scratched, and to consist of an infinite number of small broken surfaces which reflect the light in very various and differing colors. And indeed it seems impossible by art to cut the surface of any hard and brittle body smooth, since <term>putty</term> <note>a fine polishing powder, often tin oxide</note>, or even the most curious powder that can be used to polish such a body, must consist of little hard, rough particles, and each of them must cut its way, and consequently leave some kind of gutter or
<meta>catchword: furrows</meta>

<summary>Hooke uses a microscope to reveal that a razor's edge, which seems sharp to the naked eye, is actually a broad, jagged surface filled with deep scratches and furrows. He concludes that even the most finely polished surfaces, including optical lenses, are microscopically rough due to the abrasive nature of polishing powders.</summary>

And though Nature does seem to do it very readily in all kinds of fluid bodies, yet perhaps future observers may discover even these also to be rugged; it being very probable, as I show elsewhere, that fluid bodies are made up of small solid particles variously and strongly moved, and one may find reason to think there is scarcely a surface *in rerum naturâ* <note>in the nature of things</note> perfectly smooth. The black spot *m n*, I guess to be some small speck of rust, for I have often observed that to be the manner of the working of *corrosive juices*. To conclude, this *edge* and piece of a *razor*, if it had been really such as it appeared through the *microscope*, would scarcely have served to cleave wood, much less to have cut off the hair of beards—unless it were after the manner that *Lucian* merrily relates *Charon* to have used, when with a *carpenter’s axe* he chopped off the beard of a sage philosopher, whose gravity he very cautiously feared would endanger the oversetting of his *wherry* <note>a light rowing boat</note>.

## Observ. III. *Of Fine Lawn, or Linen Cloth.*

<margin>
Scheme 15.
Fig. 3.
</margin>
This is another product of art. A piece of the finest lawn I was able to get, so exquisite that the threads were scarcely discernible by the naked eye, and yet through an ordinary *microscope* you may perceive what a substantial piece of coarse *matting* it is; what large cords each of its threads are, being not unlike, both in shape and size, the bigger and coarser kind of *single rope-yarn* used to make *cables*. What makes the lawn so transparent is plainly evidenced—by the *microscope*, and even by the naked eye if attentively viewed—to be the multitude of square holes left between the threads. It appears to have much more empty space relative to the intersecting parts than is usually left in a *lattice window*, which it slightly resembles, except that the crossing parts are round and not flat.

These threads that compose this fine fabric, though they are as small as those that constitute the finer sorts of silks, nonetheless have nothing of their glossy, pleasant, and lively reflection. Nay, I have been informed both by the inventor himself and several other eyewitnesses that although the flax out of which it is made has been (by a singular art of that excellent person and noble virtuoso, *Mr. Charles Howard*, brother to the *Duke of Norfolk*) so exquisitely dressed and prepared as to appear to both the eye and the touch as *fine* and *glossy* as *sleave-silk* <note>untwisted silk fiber</note>—and to receive all kinds of colors just as well—yet when this *silken flax* is twisted into threads, it completely loses its former luster and becomes as plain and humble a thread to look at as one of the same size made of common *flax*.

The reason for this odd *phenomenon* seems to be nothing else but this: that although the exquisitely dressed *flax* has parts so exceedingly small as to equal, if not be much smaller than, the thread of a *silkworm* (especially in thickness), yet the differences between the shapes of the constituent filaments are so great, and their substances so various, that whereas

<sig>C</sig>
<meta>catchword: those</meta>

<summary>Hooke concludes that even "smooth" fluid surfaces may be microscopicially rugged and examines fine linen, noting how its threads resemble thick ropes and its structure resembles a lattice window. He also notes that specially prepared flax loses its silk-like luster once it is twisted into thread.</summary>
<keywords>microscopy, razor edge, fluid bodies, surface roughness, lawn fabric, linen, Charles Howard, flax, silk, textile structure</keywords>

--- Page 48 ---
<meta>This page continues the comparison between the fibers of fine linen (lawn) and silk, exploring why silk appears more lustrous and how flax might be modified to mimic it, before moving on to an observation of woven taffeta.</meta>

those of the silk are *small, round, hard, transparent*, and proportionally *stiff* for their size, so that each filament preserves its proper *shape*, and consequently its *vivid reflection* entirely, even when twisted into a thread (if not twisted too hard). Those of flax are *flat, limber, softer*, and less *transparent*; in twisting into a thread they join and lie so close together that they lose their own reflections and destroy each other's individual reflections. There seem, therefore, to be three particulars very necessary to make such treated flax also appear like silk when spun into threads. First, that its substance should be made more *clear* and *transparent*, as flax retains a kind of darkening brown or yellow; even the parts of the whitest kind I have yet observed with the *microscope* appear white, like flawed horn or glass, rather than clear, like transparent horn or glass. Next, each of the filaments should be *rounded*, if that could be done; however, this is not strictly necessary if the first point is achieved along with this third one: that each of the small filaments be *stiffened*. For even if they are square or flat, provided they are *transparent* and stiff, much the same appearance must necessarily follow. Now, although I have not yet attempted it, I do not doubt that both these properties may also be induced in flax—and perhaps even by one and the same method. Some trials might quickly inform any ingenious person who, considering the use and profit of such an invention, might find sufficient reason to be prompted to such inquiries. As for the *tenacity* <note>strength or cohesiveness</note> of the substance of flax from which the thread is made, it seems much inferior to that of silk, the one being a *vegetable* and the other an *animal* substance. Whether this proceeds from the better concoction <note>maturation or processing</note> or the more homogeneous makeup of *animal* substances over those of vegetables, I will not determine here. Yet, since I generally find that vegetable substances do not equal the *tenacity* of *animal* ones, nor do those equal the *tenacity* of some purified mineral substances, I am very inclined to think that the *tenacity* of bodies does not proceed from *hamous* <note>hook-shaped</note> or *hooked particles*, as the *Epicureans* and some modern *philosophers* have imagined, but rather from the more exact fit of the constituent parts. These parts are touching each other and are so substantial that they are not easily separated or shattered by small pulls or the agitation of heat.

regular pieces, *a b, c d, and e f*; *The Warp*, or the thread that ran across the ribbon, appeared like a single rope of an inch in diameter; but the *Woof* <note>The "woof" refers to the weft, or the crosswise threads in a weave.</note>, or the thread that ran the length of the ribbon, appeared not half so large. Each inch of six-penny-wide ribbon appeared no less than a piece of matting an inch and a half thick and twelve feet square; a few yards of this would be enough to floor the Long Gallery of the *Louvre* at *Paris*.

But to return to our piece of ribbon: It affords us a rather pleasant object, appearing like a bundle, or wreath, of very clear and transparent *cylinders*. If the silk is white, it is curiously tinged; if it is colored, each of those small horny *cylinders* affords, in one place or another, as vivid a reflection as if it had been sent from a cylinder of glass or horn. So much so, that the reflections of *red* appeared as if coming from many *garnets* or *rubies*. The loveliness of the colors of silks, compared to those of hairy fabrics or linen, consists—as I mention elsewhere—chiefly in the transparency and vivid reflections from the *concave* or inner surface of the transparent *cylinder*, as are also the colors of precious stones; for most of the reflections from each of these *cylinders* come from the *concave* surface of the air, which is, as it were, the foil that encompasses the *cylinder*. The colors with which each of these *cylinders* are tinged seem partly to be superficial and sticking to their outsides, and partly to be imbibed, or sunk into their substance. For *silk*, seeming to be little else than a dried thread of *glue*, may be supposed to be very easily relaxed and softened by being steeped in warm—or even cold, if penetrating—juices or liquors. And thereby those tinctures, though they tinge perhaps but a small part of the substance, yet being so highly saturated with the color as to be almost black with it, may leave an impression strong enough to exhibit the desired color.

I have seen a pretty kind of artificial material looking almost like transparent parchment, horn, or isinglass, and perhaps it may be made of some such thing. Being transparent and of a glutinous nature, and easily softened by keeping it in water (as I found upon trial), it had imbibed and remained tinged with a great variety of very vivid colors, and to the naked eye, it looked very much like the substance of *silk*. And I have often thought that a way might probably be found to create an artificial glue-like composition, much resembling—if not quite as good as, or even better than—that secretion (or whatever other substance it be) out of which the *silkworm* draws its thread. If such a composition were found, it would certainly be an easy matter to find very quick ways of drawing it out into small wires for use. I need not mention the use of such an invention, nor the benefit that is likely to come to the finder, as they are sufficiently obvious.

This hint, therefore, may, I hope, give some ingenious, inquisitive person an occasion to make some trials; if they are successful, I have reached my aim, and I suppose he will have no reason to be displeased.

# M I C R O G R A P H I A.

### Observation V. Of watered Silks, or Fabrics.

<margin>
Scheme 3.
Fig. 2.
</margin>
There are but few artificial things that are worth observing with a *microscope*; and therefore I shall speak but briefly concerning them. For the productions of art are such rude, misshapen things that when viewed with a *microscope*, there is little else observable but their deformity. The most curious carvings appear no better than those rude *Russian* images we find mentioned in *Purchas* <note>Samuel Purchas, an English cleric who published a famous collection of travel reports.</note>, where three notches at the end of a stick stood for a face. And the most smooth and burnished surfaces appear most rough and unpolished. So my first reason why I shall add but a few observations of them is their misshapen form; and the next is their uselessness. For why should we trouble ourselves in the examination of that form or shape (which is all we are able to reach with a *microscope*) which we know was designed for no higher a use than what we were able to view with our naked eye? Why should we endeavor to discover mysteries in that which has no such thing in it? And like *Rabbins* <note>Rabbis or scholars of the Talmud.</note> find out *cabalisms* <note>Mystical or secret interpretations.</note> and *enigmas* in the figure and placing of letters, where no such thing lies hidden; whereas in natural forms there are some so small, and so curious, and their designed business so far removed beyond the reach of our sight, that the more we magnify the object, the more excellencies and mysteries do appear; and the more we discover the imperfections of our senses, and the omnipotence and infinite perfections of the great Creator. I shall therefore only add one or two observations more of artificial things, and then come to the treatise concerning such matters as are the productions of a more curious Workman.

One of these shall be that of a piece of watered silk, represented in the second figure of the third *scheme*, as it appeared through the least magnifying glass; *A.B.* signifying the long way of the fabric, and *C.D.* the broad way. This fabric, if the right side of it is looked upon, appears to the naked eye all over so waved, undulated, or grained, with a curious though irregular variety of brighter and darker parts, that it adds no small gracefulness to the *gloss* of it. It is so known a property that it needs but little explanation, but it is observable—which perhaps everyone has not considered—that those parts which appear as the darker part of the wave in one position to the light appear as the lighter in another, and vice-versa; and by this means the undulations become transient and in a continual change, according as the position of the parts in respect of the incident beams of light is varied. The reason of these odd *phenomena* will be obvious enough to one who has but diligently examined it even with his naked eye. But he who observes it with a *microscope* may more easily perceive what this *Proteus* <note>A figure from mythology capable of changing shape; here referring to the shifting appearance of the silk.</note> is, and how it comes to change its shape. He may very easily perceive that it proceeds only from the variety of the *reflections* of light, which is caused by the various shape of the *particles*, or little protruding parts of the thread that compose the surface; and that those parts of the waves that

appear brighter, throw toward the eye a multitude of small reflections of light, whereas the darker parts scarcely afford any. The *Microscope* plainly discovers the reason for these reflections, as appears by the Figure. In it, you may perceive that the brighter parts of the surface consist of an abundance of large and strong reflections, denoted by *a, a, a, a, a, etc.* for the surfaces of those threads that run the *long way* are, by the mechanical process of watering, creased or angled in a different posture than they were by weaving. For by weaving, they are only *bent round* the warping threads; but by watering, they are *bent with an angle*, or *elbow*. That is, instead of lying or being *bent round* the threads—as in the third Figure, where *a, a, a, a, a, a* are around *b, b, b* (*b, b, b* representing the ends, as it were, of the cross threads they are bent about)—they are creased on the top of those threads with an *angle*, as in the fourth Figure, and that with all imaginable variety. So, whereas before they reflected the light only from *one point* of the round surface, as around *c, c, c*, now when watered, they reflect the beams from more than half the whole surface, as *de, de, de*; and in other postures, they return no reflections at all from those surfaces. Hence, in one posture they compose the brighter parts of the waves, and in another the darker. And these reflections are also varied according to how the particular parts are variously bent. We shall next examine the reason for this creasing; and here we must fetch our information from the mechanism or manner of proceeding in this operation, which, as I have been informed, is no other than this.

They double all the stuff that is to be watered; that is, they crease it exactly through the middle, the whole length of the piece, leaving the right side of the fabric inward and placing the two edges, or selvages, exactly upon one another. As nearly as they can, they position the wale <note>The ridge or texture of the fabric.</note> in the doubling so that the wale of one side may lie very nearly parallel, or even, with the wale of the other; for the nearer they lie to that posture, the greater the watering will appear, and the more obliquely or across to each other they lie, the smaller the waves are. Their way of folding it for a large wale is this: they take a pin and begin at one side of the piece in any wale, and so, moving it toward the other side, thereby direct their hands to the opposite ends of the wale, and then, as nearly as they can, place the two opposite ends of the same wale together; and so they double or fold the whole piece, repeating this inquiry with a pin at every yard or two's distance through the whole length. Then they sprinkle it with water and fold it *longways*, placing between every fold a piece of pasteboard. By this means, all the wrong side of the watered stuff becomes flat and with little wales, and the wales on the other side become the more protuberant; hence, the creasings or angular bendings of the wales become the more evident. Having folded it in this manner, they place it with an interlying pasteboard into a hot press, where it is kept very violently pressed until it is dry and stiff. By this means, the wales of either contiguous sides leave their own impressions upon each other, as is very manifest by the second Figure, where it is obvious enough that the wale of the piece *A B C D* runs parallel between the dotted lines *ef, ef, ef,* and as

clear to discern the impressions upon these wales, left by those that were pressed upon them; which, not lying exactly parallel with them but a little across them (as is denoted by the lines *o o o o, gh, gh, gh,* between which the other wales lay parallel), are so variously and irregularly creased. Because they were put into that shape when wet and kept so until they were dry, they so set each other's threads that the moldings remain almost as long as the fabric lasts.

From this, it may appear to anyone who attentively considers the Figure why the parts of the wale *a, a, a, a, a, a, a, a* should appear bright, and why the parts *b, b, b, b, b, b, b* should appear shadowed or dark; and why some, such as *d, d, d, d, d, d, d,* should appear partly light and partly dark. The varieties of these reflections and shadows are the only cause of the appearance of "watering" in silks or any other kind of fabrics.

From the variety of reflection, one may also deduce the cause of why a small breeze or gale of wind ruffling the surface of smooth water makes it appear black; and also, on the other hand, why the smoothing or burnishing of the surface of whitened silver makes it look black. Multitudes of other phenomena might be explained by this, which are too many to be dwelt upon here.

### Observ. VI. *Of small Glass Canes.*

<margin>Schem. 4.</margin>So that I might be satisfied as to whether it was not possible to make an *artificial* pore as *small* as any *natural* one I had yet found, I made several attempts with small glass pipes, melted in the flame of a lamp and then very *suddenly* drawn out to a great length. By *that means*, without much difficulty, I was able to draw some almost as thin as a *cobweb*, which nonetheless, with the *microscope*, I could plainly perceive to be *perforated* [hollow], both by looking at the *ends* of it and by looking at it *against the light*. The latter was much the *easier* way to determine whether it was solid or perforated; for, by taking a small pipe of glass and closing one end of it, then filling it *half full* of water and holding it against the light, I could very easily find what the differing *aspect* of a solid and a perforated piece of glass was. Thus, I could easily distinguish, without seeing either end, whether any cylinder of glass I looked at was a *solid stick* or a *hollow cane*. By this means, I could also presently judge of any small *filament* of glass whether it was *hollow or not*, which would have been exceedingly tedious to examine by looking at the end. I found it necessary to use many such methods in the examination of various other particulars related in this book, which would have been no easy task to determine merely by the more common way of looking at or viewing the object. For, we must first consider the very faint light with which the object is illuminated, which causes many particles to appear opaque that, when more enlightened, appear very *transparent*; so much so that I was forced to determine an object's *transparency* by one glass and its *texture* by another. Next, there is the *unmanageableness* of most *objects*, by reason

The difficulty of *finding the desired point*, and of placing it so as to reflect the *light conveniently for the investigation*; lastly, one being able to view it with only *one eye at a time*. These will appear to be no small *obstructions*, nor are they easily removed without many *inventions*. But to proceed, I could not find that water, or some deeply tinted liquids, would rise as high in small pipes as one would expect; and the *highest* I have found it yet rise in any of the pipes I have tried was 21 *inches* above the level of the water in the vessel. For though I found that in the small pipes it would *quickly enter at first* and run about 6 or 7 inches upward, I then found it to move upward *so slowly* that I have not yet had the *patience* to observe it above that height of 21 *inches*. (And that was in a pretty large pipe compared to those formerly mentioned; for I could observe the *progress* of a very deeply tinted liquid in it with my *naked eye* without much trouble, whereas many of the *other pipes were so very small* that, unless placed in a *convenient posture* to the light, I could not perceive them.) But it is very probable that greater patience and *diligence* may discover the liquids to rise, or at least to remain *suspended*, at heights that I should be loath even to *guess* at now, if at least there is any proportion kept between the height of the ascending liquid and the size of the holes of the pipes.

## An Attempt to Explain this Experiment.

<margin>Scheme 4. Figure 1.</margin>
My conjecture—*that the unequal height of the water's surfaces resulted from the greater pressure exerted on the water by the air outside the pipes A, B, and C, than by the air within them*—I shall endeavor to confirm through the truth of the following two *propositions*:

The first of which is: *That an unequal pressure of the surrounding air will cause an unequal height in the water's surfaces.*

And the second is: *That in this experiment, such an unequal pressure exists.*

That the first is true, the following experiment will demonstrate. For if you take any vessel so designed that you can at will either *increase* or *diminish* the pressure of the air upon this or that part of the *surface of the water*, the equality of the height of those parts will presently be lost; and that part of the surface that sustains the *greater pressure* will be lower than the one that undergoes the *less*. A fit vessel for this purpose will be an inverted glass *syphon*, such as the one described in the *sixth figure*. For if you put enough water into it to fill it as high as *AB*, and gently blow in at *D*, you shall depress the surface *B*, and thereby raise the opposite surface *A* to a *considerable height*; and by gently *sucking*, you may produce the exact opposite effects.

Next, that there is such an *unequal pressure*, I shall prove from this: *That there is a much greater incongruity of air to glass and some other bodies than there is of water to the same.*

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the properties of fluids and the forces that govern their behavior, transitioning from observations of capillary action to a theoretical explanation of "Congruity" and "Incongruity."</meta>

<header>M I C R O G R A P H I A.</header>
<meta>catchword: in</meta>

By Congruity, I mean a property of a fluid Body, whereby any part of it is readily *united with any other part*, either of itself, or of *any other similar, fluid, or solid body*: And by Incongruity a property of a fluid, by which it is *hindered from uniting with any dissimilar, fluid, or solid Body*.

This last property, anyone that has been observingly conversant about fluid Bodies cannot be ignorant of. For (*not now* to mention several *chemical spirits* and *oils*, which will very hardly, if at all, be brought to mix with one another; insomuch that there may be found some 8 or 9, or more, several distinct liquors, which *swimming* one upon another, will not presently *mix*) we need seek no further for examples of this kind in *fluids*, than to observe the drops of *rain* falling through the *air*, and the bubbles of air which are by any means conveyed under the surface of the *water*; or a drop of common *salad oil swimming* upon water. In all which, and many more examples of this kind that might be enumerated, the *incongruity* of two fluids is easily discernible. And as for the *Congruity* or *Incongruity* of liquids with several kinds of *firm* bodies, they have long since been taken notice of, and called by the names of *Dryness* and *Moisture* (though these two names are not comprehensive enough, being commonly used to signify only the adhering or not adhering of *water* to some other *solid bodies*). Of this kind we may observe that *water* will more readily *wet some woods* than others; and that *water*, let fall upon a *feather*, the whiter side of a *colewort* <note>a type of cabbage leaf</note>, and some other leaves, or upon almost any dusty, oily, or resinous surface, will not at all adhere to them, but easily tumble off from them, like a solid *bowl*; whereas, if dropped upon *linen, paper, clay, green wood*, etc., it will not be taken off without leaving some part of it behind adhering to them. So *quicksilver* <note>mercury</note> will very hardly be brought to stick to any *vegetable* body, but will readily adhere to, and mingle with, several clean *metallic bodies*.

And that we may the better find what the cause of *Congruity* and *Incongruity* in bodies is, it will be requisite to consider, First, what is the cause of *fluidness*; and this, I conceive, to be nothing else but a certain *pulse* or *shake* of *heat*; for heat being nothing else but a very brisk and vehement agitation of the parts of a body (as I have elsewhere made probable), the parts of a body are thereby made so loose from one another that they easily *move any way*, and become *fluid*. That I may explain this a little by a coarse analogy, let us suppose a dish of sand set upon some body that is very much agitated and shaken with some quick and strong vibrating motion, as on a *millstone* turned round upon the under stone very violently while it is empty; or on a very stiff *drumhead*, which is vehemently or very nimbly beaten with the drumsticks. By this means, the sand in the dish, which before lay like a *dull* and inactive body, becomes a perfect *fluid*; and you can no sooner make a *hole* in it with your finger, but it is immediately *filled up* again, and its upper surface *leveled*. Nor can you bury a light body, such as a piece of cork, under it, but it presently emerges or swims as it were on the top; nor can you lay a heavier one on the top of it, such as a piece of lead, but it is immediately buried

<summary>Hooke defines congruity and incongruity as the tendency of fluids to unite with or repel other substances, explaining that fluidness itself is caused by the rapid vibration of a body's parts due to heat.</summary>
<keywords>congruity, incongruity, fluidness, heat, vibration, salad oil, quicksilver, mercury, colewort, surface tension</keywords>
