<meta>This page continues Hooke's investigation into the nature of fluids, moving from the definitions of congruity and incongruity to a mechanical explanation of fluidity itself as a result of vibratory motion.</meta>

<header>MICROGRAPHIA.</header>
<meta>catchword: perfe</meta>

in sand, and (as it were) sinks to the bottom. Nor can you make a hole in the side of the dish without the sand *running out of it to a level*. This is not an *obvious property of a fluid body as such*, but this sand *imitates* it; and all this is merely caused by the vehement *agitation* of the containing vessel. For by this means, *each grain of sand comes to have a vibratory or dancing motion, so that no other heavier body can rest on it unless sustained by some* other on either side. Nor will it suffer any body to be *beneath* it, unless it is heavier than itself. 

We may find another instance of the *strange loosening* nature of a violent jarring motion, or a strong and nimble vibratory one, from a piece of *iron* grated very strongly with a *file*. For if a pin is *screwed* into that iron so firmly and hard that, even though it has a convenient head, it cannot be *unscrewed* by the fingers; if, I say, you attempt to unscrew this while it is *grated on by the file*, it will be found to loosen and turn very *easily*. 

The first of these examples demonstrates how a body actually *divided* into small parts becomes a *fluid*. The latter demonstrates by what means the agitation of heat so *easily loosens* and *unties* the parts of solid and *firm* bodies. Nor do we need to suppose heat to be anything else besides such a motion; for if we could *mechanically* produce such a motion *quickly* and *strongly* enough, we would not need to *spend fuel to melt a body*. Now, to show that I do not speak this entirely without grounds, I must refer the reader to the observations I have made upon the shining sparks of steel; for there he shall find that the *same effects* are produced upon small chips or pieces of steel by the *flame* as by a *quick and violent motion*. And if the body of steel may be melted this way (as I show there it can), I think we have little reason to doubt that almost *any other body may be as well*. 

Every blacksmith can inform you how quickly both his *file* and the *iron* grow hot with *filing*, and if you *rub* almost any two *hard* bodies together, they will do the same. And we know that a sufficient degree of heat causes *fluidity* in some bodies much sooner and in others later; that is, the *parts* of some bodies are so *loose* from one another, so *unlikely to stick together*, and so *minute and small*, that a very *small* degree of agitation keeps them always in a *state of fluidity*. 

Of this kind, I suppose, is the *Ether*, which is the *medium* or *fluid* body in which all other bodies (as it were) swim and move; and particularly the *Air*, which seems to be nothing else but a kind of *tincture* or *solution of terrestrial and aqueous particles dissolved into it* and agitated by it, just as the *tincture of cochineal* <note>a red dye made from insects</note> is nothing but some finer *dissolvable* parts of that substance absorbed or *dissolved by the fluid water*. And from this notion of it, we may easily give a more intelligible reason for how the air *becomes* so capable of *rarefaction and condensation*. For as in *tinctures*, one grain of some *strongly coloring substance* may noticeably color some *hundred thousand grains of appropriate liquids*, so that every drop of it has its proportionate share and is noticeably tinged (as I have tried both with *logwood* <note>a heartwood used to produce dark dyes</note> and *cochineal*). And as a *few grains of salt* are able to affect as great a quantity—as may be found by precipitation, though not so easily by *sight* or *taste*—so the *air*, which seems to be but (as it were) a *tincture or saline substance dissolved and agitated by the fluid and agile ether*, may dis-

For it seldom happens that any two natures have so many properties coincident or the *same*, as I have observed Solutions and Air to have, and to be *different* in the rest. And therefore I think it neither *impossible, irrational*, nay nor *difficult* to be able to *predict* what is *likely* to happen in other particulars also, besides those which *Observation* or *Experiment* have declared thus or thus; especially, if the *circumstances* that do often very much conduce to the variation of the effects are duly weighed and considered. And indeed, were there not a probability of this, our inquiries would be *endless*, our trials *vain*, and our *greatest inventions* would be nothing but the mere *products of chance*, and not of *Reason*; and, like *Mariners* in an Ocean, destitute both of a *Compass* and the sight of the *Celestial guides*, we might indeed, by *chance, steer directly* towards our desired Port, but *it is a thousand to one* but we *miss* our aim. Having therefore briefly set down my *notion of a fluid body*, I come next to consider what *congruity* is. This, as I said before, is a *relative* property of a fluid, by which it may be said to be *like* or *unlike* this or that other body, and by which it *does* or *does not mix* with that body. We will again have recourse to our *former experiment*, though it is but a simple one. Here, if we mix several kinds of sand in a dish—some of larger, others of smaller and finer sizes—we shall find that by the agitation, the *fine sand* will *eject* and *throw out* from itself all those *larger masses* of small stones and the like, and those will be gathered together all into *one place*. And if there are *other* bodies in it of different natures, those also will be separated into a place by themselves, and *united* or *tumbled up together*. And though this does not reach the highest *property* of *congruity*—which is a *cohesion* of the parts of the fluid together, or a kind of *attraction* and *tenacity*—yet this does, as it were, *foreshadow* it and somewhat resemble it. For in just the same manner, I suppose the pulse of heat agitates the *small particles of matter*; those that are of a *similar size, shape, and substance* will *hold* or *dance together*, and those which are of a differing kind will be *thrust* or *shoved* out from between them. For particles that are all *similar* will, like so many *equal musical strings* equally stretched, vibrate together in a kind of *harmony* or *unison*. Whereas others that are *dissimilar*—for whatever reason, unless the disproportion is otherwise *counterbalanced*—will, like so many strings *out of tune* with those unisons, although they have the same agitating *pulse*, yet make quite different kinds of *vibrations* and *repercussions*. So, although they may both be moved, their *vibrations* are so *different* and so *untuned*, as it were, to each other, that they *cross* and *clash* against each other, and consequently *cannot agree together*, but *fly back* from each other toward their *similar particles*. Now, to give you an instance of how the *disproportion* of some bodies in one respect may be *counterbalanced* by a *contrary disproportion* of the same body in another respect—from which we find that *subtle vinous spirit* is *congruous* with or readily mixes with *water*, which in many properties is of a very different nature—we may consider that a *unison* may be produced either by two strings of the same *size, length, and tension*; or by two strings of the same *size* but of different *length* and a *proportionally different tension*; or thirdly, by two strings of *unequal length and size* and of a different *tension*; or of *equal length* and *different size and tension*, and several other such varieties. To these three properties in strings correspond three properties also in *sand*, or the particles of bodies: their *matter* or *substance*, their *figure* or *shape*, and their *body* or *bulk*. And from the variations of these *three* may arise *infinite varieties* in fluid bodies, though all are agitated by the same pulse or *vibratory motion*. And there may be as many ways of making harmonies

Having therefore seen what is the cause of congruity or incongruity—those relative properties of fluids—we may, from what has been said, very easily gather what is the reason for those relative properties also between *fluid bodies and solids*; for since all bodies consist of particles of such a *substance, figure, and bulk*, but in some they are *united* together more *firmly* than to be *loosened* from each other by every *vibrating* motion (though I imagine that there is no body in the world, but that some degree of agitation may, as I hinted before, agitate and loosen the particles so as to make them *fluid*), those cohering particles may *vibrate* in almost the same manner as those that are loose and become *unisons* or *discords*, as I may so speak, to them. Now that the *parts of all bodies*, though ever so *solid*, do yet *vibrate*, I think we need go no further for proof than that *all bodies have some degree of heat in them*, and that there has not been yet found anything *perfectly cold*: nor can I believe indeed that there is any such thing in Nature as a body whose particles are at *rest*, or *lazy* and *inactive* in the great *Theater of the World*, it being quite contrary to the grand *Economy of the Universe*. We see therefore what is the reason for the *sympathy* or uniting of some bodies together, and of the *antipathy* or flight of others from each other: for *congruity* seems nothing else but a *sympathy*, and *incongruity* an *antipathy* of bodies; hence *similar* bodies once *united* will not *easily part*, and *dissimilar* bodies once *disjoined* will not *easily unite* again; from hence may be very easily derived the reason for the *suspension of water* and *quicksilver* above their usual *station*, as I shall more at large show shortly.

These properties therefore (always the concomitants of fluid bodies) produce these following visible *effects*:

*First*, they *unite* the parts of a fluid to its *similar solid*, or keep them *separate* from its *dissimilar*. Hence *quicksilver* will (as we noted before) *stick* to *gold, silver, tin, lead*, etc., and *unite* with them, but *roll off* from *wood, stone, glass*, etc., if ever so little situated out of its horizontal *level*; and *water* that *will wet salt* and *dissolve* it, will *slip off* from *tallow*, or the like, without at all adhering; as it may likewise be observed to do upon a dusty surface. And next, they cause the parts of *homogeneous fluid bodies* readily to adhere together and *mix*, and of *heterogeneous*, to be exceedingly averse to doing so. Hence we find that *two small drops of water*, on any surface they can roll on, will, if they chance to touch each other, readily *unite* and *mix* into one third drop: the like may be observed with two small *globules of quicksilver* upon a table or glass, provided their surfaces be not *dusty*; and with two drops of *oil* upon clear water, etc. And further, *water* put into *wine, salt water, vinegar, spirit of wine*, or the like, does immediately (especially if they be shaken together) disperse itself all over them. Now the cause why all these included fluids, newly mentioned, as well as many others that are wholly included within a heterogeneous fluid, are not *exactly* of a spherical figure (seeing that if caused by these principles only, it could be of no other) must proceed from some *other* kind of pressure against the two opposite flattened sides. This *adventitious* or *accidental pressure* may proceed from *various causes*, and accordingly must *diversify* the figure of the included heterogeneous fluid: For seeing that a body may be included either with a fluid only, or only with a solid; or partly with a fluid and partly with a solid, or partly with one fluid and partly with another; there will be found a very great variety of the *terminating surfaces*, much differing from a spherical shape, according to the various resistance or pressure that belongs to each of these encompassing bodies.

Which properties may in general be deduced from two heads, namely *Motion* and *Rest*. For either this globular figure is altered by a *natural motion*, such as *Gravity*; or a violent one, such as any accidental *motion of the fluids*, as we see in the *wind* ruffling up the water, and the *purlings* of *streams*, and foaming of *cataracts*, and the like. Or thirdly, by the *rest, firmness*, and *stability* of the surrounding *solid*. For if the including *solid* be of an *angular* or any other irregular form, the included *fluid* will be near the *same*, as a pint-pot full of *water*, or a bladder full of *air*. For the same water which, in a *glass* or wooden *vessel*, will have a concave surface upwards and will rise higher in a smaller than a larger *pipe*—the same water, I say, in the same *pipes* if they are greased or oiled, will produce quite contrary effects; for it will have a *protuberant* and *convex* surface upwards, and will not rise as high in small pipes as in larger ones. Then you shall find it (if you gently and carefully pour in more) to grow very *protuberant* and *convex*. The reason for this is plain: the solid sides of the containing body, to which the water adheres more readily than to the air, are no longer extended; it is henceforth to be enclosed by air, which would reduce it into a *hemisphere*, but because of its gravity, it is flattened into an *oval*. *Quicksilver* [mercury] also—which is more incongruous to *glass* than *air* is (and thus, when put into a *glass pipe*, will not adhere to it, but will be forced by the more congruous air to have a very *protuberant* surface and to rise higher in a larger than a smaller *pipe*)—this *quicksilver* is more congruous than *air* is to clean *metal*, especially to *gold*, *silver*, *tin*, *lead*, etc. (*iron* excepted), and will not only stick to it but have a *concave* surface like water, rising higher in a smaller than in a larger *pipe*.

In all these examples, it is evident that there is an extraordinary and external force by which the globular figure of the contained *heterogeneous* fluid is altered; nor can it be imagined how it should otherwise be any figure other than *globular*. For, being equally pushed from every direction by the *heterogeneous* fluid, any part that is *protuberant* will be *depressed* by it. For this reason, its effects very much resemble a *round spring* (such as a *hoop*). For just as in a *round spring* additional *pressure* against two opposite sides is required to reduce it into an *oval form*, or a considerable force or *protrusion* against the *concave* or inner side of the *spring* is needed to force it between the sides of a *hole* whose *diameter* is less than that of the *spring*; so, to alter this *spherical* constitution of an enclosed fluid body, more pressure is required against opposite sides to reduce it into an *oval*. And to press it into a *hole* smaller in *diameter* than itself, it requires a greater *protrusion* against all the other sides. What degrees of force are required to reduce them into increasingly long *ovals*, or to press them into smaller and smaller holes, I have not yet experimentally calculated; but I find this much by experiment in general: that a greater pressure is always required to compress them into longer *ovals* or push them into smaller holes. ...how much of the pressure of the *air* is reduced by its entry into smaller and smaller holes. From the application of this to the entry of the *air* into the larger hole of the *vessel* and into the smaller hole of the *pipe*, we shall clearly find that there is a greater pressure of the air upon the water in the *vessel* or larger pipe than there is upon the water in the smaller pipe. For since the pressure of the air in every direction is found to be equal—that is, enough to press up and support a cylinder of *mercury* two and a half feet high, or thereabouts—and since many more degrees of this pressure are required to force the *air* into a smaller hole than into a larger hole that is full of a more compatible fluid; and lastly, since those degrees of pressure required to force it in are thereby taken from the *air* within, leaving the *air* inside with that many degrees of pressure less than the *air* outside, it follows that the *air* in the smaller *tube* or *pipe* will have less pressure against the surface of the *water* within it than the *air* in the larger one; this was the minor proposition to be proved.

The conclusion, therefore, necessarily follows: *namely, that this unequal pressure of the air, caused by its entry into unequal holes, is a cause sufficient to produce this effect without the help of any other contributing factor;* and therefore it is probably the principal (if not the only) cause of these *phenomena*.

With this explained, various *phenomena* can be understood through it: such as the rising of *liquors* in a *filter*; the rising of *spirit of wine, oil, melted tallow, etc.* in the *wick* of a *lamp* (even if made of small *wire, threads of asbestos, strings of glass*, or the like); the rising of *liquors* in a *sponge*, piece of *bread, sand, etc.*; and perhaps also the ascent of the *sap* in *trees* and *plants* through their small and sometimes imperceptible *pores* (about which I have said more on another occasion), or at least its passage from the earth into their roots. Indeed, upon considering this principle, many other uses for it occurred to me, which I have not yet examined or organized well enough to propose as *axioms*, but only as *queries* and *conjectures* which may serve as hints toward further discoveries.

First, upon considering the *congruity* and *incongruity* of bodies regarding *touch*, I also found a similar *congruity* and *incongruity* (if I may put it that way) regarding the transmitting of the rays of light. In this regard, *water* (not to mention other liquids) seems to have a closer affinity to *glass* than *air* does, and *air* more than *mercury*. Thus, an oblique *ray* from *glass* will pass into *water* with very little refraction from the *perpendicular*; but no ray from *glass* into *air*, except for a *direct* one, will pass without a very great refraction from the perpendicular; indeed, any oblique ray at an angle of less than thirty degrees will not be admitted into the air at all. And *mercury* will admit neither oblique nor direct rays but reflects them all, seeming, in terms of transmitting the rays of light, to have a quite different constitution from that of *air, water, glass, etc.*, and to most resemble those opaque and strongly reflecting bodies of metals. Similarly, regarding the property of cohesion or *congruity*, water seems to maintain the same order, being

more compatible with glass than air, and air than mercury.

A second thing (which was suggested to me by considering the spherical form of the enclosed fluids, caused by the pressure of the surrounding dissimilar fluid) was whether the *phenomena* of gravity might not be explained this way: by supposing the globe of Earth, Water, and Air to be enclosed within a *fluid* dissimilar to each and all of them, so subtle that it is not only *interspersed* everywhere through the *air* (or rather the *air* through it), but *pervades* the bodies of *glass*, and even the densest *metals*. By this means, it may attempt to push all earthly bodies as far from itself as it can; and partly because of that, and partly because of its other properties, it may move them toward the center of the Earth. Now, I could produce many experiments and reasons that seem to prove there is some such fluid. But because it would take some time and space to set them down and explain them, and to consider and answer all the objections (many of which I foresee) that may be raised against it, I shall for now proceed to other *queries*, contenting myself with having only given a hint here of what I may say more about elsewhere.

A third *query* then was whether the *dissimilarity* of the surrounding *fluid* may not be considered a secondary cause of the *roundness* or *spherical form* of the *larger bodies* of the world, such as those of the *Sun*, *Stars*, and *Planets*, since the substance of each seems altogether dissimilar to the surrounding fluid *ether*? I shall say more about this in the observation of the Moon.

A fourth was whether the spherical form of the smaller portions of matter here upon the Earth—such as *fruits*, *pebbles*, or *flints*, etc. (which seem to have been a *liquid* at first)—might not be caused by the dissimilar *surrounding fluid*. For we see that melted *glass* will naturally be formed into a *round figure*; likewise, any small portion of any meltable body, if it is perfectly enclosed by the *air*, will be driven into a spherical form and, when cold, will be found to be a solid *ball*. This is clearly enough shown to us by the method of making *shot* with *drops of lead*. Since this is a very interesting curiosity known to only a few, and having been granted the liberty of publishing it by the eminent *virtuoso Sir Robert Moray*, who brought this account of it to the *Royal Society*, I have transcribed and inserted it here.

### To make small shot of different sizes; Communicated by his Highness *P. R.* <note>Prince Rupert of the Rhine</note>

Take as much lead from the ingot <note>A "pig" of lead</note> as you please, melt it down, stir and clear it with an iron ladle; gathering together the blackish parts that swim at the top like scum. When you see the color of the clear lead turn greenish, but no sooner, scatter upon it Auripigmentum <note>Orpiment, a yellow arsenic sulfide mineral used in this process</note>

<meta>This page continues Hooke's investigation into the formation of spherical bodies, transitioning from theoretical considerations of gravity and fluids to the practical application of these principles in the manufacturing of lead shot.</meta>

*pigmentum* powdered according to the quantity of *lead*; about as much as will lie upon a half-*crown* piece will serve for eighteen or twenty pounds' weight of some sorts of *lead*; others will require more or less. After the *Auripigmentum* is put in, stir the *lead* well, and the *Auripigmentum* will flame: when the flame is over, take out some of the *lead* in a *ladle* having a lip or notch in the brim for convenient pouring out of the *lead*, and being well warmed among the melted *lead*; and with a stick make some single drops of *lead* trickle out of the *ladle* into water in a *glass*. If they fall and turn out to be round and without tails, enough *Auripigmentum* has been put in, and the consistency of the heat is right; otherwise, put in more. Then lay two bars of *iron* (or some more appropriate *iron tool* made for the purpose) upon a *pail* of water, and place upon them a round *plate* of *copper*, of the size and shape of an ordinary large *pewter* or *silver trencher*. The hollow of it is to be about three inches across, with the bottom about half an inch lower than the rims, and pierced with thirty, forty, or more small holes; the smaller the holes are, the smaller the shot will be; and the rim is to be thicker than the bottom, to better conserve the heat.

The bottom of the *trencher* being some four inches distant from the water in the *pail*, lay upon it some burning *coals* to keep the *lead* melted upon it. Then, with the hot *ladle*, take *lead* from the *pot* where it stands melted, and pour it gently upon the burning *coals* over the bottom of the *trencher*, and it will immediately run through the holes into the water in small round drops. Continue to pour on new *lead* as fast as it runs through the *trencher* until all is done, blowing the *coals* now and then with *hand bellows* when the *lead* in the *trencher* cools enough to stop running.

While one person pours on the *lead*, another must, with another *ladle* thrust four or five inches under the water in the *pail*, catch from time to time some of the *shot* as it drops down to see the size of it and whether there are any defects in it. *This process can be helped by blowing the coals a little, or pouring on new lead that is hotter; but the cooler the lead, the larger the shot; and the hotter the lead, the smaller the shot. When it is too hot, the drops will crack and fly apart; then you must stop pouring on new lead and let it cool. As long as you observe the right temperature, the lead will constantly drop into very round shot, without a single one having a tail in many pounds.*

*When all is done, take your shot out of the pail of water and put it in a frying pan over the fire to dry them; this must be done carefully, shaking them constantly so they do not melt. When they are dry, you may separate the small from the large in pearl sieves made of copper or <term>lattin</term> <note>A brass-like alloy hammered into thin sheets.</note> fitted into one another, into as many sizes as you please. But if you would have your shot larger than the <term>trencher</term> <note>The perforated plate used in the process.</note> makes them, you may do it with a stick, making them trickle out of the ladle, as has been said.*

*If the <term>trencher</term> is touched only a very little when the lead stops going through it, and it is not too cool, it will begin to drop again, but it is better not to touch it at all. When melting the lead, take care that there is no kind of oil, grease, or similar substances upon the pots, ladles, or <term>trencher</term>.*

The chief cause of this *globular figure* of the *shot* seems to be the <term>Auripigmentum</term> <note>Orpiment, or arsenic trisulfide, added to the lead.</note>; for, as soon as it is put in among the melted *lead*, the lead loses its shining brightness, instantly contracting a grayish film or skin upon it when you skim it to make it clean with the *ladle*. So, when the *air* meets the falling drop of melted *lead*, that skin constricts them equally on all sides; but for what reason, and whether this is the true cause, is left to further investigation.

In much this same manner, when the *air* through which it passes is exceedingly cold, we find the drops of *rain* falling from the *clouds* frozen into round *hailstones* by the freezing *surrounding air*.

To which may be added this other known *experiment*: that if you gently let fall a drop of water upon small sand or dust, you shall find, as it were, an artificial round stone quickly formed. I cannot on this occasion omit mentioning the strange kind of *grain* which I have observed in a stone brought from *Kettering* in *Northamptonshire*, and therefore called by masons *Kettering-stone* <note>A type of oolitic limestone composed of small spherical grains.</note>, of which see the description.

Which brings to my mind what I observed long ago in the fiery sparks that are struck out of a steel. For having a great desire to see what was left behind after the spark had gone out, I purposely struck fire over a very white piece of paper; and observing diligently where some conspicuous sparks went out, I found a very little black spot no larger than the point of a pin, which through a *microscope* appeared to be a perfectly round ball, looking much like a polished ball of steel, so much so that I was able to see the image of the window reflected from it. I cannot stay here (having done it more fully in another place) to examine the particular reasons for it, but shall only hint that I imagine it to be some small particle of the steel, which by the violence of the motion of the stroke (most of which seems to be impressed upon those small particles) is made so glowing hot that it is melted into a *vitrum* <note>A glass-like or vitrified state.</note>, which by the surrounding air is thrust into the form of a ball.

A fifth thing which I thought worth examination was whether the motion of all kinds of springs might not be reduced to the principle by which the included *heterogeneous fluid* seems to be moved, or to that by which two solids, such as marbles or the like, are thrust and kept together by the *ambient fluid* <note>The surrounding fluid, such as air or water.</note>.

A sixth thing was whether the rising and bubbling up of the water out of springs and fountains (which lie much higher from the center of the Earth than the surface of the sea, from which it seems to be derived) may not be explained by the rising of water in a smaller pipe. For the seawater, being strained through the pores or crannies of the Earth, is, as it were, included in little pipes, where the pressure of the air does not have so great a power to resist its rising. But examining this way and finding in it several difficulties almost insurmountable, I thought of a way that would explain it much more naturally and understandably, which was by the following experiment: I took a *glass tube* of the form of that described in the sixth figure, and choosing two *heterogeneous fluids*, such as *water* and *oil*, I poured in as much *water* as filled up the pipes as high as A B; then putting some *oil* into the tube A C, I lowered the surface A of the water to E, and B I raised to G, which was not as high perpendicularly as the surface of the *oil F*, by the space F I; therefore, the proportion of the gravity <note>Relative density or weight.</note> of these two liquids was as G H to F E.

I also do not know whether the extreme pressure of the parts of the water against one another may not keep the salt from descending to the very bottom, as it finds little or no room to insert itself between those parts that are pushed so violently together; or else it may squeeze it upwards into the higher parts of the sea, where it may more easily find room for itself among the parts of the water because there is more heat and less pressure. To this opinion I was somewhat more inclined by the accounts I have met with in geographical writers of drawing fresh water from the bottom of the sea, which is salt above. I cannot now stop to examine whether this natural perpetual motion may be artificially imitated, nor can I stop to answer the objections which may be made against my supposition: such as, first, how it happens that there are sometimes salt springs much higher than the surface of the water? And, second, why springs do not run faster and slower according to the varying height of the cylinder of seawater caused by the ebbing and flowing of the sea?

As to the first, in short, I say the fresh water may receive a saline quality again near the surface of the Earth by passing through some salt mines, or else many of the saline parts of the sea may be kept back, though not all.

Regarding the second point, the same *spring* may be fed and supplied by various *caverns* coming from very distant parts of the *sea*, so that it may be *high tide* in one place and *low tide* in another; in this way, the spring may be equally supplied at all times. Or else the *cavern* may be so constricted and narrow that the water, not having such ready and free passage through it, cannot produce any noticeable effect at such a distance during short and rapid changes of pressure.

Furthermore, to confirm this *hypothesis*, many examples are found in *natural histories* of springs that ebb and flow like the *sea*. Specifically, those recorded by the learned *Camden*, and after him by *Speed*, to be found on this *island*. They report one of these to be on the top of a mountain by the small village of *Kilken* in *Flintshire*; *rivaling the sea, it vomits out and sucks back its waters at fixed times*; which at certain times rises and falls in the manner of the sea. A second is in *Carmarthenshire*, near *Carmarthen*, at a place called *Cantred Bichan*; *which (as Giraldus writes) twice in a natural day failing in its waves and twice overflowing, imitates the instabilities of the sea*; which, by ebbing and flowing twice in twenty-four hours, resembles the unstable motions of the sea. The *phenomena* of these two may be easily explained by supposing that the *cavern* by which they are fed originates from the bottom of the nearest sea. A third is a well upon the River *Ogmore* in *Glamorganshire*, near *Newton*, of which *Camden* reports he was informed by a letter from a learned friend of his who observed it: *The fountain is distant from here, etc.* The letter is a little too long to be inserted, but the substance is this: that this well ebbs and flows exactly contrary to the flowing and ebbing of the sea in those parts; for it is almost empty at high tide, but full at low water. This may happen because of the channel by which it is supplied, which may come from the bottom of a sea very remote from those parts, where the tides are very different from those of the nearby shores. A fourth lies in *Westmorland*, near the River *Loder* <note>Now known as the River Lowther.</note>; *which, like the Euripus <note>A strait in Greece famous for its complex and strong currents.</note>, flows and ebbs many times a day with reciprocating waves*. This may result from it being supplied by many channels coming from several parts of the sea, located far enough apart for the times of high water to differ sufficiently from one another; so that whenever it is high water at any of the places where these channels begin, it will also be so in the well; but this is only a supposition.

In the meantime, I would not willingly be guilty of that *error* which the thrice noble and learned *Verulam* justly takes notice of as such, and calls *Philoſophiæ Genus Empiricum, quod in paucorum Experimentorum Anguſtiis & Obſcuritate fundatum eſt* <note>An empirical type of philosophy, which is founded on the narrowness and obscurity of a few experiments.</note>. For I neither conclude from one single experiment, nor are the *experiments* I make use of all made upon one *subject*; nor do I twist any experiment to make it *square* with any preconceived notion. But on the contrary, I endeavor to be familiar with various kinds of experiments, and I make each and every one of those trials the standards or touchstones by which I test all my former notions, to see whether they hold out in weight, measure, and touch, etc. For as that body is no other than counterfeit *gold* which lacks any one of the properties of *gold* (such as malleability, weight, color, stability in the fire, insolubility in *aqua fortis*, and the like) though it has all the others; so will all those notions be found false and deceitful that will not undergo all the trials and tests made of them by experiments. And therefore, such as will not come up to the desired *peak* of perfection, I rather wholly reject and take new ones, than by piecing and patching, endeavor to retain the old, knowing such things at best to be but lame and imperfect. And this course I learned from Nature, whom we find neglectful of the old body and suffering its decays and infirmities to remain without repair, and altogether solicitous and careful of perpetuating the *species* by new *individuals*. And it is certainly the most likely way to erect a glorious *structure* and temple to *Nature*, such as she will be found (by any zealous *devotee*) to reside in: to begin to build anew upon a sure foundation of experiments.

But to digress no further from the consideration of the *phenomena* more immediately explicable by this experiment, we shall proceed to show that, as to the *rising of water in a filter*, the reason for it will be manifest to him who does take notice that a *filter* is constituted of a great number of small, long solid bodies which lie so close together that the air, in its getting in between them, loses some of the pressure that it has against the *fluid* without them. By which means the water or liquor—not finding as strong a resistance between them as is able to counterbalance the pressure on its surface without—is raised upward, until it meets with a pressure of the air which is able to hinder it. And as to the *rising of oil, melted tallow, spirit of wine, etc.* in the *wick* of a candle or lamp, it is evident that it differs in nothing from the former, save only in this: that in a *filter* the liquor descends and runs away by another part; and in the *wick* the liquor is dispersed and carried away by the flame;

<meta>This page continues Hooke's investigation into the movement of fluids and floating bodies, specifically examining why fluids rise in wicks and porous materials like sponges and how air pressure influences the motion of floating objects toward the sides of a container.</meta>

Flame; there is something ascribable to the heat; for it may *rarefy* the more *volatile* and *spirituous* parts of those combustible liquors, and so being made lighter than the air, they may be pushed upwards by that more ponderous fluid body in the form of vapors; but this can be ascribed to the ascent of only a very little, and most likely of that only which ascends without the wick. As for its rising in a sponge, bread, cotton, etc., above the surface of the underlying liquor, what has been said about the *filter* (if considered) will easily suggest a reason, considering that all these bodies abound with small holes or pores.

From this same principle also (*namely, the unequal pressure of the air against the unequal surface of the water*) proceeds the cause of the movement or incursion of any floating body against the sides of the containing vessel, or the approach of two floating bodies, such as *bubbles*, *corks*, *sticks*, *straws*, etc., toward one another. For instance, take a glass jar, such as A B in the seventh *Figure*, and filling it nearly to the top with water, throw into it a small round piece of cork, such as C, and plunge it all over in water so that it is wet, so that the water may rise up by its sides; then placing it anywhere upon the surface, about an inch or an inch and a quarter from any side, you shall perceive it by degrees to move *perpendicularly* toward the nearest part of the side, and the nearer it approaches, the faster it moves. The reason for this *phenomenon* will be found to be no other than this: that the air has a greater pressure against the middle of the surface than it has against those parts that approach nearer and are contiguous to the sides. Now, that the pressure is greater may (as I showed before in the explanation of the third *Figure*) be demonstrated from the flattening of the water in the middle, which arises from the gravity of the underlying *fluid*. For since, as I showed before, if there were no gravity in the underlying *fluid*, or if it were equal to that of the upper, the terminating surface would be spherical; and since it is the additional pressure of the gravity of water that makes it so flat, it follows that the pressure upon the middle must be greater than toward the sides. Hence the ball, having a stronger pressure against that side of it which faces the middle of the surface than against that which faces the nearest side, must necessarily move toward that part where it finds the least resistance, and so be accelerated as the resistance decreases. Hence, the more the water is raised under that part of its path it is passing above the middle, the faster it is moved; and therefore you will find it to move faster at E than at D, and at D than at C. Nor could I find the floating substance to be moved at all until it was placed upon some part of the surface that was sensibly elevated above the height of the middle part. Now, that this may be the true cause, you may try with a blown bladder and an exactly round ball upon a very smooth side of some pliable body, such as *horn* or *quicksilver*. For if the ball is placed under a part of the bladder which is on one side of the middle of its pressure, and you press strongly against the bladder, you shall find the ball moved from the middle toward the sides.

Having therefore shown the reason for the motion of any floating object toward the sides, the reason for the approach of any two floating bodies will easily appear: For the rising of the water against the sides of either of them is a sufficient argument to show the pressure of the air to be less there than it is further from it, where it is not so much elevated; and therefore the reason for the motion of the other toward it will be the same as toward the side of the glass; only here, for the same reason, they move mutually toward each other, whereas the side of the glass in the previous case remains fixed. If you also gently fill the jar so full with water that the water is *protuberant* above the sides, the same piece of cork that previously hurried toward the sides now flies from them just as fast toward the middle of the surface; the reason for which will be found to be none other than this: that the pressure of the air is stronger against the sides of the surface G and H than against the middle I; for since, as I showed before, the principle of congruity would make the terminating surface spherical, and since the flattening of the surface in the middle results from the reduction of the water's outward pressure by the opposing effort of its gravity, it follows that the pressure in the middle must be less than on the sides; therefore, the result will be the same as in the former case. It is very strange to someone who does not consider the reason for it to see two floating pieces of wood approach each other as though they were endowed with some magnetic power; which brings to mind what I formerly tried with a piece of cork or a similar body, which I arranged so that by putting a little stick into the same water, one part of the said cork would approach and move toward the stick, whereas another part would withdraw and fly away; indeed, it would have a kind of verticity, such that if the equator (as I may so speak) of the cork were placed toward the stick, if left alone, it would instantly turn its appropriate pole toward it and then rush at it. This was done simply by taking a dry cork and wetting one side of it with one small stroke; for by this means, when gently placed upon the water, it would depress the surface on every side of it that was dry; therefore, the greater pressure of the air being near those sides caused it either to drive away or else fly off from any other floating body, whereas only that side against which the water ascended was thereby able to attract.

It remains only for me to determine how high water or another liquid may be raised by this means in a smaller pipe above the surface of that outside it, and at what height it may be sustained. But to determine this will be exceedingly difficult, unless I could certainly know how much of the air's pressure is removed by the smallness of such and such a pipe, and whether it may be entirely removed—that is, whether there can be a hole or pore so small into which air could not enter at all, though water might with its full force; for if there were such a pore, it is manifest that the water might rise in it to some thirty-five or thirty-six English feet high. I do not know whether the capillary pipes in the bodies of small trees, which we call their *microscopical pores*, might not be of this kind, and whether the congruity of the sides of the pore might not still draw the juice

**congruity** is a principle that not only unites and holds a body joined to

And this is obvious even in a drop of water suspended under any **sim-**

keep it sustained, there is the **congruity** of the bodies that are contigu-

to those who consider a fluid body only as its parts being in a confused, irregu-

another and their incongruity to some other bodies, appears not a little
strange. So, besides the incongruity of the surrounding fluid to it, we
are to consider also the congruity of the parts of the contained fluid
with one another.

And this **congruity** (to explain it a little further here) is both
a **tenacious** and an **attractive** power; for **congruity,** in the **vi-**
**brative motions,** may be the cause of all kinds of attraction, not only **ele-**
**ctrical,** but **magnetic** also, and therefore it may also be the cause of **tenacity**
and **glutinousness.** For, from a perfect congruity of the motions of two
distant bodies, the intermediate fluid particles are separated and dri-
ven away from between them, and thereby those congruous bodies are,
by the encompassing mediums, compelled and forced closer together;
wherefore that attractiveness must necessarily be stronger when, by an im-
mediate contact, they are forced to be exactly the same: as I show more
at large in my *Theory of the Magnet.* And this hints to me the reason for
the suspension of **mercury** many inches—nay, many feet—above the usu-

similar and congruous to each other, if once united, will not easily suffer
a separation: and the parts of water that were in any way *heterogeneous,*
being exhausted by <term>exantlation</term> <note>the act of drawing out or exhausting a fluid</note> or rarefaction, the remaining parts being
also very similar, will not easily part either. And the parts of the **glass**
being solid are more difficultly disjointed; and the water, being some-
what similar to both, is, as it were, a medium to unite both the **glass** and
the **mercury** together. So that all three being united, and not very dis-
similar, by means of this contact, if care is taken that the **tube,** in e-
recting, is not jolted, the **quicksilver** will remain suspended, notwith-
standing its contrary endeavor of **gravity,** at a great height above its ordi-

mere separation of them from one another by the force of a jolt, where-
by the other becomes embodied between them and licks up from the
surface some agile parts, and so hurling them makes them air; or else

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the principle of congruity, explaining how a physical disturbance or the presence of a foreign particle allows the ether to break the attractive bond between mercury and glass, causing the fluid to fall to its standard atmospheric height.</meta>

<page-num>32</page-num>

...by some small heterogeneous, agile part of the water, or air, or quicksilver, which appears like a bubble; and by its jumbling back and forth, a way is made for the heterogeneous *ether* to push itself between the glass and either of the other fluids. The gravity of *mercury* precipitates it downward with very great violence; and if the vessel that holds the pooling <note>restagnating</note> *mercury* is suitable, the *mercury* will for a time vibrate back and forth with very large reciprocations, and at last will remain held up by the pressure of the external air at the height of near thirty inches. And whereas it may be objected that it cannot be that the mere presence of the *ether* between these bodies is the cause—since the *ether*, always having a free passage through both the pores of the glass and through those of the fluids, there is no reason why it should not cause a separation at all times while it remains suspended, as when it is violently disjointed by a jolt—to this I answer: that though the *ether* passes between the particles (that is, through the pores of bodies) so that once any chasm or separation is made, it has infinite passages to admit its entry into it, yet such is the tenacity or attractive virtue of congruity that until it is overcome by the mere strength of gravity, or by a jolt assisting that *conatus* <note>effort or inclination</note> of gravity, or by an agile particle that is like a lever agitated by the *ether*—and thereby the parts of the congruous substances are separated so far apart that the strength of congruity is so weakened as not to be able to reunite them, the parts to be gripped being removed out of the attractive sphere, as I may call it, of the congruity—such, I say, is the tenacity of congruity that it retains and holds the almost contiguous particles of the fluid and does not allow them to be separated until by mere force that attractive or retentive faculty be overcome. But the separation being once made beyond the sphere of the attractive activity of congruity, that virtue becomes of no effect at all, but the *mercury* freely falls downward until it meets with a resistance from the pressure of the surrounding air, able to resist its gravity and keep it forced up in the pipe to the height of about thirty inches.

Thus have I gently raised a steel *pendulum* by a loadstone to a great angle, until by the shaking of my hand I have happened to make a separation between them; as soon as this is made, as if the loadstone had retained no attractive virtue, the *pendulum* moves freely from it toward the other side. So vast a difference is there between the attractive virtue of the *magnet* when it acts upon a contiguous and upon a disjointed body; and much more must there be between the attractive virtues of congruity upon a contiguous and disjointed body. And in truth, the attractive virtue is so small upon a body disjointed that, though I have with a *microscope* observed very diligently whether there were any extraordinary protuberance on the side of a drop of water that was exceedingly near to the end of a green stick but did not touch it, I could not perceive the least bit; though I found that as soon as ever it touched it, the whole drop would presently unite itself with it; so that it seems an absolute contact is requisite to the exercising of the tenacious faculty of congruity.

## Observation VII. Of some Phenomena of Glass drops.

These Glass Drops are small portions of coarse green Glass taken out of the pots that contain the *Metal* (as they call it) in fusion, upon the end of an iron pipe; and being exceedingly hot, and thereby of a kind of sluggish fluid consistency, they are allowed to drop from there into a bucket of cold water, and to lie in it until they have grown noticeably cold.

Some of these I broke in the open air by snapping off a little of the small stem with my fingers, and others by crushing it with a small pair of pliers; which I had no sooner done, than the whole bulk of the drop flew violently, with a very sharp noise, into a multitude of small pieces. Some of these were as small as dust, though in some there were remaining pieces that were quite large without any flaw at all, and others were very much flawed, which were easily reduced to dust by rubbing them between one’s fingers. These dispersed in every direction so violently that some of them pierced my skin. I could not find, either with my naked eye or a *microscope*, that any of the broken pieces were of a regular shape, nor any one like another; but for the most part, those that broke off in large pieces were attractively branched.

I nipped off the ends of others of these drops while all the bodies and ends of them lay buried under the water; these, like the former, flew all to pieces with as sharp a noise and as strong a motion.

I tried to break others of these by grinding away the blunt end, and though I took a seemingly good one and had ground away near two-thirds of the ball, yet it would not fly to pieces; but now and then some small rings of it would snap and fly off, not without a sharp noise and quick motion, leaving the surface of the drop from which it flew attractively branched or creased, which was easily discoverable by the *microscope*. This drop, after I had ground it in this way without at all impairing the remnant that was not ground away, I caused to fly immediately all into sand upon nipping off the very tip of its slender end.

I began to grind away another of these drops at the smaller end, but I had not worn away more than a quarter of an inch on the stone before the whole drop flew into sand or small dust with a sharp crack; nor would it have held together that long had there not been a little flaw in the piece that I ground away, as I afterwards found.

I covered several others of these drops with a thin but very tough skin of *Icthyocolla* <note>fish glue or isinglass</note>; which, being very tough and very transparent, was the most convenient substance for these trials that I could imagine. Having dipped, I say, several of these drops in this transparent glue while hot, and allowing them to hang by a string tied about the end of them until they were cold and the skin was fairly tough; then wrapping all the body of the drop

Nor is this kind of grain, as I may call it, unique to glass drops quenched in this way; for (not to mention *copperas stones*, and various other *marcasites* and *minerals*, which I have often noticed to be flaked or grained in the very same manner, with a kind of pith in the middle;) I have observed the same in all manner of cast iron, especially the coarser sort, such as stoves, furnaces, fire-backs, and pots are made of. For upon the breaking of any of those substances, it is easy to observe how, from the outsides towards the middle, there is a kind of radiation or grain much resembling this of the glass-drop; but this grain is most conspicuous in iron bullets if they are broken. The same *phenomena* may be produced by casting *regulus* of *antimony* into a bullet-mold, as also with *glass* of *antimony*, or with almost any such kind of *vitrified substance*, either cast into a cold mold or poured into water.

Others of these drops I heated red-hot in the fire and then allowed them to cool by degrees. I found these to have quite lost all their *explosive* or flying quality, as well as their hard, brittle, and springy texture; they emerged with a much softer temper, and were much easier to be broken or snapped with one's finger. Its strong and brittle quality was quite destroyed, and it seemed much of the same consistency as other green glass well annealed in the oven.

The figure and size of these for the most part were the same as that of Figure Z; that is, all the surface of them was very smooth and polished, and for the most part round, but very rugged or knobbed around D, and all the length of the stem was here and there pitted or flattened. Around D, which is at the upper part of the drop under that side of the stem which is concave, there usually were made one or more little hillocks or prominences. The drop itself, before it is broken, appears very transparent, and towards the middle of it, appears to be very full of small bubbles of some kind of aerial substance, which by the refraction of the outward surface appear much bigger than they really are; this can be largely corrected by putting the drop under the surface of clear water, for by that means most of the refraction of the convex surface of the drop is removed, and the bubbles will appear much smaller. And this, by the way, reminds me of the apparent size of the *aperture* of the *iris*, or *pupil* of the eye, which though it appears, and is therefore judged to be very large, is yet not above a quarter of the size it appears to be, due to the lenticular refraction of the *cornea*.

The cause of all these *phenomena* I imagine to be none other than this: that the parts of the glass, being by the excessive heat of the fire kept apart and separated from one another, and thereby put into a kind of sluggish fluid consistency, are allowed to drop off with that heat or agitation remaining in them into cold water. By this means, the outsides of the drop are immediately cooled and crusted, and are thereby made of a loose texture, because the parts of it do not have time to settle themselves leisurely together and so to lie very close together. And the innermost parts of the drop, still retaining much of their former heat and agitations, remain

are also of a loose texture, and, as the cold strikes inward from the bottom and sides, they are quenched, as it were, and made rigid in the very posture in which the cold finds them. For the parts of the crust, being already hardened, will not allow the parts to shrink any more from the outward surface inward; and though it shrinks a little because of the small parcels of some aerial substances dispersed through the matter of the glass, yet that is not nearly as much as it appears (as I just now hinted); nor, if it were, would it be sufficient to consolidate and condense the body of glass into a *tough* and close texture, after it had been so excessively rarefied by the heat of the glass furnace. But that there may be such an expansion of the aerial substance contained in those little *blebs* or bubbles in the body of the drop, the following experiment will make more evident.

Take a small glass tube about a foot long, seal up one end of it *hermetically*, then put in a very small bubble of glass, almost of the shape of an *essence vial* with the open mouth towards the sealed end, then draw out the other end of the pipe very small, and fill the whole cylinder with water; then set this tube by the fire until the water begins to boil, and the air in the bubble is in good part rarefied and driven out, then by sucking at the narrowed pipe, more of the air or vapors in the bubble may be sucked out, so that it may sink to the bottom; when it is sunk to the bottom, in the flame of a candle, or lamp, seal up the slender pipe and let it cool: whereupon it is obvious to observe, first, that the water by degrees will subside and shrink into much less room; next, that the air or vapors in the glass will expand themselves so as to buoy up the little glass; thirdly, that all about the inside of the glass pipe there will appear an infinite number of small bubbles, which, as the water grows colder and colder, will swell bigger and bigger, and many of them will buoy themselves up and break at the top.

From this *departure* [disceding] of the heat in glass drops, that is, by the cooling *radiations* propagated from the surface upward and inward, by the lines CT, CT, DT, DE, etc., the bubbles in the drop have room to expand themselves a little, and the parts of the glass contract themselves; but this operation being too quick for the sluggish parts of the glass, the contraction is performed very unequally and irregularly, and thereby the particles of the glass are bent, some one way, and some another, yet so that most of them draw towards the *pith* or middle TEEE, or rather from that outward: so that they cannot extricate or unbend themselves, until some part of TEEE be broken and loosened, for all the parts about that are placed in the manner of an *arch*, and so until their hold at TEEE be loosened they cannot fly asunder, but uphold, and shelter, and fix each other much like the stones in a *vault*, where each stone concurs to the stability of the whole *structure* [fabric], and no one stone can be taken away but the whole arch falls. And wherever any of those radiating wedges DT D, etc. are removed, which are the component parts of this arch, the whole structure presently falls to pieces;

<meta>This page continues Robert Hooke's discussion on the internal tension of Prince Rupert's drops, transitioning from a description of their structure to a series of theoretical assertions about heat and matter.</meta>

<page-num>37</page-num>
<header>M I C R O G R A P H I A.</header>

pieces; for all the springs of the several parts are set at liberty, which immediately extricate themselves and fly asunder in every direction; each part by its spring contributing to the darting of itself and some other contiguous part. But if this drop is heated so hot that the parts can gradually unbend themselves, and be settled and annealed in that posture, and then be allowed to subside and cool gently; the parts, by this annealing, losing their springiness, constitute a drop of a more soft but less brittle texture. And because the parts are not at all under a flexure, even if any part of the middle or pith T E E E is broken, the drop will not fly to pieces as before.

This conjecture of mine I shall endeavor to make out by explaining each particular assertion with *analogous experiments*: The assertions are these.

First, That the parts of the glass, while in a fluid consistency and hot, are more rarefied, or take up more room, than when hard and cold.

Secondly, That the parts of the drop suffer a twofold contraction.

Thirdly, That the dropping or quenching the glowing metal in the water makes it of a hard, springy, and rarefied texture.

Fourthly, That there is a flexion or force remaining upon the parts of the glass thus quenched, from which they endeavor to extricate themselves.

Fifthly, That the fabric of the drop, which is able to hinder the parts from extricating themselves, is *analogous* to that of an arch.

Sixthly, That the sudden flying asunder of the parts proceeds from their springiness.

Seventhly, That a gradual heating and cooling does anneal or reduce the parts of glass to a texture that is more loose, and easier to be broken, but not so brittle.

That the first of these is true may be gathered from this: That *heat is a property of a body arising from the motion or agitation of its parts*; and therefore whatever body is touched by it must necessarily receive some part of that motion, whereby its parts will be shaken and agitated, and so by degrees free and extricate themselves from one another; and each part so moved does by that motion exert a <term>conatus</term> of protruding and displacing all the adjacent particles. Thus air included in a vessel, by being heated, will burst it to pieces. Thus I have broken a bladder held over the fire in my hand with such violence and noise that it almost made me deaf for the moment, and much surpassed the noise of a musket. I have done the same by throwing into the fire small glass bubbles hermetically sealed, with a little drop of water included in them. Thus water also, or any other liquid, included in a convenient vessel, by being warmed, manifestly expands itself with very great violence, so as to break the strongest vessel if, when heated, it is narrowly imprisoned in it.

<summary>Hooke proposes seven assertions to explain why Prince Rupert's drops explode, centering on the idea that heat is the internal motion of particles. He argues that rapid cooling traps this motion as tension, which is released violently when the glass is broken.</summary>

<meta>catchword: der.</meta>

This is very evident by the sealed *thermometers*, which I have, by several trials, at last brought to a great certainty and sensitivity: for I have made some with stems above four feet long, in which the expanding liquid would vary so much as to be very near the very top in the heat of summer, and pretty near the bottom at the coldest time of the winter. The stems I use for them are very thick, straight, and even pipes of glass, with a very small perforation, and both the head and body I have made on purpose at the glass-house, of the same glass from which the pipes are drawn: these I can easily, in the flame of a lamp driven by the blast of a pair of bellows, seal and join together so as to remain very firm, tight, and even; by this means I join on the body first, and then fill both it and a part of the stem—proportionate to the length of the stem and the warmth of the season I fill it in—with the best rectified *spirit of wine* highly tinged with the lovely color of *cochineal*, which I deepen further by pouring in some drops of common *spirit of urine*, which must not be too well rectified, because it will be prone to make the liquid curdle and stick in the small perforation of the stem. This liquid I have found upon trial to be the most sensitive of any spirituous liquid, and those are much more noticeably affected by the variations of heat and cold than other more phlegmatic and heavy liquids, and are as capable of receiving a deep dye, and keeping it, as any liquid whatsoever; and (which makes it even more advantageous) it is not subject to being frozen by any cold yet known. When I have thus filled it, I can very easily in the aforementioned flame of a lamp seal and join on its head.

Then, for graduating the stem, I fix that point for the beginning of my division where the surface of the liquid in the stem remains when the ball is placed in common distilled water that is so cold that it just begins to freeze and form ice flakes; and that mark I fix at a convenient place on the stem, to make it capable of showing many degrees of cold below that which is required to freeze water: the rest of my divisions, both above and below this (which I mark with a [0] or zero) I place according to the degrees of expansion or contraction of the liquid in proportion to the volume it had when it endured the newly mentioned freezing cold. And this may be very easily and accurately enough done by this following way: Prepare a cylindrical vessel of very thin plate brass or silver, *A B C D* of the figure *Z*; the diameter *A B* of whose cavity should be about two inches, and the depth *B C* the same; let each end be covered with a flat and smooth plate of the same substance, closely soldered on, and in the midst of the upper cover make a fairly large hole *E F*, about the size of a fifth part of the diameter of the other; into this fasten very well with cement a straight and even cylindrical pipe of glass, *E F G H*, the diameter of whose cavity should be exactly one-tenth of the diameter of the larger cylinder. Let this pipe be marked at *G H* with a diamond, so that *G* from *E* may be distant just two inches, or the same height with that of the cavity of the larger cylinder; then divide the length *E G* exactly into 10 parts, so the capacity of the hollow of each of these divisions will be 1/1000 part of the capacity of the larger cylinder.

->I<-

This vessel being thus prepared, the way of marking and graduating the *thermometers* may be very easily performed as follows:

Fill this cylindrical vessel with the same liquid with which the *thermometers* are filled, then place both it and the <term>thermometer</term> you are to graduate in water that is ready to be frozen, and bring the surface of the liquid in the <term>thermometer</term> to the first mark or [0]. Then adjust the amount of liquid in the cylindrical vessel so that its surface is exactly at the lower end of the small glass cylinder. Then, very gently and gradually warm the water in which both the <term>thermometer</term> and this cylindrical vessel stand; as you perceive the tinged liquid rising in both stems, use the point of a <term>diamond</term> to make several marks on the stem of the *thermometer* at those places which, by comparing the expansion in both stems, are found to correspond to the divisions of the cylindrical vessel. Having marked a few of these divisions on the stem in this way, it will be very easy to use these to mark all the rest of the stem and, accordingly, assign a proper character to every division.

A *thermometer*, thus marked and prepared, will be the most suitable instrument to serve as a standard of heat and cold that can be imagined. For, being sealed up, it is not at all subject to variation or evaporation, nor is it liable to be changed by the varying pressure of the *air*, to which all other kinds of *thermometers* open to the *air* are liable. But to proceed.

This property of <term>expansion</term> with heat and <term>contraction</term> with cold is not peculiar to liquids only, but to all kinds of solid bodies as well, especially <term>metals</term>, which will appear more clearly by this experiment.

Take the barrel of a brass <term>stopcock</term>, and let the key, which is well fitted to it, be riveted into it so that it may slip and be easily turned around. Then heat this cock in the fire, and you will find the key so swollen that you will not be able to turn it around in the barrel; but if it is allowed to cool again, as soon as it is cold, it will be as movable and as easy to be turned as before.

This quality is also very observable in *lead*, *tin*, *silver*, *antimony*, *pitch*, *rosin*, *beeswax*, *butter*, and the like; if you allow all of these to cool gently after they are melted, you shall find the parts of the upper surface subside and fall inwards, losing that plumpness and smoothness they had while in <term>fusion</term>. I have also observed the same in the cooling of *glass of antimony*, which very nearly approaches the nature of *glass*.

But because these are all examples taken from materials other than *glass*, and only suggest that there might possibly be a similar property in *glass* rather than proving there really is, we shall endeavor to demonstrate that also by three or four experiments.

The first is an observation that is very obvious even in these very drops: namely, that they all end with an unequal or irregular surface, especially around the smaller part of the drop and the whole length of the stem. Around point D, and from there to A, the entire surface—which would have been round if the drop had cooled slowly—is, by being quenched hastily, very irregularly flattened and pitted; which

<summary>Hooke describes a precise method for calibrating thermometers using a reference vessel and demonstrates that thermal expansion is a universal property affecting liquids and solids alike, including metals and glass.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the thermal expansion and contraction of solid bodies, specifically examining how glass reacts to sudden changes in temperature and providing several experimental proofs of its expansion when heated.</meta>

# MICROGRAPHIA.

I suppose this proceeds partly from the water's unequally cooling and pressing the parts of the drop, and partly from the self-contracting or subsiding quality of the substance of the glass: For the intensity of the heat of the drop causes such sudden motions and bubbles in the cold water that some parts of the water bear more forcibly against one part than against another, and consequently do more suddenly cool those parts to which they are contiguous.

A second argument may be drawn from the experiment of cutting glass with a hot iron. For in that experiment the tip of the iron heats, and thereby rarefies the parts of the glass that lie just before the crack, from which each of those agitated parts, endeavoring to expand itself and get elbow room, thrusts off all the rest of the contiguous parts, and consequently promotes the crack that was begun before.

A third argument may be drawn from the way of producing a crack in a sound piece or plate of glass, which is done two ways: either *first*, by suddenly heating a piece of glass in one place more than in another. And by this means *chemists* usually cut off the necks of glass bodies <note>Glass bodies refers to the main vessels or flasks used in chemical distillation.</note> by two kinds of instruments: either by a glowing hot round *iron ring*, which just encompasses the place that is to be cut, or else by a *sulfured thread*, which is often wound about the place where the separation is to be made, and then fired. Or *secondly*, a glass may be cracked by cooling it suddenly in any place with water, or the like, after it has been all leisurely and gradually heated very hot. Both of which *phenomena* seem manifestly to proceed from the *expansion* and contraction of the parts of the glass, which is also made more probable by this circumstance which I have observed: that a piece of common *window glass* being heated in the middle very suddenly with a live coal or hot iron usually falls into pieces at the first crack; whereas if the plate has been gradually heated very hot, and a drop of cold water or the like be put on the middle of it, it only flaws it, but does not break it asunder immediately.

A fourth argument may be drawn from this experiment: Take a glass pipe, and fit into it a solid stick of glass, so that it can just be moved in it. Then by degrees heat them while they are one within another, and they will grow stiffer; but when they are cold again, they will be as easy to be turned as before. This expansion of glass is more manifest in this experiment.

Take a stick of glass of a considerable length, and fit it between the two ends or screws of a lathe, so that it may just easily turn, and that its very ends may be just touched and sustained thereby; then, applying the flame of a candle to the middle of it and heating it hot, you will presently find the glass to stick very fast on those points, and not without much difficulty be turned on them, until, by removing the flame from it for a while, it is allowed to cool; and then you will find it as easy to be turned round as at first.

From all these experiments it is very evident that all those bodies, and particularly glass, suffer an expansion by heat, and that a very con-

considerable one, while they are in a state of fusion. For *fluidity, as I mention elsewhere, is nothing but an effect of a very strong and quick shaking motion, by which the parts are, as it were, loosened from each other and consequently leave an interjacent space or vacuum;* it follows that all those shaken particles must necessarily take up much more room than when they were at rest and lay quietly upon each other. And this is further confirmed by a pot of boiling alabaster, which will clearly rise a sixth or eighth part higher in the pot while it is boiling than it will remain at both before and after it is boiled. The reason for this odd *phenomenon* (to hint at it here only by the way) is this: there is in the fine powder of alabaster and other calcining stones a certain watery substance, which is so fixed and included within the solid particles that they will not fly away until the heat is very considerable; but after the heat is increased to such a degree, they break out in every direction as vapors, and thereby so shake and loosen the small corpuscles of the powder from each other that they become perfectly of the nature of a fluid body. One may move a stick to and fro through it and stir it as easily as water, and the vapors burst and break out in bubbles just as in boiling water and the like; whereas, both before those watery parts fly away and after they are quite gone—that is, before and after it has finished boiling—all those effects cease, and a stick is moved to and fro in it with as much difficulty as in sand or the like. Which explanation I could easily prove, had I time; but this is not a fit place for it.

To proceed therefore, I say that the dropping of this expanded body into cold water makes the parts of the glass suffer a double contraction. The first is of those parts which are near the surface of the drop. For cold—as I said before, contracting bodies, that is, *by the reduction of the agitating faculty, the parts falling closer together*—the parts next adjoining the water must necessarily lose much of their motion and impart it to the surrounding water (which its boiling and commotion manifests), and thereby become a solid and hard crust, while the innermost parts remain yet fluid and expanded; whence, as they also grow cold by degrees, their parts must necessarily be left at liberty to be condensed, but because of the hardness of the outward crust, the contraction cannot be admitted from that direction. However, there being many very small and previously inconspicuous bubbles in the substance of the glass, upon the settling of the parts of the glass, the agile substance contained in them has the liberty of expanding itself a little, and thereby those bubbles grow much bigger, which is the second contraction. And both of these are confirmed by the appearance of the drop itself: for as for the outward parts, we see, first, that it is irregular and shrunk, as it were, which is caused by the hardened skin yielding a little to a contraction after the very outermost surface is settled; and as for the internal parts, one may perceive with the naked eye an abundance of very conspicuous bubbles, and with the *microscope* many more.

The consideration of these particulars will easily make the third position probable: that is, that the parts of the drop will be of a very hard, though of a rarified texture. For if the outward parts of the drop, by reason of its hard crust, will endure very little contraction, and the agile particles, inclu-

It follows (the withdrawal of the heat being very sudden) that the parts must be left in a very loose texture; and by reason of the entanglement of the parts around one another—which, because of their sluggishness and glutinous nature, I suppose to be much like the sticks in a thorn-bush or a lock of wool—it follows, I say, that the parts will hold each other very strongly together and endeavor to draw each other nearer together, and consequently their texture must be very hard and stiff, but very much rarefied.

And this will make my next *position* probable: *That the parts of the glass are under a kind of tension or flexure, from which they endeavor to extricate and free themselves*, and thereby all the parts draw toward the center or middle. If the outward parts would give way—as they do when the outward parts cool slowly (as in the annealing <note>The original uses "baking," referring to the slow cooling process of glass.</note> of glasses)—they would contract the bulk of the drop into a much smaller space. For since, as I proved before, the internal parts of the drop, when fluid, were of a very rarefied texture and, as it were, tossed open like a lock of wool, they would be pressed close together again if they were allowed to cool slowly. And since the heat that kept them bent and open is removed, and yet the parts are not allowed to get as near together as they naturally would, it follows that the particles remain under a kind of *tension* and *flexure*, and consequently have an endeavor to free themselves from that *bending* and *distension*. This they do as soon as either the tip is broken or as soon as, by a slow heating and cooling, the parts are annealed into another posture.

And this will make my next *position* probable: *that the parts of the glass drops are joined together in the form of an arch and cannot yield or be drawn inward anywhere until, by removing some one part of it (as happens when removing one of the stones of an arch), the whole structure is shattered and falls to pieces, and each of the springs is left at liberty to suddenly extricate itself*. For since I have made it probable that the internal parts of the glass have a contractive power pulling inward, and the external parts are incapable of such a contraction, and the figure of it being spherical, it follows that the surface parts must press against each other and keep one another from being condensed into a smaller space, in the same manner as the stones of an arch contribute to upholding each other in that figure. 

And this is made more probable by another experiment which was communicated to me by an excellent person, whose extraordinary abilities in all kinds of knowledge, especially in that of natural things, and his generous disposition in communicating, encouraged me to have recourse to him on many occasions. The experiment was this: small glass balls (about the size of that represented in the *Figure &c.*) would, upon rubbing or scratching the inner surface, fly all apart with a pretty brisk noise; whereas, neither before nor after the inner surface had been thus scratched did there appear any flaw or crack.
