Now, although the pieces are not as small as those of a *fulminating drop*, they still plainly show that the outward parts of the glass have a great *conatus* <note>An inclination or tendency to move in a certain direction.</note> to fly apart, were they not held together by the tenacity of the parts of the inward surface. For we see that as soon as those parts are crazed by hard rubbing, and their tenacity thereby spoiled, the springiness of the more outward parts quickly causes a rupture; and if the concave surface of the broken pieces is further scratched with a diamond, they will fly again into even smaller pieces.

From these preceding considerations, it follows, sixthly, that the sudden flying apart of the pieces as soon as this "arch" is anywhere disordered or broken proceeds from the springing of the parts. These parts, endeavoring to extricate themselves as soon as they gain their liberty, do so with such speed that they throw one another away with very great violence. For the particles that compose the crust have a *conatus* to lie further from one another; therefore, as soon as the external parts are loosened, they dart themselves outward with great violence, just as many springs would do if they were compressed and fastened to a body and then suddenly loosened. The internal parts, drawing inward, contract so violently that they rebound back again and fly into a multitude of small shards or grains of sand. Now, although they do not appear either to the naked eye or through the *microscope*, I am very inclined to think there may be an abundance of small flaws or cracks which do not appear because the strongly reflecting air has not gotten between the *contiguous* parts. That this may be so, I argue from this: I have very often been able to make a crack or flaw in certain pieces of glass appear and disappear at will, according to whether I excluded or admitted the strongly reflecting air between the parts by pressing them together or pulling them apart. And it is very probable that there may be some substance—either very rarefied air or something *analogous* to it—which fills the bubbles of these drops; I argue this, first, from their roundness, and next, from the vivid reflection of light which they exhibit. Now, although I do not doubt that the air in them is very much rarefied, for those who well consider this experiment of the disappearing crack upon the forcing out of the air, it will seem more than probable that there is some air in them.

The seventh and last point that I shall prove, therefore, is *that the gradual heating and cooling of these extended bodies reduces the parts of the glass to a looser and softer temper.* I found this by heating them and keeping them very red hot in a fire for a pretty while; for by doing so, I found them to grow a little lighter, and the small stems could be very easily broken and snapped anywhere without making the drop shatter at all; whereas

The reason for this latter phenomenon seems to be that the slow heating and cooling of the parts does not only waste some part of the glass itself, but arranges all the parts into a better order and gives each particle an opportunity to *relax* itself. Consequently, the parts will neither hold together as strongly as before, nor be as difficult to be broken. The parts now yield more easily, and the other parts will not fly into pieces because they no longer possess the tension of bent springs. The *relaxation* in the temper of hardened steel and hammered metals by annealing them in the fire seems to proceed from much the same cause. For both by suddenly quenching such metals that have vitrified <note>Glassy or turned into glass.</note> parts interspersed, as steel does, and by hammering other kinds that do not have as many of them, such as silver, brass, etc., the parts are put into and held in a bent posture. By the agitation of heat, these parts are shaken, loosened, and allowed to unbend themselves.

## Observation VIII. Regarding the fiery sparks struck from a flint or steel.

<margin>Scheme 5.</margin>
It is a very common experiment to strike a flint against a steel to make certain fiery and shining sparks fly out from between those two colliding bodies. About eight years ago, upon casually reading the explanation of this odd *phenomenon* by the most ingenious *Descartes*, I had a great desire to be certain of what substance gave off such a shining and bright light. To that end, I spread a sheet of white paper and, observing the place on it where several of these sparks seemed to vanish, I found certain very small, black, but glistening spots of a movable substance. Examining each of these with my *microscope*, I found them to be small, round *globules*. Some of these, though they looked quite small, yielded from their surface a very bright and strong reflection on the side closest to the light; each looked almost like a bright iron ball with a regular surface, such as is represented by Figure A. In this, I could perceive the image of the window quite well, or of a stick which I moved up and down between the light and the globule. I found others which were, regarding the bulk of the ball, fairly regularly round, but their surfaces were not very smooth, being rough and more irregular; thus, the reflection from them was more faint and confused. Such were the surfaces of B, C, D, and E. which it stuck by the root F, at the end of which small stem was fastened a hemisphere, or half a hollow ball, with its mouth open away from the stem, so that it looked much like a funnel, or an old-fashioned bowl without a foot. This night, making many trials and observations of this experiment, I met, among a multitude of the globular ones which I had observed, a couple of instances which are very remarkable in confirming my *Hypothesis*.

And the first was a fairly large ball fastened to the end of a small sliver of iron, which *composite* seemed to be nothing else but a long thin chip of iron, one of whose ends was melted into a small round globule, the other end remaining unmelted and irregular, and perfectly iron.

The second instance was no less remarkable than the first; for I found, when a spark went out, nothing but a very small thin long sliver of iron or steel, unmelted at either end. So it seems that some of these sparks are the slivers or chips of the iron *vitrified*; others are only the slivers melted into balls without vitrification; and the third kind are only small slivers of the iron made red-hot by the violence of the stroke given to the steel by the flint.

He who shall diligently examine the *phenomena* of this experiment will, I doubt not, find cause to believe that the reason I have previously given for it is the true and genuine cause of it: *namely, that the spark appearing so bright as it falls is nothing else but a small piece of the steel or flint (but most commonly of the steel) which, by the violence of the stroke, is at the same time severed and heated red-hot—and sometimes to such a degree as to make it melt together into a small globule of steel. Sometimes also that heat is so very intense as to further melt it and vitrify it; but many times the heat is so gentle as to be able to make the sliver only red-hot, which nevertheless falling upon the tinder* (which is only a very fine small coal made of the small threads of linen burnt to coals and charred), it easily sets it on fire. Nor will any part of this *hypothesis* seem strange to him who considers, first, that either hammering, or filing, or otherwise violently rubbing steel will immediately make it so hot as to be able to burn one's fingers. Next, that the whole force of the stroke is exerted upon that small part where the flint and steel first touch: for the bodies being each of them so very hard, the pulse cannot be far communicated—that is, the parts of each can yield but very little—and therefore the violence of the concussion will be exerted on that piece of steel which is cut off by the flint. Thirdly, that the filings or small parts of steel are very prone, as it were, to take fire, and are immediately red-hot; that is, there seems to be a very combustible sulfurous body in iron or steel, which the air very readily preys upon as soon as the body is a little violently heated.

And this is obvious in the filings of steel or iron cast through the flame of a candle; for even by that sudden transition of the small chips of iron, they are heated red-hot, and that combustible sulfurous body is immediately preyed upon and devoured by the surrounding aerial *menstruum* <note>In early chemistry, a menstruum is a solvent or a medium that acts upon a substance.</note>, whose office in this particular I have shown in the explanation of charcoal.

# M I C R O G R A P H I A.

And in prosecution of this experiment, having taken the filings of iron and steel, and with the point of a knife cast them through the flame of a candle, I observed where some conspicuous shining particles fell; and looking on them with my *microscope*, I found them to be nothing else but such round globules as I formerly found the sparks struck from the steel by a stroke to be, only a little bigger. And shaking together all the filings that had fallen upon the sheet of paper underneath, and observing them with the *microscope*, I found a great number of small globules, such as the former, though there were also many of the parts that had remained untouched, and rough filings or chips of iron. So that, it seems, iron does contain a very *combustible sulfurous* body, which is, in all likelihood, one of the causes of this *phenomenon*, and which may be perhaps very much concerned in the business of its hardening and tempering: of which something is said in the description of *Muscovy-glass*.

So that, these things considered, we need not trouble ourselves to find out what kind of pores they are, both in the flint and steel, that contain the *atoms of fire*, nor how those *atoms* come to be hindered from running all out when a door or passage in their pores is made by the concussion. Nor need we trouble ourselves to examine by what *Prometheus* the element of fire comes to be fetched down from above the regions of the air, in what cells or boxes it is kept, and what *Epimetheus* lets it go. Nor to consider what it is that causes so great a conflux of the atomical particles of fire, which are said to fly to a flaming body like vultures or eagles to a putrefying carcass, and there to make a very great commotion. Since we have nothing more difficult in this *hypothesis* to conceive—first, as to the kindling of tinder—than how a large iron bullet, let fall red or glowing hot upon a heap of small-coal, should set fire to those that are next to it first. Nor, secondly, is this last more difficult to be explained than that a body, as silver for instance, put into a weak *menstruum*, as unrectified *aqua fortis*, should, when it is put in a great heat, be there dissolved by it, and not before; which *hypothesis* is more largely explained in the description of charcoal. To conclude, we see by this instance how much experiments may conduce to the regulating of *philosophical notions*. For if the most acute *Descartes* had applied himself experimentally to have examined what substance it was that caused that shining of the falling sparks struck from a flint and a steel, he would certainly have a little altered his *hypothesis*, and we should have found that his ingenious principles would have admitted a very plausible explanation of this *phenomenon*; whereas by not examining so far as he might, he has set down an explanation which experiment does contradict.

But before I leave this description, I must not forget to take notice of the globular form into which each of these is most curiously formed. And this *phenomenon*, as I have elsewhere more largely shown, proceeds from a property which belongs to all kinds of fluid bodies more or less, and is caused by the incongruity of the surrounding and included fluid, which so acts and modulates each other, that they acquire, as near as is possible,

<summary>Hooke demonstrates that iron filings melted in a candle flame form the same spherical globules as sparks from a flint, proving they are molten metal rather than trapped "atoms of fire." <meta>This page continues Robert Hooke's discussion on the formation of spherical particles, transitioning from his observations of iron sparks to a specific experimental method for creating metallic globules before beginning a new observation on the properties of Muscovy glass.</meta>

M I C R O G R A P H I A.

possible, a spherical or globular form; this property, and several of the *phenomena* that proceed from it, I have more fully explained in the sixth observation.

One experiment, which very much illustrates my present explanation and is in itself exceedingly pretty, I must not pass by: and that is a way of making small *globules* or balls of lead or tin, almost as small as those of iron or steel, and doing so exceedingly easily and quickly by turning the filings or chips of those metals also into perfectly round *globules*. The method, in short, as I received it from the *learned physician Doctor* I. G., is this:

Reduce the metal you would thus shape into exceedingly fine filings; the finer the filings are, the finer the balls will be. *Stratify* these filings with the fine and well-dried powder of quicklime in a crucible proportioned to the quantity you intend to make. When you have thus filled your *crucible* by continual *stratifications* of the filings and powder, so that, as near as possible, no one of the filings may touch another, place the crucible in a *gradual fire*, and by degrees let it be brought to a heat great enough to make all the filings that are mixed with the quicklime melt, and no more; for if the fire is too hot, many of these filings will join and run together. Whereas if the heat is proportioned, upon washing the lime-dust in clean water, all those small filings of the metal will sink to the bottom as a most curious powder, consisting entirely of exactly round *globules*, which, if it is very fine, is excellent for making hourglasses.

Now, though quicklime is the powder that this direction chooses, yet I do not doubt that there may be much more convenient ones found out, one of which I have tried and found very effectual; and were it not for revealing, by mentioning it, another secret which I am not free to share, I would have inserted it here.

## Observ. IX. *Of the Colours observable in Muscovy Glass, and other thin Bodies.*

Muscovy glass, or *Lapis specularis*, is a body that seems to have as many curiosities in its structure as any common mineral I have met with. For first, it is transparent to a great thickness. Next, it is composed of an infinite number of thin flakes joined or generated one upon another so closely and smoothly that many hundreds of them make one smooth and thin plate of a transparent flexible substance; this, with care and diligence, may be slit into pieces so exceedingly thin as to be hardly perceivable by the eye, and yet even those which I thought the thinnest, I have found with a good *microscope* to be made up of many other plates, yet thinner. And it is probable that, were our *microscopes*—

...much better, we might much further discover its divisibility. Nor are these flakes only regular in the smoothness of their surfaces; but thirdly, in many plates they may be perceived to be terminated naturally with edges in the shape of a *rhomboid*. This figure is much more conspicuous in our *English talc* <note>Hooke uses the period spelling "talk."</note>, much of which is found in the lead mines and is commonly called *spar* and *cawk* <note>Hooke spells this "kauck."</note>. It is of the same kind of substance as *selenite*, but is seldom found in such large flakes as that is, nor is it quite as tough; however, it is much more clear and transparent, and much more curiously shaped, and yet may be split and flaked like the other *selenite*. 

But fourthly, this stone has a property which, in respect to the *microscope*, is more notable: it exhibits several appearances of colors, both to the naked eye, but much more conspicuously to the *microscope*. To demonstrate this, I took a piece of *Muscovy glass* and, splitting or cleaving it into thin plates, I found that here and there in several parts of them I could plainly perceive several white specks or flaws, and others diversely colored with all the colors of the *rainbow*. And with the *microscope*, I could perceive that these colors were ranged in rings that encompassed the white speck or flaw, and were round or irregular, according to the shape of the spot which they terminated; and the position of colors, in respect to one another, was the very same as in the *rainbow*. 

The sequence of those colors from the middle of the spot outward was blue, purple, scarlet, yellow, green; blue, purple, scarlet, and so onwards, sometimes repeated ten times—that is, there appeared six, seven, eight, nine, or ten different colored rings or lines, each encircling the other, in the same manner as I have often seen a very vivid *rainbow* have four or five different rings of colors (that is, accounting all the gradations between red and blue as one). But the order of the colors in these rings was quite contrary to the primary or innermost *rainbow*, and the same as those of the secondary or outermost *rainbow*. These colored lines or *irises*, as I may call them, were some of them much brighter than others, and some of them also very much broader, some being ten, twenty, or, I believe, nearly a hundred times broader than others; and those that were broadest were usually nearest the center or middle of the flaw. 

And oftentimes I found that these colors reached to the very middle of the flaw, and then there appeared in the middle a very large spot, for the most part all of one color, which was very vivid, and all the other colors encompassing it gradually ascending and growing narrower toward the edges, keeping the same order as in the secondary *rainbow*—that is, if the middle were blue, the next encompassing it would be purple, the third red, the fourth yellow, etc., as above; if the middle were red, the next outside it would be yellow, the third green, the fourth blue, and so onward. And it always kept this order, whatever the middle color was.

There were further observable in several other parts of this body many lines or threads, each of them of some one peculiar color, and those so exceedingly bright and vivid that it afforded a very pleasing object.

But when we soon come to a stricter examination of these *phenomena* and inquire into the causes and reasons for these productions, I hope we shall make it more conceivable how they are produced and show them to be nothing other than the natural and necessary effects arising from the peculiar union of concurrent causes.

Since these *phenomena* are so various and so truly admirable, it will certainly be well worth our inquiry to examine their causes and reasons, and to consider whether the true causes of the production of all kinds of colors might be deduced from these demonstratively evidenced causes. I choose to do it now, instead of as an appendix or digression to this *history*, or upon the occasion of examining the colors in peacocks' or other feathers, because this subject affords more variety of particular colors and also offers much better ways of examining each circumstance. This will be made manifest to anyone who considers, first, that this laminated body is more simple and regular than the parts of peacocks' feathers, as it consists only of an indefinite number of plain and smooth plates, heaped up or *incumbent* on each other. Next, the parts of this body are much more manageable to be divided or joined than the parts of a peacock's feather or any other substance that I know. And thirdly, because in this, we are able to produce several colored bodies from a colorless body, providing all the variety of colors imaginable—and several others, which the subsequent inquiry will make manifest.

To begin, therefore, it is clear from several circumstances that the material cause of the *appearance* of these various colors is some *lamina* or plate of a transparent or pellucid body of a very specific thickness, proportioned according to the greater or lesser refractive power of the transparent body. And that this is so, an abundance of instances and particular circumstances will make clear.

As *first*, if you take any small piece of the *Muscovy-glass* <note>Muscovy-glass is a historical term for mica, a mineral that easily splits into thin, transparent sheets.</note> and, with a needle or some other convenient instrument, cleave it many times into thinner and thinner *laminae*, you shall find that until you come to a specific thinness, they shall all appear transparent and colorless; but if you continue to split and divide them further, you shall find at last that each plate, after it reaches such a specific thickness, shall appear most beautifully tinged or imbued with a specific color. If, *further*, by any means you flaw a fairly thick piece so that one part begins to cleave a little from the other, and between those two there is by some means gotten some transparent *medium*, those laminated transparent bodies that fill that space shall exhibit several rainbows or colored lines, the colors of which will be disposed and ranged according to the various thicknesses of the several parts of that plate. That this is so is yet *further* confirmed by this experiment.

Take two small pieces of ground and polished looking-glass plate, each about the size of a shilling; take these two dry, and with your forefingers and thumbs press them very hard and close together, and you shall find that when they approach each other very nearly, there will appear several *irises* or colored lines, in almost the same manner as in the *Muscovy-glass*; and you may very easily change any of the colors of any part of the interposed body by pressing the plates closer and harder together, or leaving them more loose; that is, a part which appeared colored with a red may be presently tinged with a yellow, blue, green, purple, or the like, by altering the nearness of the terminating plates. Now, that air is not necessary to be the interposed body, but that any other transparent fluid will do much the same, may be tried by wetting those contacted surfaces with water or any other transparent liquor, and proceeding with it in the same manner as you did with the air; and you will find much the same effect, only with this difference: that those compressed bodies which differ most in their refractive quality from the compressing bodies exhibit the most strong and vivid tints. Nor is it necessary that this laminated and tinged body should be of a fluid substance, as any other substance—provided it be thin enough and transparent—does the same thing. This the *laminae* of our *Muscovy-glass* suggest, but it may be confirmed by multitudes of other instances.

And first, we shall find that even glass itself may, by the help of a lamp, be blown thin enough to produce these *phenomena* of colors; which *phenomena* happening accidentally as I was attempting to shape small glasses with a lamp, did not a little surprise me at first, having never heard or seen anything of it before; though afterward, comparing it with the *phenomena* I had often

Thus I have produced them with bubbles of *pitch, rosin, colophony* <note>Colophony is a type of resin obtained from pines.</note>, *turpentine, solutions* of several *gums*, such as *gum arabic* in water; any glutinous liquor, such as *wort, wine, spirit of wine, oil of turpentine, snail slime*, etc.

It would be needless to enumerate the various instances, these being enough to show the generality or universality of this property. Only I must not omit that we have instances also of this kind even in metallic and animal bodies; for those various colors which are observed to follow each other upon the polished surface of hardened steel, when it is gradually tempered or softened by a sufficient degree of heat, are produced from nothing else but a certain thin *lamina* of a *vitrum* or vitrified part of the metal, which by that degree of heat and the concurring action of the surrounding air, is driven out and fixed on the surface of the steel.

And this suggests to me a very probable (at least, if not the true) cause of the hardening and tempering of steel, which has not, I think, been yet given, nor, so far as I know, been so much as thought of by anyone. And that is this: that its hardness arises from a greater proportion of a vitrified substance interspersed through the pores of the steel. And that the tempering or softening of it arises from the proportionately smaller portions of it left within those pores. This will seem more probable if we consider these particulars.

First, that the pure parts of metals are of themselves very *flexible* and *tough*; that is, they will endure bending and hammering, and yet retain their continuity.

Next, that the parts of all vitrified substances, such as all kinds of glass, the *scoria* <note>Scoria refers to the slag or refuse left after smelting metal.</note> of metals, etc., are very hard and also very brittle, being neither *flexible* nor *malleable*, but may be broken into small parts or powders by hammering or beating.

Thirdly, that all metals (excepting gold and silver, which do not do so as much with the fire alone, unless assisted by other saline bodies) do more or less *vitrify* by the strength of fire—that is, they are corroded by a saline substance, which I elsewhere show to be the true cause of fire—and are, as by several other *menstruums* <note>A menstruum is a solvent, especially one used in chemistry or alchemy.</note>, converted into *scoria*. And this is called *calcining* them by chemists. Thus iron and copper, by heating and quenching, eventually turn entirely into *scoria*, which are evidently vitrified substances and unite with glass, and are easily *fusible*; and when cold, they are very hard and very brittle.

Fourthly, that most kinds of *vitrifications* or *calcinations* are made by salts, uniting and incorporating with the metallic particles. Nor do I know any one calcination wherein a saline body may not, with very great probability, be said to be an agent or assistant.

Fifthly, that iron is converted into steel by means of the incorporation of certain salts, with which it is kept for a certain time in the fire.

Sixthly, That any iron may, in a very little time, be *case-hardened*, as the tradesmen call it, by encasing the iron to be hardened with clay, and putting between the clay and iron a good quantity of a mixture of *urine*, *soot*, *sea-salt*, and *horses' hoofs* (all which contain great quantities of saline bodies); and then putting the case into a good strong fire and keeping it at a considerable degree of heat for a good while, and afterwards heating and quenching or cooling it suddenly in cold water.

Seventhly, That all kinds of vitrified substances, by being suddenly cooled, become very hard and brittle. And from this arises the pretty *phenomena* of the *Glass Drops*, which I have already explained further in its own place.

Eighthly, That those metals which are not so apt to vitrify do not acquire any hardness by quenching in water, such as *silver*, *gold*, etc.

These considerations being premised, I suppose they will make way for the easier reception of the following explanation of the *phenomena* of hardened and tempered steel. That *steel* is a substance made out of iron by means of a certain proportionate *vitrification* of several parts, which are so curiously and proportionately mixed with the tougher and unaltered parts of the iron, that when this vitrified substance is melted by the great heat of the fire, and consequently rarefied—and thereby the pores of the iron are more open—if it is then suddenly cooled by means of dipping it in cold water, and the parts hardened (that is, stayed in that same degree of *expansion* they were in when hot), the parts become very hard and brittle. This happens for almost the same reason as small parcels of glass quenched in water grow brittle, which we have already explained. If after this the piece of steel is held in some appropriate heat until certain colors gradually appear upon the surface of the brightened metal, the very hard and brittle tone of the metal gradually relaxes and becomes much more tough and soft. Namely, the action of the heat gradually loosens the parts of the steel that were before stretched or set *atilt*, as it were, and held open by each other, whereby they become relaxed and set at liberty. From this, some of the more brittle interjacent parts are thrust out and melted into a thin skin on the surface of the steel, which increases from no color to a deep purple, and so onward by these gradations or successions: *white*, *yellow*, *orange*, *minium* <note>Minium refers to a bright red lead oxide pigment.</note>, *scarlet*, *purple*, *blue*, *watchet* <note>Watchet is a traditional name for a pale blue color.</note>, etc. And the parts within are more conveniently and proportionately mixed; and so they gradually settle into a texture which is much better proportioned and more closely joined, so that the rigidity of parts ceases, and the parts begin to acquire their former *ductility*.

Now, that it is nothing but the vitrified metal that sticks upon the surface of the colored body is evident from this: that if it is scraped and rubbed off by any means, the metal underneath it is white and clear; and if it is kept longer in the fire, so as to increase to a considerable thickness, it may be beaten off in flakes by blows. This is further confirmed by this observation: that iron or steel which is covered with this vitrified case will stay longer from rusting. Thus also lead will, by degrees, be

This is also observable in some way on brass, copper, silver, gold, and tin, but is most conspicuous in lead: all those colors that cover the surface of the metal are nothing else but a very thin vitrified part of the heated metal.

The other instance we have is in animal bodies, such as in pearls, mother-of-pearl shells, oyster shells, and almost all other kinds of stony shells whatsoever. I have also sometimes with pleasure observed this even in muscles and tendons. Nor is it necessary that the two bordering bodies should both be of the same kind, as may appear by the vitrified *lamina* on steel, lead, and other metals, where one surface of that *lamina* is in contact with the surface of the metal, and the other with the air.

Nor is it necessary that these colored *laminae* should be of an even thickness—that is, having their edges and centers of equal thickness, as in a looking-glass plate—which circumstance is only required to make the plate appear all of the same color. Instead, they may resemble a *lens* (having their centers thicker than their edges) or else a *double concave* (being thinner in the center than at the edges). In both cases, there will be various colored rings or lines with different sequences or orders of colors; the order of the first from the center outwards being red, yellow, green, blue, etc., and the latter being quite the opposite.

But further, it is entirely necessary that the plate, in the places where the colors appear, should be of a specific thickness. First, it must not be more than a certain thickness, for when the plate's thickness is increased beyond that, the colors cease. Besides, I have seen in a thin piece of *Muscovy-glass* <note>mica</note>, where the ends of two plates, appearing single, exhibited two distinct and different colors; but in the place where they were united and formed one double plate (as I may call it), they appeared transparent and colorless. Nor, secondly, may the plates be *thinner* than a specific size; for we always find that the very outermost rim of these flaws ends in a white and colorless ring.

Further, in this production of colors, there is no need for a specific light of a certain size and no more, nor of a specific position of that light (that it should be on this side and not on that side), nor of a bordering shadow as in the prism, and rainbow, or water-ball. And further, it is all the same whatever side of the colored rings is toward the light; for the whole ring keeps its proper colors from the middle outwards in the same order as I previously related, without varying at all upon changing the position of the light.

But above all, it is most observable that here all kinds of colors are generated in a *pellucid* <note>transparent</note> body where there is properly no such refraction as *Descartes* supposes his *globules* to acquire a *verticity* <note>rotation or spin</note> by: For in the plain and even plates it is manifest that the second refraction (according to *Descartes'* principles in the *fifth section* of the *eighth chapter* of his *Meteors*) regulates and restores the supposed *turbinated* <note>spinning</note> *globules* to their former uniform motion. This experiment, therefore, will prove to be one such as our thrice-excellent *Verulam* <note>Francis Bacon, Lord Verulam</note> calls an *Experimentum Crucis* <note>crucial experiment</note>, serving as a guide or landmark by which to direct our course in the search for the true cause of colors. It affords us this particular negative information: that for the production of colors there is necessary neither a great refraction, as in the prism; nor secondly, a determination of light and shadow, such as exists both in the prism and glass ball. Now, so that we may likewise see what affirmative and positive instruction it yields, it will be necessary to examine it a little more particularly and strictly; to do this better, it will be requisite to premise something in general concerning the nature of light and refraction.

And first, regarding light, it seems very manifest that there is no luminous body that does not have its parts in motion, more or less.

First, I think it will be very easily granted to me that all kinds of fiery, burning bodies have their parts in motion. I have elsewhere made it probable that the spark struck from a flint and steel is in rapid agitation. And I think it will be as easily conceded by those who consider that the parts of rotten wood, rotten fish, and the like are also in motion, since those parts never begin to shine until the bodies are in a state of putrefaction; and that is now generally granted by all to be caused by the motion of the parts of putrefying bodies. It is the general report of those who write of it, and of others who have seen it, that the *Bononian stone* <note>Bologna stone, a phosphorescent mineral</note> shines no longer than it is either warmed by the sunbeams, or by the flame of a fire or of a candle. And that heat implies a motion of the internal parts is (as I said before) generally granted.

But there is one more instance, which was first shown to the *Royal Society* by *Mr. Clayton*, a worthy member thereof, which makes this assertion more evident than all the rest: and that is, that a diamond, being rubbed, struck, or heated in the dark, shines for a good while afterward, as long as that motion which is imparted by any of those agents remains (in the same manner as a glass, rubbed, struck, or—by a means which I shall mention elsewhere—heated, yields a sound which lasts as long as the vibrating motion of that sonorous body). Several experiments made on this stone have since been published in a discourse of colors by the truly

# MICROGRAPHIA.

honorable Mr. *Boyle*. What may be said of those *Ignes fatui* <note>will-o'-the-wisps</note> that appear in the night, I cannot so well affirm, having never had the opportunity to examine them myself, nor to be informed by any others who had observed them: And the accounts of them in authors are so imperfect that nothing can be built on them. But I hope I shall be able in another place to make it at least very probable that there is even in those also a motion which causes this effect. That the shining of *sea-water* proceeds from the same cause may be argued from this: that it shines not unless it is beaten against a rock, or is in some other way broken or agitated by storms, or oars, or other *striking* bodies. And that the animal *energies* or agile spiritual parts are very active in *cats' eyes* when they shine seems evident enough, because their eyes never shine except when they look very intently either to find their prey, or when being hunted in a dark room they seek after their adversary or a way to escape. And the same may be said of the shining *bellies* of *glowworms*, since it is evident they can at pleasure either increase or extinguish that radiation.

It would be somewhat too long a work for this place *zetetically* <note>investigatively</note> to examine, and positively to prove, what particular kind of motion it is that must be the cause of light; for though it be a motion, yet it is not every motion that produces it, since we find there are many bodies moved very violently which yet do not afford such an effect; and there are other bodies which, to our other senses, seem not moved so much, which yet shine. Thus water and quicksilver, and most other heated liquids, do not shine; and several hard bodies, such as iron, silver, brass, copper, wood, etc., though very often struck with a hammer, do not shine immediately, though they will all of them grow exceedingly hot; whereas rotten wood, rotten fish, sea water, glowworms, etc., have nothing of tangible heat in them, and yet (where there is no stronger light to affect the senses) some of them shine so vividly that one may manage to read by them.

It would be too long, I say, here to insert the logical progression by which I inquired after the properties of the motion of light; and therefore I shall only add the result.

And, first, I found it ought to be exceedingly *quick*, such as those motions of fermentation and putrefaction, whereby, certainly, the parts are moved exceedingly nimbly and violently; and that is because we find those motions are able more minutely to shatter and divide the body than the most violent heats or *menstruums* <note>solvents</note> we yet know. And that fire is nothing else but such a *dissolution of the burning body, made by the most universal solvent of all sulfurous bodies, namely, the air*, we shall in another place of this treatise endeavor to make probable. And that, in all extremely hot shining bodies, there is a very quick motion that causes light, as well as a more robust one that causes heat, may be argued from the speed with which the bodies are dissolved.

Next, it must be a *vibratory motion*. And for this the newly mentioned *diamond* affords us a good argument; since if the motion of the parts did

And a *circular motion* of the parts is much more improbable, since, if that were granted, and they were supposed to be irregular and *angular* parts, I do not see how the parts of the diamond could hold so firmly together, or remain in the same perceivable dimensions, which they nevertheless do. Next, if they were *globular*, and moved only with a *spinning motion*, I do not know of any cause that could impress that motion upon the *transparent medium*, which is nevertheless done. Thirdly, any other irregular motion of the parts among one another would necessarily make the body of a fluid consistency, from which it is far enough removed. It must therefore be a *vibrating motion*.

And thirdly, that it is a very *short vibrating motion*, I think the instances drawn from the shining of *diamonds* will also make probable. For a *diamond* being the hardest body we yet know in the *world*, and consequently the least likely to yield or bend, must consequently also have its *vibrations* exceeding short.

And these, I think, are the three principal properties of a motion requisite to produce the effect called *light* in the *object*.

The next thing we are to consider is the way or manner of the *passage* 
of this motion through the interposed transparent body to the eye: And here it will be easily granted,

First, that it must be a body *susceptible* to and *capable of imparting* this motion that will deserve the name of a *transparent* body. And next, that the parts of such a body must be *homogeneous*, or of the same kind. Thirdly, that the constitution and motion of the parts must be such that the *impact* of the *luminous body* may be communicated or propagated through it to the greatest imaginable distance in the least imaginable time; though I see no reason to claim that it must be instantaneous: For I do not know of any single experiment or observation that proves it. And, whereas it may be objected that we see the sun risen at the very instant when it is above the visible horizon, and that we see a star hidden by the body of the moon at the same instant when the star, the moon, and our eye are all in the same line; and similar observations, or rather suppositions, may be urged. I have this to answer: that I can as easily deny as they affirm; for I would like to know by what means anyone can be more assured of the affirmative than I am of the negative. If indeed the propagation were very slow, it is possible something might be discovered by *eclipses* of the *moon*; but even if we should grant the progress of light from the *earth* to the *moon*, and from the *moon* back to the *earth* again, to take a full two minutes to perform, I know of no possible means to discover it; indeed, there may be some instances perhaps of horizontal *eclipses* that may seem very much to favor this supposition of a slower progression of *light* than most imagine. And the same may be said of the *eclipses* of the *sun*, etc. But of this only by the way. Fourthly, that the motion is propagated every way through a *homogeneous*

Fifthly, in a homogeneous *medium* this motion is propagated every way with equal velocity, whence necessarily every pulse or vibration of the luminous body will generate a sphere, which will continually increase and grow larger, just in the same manner (though infinitely swifter) as the waves or rings on the surface of the water swell into larger and larger circles about a point where, by the sinking of a stone, the motion was begun. From this it necessarily follows that all the parts of these spheres undulated through a homogeneous *medium* cut the rays at right angles.

But because all transparent media are not homogeneous to one another, we will next examine how this pulse or motion will be propagated through differently transparent *media*. And here, according to the most acute and excellent philosopher *Descartes*, I suppose the sine of the angle of inclination in the first *medium* to be to the sine of refraction in the second as the density of the first is to the density of the second. By density, I mean not the density in respect of gravity (with which the refractions or transparency of *media* hold no proportion) but in respect only to the *trajection* of the rays of light, in which respect they only differ in this: that the one propagates the pulse more easily and weakly, the other more slowly, but more strongly. But as for the pulses themselves, they will by the refraction acquire another property, which we shall now endeavor to explain.

We will suppose, therefore, in the first figure, *A C F D* to be a physical ray, or *A B C* and *D E F* to be two mathematical rays, *trajected* from a very remote point of a luminous body through a *homogeneous* transparent *medium L L L*, and *D A, E B, F C* to be small portions of the orbicular impulses which must therefore cut the rays at right angles; these rays meeting with the plain surface *N O* of a *medium* that yields an easier *transitus* to the propagation of light, and falling obliquely on it, they will in the *medium M M M* be refracted toward the perpendicular of the surface. And because this *medium* is more easily *trajected* than the former by a third, therefore the point *C* of the orbicular pulse *F C* will be moved to *H* four spaces in the same time that *F*, the other end of it, is moved to *G* three spaces; therefore the whole refracted pulse *G H* shall be oblique to the refracted rays *C H K* and *G I*; and the angle *G H C* shall be an acute angle, and so much the more acute by how much the greater the refraction is—than which nothing is more evident. For the sine of the inclination is to be the sine of refraction as *G F* to *T C* (the distance between the point *C* and the perpendicular from *G* on *C K*), which being as four to three, and *H C* being longer than *G F*, it is longer also than *T C*; therefore the angle *G H C* is less than *G T C*. So that henceforth the parts of the pulses *G H* and *I K* are moved askew, or cut the rays at *oblique* angles.

It is not my business in this place to set down the reasons why this or that body should impede the rays more and others less: as why water should transmit the rays more easily, though more weakly than air. Only thus...

But to proceed, the same kind of obliquity of the pulses and rays will also happen when the refraction occurs from a more easy into a more difficult *medium*; as shown by the calculations of *G Q* and *C S R*, which are refracted from the perpendicular. In both of these calculations, it is *obvious* to observe that the part of the ray toward which the refraction is made always has the end of the *orbicular pulse* preceding that of the other side. And always, the more often the refraction is made in the same way, or the greater the single refraction is, the greater this unequal progress becomes. So, having found this odd property to be an inseparable companion of a refracted ray—one not straightened by a contrary refraction—we will next examine the refractions of *sunbeams* as they are allowed only to pass through a small opening, obliquely out of a more difficult into a more easy *medium*.

Let us suppose, therefore, that *A B C* in the second figure represents a large *chemical glass vessel* about two feet long, filled with very clear water as high as *A B*, and tilted in a convenient position with *B* toward the sun. Let us further suppose the top of it is covered with an *opaque* body, except for the hole *a b*, through which the *sunbeams* are allowed to pass into the water and are thereby refracted to *c d e f*. If a piece of paper is spread out on the outside against that part, all the colors of the rainbow will appear; that is, the two principal colors, *scarlet* and *blue*, will be generated, along with all the intermediate ones which arise from the mixing and diluting of these two. That is, *c d* shall exhibit a *scarlet*, which toward *d* is diluted into a *yellow*; this is the refraction of the ray *i k*, which comes from the underside of the sun. And the ray *e f* shall appear of a deep *blue*, which is gradually diluted toward *e* into a pale *watchet-blue*. Between *d* and *e*, the two diluted colors, *blue* and *yellow*, are mixed and compounded into a *green*; and I imagine this to be the reason why *green* is so pleasant a color to the eye, and that either of the two extremes, if intense, are somewhat offensive—namely, [green] being placed in the middle between the two extremes and compounded from both of those, diluted also, or somewhat moderated. For the composition arising from the mixture of the two extremes *undiluted* makes a *purple*, which, though it is a lovely color and quite acceptable to the eye, is in no way comparable to the ravishing pleasure with which a fine and well-tempered *green* affects the eye. If, upon removing the paper, the eye is placed against *c d*, it will perceive the lower side of the sun (or a candle at night, which is much better because it does not offend the eye and is more easily managed) to be of a deep *red*; and if placed against *e f*, it will perceive the upper part of the luminous body to be of a deep *blue*. These colors will appear deeper and deeper as the rays from the luminous body fall more obliquely on the surface of the water, thereby undergoing a greater refraction, and the

So that on the whole, we shall find that the reason for the *phenomena* seems to depend upon the obliquity of the *orbicular pulse* to the lines of radiation; and in particular, that the ray *c d* which constitutes the *scarlet* has its inner parts—namely those which are next to the middle of the luminous body—preceding the outermost parts which are adjacent to the dark and *unradiating* sky. And that the ray *e f* which produces a *blue* has its outward part—namely, that which is adjacent to the dark sky—preceding the pulse from the innermost part, which borders on the bright *area* of the luminous body.

We may observe further, that the cause of the diluting of the colors toward the middle proceeds partly from the width of the hole through which the rays pass, whereby the rays from several parts of the luminous body fall upon many of the same parts between *c* and *f*, as is more manifest by the figure. And it also proceeds partly from the nature of the refraction itself; for the vividness or strength of the two terminating colors arises chiefly, as we have seen, from the very great difference that exists between the outsides of those oblique *undulations* and the surrounding dark rays. Because 그 disparity between the neighboring rays decays gradually the further inward toward the middle of the luminous body they are removed, the color must approach more nearly to a white or an undisturbed light.

Upon the calculation of the refraction and reflection from a *ball of water* or *glass*, we find much the same *phenomena*—namely, an obliquity of the undulation in the same manner as we have found it here. Because this is very relevant to our present purpose and affords such a *crucial instance* <note>Hooke uses the Latin "instancia crucis," a deciding experiment.</note> as no one that I know of has yet noticed, I shall examine it further. For it very plainly and positively distinguishes and shows which of the two *hypotheses*—either the *Cartesian* or this one—is to be followed, by providing a generation of all the colors in the rainbow where, according to *Cartesian* principles, no colors at all should be generated. And secondly, it provides an instance that more closely limits the cause of these *phenomena* of colors to this present *hypothesis*.

And first, regarding the *Cartesian* view, we have this to object against it: That whereas he says (*Meteors, Chapter 8, section 5*), "but I judged that at least one (refraction, namely) was required, and indeed such a one that its effect would not be destroyed by another contrary (refraction); for experience teaches that if the surfaces NM and NP (namely the refracting ones) were parallel, the rays would be restored by the second as much as they were broken by the first, and would depict no colors." This principle of his holds true indeed in a prism where the refracting surfaces are plain, but it is contradicted by the ball or cylinder, whether of water or glass, where the refracting surfaces are orbicular or cylindrical. For if we examine the passage of any globule or ray of the primary *iris* <note>The rainbow.</note>, we shall find it to pass out of the ball or cylinder again with the same inclination and refraction that it entered with; and that last refraction, by means of the *intermediate* reflection, shall be the same as if the ray had been twice refracted by two parallel surfaces without any reflection at all.

<margin>Schem. 6. Fig. 3.</margin>
*EFKNP* in the third figure is one of the rays of the primary *iris*, twice refracted at *F* and *N*, and once reflected at *K* by the surface of the water-ball. For first, it is evident that *KF* and *KN* are equal because *KN*, being the reflected part of *KF*, they both have the same inclination on the surface at *K*; that is, the angles *FKT* and *NKV* made by the two rays and the tangent of *K* are equal, which is evident by the laws of reflection. From this, it will also follow that *KN* has the same inclination on the surface *N* (or its tangent *XN*) that the ray *KF* has to the surface *F* (or its tangent *FY*). Consequently, it must necessarily follow that the refractions at *F* and *N* are equal; that is, *KFE* and *KNP* are equal. Now, that the surface *N* is made parallel to the surface at *F* by the reflection at *K* is evident from the principles of reflection; for reflection being nothing but an inverting of the rays, if we re-invert the ray *KNP* and make the same inclinations below the line *TKV* that it has above, it will be most evident that *KH* (the inverse of *KN*) will be the continuation of the line *FK*, and that *LHI* (the inverse of *OX*) is parallel to *FY*. And *HM* (the inverse of *NP*) is parallel to *EF*, for the angle *KHI* is equal to *KNO* (which is equal to *KFY*), and the angle *KHM* is equal to *KNP* (which is equal to *KFE*), which was to be proved.

So that according to the above-mentioned *Cartesian* principles, no color at all should be generated in a ball of water or glass by two refractions and one reflection. This does indeed hold most true if the surfaces are plain, as may be experimented with any kind of prism where the two refracting surfaces are equally inclined to the reflecting one; but in this case, the *phenomena* are quite different.

The cause, therefore, of the generation of color must not be what *Descartes* assigns—namely, a certain rotation of the *globuli ætherei* <note>ether globules</note>, which are the particles he supposes to constitute the *pellucid medium* <note>transparent medium</note>—but something else, perhaps what we have lately supposed and shall further investigate and explain.

But first, I shall crave leave to propound some other difficulties regarding his—nevertheless exceedingly ingenious—*hypothesis*, which I plainly confess seem problematic to me; and those are:

First, if light is (as is affirmed in *Dioptrics, chapter 1, section 8*) not so much a motion as an action or a tendency toward motion, I cannot conceive how the eye can become sensible of the *verticity* <note>rotation</note> of a *globule* that is generated in a drop of rain, perhaps a mile away from it. For that *globule* is not carried to the eye according to his formerly recited principle; and if not so, I cannot conceive how it can communicate its rotation or circular motion to the line of *globules* between the drop and the eye. It cannot be by means of every one turning the next one before him; for if so, then only all the *globules* that are in the odd places must be turned the same

Now, although the second refraction made at *Nn* is convenient—that is, it makes the rays glance more—it is not entirely necessary. The same shall also happen if the paper is placed about *Kk*, for toward *T* a *Red* shall appear, and toward *V* a *Blue*, which exactly agrees with this my *hypothesis*, as will most easily appear upon the calculation of the progress of the pulse.

Nor do these two observations—of the colors appearing to the eye around *p* being different from how they appear on the paper at *N*—contradict each other. Rather, they confirm and exactly agree with one another, as will be evident to anyone who examines the reasons set down by the ingenious *Descartes* in the 12th section of the 8th chapter of his *Meteors*. There, he gives the true reason why the colors appear in a completely contrary order to the eye compared to how they appeared on the paper, if the eye is placed in the paper's stead. And as in the *prism*, so also in the water drop or globe, the *phenomena* and reasoning are much the same.

Having therefore shown that there is such a property in the *prism* and water *globule* by which the pulse is made *oblique* to the path of progression—and all the more so the greater the refraction is—I shall next consider how this leads to the production of colors, and what kind of impression it makes upon the back of the eye. To this end, it will be necessary to examine this *hypothesis* a little more specifically.

And by the ray K C A I refracted to F, there shall be a confused stroke or impression on that part, whose strongest part—namely, that along the line C F—shall precede, and whose weakest or impeded part—namely, that along the line A F—shall follow. And all the intermediate points between F and D will receive impressions from the *converged* rays that are more like the impressions on F and D the nearer they approach one or the other.

From the consideration of the properties of these impressions, we may gather these short definitions of Colors: That *Blue* is an *impression on the retina of an oblique and confused pulse of light, whose weakest part precedes and whose strongest follows.* And that *Red* is an *impression on the retina of an oblique and confused pulse of light, whose strongest part precedes and whose weakest follows.*

These properties, as they have already been shown in the prism and falling drops of rain to be the causes of the colors generated there, may easily be found to be the causes also of the colors appearing in thin, laminated transparent bodies; it is for the explanation of these that all this has been stated beforehand.

And that this is so, a little closer examination of the *phenomena* and the *figure* of the body, by this *hypothesis*, will make evident.

For first (as we have already observed), the *laminated* body must be of a determinate thickness; that is, it must not be thinner than a certain determinate quantity. For I have always observed that near the edges of those which are exceedingly thin, the colors disappear and the part grows white. Nor must it be thicker than another determinate quantity; for I have likewise observed that beyond such a thickness, no colors appeared, but the plate looked white. Between these two determinate thicknesses were all the colored rings, of which in some substances I have found ten or twelve, and in others not half so many, which I suppose depends much upon the transparency of the *laminated* body. Thus, though the sequences are the same in the scum or the skin on the top of metals, yet in those sequences the same color is not so often repeated as in the sequences in thin glass, or in <term>soap-water</term>, or any other more transparent and glutinous liquor. For in these I have observed *Red, Yellow, Green, Blue, Purple; Red, Yellow, Green, Blue, Purple; Red, Yellow, Green, Blue, Purple; Red, Yellow*, etc., to succeed each other ten or twelve times; but in the other more opaque bodies, the sequences will not be half so many.

And therefore, secondly, the *laminated* body must be transparent; and I argue this from the fact that I have not been able to produce any color at all with an *opaque* body, no matter how thin. And this I have often tried by pressing a small *globule* of *mercury* between two smooth plates of glass, by which I have reduced that body to a much greater thinness than was required to exhibit the colors with a transparent body.

Thirdly, there must be a considerable reflecting body adjacent to the under or further side of the *lamina* or *plate*; for I always found that the greater that reflection was, the more *vivid* were the appearing colors.

From which observations, it is most evident that the reflection from the under or further side of the body is the principal cause of the production of these colors. That this is so, and how it contributes to that effect, I shall further explain in the following figure, which is described here with a very great thickness, as if it had been viewed through the *microscope*. ## **Observ. X.** *Of Metallic, and other real Colors.*

Having in the previous discourse, from the fundamental cause of color, made it probable that there are only two colors, and shown that the *Perception* of color is caused by the sensation of the *oblique* or *uneven* pulse of light, which is capable of no more than two varieties arising from the two sides of the *oblique* pulse (though each of these is capable of infinite gradations or degrees, each beginning from *White* and ending either in the deepest scarlet or *Yellow*, or the deepest *Blue*): I shall in this *Section* set down some observations I have made regarding other colors, such as *Metallic* powders, dyed or colored bodies, and several kinds of tinctures or dyed liquids. All of which, together with those I discussed in the previous observation, will, I suppose, comprise the various subjects in which color is observed to be inherent, and the various ways in which it resides or is apparent

And this being so, as I shall shortly show, it seems to be an evident argument to me that all colors whatsoever—whether in fluid or solid, whether in very transparent or seemingly opaque—have the same efficient cause, namely, some kind of *refraction* whereby the rays that proceed from such bodies have their pulse obliquated or confused in the manner I explained in the former *Section*. That is, a *Red* is caused by a duplicated or confused pulse, whose strongest pulse precedes and a weaker follows; and a *Blue* is caused by a confused pulse, where the weaker pulse precedes and the stronger follows. And according to how these are, more or less, or variously mixed and compounded, so are the sensations, and consequently the *phantasms of colors* diversified.

To proceed therefore; I suppose that all transparent colored bodies, whether fluid or solid, consist at least of two parts, or two kinds of substances, the one being a substance of a somewhat differing *refraction* from the other. That one of these substances, which may be called the *tinging substance*, consists of distinct parts or particles of a determinate size which are disseminated or dispersed all over the other. That these particles, if the body be equally and uniformly colored, are evenly ranged and dispersed over the other contiguous body; that where the body is most deeply tinged, there these particles are ranged thickest; and where it is but faintly tinged, they are ranged much thinner, but uniformly. That by the mixture of another body that unites with either of these, which has a differing refraction from either of the other, quite different effects will be produced—that is, the sequences of the confused pulses will be of another kind and consequently produce other sensations and *phantasms of colors*, and from a *Red* may turn to a *Blue*, or from a *Blue* to a *Red*, etc.

Next, they are ranged into the form of a *Quincunx*, or *equilaterotriangular* order, which I shall endeavor to show elsewhere why they are probably so. Thirdly, they are of such a nature as either more easily or more difficultly transmits the rays of light than the liquid; if more easily, a *Blue* is generated, and if more difficultly, a *Red* or *Scarlet*.

Almost all kinds of *purples*, and many sorts of *greens*, both consist of mixed colors; for if we suppose A and A in the ninth Figure to represent two pulses of clear light which follow each other at a convenient distance, A A, each of which has a *spurious* pulse preceding it, such as B B, which makes a *blue*, and another following it, such as C C, which makes a *red*—the one caused by tinging particles that have a greater refraction, the other by others that have a less refracting quality than the liquor or <term>menstruum</term> <note>a solvent</note> in which these are dissolved—whatever liquor alters the refraction of the one without altering that of the other part of the tinged liquor must necessarily very much alter the color of the liquor. For if the refraction of the *solvent* is increased, and the refraction of the tinging particles not altered, then the preceding *spurious* pulse will be shortened or stopped, and not out-run the clear pulse so much; so that B B will become E E, and the *blue* will be *diluted*, whereas the other *spurious* pulse which follows will be made to lag much more, and be further behind A A than before, and C C will become *f f*, and so the *yellow* or *red* will be heightened.

A *saline* liquor, therefore, mixed with another tinged liquor, may alter its color in several ways: first, by altering the refraction of the liquor in which the color swims; or secondly, by varying the refraction of the colored particles, by uniting more intimately either with some particular *corpuscles* of the tinging body or with all of them, according to whether it has a *congruity* <note>an affinity or compatibility</note> to some more especially, or to all alike; or thirdly, by uniting and interweaving itself with some other body that is already joined with the tinging particles, with which substance it may have a congruity, though it has very little with the particles themselves; or fourthly, it may alter the color of a tinged liquor by disjoining certain particles which were before united with the tinging particles, which, though they were somewhat congruous to these particles, have yet a greater congruity with the newly *infused saline menstruum*. It may likewise alter the color by further dissolving the tinging substance into smaller and smaller *particles*, and so diluting the color; or by uniting several particles together as in precipitations, and so deepening it, and other such ways, which many experiments and comparisons of different trials together might easily inform one of.

From these principles applied, all the varieties of colors observable either in liquors or any other tinged bodies may be explained with great ease and, I hope, intelligibly enough, there being nothing in the notion of color or in its supposed production but what is very conceivable and possible.

The greatest difficulty that I find against this *hypothesis* is that there seem to be more distinct colors than two—that is, more than yellow and blue. This objection is grounded on the reason that there are several reds which, when diluted, do not make a saffron or pale yellow; therefore, red or scarlet seems to be a third color distinct from a deep degree of yellow.

To which I answer that saffron affords us a deep scarlet tincture, which may be *diluted* into as pale a yellow as any, either by making a weak so-

He addresses the objection that red is a primary color by demonstrating that deep red tinctures like saffron can be diluted into pale yellow.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Robert Hooke’s investigation into how the concentration and particle size of a substance, such as saffron, affect the perception of its color through refraction and light pulses.</meta>

# MICROGRAPHIA.

solution of the saffron, by infusing a small portion of it into a large quantity of liquid, as in spirit of wine, or else by looking through a very thin amount of the tincture, which may be heightened into the loveliest scarlet by looking through a very thick body of this tincture, or through a thinner portion of it that is highly *impregnated* with the coloring substance, by having had a larger quantity of the saffron dissolved in a smaller amount of the liquid.

Now, although there may be some particles of other coloring substances that also produce a lovely scarlet, which, no matter how much they are diluted with liquid or viewed through a very thin layer of tinted liquid, will still not provide a pale yellow, but only a kind of faint red; yet this is no argument that those tinted particles may not have within them the faintest degree of yellow, even if we are unable to make them show it. For that power of being *diluted* depends upon the divisibility of the tinted substance; if I am unable to make the coloring particles so thin as to show that color, it does not therefore follow that the thing is impossible to be done. Now, the coloring particles of some substances are of such a nature that unless some way is found to break them down into smaller sizes than the liquid dissolves them into, all the rays that pass through them must necessarily receive a tint as deep as their appropriate refractions and sizes, compared with the properties of the dissolving liquid, must necessarily incline them to impart—which may perhaps be a pretty deep yellow or pale red.

And to show that this is not a mere assertion without proof <note>from the Latin *gratis dictum*</note>, I shall add one instance of this kind, in which the fact is most obvious.

If you take blue *smalt* <note>a pigment made of ground blue glass</note>, you will find that the deepest blue is produced by the largest particles or grains, all other things being equal <note>from the Latin *ceteris paribus*</note>; and if you further divide or grind those particles on a grindstone or *porphyry* stone, you may, by breaking down the grains of it, dilute the blue into as pale a shade as you please. This you cannot do by simply laying the color thin; for wherever any single particle is, it displays as deep a blue as the whole mass. Now, there are other blues which, no matter how much they are ground, will not be *diluted* by grinding, because they consist of very small particles that are very deeply tinted; they cannot be actually separated into smaller particles by grinding than the action of the fire or some other dissolving *menstruum* <note>solvent</note> has already reduced them to.

Thus all kinds of *metallic* colors—whether precipitated, *sublimed*, *calcined*, or otherwise prepared—are hardly changed by grinding; for example, *ultramarine* is not further diluted, nor is *vermilion* or *red-lead* made into a fainter color by grinding. For the smallest particles of these, which I have viewed with my greatest magnifying glass, appear very deeply tinted with their peculiar colors if they are well lit. Although I have magnified and lit the particles exceedingly, I could not perceive many of them to be transparent or to be single, whole particles; instead, the smallest specks that I could find among well-ground *vermilion* and *red-lead* seemed to be a red mass composed of a multitude of smaller and smaller motes which, sticking together, composed a size not one-millionth part of the smallest visible grain of sand or mote.

# MICROGRAPHIA.

And I find this generally in most metallic colors: though they consist of such exceedingly small parts, they are very deeply tinted, being so heavy and having such a multitude of terrestrial particles crowded into a small space. So it is difficult to find any particle that is transparent or resembles a precious stone, though it is not impossible. For I have observed various such shining and resplendent colors mixed with the particles of *Cinnabar*, both natural and artificial, before it has been ground and broken or flawed into *Vermilion*. I have also seen this in *Orpiment*, *Red-lead*, and *Bise*, which leads me to suppose that those *metallic colors* are, by grinding, not only actually broken and separated into smaller pieces, but that they are also flawed and bruised. Because of this, for the most part, they become opaque, like flawed crystal or glass, etc. But for *smalts* and *verditures*, I have been able with a *Microscope* to perceive that very many of their particles are transparent.

Now, it may be made probable by this experiment that the others may also be transparent, even though they do not appear so under the *Microscope*: if you take enamel <note>ammel</note> that is almost opaque and grind it very well on a *Porphyry* or *Serpentine* stone, the small particles will appear perfectly opaque because of their flaws. That it is the flaws which produce this opacity may be argued from the fact that much thicker particles of the same enamel, if unflawed, will appear somewhat transparent even to the eye. It can also be argued from the fact that the most transparent and clear crystal, if heated in a fire and then suddenly quenched so that it becomes flawed all over, will appear opaque and white.

And it may be argued further that the particles of *metallic colors* are transparent because the crystals, or *vitriols* <note>metallic salts, often sulfates</note> of all metals, are transparent. Since these consist of metallic as well as *saline* particles, those *metallic* ones must be transparent. This is further confirmed by the fact that they have, for the most part, *appropriate* colors: the vitriol of *Gold* is *yellow*; of *Copper*, *blue* and sometimes *green*; of *Iron*, *green*; of *Tin* and *Lead*, a pale white; of *Silver*, a pale blue, etc.

Next, the *solutions* of all metals into *menstruums* <note>solvents</note> are much the same as the *vitriols* or crystals. It seems very probable, therefore, that those colors produced by the precipitation of those particles out of the *menstruums* by transparent precipitating liquids should also be transparent. Thus, *gold* precipitates with *oil of Tartar* or *spirit of Urine* into a brownish *yellow*. *Copper* precipitates with *spirit of Urine* into a *mucous blue* which retains its transparency. A solution of sublimate (as the same illustrious author I lately mentioned shows in his 40th Experiment) precipitates with *oil of Tartar per deliquium* <note>liquid potassium carbonate formed by exposing the salt to air</note> into an orange-colored *precipitate*. Nor is it less probable that the calcination of those *vitriols* by fire should result in transparent particles. Thus *Saccarum Saturni* <note>sugar of lead</note>, or the *vitriol of lead*, becomes a deep orange-colored *minium* <note>red lead</note> by calcination, which is a kind of precipitation by some salt proceeding from the fire; common *vitriol calcined* yields a deep brownish red, etc.

A third argument that the particles of metals are transparent is that, when *calcined* and melted with *glass*, they tint the *glass* with transparent

And that the parts of metals are transparent may be further argued from the transparency of gold leaf, which, when held against the light, exhibits a deep green to both the naked eye and the *microscope*. And although I have never seen other metals laminated so thinly that I was able to perceive them as transparent, yet, for copper and brass, if we had the same convenience for laminating them as we have for gold, we might perhaps find very different degrees of blue or green through such plates or leaves. For it seems very probable that those rays that rebound from them, tinted with a deep yellow or pale red (as from copper) or with a pale yellow (as from brass), have passed through them; for I cannot conceive, according to any existing *hypothesis*, how those rays could receive a tint by reflection alone.

So we see that a sufficient reason may be drawn from these instances why those colors which we are unable to dilute to the palest yellow, blue, or green should not therefore be concluded to be anything other than a deeper degree of them. For suppose we had a large collection of small globular essence bottles, or round glass bubbles about the size of a walnut, each filled with a very deep mixture of saffron, and that every one of them appeared to be a deep scarlet color, and all of them together exhibited a deep-dyed scarlet body from a distance. It does not follow that because we find them to have much the same color as the whole mass after coming nearer to this *congeries* (or mass) and dividing it into its parts and examining each part individually—it does not, I say, follow that if we could break those globules smaller, or in any other way see a smaller or thinner portion of the tinted liquor that filled those bubbles, that the tinted liquor must always appear red or of a scarlet hue. For if an experiment is made, the quite contrary will occur, as it is capable of being diluted into the palest yellow.

Now, to avoid all *objections* of this kind by presenting an experiment that might convince by ocular proof those whom other reasons would not persuade, I provided myself with a *prismatical glass* made hollow, exactly in the form of a wedge, such as is represented in the tenth figure of the sixth scheme. The two parallelogram sides *A B C D* and *A B E F*, which met at a point, were made of the clearest looking-glass plates, well ground and polished, that I could find; these were joined with hard cement to the *triangular* sides, *B C E* and *A D F*, which were made of wood. The parallelogram base, *B C E F*, was likewise made of wood and joined to the rest with hard cement. The whole *prismatical* box was exactly sealed everywhere, except for one small hole left near the base, by which the vessel could be filled with any liquor or emptied again at pleasure.

But instead of meeting with what I looked for, I met with something more admirable; and that was, that I found myself utterly unable to see through them when placed both together, though they were transparent enough when apart; and though I could see through twice the thickness when both of them were filled with the same colored liquors, whether both with the yellow or both with the blue, yet when one was filled with the yellow and the other with the blue and both were looked through, they both appeared dark, only when the parts near the tops were looked through, they exhibited greens, and those of very great variety, as I expected, but the purples and other colors I could not by any means make, whether I endeavored to look through them both against the sun, or whether I placed them against the hole of a darkened room.

But notwithstanding this misguessing, I proceeded with my trial in a dark room, and having two holes near one another, I was able, by placing my wedges against them, to mix the tinted rays that passed through them and fell on a sheet of white paper held at a convenient distance from them as I pleased; so that I could make the paper appear of whatever color I would by varying the thicknesses of the wedges and consequently the tincture of the rays that passed through the two holes, and sometimes also by varying the paper—that is, instead of a white paper, holding a gray or a black piece of paper.

Whence I experimentally found what I had before imagined, that all the varieties of colors imaginable are produced from several degrees of these two colors, namely, yellow and blue, or the mixture of them with light and darkness, that is, white and black.
