Now, whereas it may again be objected that neither can reds be made out of yellows, even when added together or applied in greater or lesser quantities, nor can yellows be made out of reds, even if they are applied very thinly; and as for the addition of white or black, they do nothing but either whiten or darken the colors to which they are added, and do not make them any other kind of color at all. For instance, *vermilion*, by being mixed with white lead, does not become more yellow at all, but only a whiter kind of red. Nor does *yellow ochre*, even when applied very thickly, produce the color of *vermilion*; nor, though it be mixed with black, does it make a red at all. Indeed, even if it is mixed with white, it will not yield a fainter kind of yellow, such as <term>masticot</term>, but only a whitened yellow. Nor will blues be diluted or deepened in the manner I describe; for example, <term>indigo</term> will never yield as fine a blue as *ultramarine* or <term>bice</term>; nor will it, mixed with *vermilion*, ever produce a green, even if each of them is mixed extensively with white.

To which I answer that there is a great difference between diluting a color and whitening it. Diluting a color is to make the colored parts thinner, so that the tinted light—which is created by passing through those tinted bodies—does not receive such a deep tincture. However, whitening a color is only an intermixing of many clear reflections of light among those same tinted parts. Likewise, deepening and darkening (or blackening) a color are very different: deepening a color is to make the light pass through a greater quantity of the same tinting body, while darkening or blackening a color is only the interposing of a multitude of dark or black spots among those same tinted parts, or placing the color in a fainter light.

First, therefore, as to the former of these operations—that is, diluting and deepening—most of the colors used by <term>limners</term> and painters are incapable of them, specifically *vermilion*, *red lead*, and *ochre*. This is because the tinted parts are so exceedingly small that even the most meticulous grindstones we have are not able to separate them into parts actually divided as small as the tinted particles are. For looking at the most finely ground *vermilion*, *ochre*, and *red lead*, I could perceive that even those small <term>corpuscles</term> of the bodies they left behind were compounded of many pieces; that is, they seemed to be small pieces composed of a multitude of smaller tinted parts. Each piece seemed almost like a piece of red glass or tinted crystal, full of flaws. Consequently, unless the grindstone could actually divide them into smaller pieces than those flawed particles were—which composed that tinted mote I could see with my <term>microscope</term>—it would be impossible to *dilute* the color by grinding. Because the finest stones we have will not succeed in doing this with *vermilion* or *ochre*, they cannot be diluted at all, or only with great difficulty.

Other colors, indeed, whose tinted particles are such that they may be made smaller by grinding their color, may be *diluted*. Thus several of the

# MICROGRAPHIA.

Blues may be *diluted*, such as *smalt* and *bice*; and *masticot*, which is **yellow**, may be made fainter. And even *vermilion* itself may, by too much grinding, be brought to the color of *red lead*, which is only an orange color, and which is admitted by all to be very close to yellow. Now, although perhaps some of this dilution of *vermilion* by overmuch grinding may be attributed to the grindstone or muller (because some of their parts may be worn off and mixed with the color), yet it seems not to be very much, for I have done it on a serpentine stone with a muller made of a pebble, and yet observed the same effect follow.

And secondly, as to the other of these operations on colors—that is, the deepening of them—limners' and painters' colors are for the most part also incapable of it. For they are mostly *opaque*; and that *opaqueness*, as I said before, proceeds from the particles being very flawed. Unless we were able to join and reunite those flawed particles again into one piece, we shall not be able to deepen the color. Since we are unable to do this with most of the colors which are considered *opaque* by painters, we are therefore unable to deepen them by adding more of the same kind.

But because all those opaque colors have two kinds of beams or rays reflected from them—that is, untinted rays, which are only reflected from the outward surface without at all penetrating the body, and tinted rays, which are reflected from the inward surfaces or flaws after they have suffered a twofold refraction—and because transparent liquids mixed with such *corpuscles* do, for the most part, remove the former kind of reflection; therefore these colors mixed with water or oil appear much deeper than when dry, for most of that white reflection from the outward surface is removed. Indeed, some of these colors are very much deepened by the mixture with some transparent liquid, and that is because they may perhaps get between those two flaws, and so consequently join two or more of those flawed pieces together; but this happens in only a very few cases.

Now, to show that all this is not *gratis dictum* <note>a statement made without proof</note>, I shall set down some experiments which demonstrate that these things I have delivered here are probable and likely.

For, first, if you take any tinted liquid whatsoever—especially if it is quite deeply tinted—and by any means work it into a froth, the *congeries* <note>a collection or mass</note> of that froth shall seem to be an opaque body and appear to be of the same color, but much whiter than the liquid from which it is made. For the abundance of reflections of the rays against those surfaces of the bubbles of which the froth consists so often rebounds the rays backward that little or no light can pass through, and consequently the froth appears opaque.

Again, if to any of these tinted liquids that will endure boiling there is added a small quantity of fine flour (the parts of which through the *microscope* are clearly enough perceived to consist of transparent *corpuscles*) and allowed to boil until it thickens the liquid, the mass of the liquid will appear *opaque* and tinted with the same color, but very much whitened.

<summary>Hooke explains how grinding pigments into smaller, flawed particles makes them appear lighter (whiter) by increasing surface reflections, while mixing them with liquids deepens their color by reducing those reflections.</summary>

Thus, if you take a piece of well-colored transparent glass and flaw it all over by heating it and then quenching it in water, it will become *opaque* and will exhibit the same color with which the piece is tinted, but fainter and whiter.

Or, if you take a tube of this transparent glass and melt it in the flame of a lamp, then blow it into very thin bubbles, break those bubbles, and collect a large amount of those *plates* together in a paper, you shall find that a small thickness of those plates will constitute an *opaque* body. You may see through the mass of glass, before it was thus *laminated*, at more than four times that thickness. Besides, they will now provide a color by reflection, just as other colors called *opaque* do, but much fainter and whiter than that of the lump or tube out of which they were made.

In the same way, if you take <term>putty</term> <note>a powder used in glassmaking, typically tin oxide, to create opacity</note> and melt it with any transparent colored glass, it will make it become an opaque colored lump and yield a paler and whiter color than the lump did by reflection.

The same thing may be done by a preparation of *antimony*, as has been shown by the learned *physician* Dr. *C. M.* <note>Dr. Christopher Merret</note> in his excellent observations and notes on *Neri's Art of Glass*; by this means, all transparent colors become *opaque*, or *enamels*. And although they lose very much of their color by being ground, growing much whiter because of the multitude of single reflections from their outward surfaces (as I showed before), the fire in the <term>annealing</term> or melting reunites them. This renews those *spurious* reflections and also removes those whitenings of the color that proceed from them.

As for the other colors that painters use, which are transparent and used to varnish over all other paintings, it is well enough known that applying them thinner or thicker very much dilutes or deepens their color.

Since painters' colors consist mostly of solid particles so small that they cannot be reunited into thicker particles by any art yet known (and consequently cannot be deepened), nor divided into particles as small as the flawed particles that exhibit that color (much less smaller, and consequently cannot be diluted), it is necessary that those who wish to imitate all kinds of colors should have as many degrees of each color as can be procured.

To this purpose, both <term>limners</term> <note>painters of miniatures or manuscript illustrators</note> and painters have a very great variety of both *yellows* and *blues*, besides several other colored bodies that exhibit very composite colors, such as greens and purples. Others are compounded of several degrees of yellow, or several degrees of blue, sometimes unmixed and sometimes compounded with several other colored bodies.

The *yellows*, ranging from the palest to the deepest red or scarlet (which has no intermixture of blue), are *pale and deep masticot*, *orpiment*, *English ochre*, *brown ochre*, *red lead*, and *vermilion*, *burnt English ochre*, and *burnt brown ochre* (the last of which have a mixture of dark or dirty parts within them), etc.

# M I C R O G R A P H I A.

Their blues consist of several kinds of *smalts*, *verditers*, *bice*, *ultramarine*, and *indigo*, the last of which has many dirty or dark parts mixed in with it.

Their compound colored bodies, such as <term>pink</term> <note>a yellow pigment derived from vegetable matter, used in Hooke's time to mix greens</note> and *verdigris*, are greens—the one a *popinjay*, the other a *sea-green*; then *lac*, which is a very lovely *purple*.

To these may be added their black and white, which they also usually call colors. Of each of these, they have several kinds, such as *bone black*, made of *ivory* burnt in a closed vessel; *blue black*, made of the small coal of *willow* or some other wood; and *Cologne earth*, which is a kind of brown-black, etc. Their usual whites are either artificial or natural *white lead*, the latter being the best they have yet; and by mixing and tempering these colors together, they are able to create an imitation of any color whatsoever. They can *dilute* their reds or deep yellows by mixing pale yellows with them, and deepen their pale colors by mixing deeper ones with them. For it is not the same with *opaque* colors as it is with *transparent* ones, where adding more yellow to a transparent yellow deepens it; rather, in *opaque* colors, it is diluted. They can whiten any color by mixing white with it and darken any color by mixing black or some dark and dirty color. In short, most of the colors or colored bodies they use in limning and painting are such that, even though mixed with any other of their colors, they preserve their own hue. By being dispersed in such very small parts through the other colored bodies, they both, or altogether, represent a *composite* of all to the eye. The eye is unable, because of their smallness, to distinguish the uniquely colored particles, but receives them as one entire *composite*. However, in many of these, the *microscope* very easily distinguishes each of the compounding colors as distinct, exhibiting its own color.

Thus, by gently mixing dry *vermilion* and *bice*, I produced a very fine purple or mixed color. But looking at it with the *microscope*, I could easily distinguish both the red and the blue particles, which did not at all produce the *appearance* of purple.

To sum up everything in a word, I have not yet found any solid colored body that I have examined to be perfectly *opaque*. Those that are least transparent are *metallic* and *mineral* bodies, whose particles generally—seeming either to be very small or very flawed—appear for the most part opaque. Yet, there are very few of them that I have looked at with a *microscope* that have not very plainly or circumstantially shown themselves to be transparent.

And indeed, there seem to be so few bodies in the world that are <term>in minimis</term> <note>in their smallest parts</note> opaque, that I think one may make it a rational *query*: whether there be any body absolutely opaque? For I do not doubt at all (and I have taken notice of many circumstances that make me of this mind) that if we could greatly improve the *microscope*, we might be able to see all those bodies as plainly transparent which we are now only forced to guess at by circumstances. Indeed, the object glasses we currently use are such that they make many bodies transparent to the eye,

Now, as for all kinds of colors that are dissolvable in water or other liquids, nothing is so manifest as that all those tinted liquids are transparent; and many of them are capable of being *diluted* and compounded or mixed with other colors, and several of them are capable of being very much changed, heightened, and fixed with various kinds of <term>saline menstruums</term> <note>salt-based solvents or chemical solutions</note>. In the true ordering, *diluting*, deepening, mixing, and fixing of each of these consists one of the greatest mysteries of the dyers; because our *microscope* affords us very little information on these particulars, I shall add nothing more at present, except that with a very few tinctures ordered and mixed in certain ways (too long to be set down here), I have been able to create the appearance of all the various colors imaginable, without using the help of *salts* or *saline menstruums* to vary them.

As for the change of colors by *saline menstruums*, they have already been so fully and excellently handled by the lately mentioned incomparable *author* <note>Robert Boyle</note>, that I can add nothing, except that of a multitude of trials that I made, I have found them exactly to agree with his rules and theories; and though there may be infinite instances, yet they may be reduced under a few heads and comprised within a very few rules. And generally, I find that *saline menstruums* are most operative upon those colors that are purple, or have some degree of purple in them, and upon the other colors much less. The *spurious pulses* that compose them being (as I formerly noted) so very near the middle between the true ones, that a small variation throws them both to one side or both to the other, and so consequently must make a vast change in the previously appearing color.

### Observation XI. Of Figures observed in small Sand.

Sand generally seems to be nothing else but exceedingly small pebbles, or at least some very small pieces of a larger stone; the whiter kind seems through the *microscope* to consist of small transparent pieces of some *pellucid* <note>translucent or clear</note> body, each of them looking much like a piece of *alum* or <term>Salt Gem</term> <note>rock salt</note>; and this kind of sand is angled for the most part irregularly, without any certain shape, and its granules are mostly flawed; though among many of them it is not difficult to find some that are perfectly *pellucid*, like a piece of clear *crystal*, and various others most curiously shaped, much like the larger <term>stiriæ</term> <note>icicle-like or columnar crystals</note> of *crystal*, or like the small *diamonds* I observed in certain flints, of which I shall shortly give an account; this last particular seems to argue that this kind of sand is not

made by the pulverizing <note>comminution</note> of larger transparent crystalline bodies, but by the solidifying or coagulation of water, or some other fluid substance.

There are other kinds of coarser sands, which are browner and have much larger particles; when viewed with a *microscope*, these seem to be much coarser and more opaque substances, and most of them have irregularly rounded shapes. Although they do not seem so opaque to the naked eye, they appear very foul and cloudy; but these also do not lack beautifully transparent particles, any more than they lack regularly shaped and well-colored ones, as I have often found.

There are multitudes of other kinds of sands which, in many particulars plainly enough discoverable by the *microscope*, differ both from these last-mentioned kinds of sands and from one another. There seems to be as great a variety of sands as there is of stones. And just as among stones some are called precious because of their excellence, so also are there sands which deserve the same epithet for their beauty. For when viewing a small parcel of *East-India* sand (which was given to me by my highly honored friend, Mr. *Daniel Colwall*) and, since then, another parcel of much the same kind, I found several of them to be both very transparent like precious stones and regularly shaped like *crystal* or *Cornish diamonds*, some like *rubies*, etc., and also tinged with very lively and deep colors, like *rubies*, *sapphires*, *emeralds*, etc. I have often found these kinds of granules in *English* sand as well. And it is easy to make such counterfeit sand with deeply tinged glass, enamels, and painters' colors.

It would be endless to describe the multitudes of figures I have encountered in these kinds of minute bodies, such as *spherical*, *oval*, *pyramidal*, *conical*, and *prismatical*, of each of which I have taken notice.

But among many others, I met with none more noteworthy than this pretty shell (described in *Figure X* of the *fifth scheme*). Although it was happened upon by chance and deserved to have been omitted (since I am unable to direct anyone to find the like), yet for its rarity, it was not insignificant, especially on account of the information it may afford us. For by it, we have a very good instance of the ingenuity <note>curiosity</note> of nature in another kind of animal which is hidden, by reason of its smallness, beyond the reach of our eyes. Just as there are several sorts of *insects*, such as *mites* and others, so small as not yet to have had any names (some of which I shall describe later); and small fish, such as *leeches* in *vinegar*; and small vegetables, such as *moss* and *rose-leaf plants*; and small *mushrooms*, such as mold: so there are, it seems, small shellfish likewise, nature showing her ingenuity in every tribe of *animals*, *vegetables*, and *minerals*.

I was testing several small and single magnifying glasses and casually viewing a parcel of white sand, when I perceived one of the grains exactly shaped and coiled like a shell. But when I endeavored to distinguish it with my naked eye, it was so very small that I was obliged to use the glass again to find it. Then, while I looked at it this way, I separated all the rest of the granules of sand with a pin and found it afterwards to appear to the naked eye as an exceedingly small white spot, no bigger than the point of a pin.

### Observation XII. Regarding Gravel in Urine.

I have often observed the sand or gravel of *urine*, which seems to be a tartareous <note>resembling tartar or mineral scale</note> substance, generated from a saline and an earthy substance crystallized together in the form of tartar. Sometimes it sticks to the sides of the *urinal* <note>a vessel for collecting urine</note>, but for the most part it sinks to the bottom, lying there in the form of coarse common sand. Through the *microscope*, these appear to be a collection of small bodies, partly transparent and partly opaque—some white, some yellow, some red, and others of more brown and dusky colors.

The shape of them is for the most part flat, like slate or similar layered stones; that is, each of them seems to be made up of several other thinner plates, much like *Muscovy glass* <note>mica</note> or *English spar* <note>calcite</note>. The white plated gravel seems most similar to the latter; for they seem not only layered like that, but their sides are also shaped into *rhombs*, *rhomboids*, and sometimes into *rectangles* and *squares*. Their size and shape may be seen in the second *figure* of the sixth *plate*, which represents about a dozen of them lying upon a plate ABCD. Some of these, such as a, b, c, and d, seemed more regular than the rest, and e, which was a small one sticking on the top of another, was a perfect *rhomboid* on the top and had four *rectangular* sides.

The line E, which was the scale of the *microscope*, is 1/32 part of an *English* inch, so that the greatest breadth of any of them did not exceed 1/320 part of an inch.

Putting these into several liquids, I found *oil of vitriol* <note>sulfuric acid</note>, *spirit of urine* <note>ammonia</note>, and several other *saline* <term>menstruums</term> <note>solvents</note> to dissolve them; the first of these did so in less than a minute without *ebullition* <note>bubbling or boiling</note>. *Water* and several other liquids had no immediate effect upon them. I mention this because those liquids that dissolve them first make them very white—not distorting, but rather sharpening their shape—and thereby make them a very beautiful object for the *microscope*.

How great an advantage it would be to those troubled with the stone to find some <term>menstruum</term> that might dissolve them without hurting the bladder is easily imagined, since some *injections* made of such substances might likewise dissolve the stone, which seems to be of much the same nature.

## Observation XIII. *Of the small Diamonds, or Sparks in Flints.*

By chance, having broken a flint stone into pieces, I found within it a certain cavity all crusted over with a very pretty candied substance, some parts of which, upon changing the position of the stone in respect to the *incident* light, exhibited a number of small but very vivid reflections; and having made use of my *microscope*, I could perceive the whole surface of that cavity to be covered with a multitude of little *crystalline* or *adamantine* <note>diamond-like</note> bodies, so curiously shaped that it provided a quite pleasing object.

Having considered those vivid repercussions of light, I found them to be made partly from the flat external surface of these regularly figured bodies (which provided the vivid reflections) and partly to be made from within the somewhat *pellucid* <note>transparent or translucent</note> body—that is, from some surface of the body opposite to the surface that was nearest the eye.

And because these bodies were so small that I could not easily perform experiments and examinations on them, I provided myself with several small *striae* <note>crystalline rods or growths</note> of crystals or diamonds found in great quantities in *Cornwall*, which are therefore commonly called *Cornish diamonds*. These being very *pellucid* and growing in a hollow cavity of a rock (as I have been several times informed by those who have observed them) much in the same manner as these do in the flint, and having, besides their outward surface, very regular shapes, retaining nearly the same figures as some of those I observed in the other, they became a convenient help to me for the examination of the properties of those kinds of bodies.

And first, regarding the reflections: in these I found it very notable that the brightest reflections of light proceeded from within the *pellucid* body; that is, that the rays admitted through the *pellucid* substance, as they exited on the opposite side, were very vividly reflected by the contiguous and strongly reflecting surface of the air, so that more rays were reflected to the eye by this surface (even though the ray had suffered a double refraction in entering and exiting the crystal) than there were from the outward surface of the glass where the ray had suffered no refraction at all.

And that this was the surface of the Air that gave such a vivid *re-percussion*, I tried by this means: I sank half of a *stiria* in water, so that only water was contiguous to the under surface, and then the internal reflection was so exceedingly faint that it was scarcely discernible. Again, I tried to alter this vivid reflection by keeping off the air with a body that was not fluid, and that was by rubbing and holding my finger very hard against the under surface, so that in many places the pulp of my finger touched the glass without any *interjacent* air between them; then observing the reflection, I found that wherever my finger or skin touched the surface, there was no reflection from that part; but in the little furrows or creases of my skin, where small lines of air remained, a very vivid reflection was returned from them as before. I tried further by making the surface of very pure quicksilver touch the under surface of this *pellucid* body, and then the reflection from that was as much more vivid than from the air as the reflection from air was than the reflection from the water; from all these trials I plainly saw that the strong reflecting air was the cause of this *phenomenon*.

And this agrees very well with the *hypothesis* of light and *pellucid* bodies which I have mentioned in the description of *Muscovy-glass*; for we there suppose glass to be a *medium* which less resists the pulse of light, and consequently, that most of the rays incident on it enter into it and are refracted towards the *perpendicular*; whereas I suppose the air to be a body that resists it more, and consequently more rays are *repercussed* than enter it. I have made the same kind of trials with *crystalline glass*, with drops of fluid bodies, and several other ways, all of which seem to agree very exactly with this *theory*. So, from this well-established principle, we may deduce several corollaries not unworthy of observation.

And the first is, that it clearly appears by this that the production of the Rainbow is as much to be ascribed to the reflection of the concave surface of the air as to the refraction of the *globular* drops. This will be evidently manifest by these experiments: if you *foliate* that part of a glass ball that is to reflect an *iris*, as in the *Cartesian* experiment mentioned above, the reflections will be abundantly stronger and the colors more vivid; and if that part of the surface is touched with water, <note>Likely a printing error for "Water".</note> it scarcely affords any sensible color at all.

Next, we learn that the great reason why pellucid bodies are white when beaten small is because of the multitude of reflections, not from the particles of the body itself, but from the contiguous surface of the air. And this is clearly demonstrated by filling the *intersticia* of those powdered bodies with water, whereby their whiteness immediately disappears. From the same reason proceeds the whiteness of many kinds of sands, which in the *microscope* appear to be made up of a multitude of little *pellucid* bodies, whose brightest reflections can be clearly perceived by the *microscope* to come from their internal surfaces; and much of the whiteness of it can be destroyed by the pouring on of clean water to be contiguous to those surfaces.

The whiteness also of froth is for the most part to be ascribed to the

reflection of the light from the surface of the air within the bubbles, and very little to the reflection from the surface of the water itself: for this latter reflection does not return a quarter as many rays as that which is made from the surface of the air, as I have certainly found through many observations and experiments.

The whiteness of *linen*, *paper*, *silk*, etc., proceeds largely from the same reason, as the *microscope* will easily discover; for the paper is made up of an abundance of *pellucid* bodies, which afford a very plentiful reflection from within—that is, from the concave surface of the air contiguous to its component particles. Therefore, by the application of water, oil, tallow, turpentine, etc., all those reflections are made more faint, and the beams of light are allowed to pass and run through the paper more freely.

Furthermore, from this we may learn the reason for the whiteness of many bodies, and by what means they may be made partially *pellucid*: as white marble, for instance. This body is composed of a *pellucid* substance that is exceedingly flawed—that is, there are an abundance of thin and very fine cracks or chinks among the multitude of particles of the body which contain small parcels of air. These so *reflect* and drive back the penetrating beams that they cannot enter very deep within that body, which the *microscope* plainly informs us is made up of a *collection* of *pellucid* particles. And I further found it somewhat more evidently by some attempts I made toward making transparent marble; for by heating the stone a little and soaking it in oil, turpentine, oil of turpentine, etc., I found that I was able to see much deeper into the body of the marble than before. One trial, which was not with an oily substance, succeeded better than the rest; when I have a better opportunity, I shall make further trials of it.

This also gives us a probable reason for the much-admired *phenomena* of the *Oculus Mundi*, an *oval* stone which commonly looks like white alabaster; but after being laid for a certain time in water, it grows *pellucid* and transparent, and when allowed to lie dry again, it gradually loses that transparency and becomes white as before. For the stone, being of a hollow, spongy nature, has all those pores filled with the dulling and reflecting air in the first and last of these appearances; whereas in the second, all those pores are filled with a *medium* that has much the same refraction as the particles of the stone. Therefore, those two being contiguous make, as it were, one continuous *medium*, of which more is said in *Observation 15*.

There are a multitude of other *phenomena* produced from this same principle, which, as it has not yet been noticed by anyone else that I know of, I think will be found not the least considerable upon more diligent observation. But I only have time here to hint at *hypotheses* and not to prosecute them as fully as I could wish; many of them have a vast extent in the production of a multitude of *phenomena* which have either not been attempted to be explained by others or else attributed to some cause other than what I have assigned, and perhaps other than the right one. Therefore, I shall leave this to the pursuit of those who have more leisure:

Only before I leave it, I must not fail to mention that by this principle, a multitude of the *phenomena* of the air—such as *mists*, *clouds*, *meteors*, *haloes*, etc.—are most plainly and (perhaps) truly explicable; many *phenomena* in colored bodies, such as *liquors*, etc., are also deducible from it.

And from this I shall proceed to a second significant *phenomenon* which these *diamonds* exhibit, and that is the regularity of their *figure*, which is a property no less general than the former; it includes within its scope all kinds of *metals*, all kinds of *minerals*, most *precious stones*, all kinds of *salts*, many *earths*, and almost all kinds of *fluid bodies*. And this is another property which, though noted superficially by some, has not, as far as I know, been even attempted to be explained by anyone.

This property of bodies, as I think it most worthy and next in order to be considered after the contemplation of the *globular figure*, is one I have long desired and intended to pursue if I had the opportunity. I long ago proposed to myself a method for my inquiry into it, as it contains all the attractions that I think any inquiry is capable of: For, first, I consider it to proceed from the simplest principle that any kind of form can come from, next to the *globular*, which was therefore the first I addressed; and what I have accomplished there, I leave the judicious reader to determine. For as that form proceeded from a property of fluid bodies, which I have called *congruity* or *incongruity*, so I think, had I time and opportunity, I could make it probable that all these regular figures that are so conspicuously *various* and *curious*, and which so adorn and beautify such a multitude of bodies as I have hinted at above, arise only from three or four different positions or postures of *globular* particles. These are the most plain, obvious, and necessary conjunctions of such shaped particles that are possible. So, assuming such plain and obvious causes occur together, the coagulating particles must necessarily compose a body of such a determined regular *figure*, and no other; and this with as much necessity and obviousness as a fluid body surrounded by a *heterogeneous* fluid must be pushed into a spherule or globe. And this I have demonstrated *ad oculum* <note>before the eyes; visually</note> with a collection of bullets and a few other very simple bodies; so that there was no regular *figure* which I have hitherto encountered among any of those bodies I named above that I could not imitate with the arrangement of bullets or globules and one or two other bodies, even almost by shaking them together. And thus, for instance, we may find that globular bullets will of themselves—if put on an inclined plane so that they may run together—naturally run into a triangular order, composing all the variety of figures that can be imagined to be made out of *equilateral triangles*. And you will find upon trial that all the surfaces of *alum* are composed of such shapes: For three bullets lying on a plane as close to one another as possible compose an *equilateral-triangular* form, as in A in the *7th scheme*. If a fourth be joined to them on either side as closely as it can be, the four compose the most regular *rhombus*, consisting of two *equilateral triangles*,

If a sixth is added, as before, it either makes an *equilateral triangle*, as D, or a *rhomboid*, as E, or a *hexangular* figure, as F, which is composed of two primary *rhombuses*. If a seventh is added, it makes either an *equilateral hexagonal* figure, as G, or some kind of six-sided *figure*, as H or I. And no matter how many are placed together, they may be arranged into some of these recently mentioned figures, all the angles of which will be either 60 degrees or 120, like figure K, which is an *equiangular hexagonal figure* compounded of 12 *globules*, or it may be of 25, 27, 36, 42, etc. By these kinds of textures, or positions of globular bodies, you may find all the variety of regular shapes into which the smooth surfaces of <term>alum</term> are formed, as anyone may easily find upon examination; nor does it apply only to surfaces, but in solid form also; for it is obvious that a fourth *globule* laid upon three others in this texture composes a regular <term>tetrahedron</term>, which is a very common *figure* of the *crystals* of <term>alum</term>. And (to be brief) there is no single figure into which <term>alum</term> is observed to be crystallized that cannot be imitated by this texture of *globules*, and by no other.

I could also give the example of the figure of <term>sea salt</term> and <term>sal-gem</term> <note>Rock salt.</note>, which is composed of a texture of *globules* placed in a cubical form, as L; and all the figures of those salts may be imitated by this texture of *globules*, and by no other whatsoever. And the forms of <term>vitriol</term> <note>Sulfate minerals.</note> and of <term>saltpeter</term>, as also of <term>crystal</term>, <term>hoar frost</term>, etc., are compounded of these two textures, but modified by certain properties. But I do not have time here to dwell on this, nor to show by what means *globules* come to be thus interconnected, what those *globules* are, and many other particulars required for a full and intelligible explanation of this property of bodies. Nor have I yet found an opportunity to pursue the inquiry as far as I intended; nor do I know when I might, as it requires an abundance of time and a great deal of assistance to complete what I planned, the model of which was this:

First, to obtain as exact and full a collection as I could of all the different kinds of geometrically shaped bodies, with some three or four individual bodies of each kind.

Second, along with them to get as exact a history as I possibly could of their places of origin or discovery, and to inquire after as many circumstances that tended to illustrate this inquiry as I possibly could observe.

Third, to conduct as many trials as I might find necessary based on experience in the dissolving and thickening of several crystallizing salts, for the necessary instruction and information in this inquiry.

Fourth, to perform several trials on various other bodies, such as metals, minerals, and stones, by dissolving them in several <term>menstruums</term> <note>Solvents.</note> and crystallizing them, to see what figures would arise from those several <term>compositums</term> <note>Compounds or mixtures.</note>.

<meta>catchword: Fifthly,</meta>

<summary>Robert Hooke explains how various crystal shapes, such as those of alum and sea salt, result from the geometric arrangement of spherical globules and outlines his four-part plan for a systematic study of mineralogy and crystallization.</summary>
<keywords>Robert Hooke, Micrographia, crystallization, geometry, alum, sea salt, sal-gem, vitriol, saltpeter, tetrahedron, globules, chemistry, minerals</keywords>

Fifthly, to create compositions and coagulations of several salts together into the same mass, to observe what figure would result from them; and in all cases, to note as many circumstances as I should judge conducive to my enquiry.

Sixthly, to investigate the density or rarity of the texture of these bodies by examining their gravity, their refraction, and so on.

Seventhly, to investigate particularly what effects fire has upon several kinds of salts, and what changes it causes in their figures, textures, or properties.

Eighthly, to examine their manner of dissolution, or how they act upon those bodies dissolvable in them; the texture of those bodies before and after the process. And this for the history.

Next, for the solution: to have examined by what and how many means such figures, actions, and effects could possibly be produced.

And lastly, from all circumstances well weighed, I should have endeavored to show which of them was most likely, and (if the information from these enquiries would have borne it) to have demonstrated which of them it must be, and was.

But to proceed: as I believe it to be, next to the globular form, the most simple; so do I, in the second place, judge it no less pleasant. For that which makes an enquiry pleasant is, first, a noble *Inventum* <note>Discovery.</note> that promises to crown a successful endeavor; and such must certainly be the knowledge of the efficient and concurrent causes of all these curious geometrical figures, which has led philosophers until now to conclude that nature plays the geometrician in these things, according to that saying of Plato, 'o Θεὸς γεωμετρεῖ <note>God geometrizes.</note>. Or next, a great variety of matter in the enquiry; and here we meet with nothing less than the mathematics of nature, having every day a new figure to contemplate, or a variation of the same in another body.

These afford us a third thing, which will yet more sweeten the enquiry, and that is, a multitude of information. We do not have to grope in the dark as much as in most other enquiries where the *Inventum* is great; for having such a multitude of instances to compare, and such easy ways of generating, or compounding and of destroying the form—as in the *solution* and *crystallization* of salts—we cannot help but gain plentiful information to proceed by. And this will further appear from the universality of the principle which Nature has used in almost all inanimate bodies. Therefore, as the contemplation of them all leads to the knowledge of any one, so from a scientific knowledge of any one follows <margin>Salts, etc. <br/> p. 43</margin> the same of all and every one.

And fourthly, regarding the usefulness of this knowledge once acquired, certainly no one can doubt it who considers that it carries us a step forward into the labyrinth of Nature, on the right path toward the goal we propose for ourselves in all philosophical enquiries. So, by knowing the form of inanimate or mineral bodies, we shall be better able to proceed in our next enquiry after the forms of vegeta-

## Observ. XIV. Of several kinds of frozen figures.

I have very often in a morning, when there has been a great *hoar-frost*, with a moderately magnifying *microscope*, observed the small *stiriæ* <note>Small icicle-shaped crystals.</note>, or *crystalline* beard, which then usually covers the face of most bodies that lie open to the cold air, and found them to be generally *hexagonal prismatic* bodies, much like the long *crystals* of *saltpeter*, except only that their ends were different: for whereas those of *nitre* are for the most part pyramidal, being terminated either in a point or edge; these of *frost* were hollow, and the cavity in some seemed pretty deep, and this cavity was the more plainly to be seen because usually one or other of the six *parallelogram* sides was wanting, or at least much shorter than the rest.

But this was only the figure of the bearded *hoar-frost*; and as for the particles of other kinds of *hoar-frosts*, they seemed for the most part irregular, or of no certain figure. Indeed, the parts of those curious branchings, or *vortices*, that usually in cold weather tarnish the surface of glass, appear through the *microscope* very crude and unshapen, as do most other kinds of frozen *figures*, which to the naked eye seem exceedingly neat and curious, such as the figures of *snow*, frozen *urine*, *hail*, several *figures* frozen in common water, etc. Some observations of each of which I shall annex hereunto, because if well considered and examined, they may, perhaps, prove very instructive for finding out what I have endeavored in the preceding observation to show: to be (next to the globular figure which is caused by congruity, as I hope I have made probable in the sixth *observation*) the most simple and plain operation of nature, of which, notwithstanding, we are yet ignorant.

3 None of all these figures I have yet taken notice of had any regular position in respect of one another, or of the sides of the vessel; nor did I find any of them extended with exactness in every direction from the center *a*.

4 Wherever there was a center, the branches from it—*ab*, *ac*, *ad*, *ae*, *af*, *ag*—were never fewer or more than six. These usually converged or met one another very near the same point or center, *a*, though often not exactly. They were inclined toward each other by an angle of very near sixty degrees. I say "very near" because, although I endeavored to measure them as accurately as I was able with the largest compasses I had and could not find any noticeable variation from that measurement, yet because the whole six-branched figure seems to compose a solid angle, they must necessarily be somewhat less.

5 The middle lines or stems of these branches—*ab*, *ac*, *ad*, *ae*, *af*, *ag*—seemed somewhat whiter and a little higher than any of the *intermediate* branchings of these figures. The center, *a*, was the most *prominent* part of the whole figure, appearing to be the *apex* of a solid angle or *pyramid*, with each of the six planes being slightly inclined below the surface of the *urine* <note>Hooke is likely observing frozen urine or a similar solute-heavy liquid, as mentioned in his broader study of crystallization.</note>.

6 The lateral branchings issuing out of the large ones, such as *op*, *nq*, etc., were each inclined toward the large ones by the same angle of about sixty degrees, just as the large ones were to one another. Always the larger branches were *prominent* above the smaller, and the smaller above the smallest, by proportionate gradations.

7 The *lateral* branches shooting out of the large ones all grew away from the center, and each of them was parallel to the large branch next to which it lay. Thus, just as all the branches on one *side* were parallel to one another, they were also all parallel to the *nearby* large branch; for example, as *po* and *qr* were parallel to each other and grew from the center, they were also parallel to the large branch *ab*.

8 Some of the stems of the six branches proceeded straight and had a thickness that gradually grew sharper towards the end, as in *ag*.

9 Others of the stems of those branches grew larger and knotty toward the middle, and the branches as well as stems grew from cylinders into plates in a most admirable and curious order—so exceedingly regular and delicate that nothing could be more so, as is visible in *ab*, *ac*, *ad*, *ae*, and *af*. However, toward the end of some of these stems, they began again to grow smaller and to recover their former branching shapes, as seen around *k* and *n*.

10 Many of the *lateral* branches had collateral branches (if I may call them that), such as *qm* having many like *st*. Most of those, in turn, had *sub-collateral* branches, like *vw*, and these again had other smaller ones, which one might call *latero-subcollateral*; these had others, and those yet others, etc., in larger figures.

11 The branchings of the main stems did not join together along any regular line, nor did one side of one lie over the side of another, but the small collateral and sub-collateral branches did lie at the top of one

12 That side of a *collateral* or *sub-collateral*, etc. branch, lay over the side of the *adjacent* one (like the feathers in the wing of a bird) whose branchings proceeded parallel to the last largest stem from which it grew, and not to the main stem of all, unless that happened to be a second stem back.

13 This rule that applied to the branchings of the *Sexangular Figure* also applied to the branchings of any other large or small stem, even if it did not originate from a center.

14 The exactness and intricacy of the shape of these branches was so remarkable in every detail that I judge it almost impossible for human art to imitate.

15 Tasting several clear pieces of this *ice*, I could not find any *urinous* taste in them; those few I tasted seemed as tasteless as water.

16 I have several times observed a formation somewhat like this, though indeed much more intricate in some details, in *regulus martis stellatus* <note>A star-shaped crystalline structure of antimony, often produced by smelting it with iron.</note>, but with this difference: all the stems and branches are curved in a most excellent and regular order, whereas in *ice* the stems and branches are straight. In all other details it agrees with this, and indeed seems to be nothing but one of these stars or branched figures frozen on *urine*, distorted or twisted a little in a certain proportion. I have also found that *lead* mixed with *arsenic* and certain other things has its surface, when allowed to cool, shaped somewhat like the branches of *urine*, but much smaller.

17 But there is a *plant* which very closely imitates these branches, and that is the *fern*, where the main stem can be observed to shoot out branches, and the stems of each of these *lateral* branches send forth *collateral* ones, and those *sub-collateral*, and those *latero-sub-collateral*, and so on. All of these follow much the same order as the branchings, divisions, and subdivisions in the branches of these figures in frozen *urine*. Thus, if the shapes of both are well considered, one would guess that there was no greater need for a *seminal principle* <note>A biological "seed" or formative soul believed at the time to guide the growth and form of living things.</note> to produce a *fern* than to produce the branches of *urine* or the *stella martis* <note>Another name for the star-shaped crystalline antimony mentioned above.</note>. There seems to be as much form and beauty in the one as in the other.

And indeed, this plant, the *fern*, if all details are well considered, will seem to have as simple and uncompounded a form as any *plant*, second only to *mold* or *mushrooms*. After the forms of those are understood, it would deserve to be investigated next. For although several have claimed that it has seeds and is propagated by them, yet, though I have made a very diligent inquiry into that detail, I cannot find any part of it that can be imagined to be more seminal than another. But this is only mentioned here in passing.

To create these freezing figures in *urine*, I found it necessary:

First, that the surface not be disturbed by any wind, or other commotion of the air, or the like.

Secondly,

## II.
### Observations in figured snow.

<margin>Scheme 8. Fig. 2.</margin>
By exposing a piece of black cloth or a black hat to the falling *snow*, I have often, with great pleasure, observed such an infinite variety of intricately figured *snow* that it would be as impossible to draw the figure and shape of every one of them as to imitate exactly the intricate and geometrical *mechanism* of nature in any one. Some coarse drawings—such as the coldness of the weather and the poor materials I had on hand for such a purpose would permit me to make—I have added here in the second figure of the eighth scheme.

In all of these, I observed that if they had any regular figures, they were always branched out with six principal branches, all of equal length, shape, and make, from the center; each of them was inclined to the next branch on either side by an angle of sixty degrees.

Now, just as all these stems within one flake were for the most part exactly of the same make, so they were of very different makes in different figures; so that in a very short time, I have observed over a hundred different sizes and shapes of these starry flakes.

The branches stemming from each main stem of any one of these flakes were also exactly alike in the same flake. Thus, whatever the figure of one branch, the other five were certain to be exactly the same; that is, if the branchings of one were small *parallelepipeds* or *plates*, the branchings of the other five were the same. Generally, the branchings were very conformable to the rules and method observed before in the figures on *urine*; that is, the branchings from each side of the stems were parallel to the next stem on that side, and if the stems were plated, the branches also were the same; if the stems were very long, the branches also were so, etc.

Observing some of these figured flakes with a *microscope*, I found that they did not appear as intricate and exactly figured as one would have imagined, but like artificial figures; the more they were magnified, the more irregularities appeared in them. However, this irregularity seemed attributable to the thawing and breaking of the flake by the fall, and not at all to a defect in the formative power of nature, whose intricacy in the formation of most of these kinds of regular figures—such as those of *salt*, *minerals*, etc.—

For since I have observed the figures of *salts* and *minerals* to be some of them so exceedingly small that I have scarcely been able to perceive them with the *microscope*, and yet they have been regular; and since (as far as I have yet examined it) there seems to be but one and the same cause that produces both these effects, I think it not irrational to suppose that these pretty figured stars of *snow*, when first generated, might also be very regular and exact.

### III.

### *Several kinds of figures in frozen water.*

Putting clear water into a large, capacious vessel of *glass*, and exposing it to the cold, I observed after a little time several broad, flat, and thin *laminae*, or plates of *ice*, crossing the bulk of the water and one another very irregularly; only most of them seemed to turn one of their edges toward that side of the *glass* which was next to it, and seemed to grow, as it were, from the inside of the vessel inward toward the middle, almost like so many blades of *fern*. Having taken several of these plates out of the water on the blade of a *knife*, I observed them figured much after the manner of *herring bones* or *fern blades*; that is, there was one larger stem in the middle like the backbone, and out of it, on either side, were a multitude of small *striae* <note>small needle-like projections or icicles</note>, like the smaller bones or the smaller branches in *fern*. Each of these branches on one side was parallel to all the rest on the same side, and all of them seemed to make an angle with the stem, toward the top, of sixty degrees, and toward the bottom or root of this stem, of 120 degrees. See the fourth *figure* of the 8th *plate*.

I likewise observed several very pretty varieties of figures in water frozen on the top of a broad, flat marble stone, exposed to the cold with a little water on it: some like feathers, some of other shapes; many of them were very much like the shape expressed in the fifth figure of the 8th *scheme*, which is extremely different from any of the other figures.

I likewise observed that the shootings of *ice* on the top of water, beginning to freeze, were in straight *prismatical* bodies much like those of *roch-peter* <note>saltpeter or nitre</note>; that they crossed each other usually without any kind of order or rule; that they were always a little higher than the surface of the water that lay between them; and that by degrees those *interjacent* [lying between] spaces would be filled with *ice* also, which usually would be as high as the surface of the rest.

But indeed (which I also hinted at there) I judge it the second step by which the *Pyramid* of natural knowledge (which is the knowledge of the *form of bodies*) is to be ascended: And whoever will climb it, must be well furnished with that which the Noble *Verulam* <note>Francis Bacon, Lord Verulam</note> calls *Scalam Intellectûs* <note>The ladder of the intellect</note>; he must have scaling ladders, otherwise the steps are so large and high, there will be no getting up them, and consequently little hope of attaining any higher station, such as to the knowledge of the most simple principle of Vegetation manifested in Mould and Mushrooms, which, as I elsewhere endeavored to show, seems to be the third step; for it seems to me, that the intellect of man is like his body, destitute of wings, and cannot move from a lower to a higher and more sublime station of knowledge, otherwise than step by step, nay, even there where the way is prepared and already made passable; as in the *Elements of Geometry*, or the like, where it is obliged to climb a whole *series* of *Propositions* by degrees, before it attains the knowledge of one *Problem*. But if the ascent be high, difficult, and above its reach, it must have recourse to a *novum organum* <note>a new instrument or method</note>, some new engine and contrivance, some new kind of *Algebra*, or *Analytic Art* before it can surmount it.

## Observation XV. *Of Kettering-stone, and of the pores of Inanimate bodies.*

<margin>Scheme 9. Figure 1.</margin>
This Stone which is brought from *Kettering* in *Northamptonshire*, and dug out of a Quarry, as I am informed, has a grain altogether admirable, nor have I ever seen or heard of any other stone that has the like. It is made up of an innumerable company of small bodies, not all of the same size or shape, but for the most part, not much differing from a globular form, nor do they exceed one another in diameter above three or four times; they appear to the eye like the roe or ovary of a *herring*, or some smaller fishes, but for the most part, the particles seem somewhat smaller, and not so uniform; but their variation from a perfect globular ball seems to be only by the pressure of the contiguous balls which have a little depressed and protruded those touched sides inward, and forced

Where these grains touch each other, they are so firmly united or settled together that they seldom part without breaking a hole in one or the other of them, such as *a, a, a, b, c, c,* etc. Some of which fractures, as *a, a, a, a,* where the contact has been only light, break no more than the outward crust, or first shell of the stone, which is of a white color, a little dashed with a brownish yellow, and is very thin, like the shell of an egg: and I have seen some of those grains perfectly resemble some kind of eggs, both in color and shape: But where the union of the contiguous granules has been more firm, there the separation has made a greater chasm, as at *b, b, b,* so much so that I have observed some of them quite broken in two, as at *c, c, c,* which has discovered to me a further resemblance they have to eggs, they having an appearance of a white and yolk, by two differing substances that envelope and encompass each other.

That which we may call the white was pretty whitish near the yolk, but more dusky towards the shell; some of them I could plainly perceive to be shot or radiated like a *pyrite* or *fire-stone*; the yolk in some I saw hollow, in others filled with a dusky brown and porous substance like a kind of pith.

The small pores, or *interstices e e e e* between the globules, I plainly saw, and found by other trials to be every way pervious to air and water, for I could blow through a piece of this stone of a considerable thickness as easily as I have blown through a cane, which reminded me of the pores which *Descartes* allows his *materia subtilis* <note>The "subtle matter" or ether in Cartesian physics</note> between the ethereal globules.

<margin><insert>Not such tumblings at the bottom of the sea; a mere conceit.</insert></margin>
The object, through the *microscope*, appears like a *congeries* or heap of pebbles, such as I have often seen cast up on the shore by the working of the sea after a great storm, or like (in shape, though not color) a company of small globules of quicksilver looked on with a *microscope*, when reduced into that form by the way lately mentioned. And perhaps this last may give some hint at the manner of the formation of the former: For supposing some *lapidescent* <note>Stone-forming</note> substance to be generated, or some way brought (either by some mixture of bodies in the sea itself, or protruded in, perhaps, out of some *subterraneous* caverns) to the bottom of the sea, and there remaining in the form of a liquor like quicksilver, *heterogeneous* to the surrounding *saline* fluid, it may by the working and tumblings of the sea to and fro be jumbled and broken down into such globules as may afterwards be hardened into flints, the lying of which one upon another, when in the sea, being not very hard, by reason of the weight of the encompassing fluid, may cause the undermost to be a little, though not much, varied from a globular figure. But this only by the by.

# M I C R O G R A P H I A.

I cannot learn in what manner this Kettering stone might be generated, having never been there to view the place and observe the circumstances; but it seems to me from its structure to be generated from some substance that was once more fluid, and afterwards by degrees grew harder, in almost the same manner as I supposed the generation of flints to be made.

But whatever was the cause of its curious texture, we may learn this information from it: that even in those things which we account vile, rude, and coarse, Nature has not failed to show an abundance of curiosity and excellent mechanism.

We may here find a stone, by help of a *microscope*, to be made up of an abundance of small balls which only just touch each other; and yet, there being so many points of contact, they make a firm hard mass, or a stone much harder than freestone.

Next, though we can discern such a curious shape in the particles by a *microscope*, yet to the naked eye there scarcely appears any such thing. This may afford us a good argument to think that even in those bodies whose texture we are not able to discern, though helped with *microscopes*, there may yet be latent such a curious <term>schematism</term> that it might abundantly satisfy the curious searcher who shall be so happy as to find some way to discover it.

Next, we here find a stone that is a very solid one to the naked eye, yet it is every way perforated with innumerable pores, which are nothing else but the <term>interstitia</term> between those multitudes of minute globular particles that compose the bulk itself; and these pores are discovered not only by the *microscope*, but by this contrivance:

I took a fairly large piece of this stone and, covering it all over with cement except only at two opposite parts, I found myself able, by blowing in at one end that was left open, to blow my saliva (with which I had wet the other end) into an abundance of bubbles. This proved these pores to be open and pervious through the whole stone, which affords us a very fine instance of the porousness of some seemingly solid bodies, of which kind I shall soon have occasion to add many more, tending to prove the same thing.

I must not here omit to take notice that in this body there is not a <term>vegetative faculty</term> that should so design this structure for any peculiar use of vegetation or growth; whereas in the other instances of vegetable porous bodies, there is an <term>anima</term>, or <term>forma informans</term>, that designs all the structures and mechanisms of the constituting body to make them subservient and useful to the great work or function they are to perform. And so I guess the pores in wood and other vegetables, in bones, and other animal substances, to be like so many channels provided by the Great and All-wise Creator for the conveyance of specific juices to particular parts. Therefore, these may lead or be pervious all towards one part, and may have impediments, such as valves or the like, to any other; but in this body we have very little reason to suspect there should be any such design, for it is equally pervious every way, not only forward,

And, according as these pores are more numerous or larger in respect to the *interstitial* bodies, the more transparent are the so-constituted *concretes*; and the smaller those pores are, the weaker is the *impulse* of light communicated through them, though the more quick its progress.

Upon this occasion, I hope it will not be altogether unseasonable if I propose my conjectures and *hypothesis* about the *medium* and conveyance of light.

I suppose then that the greatest part of the *interstitia* of the world, which lies between the bodies of the sun, stars, planets, and the Earth, is an exceedingly fluid body, very apt and ready to be moved, and to communicate the motion of any one part to any other part, no matter how far distant. Nor do I concern myself much with determining what the shape of the particles of this exceedingly subtle fluid *medium* must be, nor whether it has any interstitial pores or vacancies, it being sufficient to solve all the *phenomena* to suppose it an exceedingly fluid—or the most fluid—body in the world, as it is yet impossible to determine the other difficulties.

Being such an exceedingly fluid body, it easily allows all other bodies to move to and fro within it.

That it neither receives from any of its parts, or from other bodies, nor communicates to any of its parts, or to any other body, any impulse or motion in a direct line that is not of a determinate quickness. And that when the motion is of such determinate swiftness, it both receives and communicates or propagates an impulse or motion to any imaginable distance in straight lines, with an unimaginable celerity and vigor.

That all kinds of solid bodies consist of fairly massive particles in respect to the particles of this fluid *medium*, which in many places touch each other so that none of this fluid *medium* interposes much—in the same manner (to use a gross comparison) as a heap of large stones forms one large mass in the midst of the water.

That all fluid bodies which we may call *tangible* are nothing but some more subtle parts of those particles that serve to constitute all *tangible* bodies.

That water and such other fluid bodies are nothing but a congeries of particles agitated or made fluid by it in the same manner as the particles of *salt* are agitated or made fluid by a portion of water in which they are dissolved; and, subsiding to the bottom of it, they constitute a fluid body much more massive and dense, and less fluid than the pure water itself.

That the air, on the other hand, is a certain collection of particles of quite another kind—that is, such as are very *much smaller* and more easily moved by the motion of this fluid *medium*; much like those very subtle parts of *cochineal*, and other very deep-dyeing bodies, where by a very

Further, as these solutions and tinctures do alter the nature of these fluid bodies regarding their ability to propagate a motion or impulse through them, even so do the particles of the Air, Water, and other fluid bodies, and of Glass, Crystal, *etc.* which are mixed with this bulk of the Ether, alter the motion of the propagated pulse of light; that is, where these more bulky particles are more plentiful, and consequently a smaller quantity of the Ether between them to be moved, there the motion must necessarily be the swifter, though not so robust, which will produce those effects which I have (I hope) with some probability ascribed to it in the digression about Colors at the end of the *Observations* on *Muscovy-glass*.

Now, that other stones, and those which have the closest and hardest textures and seem (as far as we are able to discover with our eyes, even when helped with the best *Microscopes*) freest from pores, are nonetheless filled with them, an instance or two will, I suppose, make more probable.

A very solid and flawless piece of clear white *Marble*, if it is well polished and glazed, has so remarkably smooth a surface that the best and most polished surface of any worked glass does not seem to the naked eye, nor through a *Microscope*, to be smoother or less porous. And yet, that this hard, close body is filled with an abundance of pores, I think these following experiments will sufficiently prove.

The first is that if you take such a piece and boil it for a good while in turpentine and oil of turpentine, you shall find that the stone will be all imbued with it. Whereas before it looked more white but more opaque, now it will look more greasy but be much more transparent; and if you let it sit for just a little while and then break off a part of it, you shall find the oily substance to have penetrated it to a specific depth every way within the surface. This may be even more easily tried with a piece of the same *Marble*, warmed a little in the fire, and then having a little pitch or tar melted on the top of it; for these black bodies, by working their way into the invisible pores of the stone, tinge it with such a black hue that there can be no further doubt of the truth of this assertion: that it abounds with small, imperceptible pores.

Nor is Marble the only seemingly dense stone which, by other kinds of experiments, may be found porous; for I have, by this kind of experiment on various other stones, found much the same effect—and in some, indeed, much more notable. I have found other stones so porous that with the *Microscope* I could perceive several small winding holes, much like worm-holes, as I have noted in some kinds of *Purbeck stone* by looking on the surface of a piece newly chipped off; for if, otherwise, the surface has been long exposed to the air or has been scraped with any tool, those small cavities are filled with dust and disappear.

A small stone of the kind called by some authors *Oculus Mundi*, being dry and cloudy, weighed 5 <sup>209</sup>/<sub>256</sub> *grains*.

The same, put under water for a night and somewhat more, became transparent; and the surface being wiped dry, it weighed 6 <sup>3</sup>/<sub>256</sub> *grains*.

The difference between these two weights: 0 <sup>50</sup>/<sub>256</sub> of a *grain*.

The same stone, kept out of water for one day and becoming cloudy again, weighed 5 <sup>225</sup>/<sub>256</sub> *grains*.

Which was more than the first weight by 0 <sup>16</sup>/<sub>256</sub> of a *grain*.

The same, being kept two days longer, weighed 5 <sup>202</sup>/<sub>256</sub> *grains*.

Which was less than at first by 0 <sup>7</sup>/<sub>256</sub> of a *grain*.

Being kept dry somewhat longer, it did not grow noticeably lighter.

Being put under water for a night and becoming again transparent and wiped dry, the weight was 6 <sup>3</sup>/<sub>256</sub> *grains*—the same as the first time after being put in water—and 0 <sup>57</sup>/<sub>256</sub> of a *grain* more than the last weight after keeping it dry.

Bodies which we think are the most solid ones, and appear so to our sight, nevertheless have an abundance of those larger kinds of pores which will admit several kinds of liquids into them. Why should we not believe that glass, and all other transparent bodies, abound with them as well, since we have many other arguments, besides the propagation of light, which seem to argue for it?

And whereas it may be objected that the propagation of light is no argument that there are those minute pores in glass, since there are *hypotheses* plausible enough to solve those *phenomena* by supposing the pulse only to be communicated through the transparent body.

To this I answer, that the *hypothesis* which the industrious *Moreanus* <note>Likely referring to a contemporary optical theorist; Hooke often engaged with the theories of Marin Mersenne or similar scholars regarding the speed of light.</note> has published—about the slower motion of the end of a ray in a denser *medium* than in a more rare and thin one—seems altogether insufficient to solve an abundance of *phenomena*. Of these, it is not the least significant that it is impossible, based on that supposition, for any colors to be generated from the refraction of the rays. For since by that *hypothesis* the undulating pulse is always carried perpendicular, or at right angles, to the ray or line of direction, it follows that the stroke of the pulse of light, after it has been once or twice refracted (through a prism, for example), must affect the eye with the same kind of stroke as if it had not been refracted at all. Nor will it be enough for a defender of that *hypothesis* to say that perhaps it is because the refractions have made the rays weaker; for if so, then two refractions in the two parallel sides of a *quadrangular prism* would produce colors, but we have no such *phenomena* produced.

There are several arguments that I could bring to prove that there are such minute pores in all transparent bodies, and that there is such a fluid body as I am arguing for, which is the *medium*, or instrument, by which the pulse of light is conveyed from the luminous body to the illuminated one. But as that would be a digression from the observations I was recording about the pores of *Kettering Stone*, it would be excessive if I should prolong it too long; and therefore I shall proceed to the next *observation*.

### Observation XVI. Of Charcoal, or Burnt Vegetables.

Charcoal, or a vegetable burnt black, affords an object no less pleasant than instructive; for if you take a small round piece of charcoal and snap it with your fingers, you may perceive it to break with a very smooth and sleek surface, almost like the surface of black sealing wax. This surface, if it is looked at with an ordinary *microscope*, reveals an abundance of those pores which are also visible to the eye in many kinds of wood, arranged around the pith, both in a kind of circular order and a radiating one. There are a multitude of these in the substance of the coal, almost everywhere perforating and drilling it from end to end; by

But this is not all, for besides those many great and conspicuous irregular spots or pores, if a better *microscope* is used, there will appear an infinite company of exceedingly small and very regular pores. They are so thick, so orderly set, and so close to one another that they leave very little room or space between them to be filled with a solid body; for the apparent *interstitia*, or separating sides of these pores, seem so thin in some places that the texture of a honeycomb cannot be more porous. Though this is not so everywhere, the intercurrent partitions in some places being much thicker in proportion to the holes.

Most of these small pores seemed to be quite round and were arranged in rows that radiated from the pith to the bark; they all seemed to be continuous open pores running the whole length of the stick. I tested that they were all perforated by breaking off a very thin sliver of the coal crossways and then, with my *microscope*, diligently surveying them against the light; for by that means, I was able to see quite through them.

<margin>1/18</margin>
These pores were so exceedingly small and thick that in a line of them, 1/18th of an inch long, I found by numbering them no less than 150 small pores; and therefore, in a line of them an inch long, there must be no less than 2,700 pores, and in a circular *area* of an inch diameter, there must be about 5,725,350 such pores. So, a stick an inch in diameter may contain no less than five million, seven hundred and twenty-five thousand pores; which would, I doubt not, seem even incredible, were not everyone left to believe his own eyes. Indeed, having since examined *Cocus*, black and green *ebony*, *Lignum Vitae*, etc., I found that all these woods have pores abundantly smaller than those of soft, light wood; so much so that those of *Guajacum* seemed not above an eighth part of the size of the pores of beech, but then the *interstitia* were thicker. So prodigiously curious are the contrivances, pipes, or sluices by which the *Succus nutritius* <note>The "nutritive juice" or sap of the plant.</note>, or juice of a vegetable, is conveyed from place to place.

This observation seems to afford us the true reason for several *phenomena* of coals; such as:

First, why they look black; and for this we need go no further than the *scheme* <note>Referring to the diagram or illustration in the original plate.</note>, for certainly, a body that has so many pores in it as this is discovered to have—from each of which no light is reflected—must necessarily look black. This is especially true when the pores are somewhat larger in proportion to the intervals than they are drawn in the *scheme*. Black is nothing else but a privation of light, or a lack of reflection; and wherever this reflecting quality is deficient, that part looks black, whether it is from the porousness of the body, as in this instance, or from a deadening and dulling quality, such as I have observed in the *scoria* <note>The dross or slag of metal.</note> of lead, tin, silver, copper, etc.

Next, we may also as plainly see the reason for its shining quality, and

That is, from the clean breaking off of the stick, the solid *interstitia* having a regular surface and a fairly strong reflecting quality, many small reflections become united to the naked eye and create a very attractive shining surface.

Thirdly, the reason for its hardness and brittleness seems evident; for since all the watery or liquid substances that moistened and toughened those *interstitia* of the more solid parts are evaporated and removed, what is left behind becomes almost like a stone, which will not bend at all, or very little, without a *divulsion* <note>a pulling apart</note> or *solution* of its *continuity* <note>a breaking of its continuous structure</note>.

It is not my design at present to examine the use and *mechanism* of these parts of wood, as that is more proper for another inquiry; but rather to suggest that from this experiment we may learn:

First, the cause of the blackness of many burnt bodies, which we may find to be nothing else but this: that the heat of the fire, agitating and rarefying the watery, transparent, and volatile liquid that is contained in them, through the continuation of that action, so totally expels and drives away everything that previously filled the pores and was also dispersed through the solid mass of it. This action, which caused a universal kind of transparency, not only leaves all the pores empty but also leaves all the *interstitia* so dry and opaque—and perhaps even further perforated—that only the light which falls upon the very outer edges of the pores is reflected back. All those rays that enter into the pores of the body never return but are lost within it.

Now, that the charring or coaling of a body is nothing else may be easily believed by anyone who considers the means of its production, which may be done in this or any similar manner. The body to be charred or coaled may be put into a crucible, pot, or any other vessel that can endure being made red-hot in the fire without breaking, and then covered over with sand so that no part of it is allowed to be open to the air. It is then placed in a good fire and kept there until the sand has remained red-hot for a quarter, half, an hour, two, or more, according to the nature and size of the body to be coaled or charred. Then, taking it out of the fire and letting it stand until it is quite cold, the body may be taken out of the sand, well charred and cleansed of its watery parts. However, in taking it out, care must be taken that the sand is very near cold; otherwise, when it comes into the free air, it will catch fire and readily burn away.

This may also be done in any closed glass vessel, such as a *retort* or similar container, and the various fluid substances that come over may be received in a suitable *recipient*, which will further support this *hypothesis*. Their manner of charring wood in great quantities amounts to much the same thing: namely, an application of great heat to the body and protecting it from the free access of the devouring air. This can be easily learned from the history of charring coal, most excellently described and published by that most accomplished gentleman, *Mr. John Evelyn*, on pages 100, 101, and 103 of his *Sylva*, to which I shall therefore refer the curious reader who desires full information on the subject.
