M I C R O G R A P H I A.

Next, we may learn what part of the wood is the *combustible matter*; for since we find that none, or very little, of those fluid substances driven over into the receiver are *combustible*, and that most of what is left behind is, it follows that the solid *interstitia* of the wood are the *combustible matter*. Further, the reason why uncharred wood burns with a greater flame than that which is charred is just as evident: because those watery or volatile parts issuing out of the fired wood in every direction not only shatter and open the body, making it easier for the fire to enter, but issuing out in vapors or wind, they become like so many little *aeolipiles*, or bellows, by which they blow and agitate the fired part, and contribute to the more speedy and violent consumption or dissolution of the body.

Thirdly, from the experiment of charring coals (whereby we see that notwithstanding the great heat and its duration, the solid parts of the wood remain as long as they are preserved from the free access of air without being dissipated), we may learn something which has not, that I know of, been published or hinted at—no, not so much as thought of by anyone; and that in short is this:

First, *that the air in which we live, move, and breathe, and which encompasses very many and cherishes most bodies it encompasses, is the <term>menstruum</term> <note>a solvent</note>, or universal dissolvent of all sulfurous bodies.*

Secondly, *that it does not perform this action until the body is first sufficiently heated, as we find is also necessary for the dissolution of many other bodies by various other menstruums.*

Thirdly, *that this action of dissolution produces or generates a very great heat, and that which we call fire; and this is common also to many dissolutions of other bodies made by menstruums, of which I could give multitudes of instances.*

Fourthly, *that this action is performed with such great violence, and acts so minutely and rapidly agitates the smallest parts of the combustible matter, that it produces in the transparent medium of the air the action or pulse of light, the nature of which I have already shown elsewhere.*

Fifthly, *that the dissolution of sulfurous bodies is made by a substance inherent in and mixed with the air, which is like, if not the very same, as that which is fixed in saltpeter; this, I think, will be most clearly demonstrated by the many experiments that can be made with saltpeter.*

Sixthly, *that in this dissolution of bodies by the air, a certain part is united and mixed, or dissolved and turned into the air, and made to fly up and down with it in the same manner as a metallic or other body dissolved in any menstruum follows the motions and progress of that menstruum until it is precipitated.*

Seventhly, that just as there is one part that is dissolvable by the air, so there are other parts with which the parts of the air, mixing and uniting, create a *coagulum* <note>a thickened or clotted mass</note>, or precipitation, as one might call it, which causes it to be separated from the air. But this precipitate is so light, and in such small and rarefied or porous clusters, that it is very volatile and is easily carried up by the motion of the air, though afterwards, when the heat and agitation

<summary>Hooke proposes a revolutionary theory of combustion, arguing that air contains a specific substance—similar to that in saltpeter—which acts as a universal solvent for heated sulfurous materials, creating fire and light. He explains that flame is caused by volatile parts of wood acting like tiny bellows to accelerate this dissolution process.</summary>

Eighthly, that many indissoluble parts being very apt and ready to be rarefied, and so, while they continue in that heat and agitation, are lighter than the ambient air, they are thereby thrust and carried upwards with great violence. By that means, they carry along with them not only that *saline concrete* <note>a solid mass of particles</note> I mentioned before, but many terrestrial, or indissoluble and irrarefiable parts—indeed, many parts also which are dissolvable but are not allowed to stay long enough in a sufficient heat to make them ready and apt for that action. And therefore we find in *soot* not only a part that, being continued longer in a competent heat, will be dissolved by the air or take fire and burn, but also a part which is fixed, terrestrial, and irrarefiable.

Ninthly, that as there are these several parts that will rarefy and fly, or be driven up by the heat, so are there many others that, as they are indissoluble by the *aerial menstruum* <note>the air acting as a solvent</note>, so are they of such sluggish and gross parts that they are not easily rarefied by heat, and therefore cannot be raised by it. The volatility or fixity of a body seems to consist only in this: that one has a texture, or component parts, that will be easily rarefied into the form of air, and the other has such as will not, without much effort, be brought to such a condition. And this is that part which remains behind in a white body called *ashes*, which contains a substance, or *salt*, which chemists call *alkali*. What the particular natures of each of these bodies are, I shall not examine here, intending to do so in another place; but I shall rather add that this *hypothesis* does so exactly agree with all *phenomena* of fire, and so naturally explains each particular circumstance that I have hitherto observed, that it is more than probable that this cause which I have assigned is the true, adequate, real, and only cause of those *phenomena*. And therefore I shall proceed a little further to show the nature and use of the air.

Tenthly, therefore the dissolving parts of the air are but few; that is, it seems to be of the nature of those saline <term>menstruums</term>, or spirits, that have very much phlegm <note>inert or watery dilution</note> mixed with the spirits, and therefore a small parcel of it is quickly saturated and will dissolve no more. And therefore, unless some fresh part of this *menstruum* be applied to the body to be dissolved, the action ceases, and the body stops being dissolved and stops shining (which is the *indication* of it), even if placed or kept in the greatest heat. Whereas *salt-peter* is a *menstruum* which, when melted and red-hot, abounds more with those dissolving particles; and therefore, as a small quantity of it will dissolve a great sulfurous body, so will the dissolution be very quick and violent.

Therefore in the *eleventh* place, it is observable that, as in other solutions, if a copious and quick supply of fresh *menstruum*, though but weak, be poured on or applied to the dissolvable body, it quickly consumes it. So this *menstruum* of the air, if by bellows or any other such contrivance it be copiously applied to the shining body, is found to

Therefore twelfthly, it seems reasonable to think that there is no such thing as an Element of Fire that should attract or draw up the flame, or towards which the flame should endeavor to ascend out of a desire or appetite of uniting with that as its *Homogeneal* <note>of the same kind</note> primitive and generating Element; but that that shining transient body which we call *Flame*, is nothing else but a mixture of *Air*, and volatile sulfurous parts of dissolvable or combustible bodies, which are acting upon each other while they ascend. That is, flame seems to be a mixture of *Air* and the combustible volatile parts of any body, which parts the encompassing *Air* does dissolve or work upon; this action, as it increases the heat of the *aerial* parts of the dissolvent, so does it thereby further rarefy those parts that are acting, or that are very near them, whereby they, growing much lighter than the heavy parts of that *Menstruum* that are more remote, are thereby protruded and driven upward; and this may be easily observed also in dissolutions made by any other *menstruum*, especially such as either create heat or bubbles. Now, this action of the *Menstruum*, or *Air*, on the dissolvable parts, is made with such violence, or is such, that it imparts such a motion or pulse to the *diaphanous* <note>transparent</note> parts of the Air, as I have elsewhere shown is requisite to produce light.

This *Hypothesis* I have endeavored to raise from an infinite number of Observations and Experiments, the process of which would be much too long to be here inserted, and will perhaps another time afford matter copious enough for a much larger Discourse. The Air is a Subject which (though all the world has hitherto lived and breathed in it, and been familiar with it) has yet been so little truly examined or explained, that a diligent inquirer will be able to find but very little information from what has been (until lately) written of it: But being once well understood, it will, I doubt not, enable a man to render an intelligible, nay probable, if not the true reason of all the *Phenomena* of Fire. As fire has been found by Writers and Philosophers of all Ages to be a matter of no small difficulty—as may be sufficiently understood by their strange *Hypotheses*, and unintelligible Solutions of some few *Phenomena* of it—so will it prove a matter of no small concern and use in human affairs, as I shall elsewhere endeavor to manifest when I come to show the use of the Air in *respiration*, and for the preservation of the life, nay, for the conservation and restoration of the health and natural constitution of mankind as well as all other *aerial* animals, as also the uses of this principle or property of the Air in chemical, mechanical, and other operations. In this place I have only time to hint a *Hypothesis*, which, if God permit me life and opportunity, I may elsewhere prosecute, improve and publish. In the mean time, before I finish this Discourse, I must not forget to acquaint the Reader, that having had the liberty granted me of making some trials on a piece of *Lignum fossile* <note>fossilized wood</note> shown to the *Royal Society*, by the eminently Ingenious and Learned Physician, *Doctor Ent*, who received it as a Present from the famous *Ingenioso Cavalliero de Pozzi*, it being one of the fairest

and the best pieces of *Lignum fossile* <note>fossil wood</note> he had seen; Having (I say) taken a small piece of this wood and examined it, I found it to burn in the open air almost like other wood. Instead of a resinous smoke or fume, it yielded a very bituminous one, smelling much of that kind of scent. But that which I chiefly took notice of was that, cutting off a small piece of it about the size of my thumb and charring it in a *crucible* with sand, after the manner I described above, I found it to abound infinitely with the smaller sort of pores. These were so extremely thick and so regularly perforating the substance of it lengthwise that, breaking it across, I found it to look very much like a honeycomb. However, as for any of the second or larger kind of pores, I could not find that it had any. So it seems that, whatever was the cause of its production, it was not without those small kinds of pores which we have only found so far in vegetable bodies. Comparing them with the pores which I have found in the charcoals that I made by this means from several other kinds of wood, I find it resembles none so much as those of fir, to which it is not much unlike in grain also, and several other properties.

And therefore, whatever is affirmed by some who have written of it—and particularly by *Francisco Stelluto*, who wrote a treatise in *Italian* on that subject which was printed at *Rome* in 1637—that it is a certain kind of clay or earth which in the course of time is turned into wood, I rather suspect the quite contrary: that it was at first certain great trees of fir or pine which, by some earthquake or other accident, came to be buried under the earth. There, after a long time's residence (according to the several natures of the surrounding adjacent parts), it was either rotted and turned into a kind of clay, or petrified and turned into a kind of stone, or else had its pores filled with certain mineral juices which, being stayed in them and in the course of time coagulated, appeared, upon being cleaved out, like small metallic wires. Or perhaps, from some flames or scorching heat that often occurs and usually accompanies earthquakes, it might be blasted and turned into coal. Or else, from certain subterranean fires which are affirmed by that author to abound much about those parts (namely, in a province of *Italy* called *Umbria*, now the *Duchy of Spoleto*, in the territory of *Todi*, anciently called *Tudor*; and between the two villages of *Collesecco* and *Rosaro*, not far distant from the highway leading to *Rome*, where it is found in greater quantity than elsewhere), they are, by reason of being surrounded with earth and so kept closed from the dissolving air, charred and converted into coal. ## Observation XVII. *Of Petrified wood, and other Petrified bodies.*

Of this sort of substance, I observed several pieces of very different kinds, both for their outward shape, color, grain, texture, hardness, etc. some being brown and reddish; others gray, like a hone; others black, and flint-like: some soft, like a slate or whetstone, others as hard as a flint, and as brittle. That which I more particularly examined, was a piece about the size of a man's hand, which seemed to have been a part of some large tree, that by rottenness had been broken off from it before it began to be petrified.

And indeed, all that I have yet seen, seem to have been rotten wood before the petrification was begun; and not long since, examining and viewing a huge great oak, that seemed with mere age to be rotten as it stood, I was very much confirmed in this opinion; for I found, that the grain, color, and shape of the wood, was exactly like this petrified substance; and with a *microscope*, I found, that all those *microscopical* pores, which in sappy or firm and sound wood are filled with the natural or innate juices of those <term>vegetables</term> <note>plants</note>, in this they were all empty, like those of <term>vegetables charred</term>; but with this difference, that they seemed much larger than I have seen any in charcoals; nay, even than those of coals made of great blocks of timber, which are commonly called <term>Old-coals</term>.

The reason of which difference may probably be, that the charring of vegetables, being an operation quickly performed, and while the wood is sappy, the more solid parts may more easily shrink together, and contract the pores or <term>interstitia</term> <note>spaces</note> between them, than in the rotten wood, where that natural juice seems only to be washed away by adventitious or unnatural moisture; and so though the natural juice be wasted from between the firm parts, yet those parts are kept asunder by the adventitious moistures, and so by degrees settled in those positions.

And this I likewise found in the petrified wood, that the pores were somewhat bigger than those of charcoal, each pore being nearly half as big again, but they did not bear that disproportion which is expressed in the tenth *scheme*, between the small specks or pores in the first *Figure* (which represents the pores of coal or wood charred) and the black spots of the second *Figure* (which represent the like *microscopical* pores in the petrified wood) for these last were drawn by a *microscope* that magnified the object above six times more in *diameter* than the *microscope* by which those pores of coal were observed.

Now, though they were a little bigger, yet did they keep the exact shape and order of the pores of coals and of rotten wood, which last also were much of the same size.

The other observations on this petrified substance, that a while since, by the appointment of the *Royal Society*, I made, and presented to them an account of, were these that follow, which had the honor done them

...by the most accomplished Mr. *Evelyn*, my highly honored friend, to be inserted and published among those excellent observations with which his *Sylva* is replenished, and would therefore have been here omitted, had not the figure of them, as they appeared through the *microscope*, been engraved before that time.

This *petrified* substance resembled wood, in that:

First, all its parts seemed not at all dislocated or altered from their natural position while they were wood, but the whole piece retained the exact shape of wood, having many of the conspicuous pores of wood still remaining as pores, and showing a manifest difference, visible enough, between the grain of the wood and that of the bark, especially when any side of it was cut smooth and polished; for then it appeared to have a very lovely grain, like that of some exquisite dense wood.

Next (it resembled wood) in that all the smaller and (if I may so call those which are only visible with a good magnifying glass) *microscopical pores* of it appear (both when the substance is cut and polished transversely and parallel to its pores) perfectly like the *microscopical* pores of several kinds of wood, especially like and equal to those of several sorts of rotten wood which I have since observed, retaining both the shape, position, and magnitude of such pores. It differed from wood:

First, in *weight*, being to common water as 3 1/4 to 1, whereas there are few of our *English* woods that, when very dry, are found to be as heavy as water.

Secondly, in *hardness*, being very nearly as hard as a flint; and in some places also resembling the grain of a flint; and, like it, it would very readily cut glass, and would not without difficulty, especially in some parts of it, be scratched by a black hard flint. It would also as readily strike fire against a steel, or against a flint, as any common flint.

Thirdly, in its *closeness*, for though all the *microscopical* pores of this *petrified* substance were very conspicuous in one position, yet by altering that position of the polished surface to the light, it was also manifest that those pores appeared darker than the rest of the body, only because they were filled up with a darker substance, and not because they were hollow.

Fourthly, in its *incombustibility*, in that it would not burn in the fire; nay, though I kept it a good while red-hot in the flame of a lamp made very intense by the blast of a small pipe and a large charcoal, yet it seemed not at all to have diminished its size; but only I found it to have changed its color and to appear of a more dark and dusky brown color. Nor could I perceive that those parts which seemed to have been wood at first were at all wasted, but the parts appeared as solid and dense as before. It was further observable also that, as it did not consume like wood, so neither did it crack and fly apart like a flint or similar hard stone, nor was it long before it appeared red-hot.

Fifthly, in its *solubility*; for putting some drops of distilled vinegar upon the stone, I found it presently to yield very many bubbles, just like those which may be observed in spirit of *vinegar* when it corrodes corals, though

MICROGRAPHIA.

...though perhaps many of those small bubbles might proceed from some small parcels of air which were driven out of the pores of this *petrified* substance by the insinuating liquid *menstruum*.

Sixthly, in its rigidity and friability, being not at all flexible but brittle like a flint, so much so that I could with one knock of a hammer break off a piece of it, and with a few more, reduce that into a fairly fine powder.

Seventhly, it also seemed very different from wood *to the touch, feeling* colder than wood usually does, and much like other dense stones and minerals.

The reasons for all of these *phenomena* seem to be:

That this *petrified* wood, having lain in some place where it was well soaked with *petrifying* water (that is, water that is well impregnated with stony and earthy particles), did by degrees separate—either by straining and filtration, or perhaps by precipitation, cohesion, or coagulation—an abundance of stony particles from the permeating water. These stony particles, being conveyed by means of the fluid *vehicle* not only into the *microscopical* pores, and so perfectly stopping them up, but also into the pores or *interstices* which may, perhaps, be even in the texture or *schematism* of that part of the wood which, through the *microscope*, appears most solid, thereby so augment the weight of the wood as to make it more than three times heavier than water, and perhaps six times as heavy as it was when it was wood.

Next, they thereby so lock up and fetter the parts of the wood that fire cannot easily make them fly away; rather, the action of the fire upon them is only able to *char* those parts. Just as a piece of wood, if it is closed very tightly in clay and kept for a good while red-hot in the fire, will by the heat of the fire be charred and not consumed, which may, perhaps, also be part of the reason why the *petrified* substance appeared a dark brown color after it had been burnt.

By this *intrusion* of the petrifying particles, this substance also becomes hard and *friable*; for the smaller pores of the wood being perfectly wedged and stuffed up with those stony particles, the small parts of the wood have no places or pores into which they may slide upon bending, and consequently little or no flexion or yielding at all can be caused in such a substance.

Likewise, the remaining particles of the wood among the stony particles may keep them from cracking and flying when put into the fire, as they are very prone to do in a flint.

Nor is wood the only substance that may by this kind of *transmutation* be changed into stone; for I myself have seen and examined very many kinds of substances, and among very credible authors, we may meet with accounts of such *metamorphoses* wrought almost on all kinds of substances, both *vegetable* and *animal*. It is not my business at present to either relate or *epitomize* these *accounts*, but only to set down some observations I lately made on several kinds of *petrified shells* found around *Keynsham*, which lies within four or five miles of *Bristol*, and which are commonly called *serpentine-stones*.

He notes that this process of mineralization applies to various organic substances, including the fossilized shells found near Keynsham.</summary>

# MICROGRAPHIA.

Examining several of these very curiously figured bodies (which are commonly thought to be stones formed by some extraordinary *plastic virtue* <note>A hypothetical formative power once thought to exist within the Earth that shaped minerals into life-like forms.</note> latent in the Earth itself), I took notice of these particulars:

First, that these figured bodies, or stones, were of very different substances regarding hardness: some of clay, some marl, some soft stone, almost of the hardness of those soft stones which masons call *firestone*, others as hard as *Portland* stone, others as hard as marble, and some as hard as flint or crystal.

Next, they were of very different substances regarding transparency and color; some white, some almost black, some brown, some metallic, or like marcasites; some transparent like white marble, others like flawed crystal, some gray, some of diverse colors; some radiated like those long petrified *drops* <note>Stalactites.</note>, which are commonly found at the *Peak* <note>The Peak District in Derbyshire.</note>, and in other subterranean caverns, which have a kind of pith in the middle.

Thirdly, that they were very different regarding the manner of their outward figuration; for some of them seemed to have been the substance that had filled the shell of some kind of shellfish; others, to have been the substance that had contained or wrapped one of these shells. On both of these, the perfect impression of either the inside or outside of such shells seemed to be left, but for the most part, those impressions seemed to be made by an imperfect or broken shell; the large end or mouth of the shell was always missing, and often the small end, and sometimes half. In some, there were impressions just as if there had been holes broken in the figuring, imprinting, or molding shell; some of them seemed to be made by such a shell being very much bruised or flawed, so much so that one would truly have thought that very figured stone had been broken or bruised while it was like a jelly, as it were, and so hardened; but within the grain of the stone, there appeared not the least sign of any such bruise or breaking, but only on the very outermost surface.

Fourthly, they were very different regarding their outward covering; some had the perfect shell—both in figure, color, and substance—sticking onto its surface and adhering to it, but it could very easily be separated from it. Like other common *cockle* or *scallop shells*, which some of them most accurately resembled, these were very dissolvable in common *vinegar*. Others of them, especially those *serpentine* or *helical* stones <note>Ammonites.</note>, were covered with or retained the shining or pearl-colored substance of the inside of a shell. This substance, on some parts of them, was exceedingly thin and could very easily be rubbed off; on other parts, it was quite thick and retained a white coat or flaky substance on the top, just like the outsides of such shells. Some of them had very large pieces of the shell very plainly sticking to them, which were easily broken or flaked off by degrees. They likewise, some of them, retained all along their surface very pretty kinds of *sutures*, such as are observed in the skulls of several kinds of living creatures; these *sutures* were most curiously shaped in the manner of leaves, and every one of them in the same shell was exactly like the others. I was able to discover these plainly enough with my naked eye, but more perfectly and distinctly with my *microscope*; all these

# MICROGRAPHIA.

By breaking some of these stones, I found these *sutures* to be the *termini*, or boundaries, of certain *diaphragms* or partitions. These seemed to divide the cavity of the shell into a multitude of very proportionate and regular *cells* or *caverns*. In many of them, I found these *diaphragms* to be very perfect and complete, made of a very distinct substance from that which filled the cavities, and exactly of the same kind as that which covered the outside—being for the most part whitish or *mother-of-pearl* colored.

As for the cavities between those *diaphragms*, I found some of them filled with marl, and others with several kinds of stones. Others were for the most part hollow, with only the entire cavity usually covered over with a kind of tartareous petrified substance which stuck to the sides. There, it had crystallized into very curious, regular figures, just as *tartar* or other dissolved salts are observed to stick and *crystallize* around the sides of the vessels containing them; or like those little *diamonds* which I previously observed covering the vaulted cavity of a *flint*. Others had these cavities all lined with a kind of metallic or *marcasite*-like substance, which I could see with a *microscope* just as plainly and curiously figured as I had seen those in a flint.

From all of this, and several other particulars which I observed, I cannot help but think that all these, and most other kinds of stony bodies found so strangely shaped, owe their formation and shape not to any kind of *plastic virtue* <note>A hypothetical formative power once thought to exist within the Earth that shaped minerals into life-like forms.</note> inherent in the earth, but to the shells of certain shellfish. These shells, by some deluge, flood, earthquake, or other such means, were thrown to that place and there became filled with some kind of mud, clay, *petrifying water*, or some other substance. In the course of time, this substance settled and hardened within those shelly moulds into the shaped objects we now find. The large and thin end of these shells was broken off by that earthquake—or whatever other extraordinary cause brought them there—and many others were otherwise broken, bruised, and disfigured. These shells, which are thus spiraled and separated by *diaphragms*, were some kind of *nautili* or *porcelain shells*; and others were shells of *cockles*, *mussels*, *periwinkles*, *scallops*, etc., of various sorts. In many cases, due to the particular nature of the surrounding or enclosed earth, or some other cause, these shells have rotted and moldered away over time, leaving only their impressions on both the surrounding and the enclosed substances. This left them quite loose one within another, so that they may be easily separated by a knock or two of a hammer. Other shells, according to the nature of the substances adjacent to them, have been petrified and turned into stone through long continuance in that position, just as I recently observed with several sorts of wood. Often the shell may be found with one kind of substance inside and quite another outside, having perhaps been filled in one place and afterwards moved to another—something I have very frequently observed in *cockle*, *mussel*, *periwinkle*, and other shells found by the seaside. Furthermore, some parts of the same shell may be filled in one place, and some

<summary>Hooke argues that fossils are not naturally occurring "figured stones" but are actually the remains of organic shells that were filled with mineral matter and petrified over time. He supports this by describing the internal chambers, partitions, and crystallization patterns he observed inside them using a microscope.</summary>

some other caverns in another, and others in a third, or a fourth, or a fifth place, for I have found so many different substances in one of these petrified shells, and perhaps all these differ from the encompassing earth or stone. The means by which all these varieties may be caused will not, I think, be difficult to conceive for anyone who has taken notice of those shells which are commonly found on the seashore. And whoever shall thoroughly examine several kinds of such curiously formed stones will (I am very inclined to think) find reason to suppose their generation or formation is ascribable to some such accidents as I have mentioned, and not to any *Plastic virtue* <note>A hypothetical formative power once thought to exist within the Earth that shaped minerals into life-like forms.</note>. For it seems to me quite contrary to the infinite prudence of Nature, which is observable in all its works and productions, to design everything for a specific end, and for the attaining of that end, to make use of such ways as are (as far as the knowledge of man has yet been able to reach) altogether consistent and most agreeable to human reason, and no way or means that contradicts or is contrary to *human reasoning*. For this reason, it has for a long time been a general observation and maxim that *Nature does nothing in vain*. It seems, I say, contrary to that great wisdom of Nature that these prettily shaped bodies should have all those curious figures and structures (with which many of them are adorned and designed) generated or wrought by a *Plastic virtue* for no higher end than only to exhibit such a form. Anyone who thoroughly considers all the circumstances of such kinds of figured bodies will, I think, have great reason to believe this, though I confess one cannot immediately find out what Nature's designs are. It would, therefore, be very desirable for a good collection of such kinds of figured stones to be gathered, and as many particulars, circumstances, and pieces of information collected with them as could be obtained, so that from such a history of observations—well arranged, examined, and digested—the true origin or production of all those kinds of stones might be perfectly and surely known. These include such stones as *Thunder-stones, Lapides Stellares, Lapides Judaici*, and multitudes of others mentioned in *Aldrovandus*, *Wormius*, and other writers on minerals.

## Observation XVIII. Of the Schematism or Texture of Cork, and of the Cells and Pores of some other such frothy Bodies.

I took a good clear piece of cork, and with a penknife sharpened as keen as a razor, I cut a piece of it off, and thereby left the surface of it exceedingly smooth. Then, examining it very diligently with a *microscope*, I thought I could perceive it to appear a little porous; but I could not distinguish them so plainly as to be sure they were pores, much less what shape they were. But judging from the lightness and yielding quality of the cork, I was certain the texture could not be so

First, in that it had a very little solid substance, in comparison to the empty cavity that was contained between, as does more manifestly appear by the Figure A and B of the XI. *Scheme* <note>An illustrated plate or diagram.</note>, for the *Interstitia* <note>The spaces or walls between the pores.</note>, or walls (as I may so call them) or partitions of those pores were near as thin in proportion to their pores, as those thin films of wax in a honeycomb (which enclose and constitute the *sexangular* <note>six-angled or hexagonal</note> *cells*) are to theirs.

Next, in that these pores, or cells, were not very deep, but consisted of a great many little boxes, separated out of one continued long pore, by certain *Diaphragms* <note>Dividing membranes or walls.</note>, as is visible by the Figure B, which represents a sight of those pores split lengthwise.

I no sooner discerned these (which were indeed the first *microscopic pores* I ever saw, and perhaps, that were ever seen, for I had not met with any writer or person, that had made any mention of them before this) but it occurred to me that I had, with the discovery of them, presently hinted to me the true and intelligible reason of all the *Phænomena* <note>Observed phenomena or characteristics.</note> of cork; as,

First, if I enquired why it was so exceedingly light a body? my *Microscope* could presently inform me that here was the same reason evident that there is found for the lightness of froth, an empty honeycomb, wool, a sponge, a pumice-stone, or the like; namely, a very small quantity of a solid body, extended into exceedingly large dimensions.

Next, it seemed nothing more difficult to give an intelligible reason, why cork is a body so very unapt to suck and drink in water, and consequently preserves itself, floating on the top of water, though left on it never so long: and why it is able to stop and hold air in a bottle, though it be there very much condensed and consequently presses very strongly to get a passage out, without suffering the least bubble to pass through its substance. For, as to the first, since our *Microscope* informs us that the substance of cork is altogether filled with air, and that that air is perfectly enclosed in little boxes or cells distinct from one another. It seems very plain, why neither the water, nor any other air can easily insinuate itself into them, since there is already within them an *intus existens* <note>Something already existing within.</note>, and consequently, why the pieces of cork become so good floats for nets, and stoppers for *vials*, or other close vessels.

And thirdly, if we enquire why cork has such a springiness and swelling nature when compressed? and how it comes to suffer so great a compression, or seeming penetration of dimensions, so as to be made a substance as heavy again and more, bulk for bulk, as it was before compression, and yet allowed to return, is found to extend itself again into the same space? Our *Microscope* will easily inform us, that the whole mass

And if we could as easily and certainly discover the *schematism* <note>The internal structure or arrangement of parts.</note> and texture even of these films, and of several other bodies, as we can those of cork; there seems no probable reason to the contrary but that we might as readily provide the true reason for all their *phenomena*; namely, what causes the springiness and toughness of some, regarding both their flexibility and restoration. What causes the friability or brittleness of others, and the like; but until such time as our *microscope*, or some other means, enables us to discover the true *schematism* and texture of all kinds of bodies, we must grope, as it were, in the dark, and only guess at the true reasons of things by similarities and comparisons.

But, to return to our observation. I counted several lines of these pores, and found that there were usually about sixty of these small cells placed end-to-end in the eighteenth part of an inch in length, from which I concluded there must be near 1,100 of them, or somewhat more than 1,000 in the length of an inch, and therefore in a square inch above a million, or 1,166,400, and in a cubic inch, above 1,200 million, or 1,259,712,000. This is a thing almost incredible, did not our *microscope* assure us of it by visual proof; indeed, it discovers to us the pores of a body which, were they *diaphragmed* <note>Divided by membranes.</note>, like those of cork, would provide us in one cubic inch more than ten times as many little cells, as is evident in several charred vegetables. So prodigiously intricate are the works of Nature, that even these conspicuous pores of bodies, which seem to be the channels or pipes through which the *succus nutritius* <note>Nutritional sap or juices.</note>, or natural juices of vegetables, are conveyed, and seem to correspond to the veins, arteries and other vessels in sentient creatures—that these pores, I say, which seem to be the vessels of nutrition to the largest body in the world, are yet so exceedingly small that the *atoms* which *Epicurus* imagined would be nearly too large to enter them, much less to constitute a fluid body within them. And how infinitely smaller, then, must be the vessels of a mite, or the pores of one of those little vegetables I have discovered to grow on the back of a rose-leaf, and shall shortly more fully describe, whose bulk is many millions of times smaller than the bulk of the small shrub it grows on; and even that shrub, many millions of times smaller in bulk than several trees (that have previously grown in *England*, and are today flourishing in other hotter climates, as we are very credibly informed) if at least the pores of this small vegetable should keep any such proportion to its body, as we have found these pores

To proceed then, cork seems to be, by the transverse arrangement of its pores, a kind of *fungus* or mushroom; for the pores lie like so many rays tending from the center, or pith of the tree, outwards. So, if you cut a piece from a sheet of cork transverse to its flat surface, you will, as it were, split the pores, and they will appear just as they are shown in Figure B of the XI. *scheme*. But if you shave off a very thin piece from this sheet, parallel to its plane, you will cut all the pores transversely, and they will appear almost as they are shown in Figure A, except that the solid *interstitia* <note>The solid walls or spaces between the pores.</note> will not appear as thick as they are represented there.

So that cork seems to draw its nourishment immediately from the underlying bark of the tree, and to be a kind of excrescence, or a substance distinct from the substances of the entire tree, somewhat analogous to the mushroom or moss on other trees, or to the hair on animals. And having inquired into the history of cork, I find it is considered an excrescence of the bark of a certain tree, which is distinct from the two barks that lie beneath it, which are also common to other trees. I find that it is some time before the cork covering the young and tender sprouts becomes discernable; that it cracks, flaws, and splits into many large gaps, while the bark underneath remains entire; and that it may be separated and removed from the tree, and yet the two under-barks (which are common to that and other trees) are not at all injured, but rather helped and freed from an external injury. Thus *Jonstonus* in *Dendrologia*, speaking *about cork*, says,

> *Arbor est procera, Lignum est robustum, dempto cortice in aquis non fluitat, Cortice in orbem detracto juvatur, crassescens enim præstringit & strangulat, intra triennium iterum repletur: Caudex ubi adolescit crassus, cortex superior densus carnosus, duos digitos crassus, scaber, rimosus, & qui nisi detrahatur dehiscit, alioque subnascente expellitur, interior qui subest novellus ita rubet ut arbor minio picta videatur.*

These accounts, if well considered, and if the tree, substance, and manner of growth were well examined, would, I am very apt to believe, strongly confirm my conjecture about the origin of cork.

Nor is this kind of texture unique to cork alone; for upon examination with my *microscope*, I have found that the pith of an elder, or almost any other tree, and the inner pulp or pith of the cany, hollow stalks of several other vegetables—such as fennel, carrots, <term>Daucus</term> <note>A genus of plants that includes the carrot.</note>, burdocks, teasels, fern, some kinds of reeds, etc.—have much the same kind of <term>schematism</term> <note>Internal structural arrangement.</note> as I have lately shown in cork, except that here the pores are arranged lengthwise, or in the same direction as the length of the stalk, whereas in cork they are transverse.

The pith also that fills that part of the shaft of a feather that is above the quill has much the same kind of texture, except that no matter which way I positioned this light substance, the pores seemed to be cut transversely. Now, though I have with great diligence endeavored to find whether there be any such thing in those *microscopical* pores of wood or piths as the *valves* in the heart, veins, and other passages of animals, that open and give passage to the contained fluid juices one way, and shut themselves and impede the passage of such liquors back again, yet have I not hitherto been able to say anything positive about it; though, it seems to me very probable that Nature has in these passages, as well as in those of animal bodies, very many appropriated instruments and contrivances whereby to bring her designs and ends to pass, which it is not improbable that some diligent observer, if helped with better *microscopes*, may in time detect.

And that this may be so seems with great probability to be argued from the strange *phenomena* of sensitive plants, wherein Nature seems to perform several *animal* actions with the same *schematism* <note>Structural organization or arrangement.</note> or *organization* that is common to all vegetables, as may appear by some no less instructive than curious observations that were made by various eminent members of the *Royal Society* on some of these kind of plants, of which an account was delivered to them by the most ingenious and excellent *physician, Doctor Clark*, which, having that liberty granted me by that most illustrious society, I have hereunto adjoined.

The distances between the sprouts are usually somewhat more than an inch, and there are many upon a branch, according to its length; and they grow so that if the lower sprout is on the left side of the branch, the next above is on the right, and so to the end, not sprouting in pairs.

At the end of each sprout are generally four sprigs: two at the extremity, and one on each side, just under it. At the first sprouting of these from the branch to the sprig where the leaves grow, they are full of little short white hairs, which wear off as the leaves grow, and then they are as smooth as the branch.

Upon each of these sprigs are, for the most part, eleven pairs of leaves, neatly set into the uppermost part of the little sprig, exactly opposite one another, as if in little articulations, such as anatomists call <term>*Enarthrosis*</term>, where the round head of a bone is received into another fitted for its motion; and standing very fitly to shut themselves and touch, the pairs just above them closing somewhat upon them, as in the shut sprig; so is the little round <term>*Pedunculus*</term> of this leaf fitted into a little cavity of the sprig, visible to the eye in a sprig newly plucked, or in a sprig withered on the branch, from which the leaves easily fall when touched.

The leaf, being almost an oblong square and set into the <term>*Pedunculus*</term> at one of the lower corners, receives from that not only a <term>*spine*</term>, as I may call it—which, passing through the leaf, divides it lengthwise so that the outer side is broader than the inner side next the sprig—but little <term>*fibers*</term> passing obliquely towards the opposite broader side, which seem to make it here a little muscular and fitted to move the whole leaf; these, together with the whole sprig, are covered with little short whitish hairs.

One of these plants, whose branch seemed to be older and more grown than the other, has only its tender sprouts fall and hang down after the leaves are closed; of the other, the whole branches fall to the ground if the sun shines very warmly upon the first removal of the glass, which I therefore call the *humble plant*.

The sprouts from them have several pairs of sprigs, with much smaller leaves than the others, and generally have seventeen pairs on each sprig.

Upon touching any of the sprigs with leaves on them, all the leaves on that sprig, contracting themselves by pairs, joined their upper surfaces close together.

Upon the dropping of a drop of <term>*aqua fortis*</term> on the sprig between the leaves *f f*, all the leaves above closed immediately; those below closed by pairs successively after, and then the lower leaves of the other branches, *l l*, *k k*, etc., and so every pair successively, with some small interval of time between, to the top of each sprig; and they continued closed all the time we were there. But I, returning the next day and several days since, found all the leaves expanded again on two of the sprigs; but from *f f* upwards, where the <term>*aqua fortis*</term> had dropped, they were dead and withered; however, those below on the same sprig were green and closed upon being touched, and remain so at this day, *August* 14.

With a pair of scissors, as suddenly as it could be done, one of the leaves *b b* was clipped off in the middle, upon which that pair and the pair above closed immediately; after a little interval, *d d* closed, then *e e*, and so the rest of the pairs to the bottom of the sprig; then the motion began in the lower pairs, *l l*, on the other sprigs, and so closed them by pairs upwards, though not with such distinct intervals of time.

Beneath a fairly large branch with its sprigs attached, there was a large shell lying between two and three inches below it. A strong-scented oil was rubbed onto the shell; after a short time, all the leaves on that sprig closed, and they remained closed during the entire duration of our stay there. However, upon my return the next day, I found the position of the shell was altered, and the leaves were expanded as before, closing again upon being touched.

Upon applying the sun's rays with a burning glass, the *more humble Plant* fell, while the other shut its leaves.

We could not apply the smoke of sulfur in such a way as to have any visible effect from two or three trials; but on another trial, when the smoke touched the leaves, it succeeded.

The *humble Plant* fell upon removing the glass with which it was covered.

Upon cutting off one of the little sprouts, two or three drops of liquid were pushed out from the part where it was cut; it was very clear and transparent, of a bright greenish color, tasting a little bitter at first, but afterwards leaving a licorice-like taste in my mouth.

Since then, having gone two or three times when it was cold, I took the glasses off from the *more humble Plant*, and it did not fall as it had previously, but only shut its leaves. But coming back later, when the sun shone very warmly, as soon as the glass was taken off, it fell as before.

Since then, I plucked off another sprig whose leaves were all shut and had been so for some time, thinking to observe the liquid that should come from where I had broken it off; but finding none come, even with pressing, I as skillfully as I could pulled off one whose leaves were expanded. Then, upon the shutting of the leaves, I obtained a little of the mentioned liquid from the end of the sprig I had broken from the plant. This happened twice in succession—almost as often as I dared to rob the plant.

liquid, both from the part I had cut and from the part I had cut it from, without any pressure.

This led me to think that the motion of this plant upon being touched might result from a constant *intercourse* between every part of this plant and its root, either by a *circulation* of this liquid or a constant pressing of its more subtle parts to every extremity of the plant. Upon any pressure, from whatever cause it proceeds, if it is greater than the pressure that holds it up, the subtle parts of this liquid are thrust downwards toward the *articulations* of the leaves. There, having no immediate room to get into the sprig, the little round *pedunculus*—from which the *Spine* and those oblique *Fibres* I mentioned arise—becomes dilated. Consequently, the *Spine* and *Fibres* (being continuous with it) must be contracted and shortened, and so draw the leaf upward to join with its fellow, which is in the same condition as itself. Once they are closed, they are held together by the entanglements of the little whitish hairs, as well as by the liquid still retreating; this distends the *Fibres* that continue lower toward the branch and root, shortening them above. When the liquid is forced so much from the sprout—whose *Fibres* are still tender and unable to support themselves except by the tension provided by the liquid filling their *interstices*—the sprout hangs and flags.

But perhaps someone who had the ability and leisure to provide an exact *Anatomy* of this pretty plant—to show its fibers and visible *Canales* through which this fine liquid circulates or is moved, and who had the faculty of expressing his observations and thoughts better and more copiously—would easily use the motion of this liquid to solve all the *Phænomena*. Such a person would not fear to affirm that the plant possesses a distinct sensation. But I have said too much; I humbly submit these thoughts and am ready to be corrected.

I have not yet made such complete and satisfactory observations on this plant as I desire, for it seems to be a subject that will provide a wealth of information.

<summary>Hooke hypothesizes that the movement of the sensitive plant is caused by the hydraulic flow and pressure of internal liquids through its fibers and joints. He suggests that a detailed anatomical study of these channels would reveal that the plant possesses a genuine sense of feeling.</summary>

### Observ. XIX. Of a Plant growing in the blighted or yellow specks of Damask-rose-leaves, Bramble-leaves, and some other kind of leaves.

I Have for several years together, in the months of *June, July, August*, and *September* (when any of the green leaves of *Roses* begin to dry and grow yellow) observed many of them, especially the leaves of the old shrubs of *Damask-Roses*, all speckled with yellow stains, and the undersides just against them, to have little yellow hillocks of a gummy substance, and several of them to have small black spots in the midst of those yellow ones, which, to the naked eye, appeared no bigger than the point of a Pin, or the smallest black spot or dot of Ink one is able to make with a very sharp pointed Pen.

<margin>not like the seeds of moss, but in shapes very like barberries</margin>
Examining these with a *Microscope*, I was able plainly to distinguish, up and down the surface, several small yellow knobs, of a kind of yellowish red gummy substance, out of which I perceived there sprung multitudes of little cases or black bodies like Seed-pods, and those of them that were quite without the hillock of gum, revealed themselves to grow out of it with a small straw-colored and transparent stem, the which seed and stem appeared very like those of common Moss (which I elsewhere describe) but that they were abundantly smaller, many hundreds of them not being able to equal one single seed pod of Moss.

I have often doubted whether they were the seed pods of some little plant, or some kind of small buds, or the eggs of some very small insect; they appeared of a dark brownish red, some almost quite black, and of a figure much resembling the seed-pod of Moss, but their stalks on which they grew were of a very fine transparent substance, almost like the stalk of mold, but that they seemed somewhat more yellow.

That which makes me to suppose them to be plants is because I perceived many of those hillocks bare or destitute, as if those bodies lay yet concealed, as at G. In others of them, they were just springing out of their gummy hillocks, which all seemed to shoot directly outwards, as at A. From this putrefied scab breaks out this little vegetable, which may be something like a *mould* or *moss*. This is set in motion by the *putrefactive* and *fermentative* heat, joined with that of the surrounding air, when (by the putrefaction and decay of some other parts of the vegetable that for a while stalled its progress) it is unfettered and left at liberty to move in its former course. But by reason of its regulators, it moves and acts in a completely different manner than it did when it was a co-agent in the more complex *machine* of the more perfect vegetable.

And from this very same principle, I imagine the *mistletoe* of oaks, thorns, apple trees, and other trees to have its origin: it seldom or never grows on any of those trees until they begin to become decrepit and decay with age, and are troubled with many other infirmities.

And we see this to be very much the method of nature throughout its operations: *putrefactive vegetables* very often producing a vegetable of a much less complex nature and of a much inferior tribe; and *putrefactive animal* substances degenerating into some kind of animal production of a much inferior rank and of a more simple nature.

Thus we find the humors and substances of the body, upon *putrefaction*, produce strange kinds of moving vermin: the *putrefaction* of the slimes and juices of the stomach and guts produce worms almost like earthworms; the wheals <note>Small swellings or pimples on the skin.</note> in children's hands produce a little worm called a *wheal-worm*; the blood and milk, and other humors, produce other kinds of worms—at least, if we may believe what is delivered to us by very famous authors; though, I confess, I have not yet been able to discover such myself.

And while it may seem strange that *vinegar*, *meal*, musty *casks*, etc., are observed to breed their different kinds of insects or living creatures—since, being vegetable substances, they seem to be of an inferior kind and thus unable to produce a creature more noble or of a more complex nature than they themselves are, and so without some concurrent seminal principle might be thought utterly unfit for such an operation—I must add that we cannot immediately say for certain that there are no animal substances joined with them, either indirectly, such as through the soil or fertilizer of the plant from which they sprang, or more directly, by the real mixture or composition of such substances. Or perhaps some kind of insect, in places where such kinds of *putrefying* or *fermenting* bodies are, may, by a certain instinct of nature, eject some sort of seminal principle which, cooperating with various kinds of putrefying substances, may produce various kinds of insects or animate bodies. For we find in most sorts of those lower degrees of animate bodies that the *putrefying* substances on which these eggs, seeds, or seminal principles are cast by the insect become, as it were, the *matrices* or *wombs* that contribute very much to their generation, and perhaps also to their variation and alteration; much in the same manner as several new kinds of animals are produced by strange and unnatural copulations, such as *mules* and the like, which are usually called monstrous because they are a little unusual, though many of them have all their principal parts as perfectly shaped and adapted for their peculiar uses as any of the most perfect animals. If, therefore, the *putrefying* body on which any kind of seminal or vital principle happens to be cast becomes something more than merely a nursing and fostering helper in the generation and production of any kind of animate body, the nearer it approaches the true nature of a womb, the more power will it have over the offspring <note>Hooke uses the term "by-blow," which refers to an offspring produced outside the typical or "legitimate" course of nature.</note> it encloses. Perhaps some more accurate inquiries and observations about these matters might bring the question to some certainty, which would be of no small concern in natural philosophy.

For we do not know but that the Omnipotent and All-wise Creator might as directly design the structure of such a vegetable, or such an animal, to be produced out of such or such a putrefaction or change of this or that body—towards the constitution or structure of which he knew it necessary, or thought it fit, to make it an ingredient—as that the digestion or moderate heating of an egg, either by the female, or the sun, or the heat of the fire, or the like, should produce this or that bird; or that *putrefactive* and warm steams should, out of the "blowings," as they call them (that is, the eggs of a fly), produce a living maggot, and that, by degrees, be turned into an *aurelia*, and that, by a longer and a proportioned heat, be transmuted into a fly. Nor do we need therefore to suppose it more imperfect in its kind than the more complex vegetable or animal of which it is a part; for he might as completely furnish it with all kinds of contrivances necessary for its own existence and the propagation of its own species, and yet make it a part of a more complex body: as a clock-maker might make a set of chimes to be a part of a clock, and yet, when the watch part or striking part are taken away and the hindrances of its motion removed, this chiming part may go as accurately, and strike its tune as exactly, as if it were still a part of the complex *automaton*. Nor are damask-rose leaves the only leaves that produce these kinds of vegetable sproutings; for I have observed them also in several other kinds of rose leaves, and on the leaves of several sorts of briars, and on bramble leaves they are often to be found in very great clusters; so that I have found in one cluster, three, four, or five hundred of them, making a very conspicuous black spot or scab on the back side of the leaf.

### Observation XX. Of blue Mold, and of the first Principles of Vegetation arising from Putrefaction.

The blue and white and several kinds of hairy moldy spots, which are observable upon various kinds of putrefied bodies, whether animal substances or vegetable—such as the skin (raw or dressed), flesh, blood, humors, milk, green cheese, etc., or rotten sappy wood, or herbs, leaves, barks, roots, etc., of plants—are all of them nothing else but several kinds of small and variously shaped mushrooms. These, from convenient materials in those putrefying bodies, are, by the concurrent heat of the air, excited to a certain kind of vegetation, which will not be unworthy of our more serious speculation and examination, as I shall shortly show. But, first, I must premise a short description of this *specimen*, which I have added of this tribe, in the first figure of the XII scheme, which is nothing else but the appearance of a small white spot of hairy mold. I found multitudes of these to bespeck and whiten over the red covers of a small book, which, it seems, were of sheepskin, that being more apt to gather mold, even in a dry and clean room, than other leathers. These spots appeared, through a good microscope, to be a very pretty shaped vegetative body, which, from almost the same part of the leather, shot

Both their smell and taste, which are active enough to make a sensible impression upon those organs, are unpleasant and offensive.

I did not find that they would be so quickly destroyed by the actual flame of a candle as I had imagined at first sight; they remained entire after I had passed that part of the leather on which they grew through the flame of a candle three or four times. Thus, it seems they are not very likely to catch fire, any more than common white mushrooms are when they are sappy.

There are a multitude of other shapes in which these *microscopical* mushrooms are formed, which would have been a long work to describe and would not have suited my design in this treatise so well. However, among the rest, I must not forget to mention one that was somewhat like, or resembled, a sponge, consisting of a multitude of little ramifications almost as that body does, which indeed seems to be a kind of water-mushroom of a very pretty texture, as I manifest elsewhere. And a second, which I must not omit because it was often mingled with and near adjoining those I have described, appeared much like a thicket of bushes or brambles, very much branched and extended—some of them to a great length in proportion to their diameter—like creeping brambles.

The manner of the growth and formation of this kind of vegetable is the third head of inquiry, which I would follow had I time. The figure and method of generation in this solid object seems to me, next after the inquiry into the formation, shape, or crystallization of salts, to be the most simple, plain, and easy; and it seems to be a *medium* through which anyone must necessarily pass who would, with any likelihood, investigate the *forma informans* <note>The inherent form or organizing principle.</note> of vegetables. Thus, the inquiry into the forms of vegetables will be no less, if not much more difficult, without the foreknowledge of the forms of mushrooms. These several inquiries have no less dependence upon one another than any select number of propositions in the elements of mathematics may be made to have.

Nor do I imagine that the skips from one to another will be found very great, if—beginning from fluidity, or a body without any form—we descend gradually until we arrive at the highest form of a brute animal's soul, making the steps or foundations of our inquiry: *Fluidity, Orbiculation, Fixation, Angulization or Crystallization, Germination or Ebullition, Vegetation, Plantanimation, Animation, Sensation, Imagination.*

Now, so that we may better proceed in our inquiry, it will be necessary to consider:

First, that mold and mushrooms require no seminal property <note>reproductive seeds</note>, but the former may be produced at any time from any kind of putrefying animal or vegetable substance, such as flesh, *etc.*, kept moist and warm. The latter, if what *Mathiolus* relates about making them by art is true, are just as much within our command. Of this matter, take the *epitome* which Mr. *Parkinson* has delivered in his Herbal, in his chapter on *Mushrooms*, because I do not have *Mathiolus* with me now: *To these mushrooms (he says) may also be added those which are made by art (of which* Mathiolus *makes mention) that grow naturally among certain stones in* Naples; *and that when the stones were dug up and carried to* Rome *and other places, where they set them in their wine cellars, covering them with a little earth and sprinkling a little warm water on them, they would within four days produce mushrooms fit to be eaten, at whatever time one wished. Also, that mushrooms may be made to grow at the foot of a wild poplar tree within four days after warm water—in which some leaves have been dissolved—is poured into the root (which must be slit) and the stock above ground.*

Next, just as mushrooms may be generated without seed, it also does not appear that they have any such thing as seed in any part of them. For having considered several kinds of them, I could never find anything in them that I could with any probability guess to be the seed. So, it does not as yet appear (that I know of) that mushrooms may be generated from a seed, but they rather seem to depend merely upon a convenient constitution of the matter out of which they are made, and a concurrence of either natural or artificial heat.

Thirdly, that by various bodies (such as salts and metals, both in water and in the air, and by several kinds of sublimations in the air) actuated and guided by a consistent heat, there may be produced several kinds of bodies of as curious, if not of a more composed figure. This is manifested by several kinds of rising or ebulliating <note>bubbling or boiling up</note> figures, as witnessed in the shooting during the rectification of spirits of *urine, hartshorn <note>aqueous solution of ammonia</note>, blood, etc.* Witness also the intricate branches of evaporated solutions, some of them against the

But above all the rest, a very beautiful kind of germination is provided to us in the Silver Tree—the method of making which with mercury and silver is well known to the chemists. In this, there is an ebullition or germination very much like that of mushrooms, if I have been rightly informed of it.

Fourthly, I have very often noticed, and also observed with a *microscope*, certain excrescences or ebullitions in the snuff of a candle. These, partly from the sticking of the smoky particles as they are carried upward by the current of the rarefied air and flame, and partly also from a kind of germination or ebullition of some activated oily parts which creep along and filter through some small string of the wick, are formed into pretty round and uniform heads, very much resembling the shape of hooded mushrooms. When these are exposed by any means to the fresh air, or that air which encompasses the flame, they are immediately licked up and devoured by it, and they vanish.

The reason for this *phenomenon* seems to me to be nothing other than this: when a suitable thread of the wick is so bent out by the sides of the snuff that it is about half an inch or more removed above the bottom or lowest part of the flame, and this part is entirely included within the flame, the oil—for the reason of filtration, which I have explained elsewhere—is continually driven up the wick and likewise into this ragged, bent end. Since this part is removed a good distance (as half an inch or more) above the bottom of the flame, the parts of the air that pass by it are already almost saturated with the dissolution of the boiling oily vapors that issued out below. Therefore, the air is not only glutted—that is, it can dissolve no more than what it is already acting upon—but it also carries up with it an abundance of oily and sooty particles. When these meet that rag of the wick, which is plentifully filled with oil and only loses it as fast as it evaporates (and not at all by dissolution or burning), and because the steamy parts of the filtered oil issuing from the sides of this rag are enclosed by air that is already saturated and cannot prey upon or burn them, the ascending sooty particles are stopped and fixed around it. Thus, around the end of that rag or filament of the snuff, from which the greatest part of the vapors issue, a round and fairly uniform cap is conglobated <note>collected into a ball</note> or fixed, much resembling the head of a mushroom. If it is of any great size, you may observe that its underside will be larger than the part above the rag or stem; for the oil brought into it by filtration is somewhat sheltered from the heat of the flame by the bulk of the cap. By that means, it issues as much from beneath the stalk or downwards as it does upwards, and because of the great arrival of additional smoke from below, it increases most in that direction. That this may be the true reason for this *phenomenon*, I could produce many arguments and experiments to make it probable: First, that filtration carries the oil to the top of the wick, at least

In the first place, the droppings or tricklings of *lapidescent* (stone-forming) waters in vaults underground seem to constitute a kind of petrified body, formed almost like certain kinds of *mushrooms* inverted, so much so that I have seen some knobby at the lower end, though for the most part, indeed, they are otherwise shaped and tapered toward the end. The generation of these seems to be for no other reason than this: the water, by soaking through the earth and lime (for I guess that substance adds much to its petrifying quality), so impregnates itself with stony particles that as it hangs in drops from the roof of the vault—because the soaking of the water is slow—it becomes exposed to the *air*. Thereby, the outward part of the drop gradually grows hard because, as the water gradually evaporates, the stony particles near the outside of the drop begin to touch, and by degrees dry and grow closer together, and at length constitute a crust or shell around the drop. As this soaking is gradually supplied with more water, the drop grows longer and longer, and the sides harden and thicken into a *quill* or *cane*; and at length, that hollow or pith becomes almost stopped up and solid. Afterwards, the soaking petrifying water, finding no longer a passage through the middle, bursts out and trickles down the outside, and as the water evaporates, leaves new superimposed shells which more and more increase the bulk of those *icicles*. Because of the great supply of petrifying water from the vault, those bodies grow larger and larger near the vault and taper or sharpen toward the point; for since the supply from the arch of the vault is very slow, and consequently the water is spread very thinly over the surface of the *icicle*, the water begins to settle before it can reach the bottom or lower end of it. From this, if you break one of these, you would almost imagine it to be a stick of *wood* petrified, as it has such a beautiful resemblance to pith and grain; and if you look on the outside of a piece, or of one whole, you would think no less, both from its vegetable-like roundness and

By these last observations, we see that there may be a quite pretty body shaped and solidified by mechanical principles, without the least show or probability of any other seminal *formatrix*.

And since we find that the primary reason for the *phenomena* of this pretty *petrifaction* is to be reduced from the gravity of a fluid and quite volatile body impregnated with stony particles, why may not the *phenomena* of ebullition or germination be, in part, possibly enough deduced from the levity of an impregnated liquor? This liquor, therefore, perpendicularly ascending by degrees, evaporates and leaves the more solid and fixed parts behind in the form of a mushroom, which is yet diversified and specified by the forms of the parts that impregnated the liquor and compose or help to constitute the mushroom.

That the aforementioned figures of growing salts, and the *Silver Tree*, are from this principle, I could very easily manifest; but I do not now have a convenient opportunity of pursuing it, nor have I made a sufficient number of experiments and observations to propound, explain, and prove so useful a *theory* as this regarding mushrooms. For, though the contrary principle to that of *petrified* icicles may be in part a cause, yet I cannot but think that there is a somewhat more complicated cause, though still mechanical, and possible to be explained.

We therefore have further to inquire of it: what makes it such a liquor and causes it to ascend—whether the heat of the Sun and air, or whether that of *fermentation* and *putrefaction*, or both together? Also, whether there is not a third or fourth cause; whether a saline principle is not a considerable agent in this business as well as heat; and whether also a fixation, precipitation, or settling of certain parts out of the aerial mushroom may not also be a considerable contributor in the business. Since we find that many pretty beards or *stiriæ* of silver particles may be precipitated upon a piece of brass put into a *solution* of silver very much diluted with clear water (which looks not unlike a kind of mould or frost upon that piece of metal), and the hoar frost looks like a kind of mould; and whether there may not be several other factors that concur in the production of a mushroom—having not yet had sufficient time to prosecute this according to my desires, I must refer this to a better opportunity of my own, or leave and recommend it to the more diligent inquiry and examination of those who can be masters of both leisure and conveniences for such an inquiry.

And in the meantime, I must conclude that as far as I have been able to look into the nature of this primary kind of life and vegetation, I cannot find the least probable argument to persuade me there is any other concurrent cause than such as is purely mechanical; and that the *effects* or *productions* are as necessary upon the concurrence of those causes as that a ship—when the sails are hoisted and the rudder is set to such a position—should, when the wind blows, be moved in such a way or course.

## Observation XXI. Of Moss, and several other small vegetative substances.

Moss is a plant that the wisest of kings thought neither unworthy of his speculation nor his pen; and though among plants it is in bulk one of the smallest, yet it is not the least considerable. For, as to its shape, it may compare for its beauty with any plant that grows and bears a much greater breadth. It has a root almost like a seedy parsnip, furnished with small strings and suckers, which are all of them finely branched, like those of the roots of much bigger vegetables. Out of this springs the stem or body of the plant, which is somewhat quadrangular, rather than cylindrical, most curiously fluted or strung with small creases, which run, for the most part, parallel to the whole stem. On the sides of this are closely and thickly set a multitude of fair, large, well-shaped leaves, some of them of a rounder, others of a longer shape, according as they are younger or older when plucked; as I guess by this, that those plants that had the stalks growing from the top of them had their leaves of a much longer shape, all the surface of each side of which is curiously covered with a multitude of little oblong transparent bodies, in the manner as you see it expressed in the leaf B, in the XIII. scheme.

This plant, when young and springing up, much resembles a houseleek, having thick leaves almost like that, and seems to be somewhat of kin to it in other particulars; also from the top of the leaves, there shoots out a small white and transparent hair, or thorn. This stem, in time, comes to shoot out into a long, round, and even stalk, which by cutting transversely when dry, I manifestly found to be a stiff, hard, and hollow cane or reed, without any kind of knot or stop from its bottom, where the leaves encompassed it, to the top, on which there grows a large seed case, A, covered with a thin and more whitish skin, B, terminated in a long thorny top, which at first covers all the case, and by degrees, as that swells, the skin cleaves, and at length falls off with its thorny top and all (which is a part of it) and leaves the seed case to ripen, and by degrees, to shatter out its seed at a place underneath this cap, B, which before the seed is ripe, appears like a flat barred button, without any hole in the middle; but as it ripens, the button grows bigger, and a hole appears in the middle of it, E, out of which, in all probability, the seed falls. For as it ripens by a provision of Nature, that end of this case turns downward after the same manner as the ears of wheat and barley usually do; and opening several of these dry red cases, F, I found them to be

quite hollow, without anything at all in them; whereas when I cut them asunder with a sharp penknife when green, I found in the middle of this great case another smaller round case. Between these two, the interstices were filled with multitudes of stringy fibers, which seemed to suspend the smaller case in the middle of the other. This (as far as I was able to discern) seemed full of exceedingly small white seeds, much like the seed-bag in the bud of a carnation after the flowers have been fallen off for two or three days, or a week; but I could not discern this perfectly, and therefore cannot positively affirm it.

After the seed had fallen away, I found both the case, stalk, and plant all grew red and withered, and from other parts of the root, new branches or slips continually sprang, which by degrees increased and grew as big as the former, seeded, ripened, shattered, and withered.

I could not find that it observed any particular seasons for these several kinds of growth, but rather found it to be springing, mature, ripe, seedy, and withered at all times of the year; but I found it most to flourish and increase in warm and moist weather.

It gathers its nourishment, for the most part, out of some stony or other substance corrupted or changed from its former texture or substantial form; for I have found it to grow on the rotten parts of stone, of bricks, of wood, of bones, of leather, *etc.*

It often grows on the bark of several trees, spreading itself sometimes from the ground upwards, and sometimes from some chink or cleft of the bark of the tree which has some putrefied substance in it; but this seems of a distinct kind from that which I observed to grow on putrefied inanimate bodies and rotten earth.

There are also great varieties of other kinds of mosses which grow on trees and several other plants, of which I shall make no mention here, nor of the moss growing on the skull of a dead man, which much resembles that of trees.

Whether this plant sometimes originally springs or rises out of corruption without any disseminated seed, I have not yet made enough trials to be very positive or negative. For as it seems very hard to conceive how the seed should be generally dispersed into all parts where a corruption has begun, unless we may rationally suppose that this seed—being so exceedingly small and consequently exceedingly light—is thereby taken up and carried to and fro in the air into every place, and by the falling drops of rain is washed down out of it and so dispersed into all places, and there only takes root and propagates where it finds a convenient soil or matrix for it to thrive in; so if we will have it proceed from corruption, it is no less difficult to conceive,

First, how the corruption of any vegetable, much less of any stone or brick, should be the parent of so curiously figured and so perfect a plant as this is. But here indeed, I cannot but add that it seems rather to be a product of the rain in those bodies where it is stayed, than of the very bodies themselves, since I have found it growing on marble and flint; but always the *Microscope*, if not the naked eye, would discover some little hole of dirt in which it was rooted.
