->MICROGRAPHIA.<-

Next, how the corruption of each of those exceedingly different bodies should all conspire to produce the same plant—that is, that stones, bricks, wood, or vegetable substances, and bones, leather, horns, or animate substances—unless we may with some plausibility say that air and water are the helpers, or *menstruums*, in all kinds of putrefactions. Thereby, though the bodies were of exceedingly different natures while they retained their substantial forms, they may be very homogeneous since they are dissolved and mixed into another. They are almost resolved again into air, water, and earth, perhaps retaining one part of their vegetative faculty yet entire; which, meeting with suitable assistants, such as the heat of the air and the fluidity of the water and similar helpers and conveniences, acquires a certain growth for a time, wholly differing perhaps from that kind of growth it had before.

To explain my meaning a little better by a simple similitude: Suppose a curious piece of clockwork that had several motions and contrivances in it which, when in order, would all have moved in their designed methods and periods. We will further suppose, by some means, that this clock becomes broken, damaged, or otherwise disordered, so that several parts of it being displaced are obstructed, and so stand still, not only hindering its own progressive motion and failing to produce the effect they were designed for, but because the other parts also have a dependence upon them, they put a stop to their motion likewise; and so the whole instrument becomes unserviceable and not fit for any use. This instrument afterwards, by some shaking and tumbling and throwing up and down, comes to have several of its parts shaken out, and several of its curious motions, contrivances, and particles all fall asunder; here a pin falls out, and there a pillar, and here a wheel, and there a hammer and a spring, and the like; and among the rest, away fall those parts also which were damaged and disordered, and had all this while obstructed the motion of all the rest. Upon this, several of those other motions that yet remain, whose springs were not quite run down, being now at liberty, begin each of them to move in this or that way, but quite after another method than before, there being many regulating parts and the like fallen away and lost. Because of this, the owner, who chances to hear and observe some of these effects, being ignorant of the watchmaker's art, wonders what has happened to his clock and immediately imagines that some artist has been at work and has set his clock in order and made a new kind of instrument of it. But upon examining the circumstances, he finds there was no such matter, but that the casual slipping out of a pin had made several parts of his clock fall to pieces, and that thereby the obstacle that all this while hindered his clock, together with other useful parts, were fallen out, and so his clock was set at liberty. And upon winding up those springs again when run down, he finds his clock to go, but quite in another manner than it was accustomed to previously.

And thus may it be perhaps in the matter of moss, mold, and mushrooms, and several other spontaneous kinds of growth, which

may be caused by a vegetative principle, which was a helper to the life and growth of the larger vegetable, and was by the destroying of its life stopped and hindered from performing its office; but afterwards, upon a further corruption of several parts that had hindered it all the while, the heat of the Sun winding up the spring, as it were, sets it again into a vegetative motion. This being single, and not at all regulated as it was before (when it was a part of that larger machine, the original vegetable), it is moved in quite a different manner, and produces effects very different from those it did before.

But I propose this only as a conjecture, not because I am more inclined to this *Hypothesis* than the seminal one, which I guess for good reason to be mechanical also, as I may elsewhere more fully show. But I do so because I may, by this, hint at a possible way how this appearance may be solved, supposing we should be driven to confess—from certain experiments and observations made—that such or such vegetables were produced out of the corruption of another, without any concurrent seminal principle (as I have given some reason to suppose in the description of a *microscopical mushroom*), without derogating at all from the infinite wisdom of the Creator. For this accidental production, as I may call it, demonstrates as much, if not very much more, of the excellence of his design than anything in the more perfect vegetative bodies of the world, even as the accidental motion of the *Automaton* makes the owner see that there was much more design in it than he at first imagined. But of this I have added more in the description of *Mould*, and the vegetables on *Rose leaves, etc.*, those being much more likely to have their origin from such a cause than this which I have described here in the 13th *scheme*, which indeed I cannot conceive of otherwise than as a most perfect vegetable, lacking nothing of the perfections of the most conspicuous and largest vegetables of the world, and being of a rank so high that it may very properly be reckoned with the tall *cedar of Lebanon*, as that Kingly Botanist <note>A reference to King Solomon, who was said to have described plants from the cedar to the hyssop.</note> has done.

We know there may be as much intricacy of design and excellence of form in a very small pocket-watch that takes up less than an inch square of space as there may be in a church clock that fills a whole room. And I do not know whether all the designs and *mechanisms* required for a perfect vegetable may not be crowded into an exceedingly smaller space than this *moss*, just as I have heard of a striking watch so small that it served for a pendant in a lady’s ear; and I have already given you the description of a plant growing on *rose leaves* that is abundantly smaller than *moss*, so much so that near 1,000 of them would hardly equal the size of one single plant of *moss*. And by comparing the bulk of *moss* with the bulk of the largest kind of vegetable we meet with in history (of which kind we find in some hotter climates, such as *Guinea* and *Brazil*, the trunk or body of some trees to be twenty feet in diameter, whereas the body or stem of *moss*, for the most part, is not more than one-sixtieth of an inch), we shall find that the bulk of the one will exceed the bulk of the other by no less than 2,985,984 million,

So prodigiously various are the works of the Creator, and so all-sufficient is he to perform what to man would seem impossible; they being both alike easy to him, even as one day and a thousand years are to him as one and the same time.

I have taken notice of such an infinite variety of those smaller kinds of vegetation that, had I described every one of them, they would almost have filled a volume and proved large enough to have made a new herbal. Such multitudes are to be found in moist, hot weather, especially in the summer time, on all kinds of putrefying substances; whether they more properly belong to the *classes* of *mushrooms*, or *molds*, or *mosses*, I shall not now dispute, as there are some that seem more properly of one kind and others of another, their colors and sizes being as different as their shapes and substances.

Nay, I have observed that by putting clean water (whether rain water, pump water, May dew, or snow water, it was almost all the same)—I have often observed, I say, that this water would, with a little standing, tarnish and cover all the sides of the glass that lay under water with a lovely green. But though I have often endeavored to discover with my *microscope* whether this green were like moss, or long striped seaweed, or any other peculiar form, yet so poor and imperfect are our *microscopes* that I could not certainly distinguish any.

Living trees also, and any kinds of wood, stones, bones, etc., that have been long exposed to the air and rain, will be covered all over with a greenish scurf, which will very much stain and turn green any kind of clothes that are rubbed against it. Viewing this, I could not certainly perceive a definite form in many parts of it, though in many I could perceive a bed, as it were, of young moss; but in other parts it looked almost like green bushes and very confused. However, regardless of whatever irregular shapes the parts appeared to have, they were always green and seemed to be either some vegetable or to have some vegetating principle.

### Observation XXII. *Of common sponges, and several other spongy fibrous bodies.*

A sponge is commonly reckoned among the <term>zoophytes</term>, or plant-animals; and the *texture* of it, which the *microscope* discovers, seems to confirm it. For it is of a form unlike any other vegetable I have ever observed, and indeed, it seems impossible that any should be of it, for it consists of an infinite number of small short fibers, or nervous parts, of much the same size, curiously jointed or woven together in the form of a net, as is more plainly manifest by the little illustration which I have added

<summary>Hooke discusses the immense variety and staggering number of microscopic plants found on decaying matter and submerged surfaces before transitioning to a microscopic analysis of the net-like structure of sponges.</summary>
<keywords>microscopy, botany, spontaneous generation, Robert Hooke, sponges, zoophytes, decomposition, microbiology</keywords>

--- Page 200 ---
<meta>This page transitions from Hooke's discussion on microscopic vegetation and molds to his detailed observation of the structure of a sponge under the microscope.</meta>

->M I C R O G R A P H I A.<-

added in the third *Figure* of the IX. *Scheme*, of a piece of it, which you may perceive represents a confused heap of the *fibrous* parts curiously jointed and entwined. The joints are, for the most part, where only three *fibres* meet, for I have very seldom met with any that had four.

At these joints, no one of the three seems to be the stock upon which the others grow, but each of the *fibres* is, for the most part, of an equal size and seems to have an equal share in the joint; the *fibres* are all of much the same size, not smaller toward the top of the sponge and larger near the bottom or root, as is usual in plants. The length of each between the joints is very irregular and different; the distance between some two joints being ten or twelve times more than between some others.

Nor are the joints regular and of an *equitriagonal figure* <note>an equilateral triangle</note>, but for the most part, the three *fibres* meet so that they compose three angles that are all very different from one another.

The meshes likewise, and holes of this reticulated body, are no less various and irregular: some *bilateral*, others *trilateral*, and *quadrilateral figures*; indeed, I have observed some meshes to have 5, 6, 7, 8, or 9 sides, and some to have only one, so exceedingly various is the *Lusus Naturae* <note>the play of nature</note> in this body.

As to the outward appearance of this *vegetative* body, they are so common everywhere that I need not describe them, consisting of a soft and porous substance resembling a lock, sometimes a fleece of wool. But besides these small *microscopical* pores which lie between the *fibres*, it has a multitude of round pores or holes which pierce into the body from the top and sometimes go quite through to the bottom.

I have observed many of these sponges to have included, likewise in the midst of their fibrous textures, quite large crumbly stones, which must either have been enclosed while this vegetable was in formation or generated in those places after it was perfectly shaped. The latter of which seems the more improbable because I did not find that any of these stony substances were perforated with the *fibres* of the sponge.

I have never seen nor been informed of the true manner of sponges growing on a rock: whether they are found to increase from small to large like vegetables (that is, part by part), or like animals (all parts growing together equally); or whether they be *matrices* <note>breeding places or wombs</note> or seed-bags of any kind of fish or some kind of watery *insect*; or whether they are at any time more soft and tender, or of another nature and texture—things which, if I knew them, I would very much desire to be informed of. But from a cursory view that I first made with my *microscope* and some other trials, I supposed it to be some animal substance cast out and fastened upon the rocks in the form of a froth or *congeries* <note>a collection or mass</note> of bubbles—like that which I have often observed on rosemary and other plants (wherein a little *insect* is included)—and that all the little films which divide these bubbles from one another did, almost immediately after the substance began to grow a little harder, break and leave only the thread behind, which might be, as it were, the angle or thread between the bubbles, that the

->M I C R O G R A P H I A.<-

The great holes or pores observable in these sponges were made by the eruption of the included heterogeneous substance (whether air, or some other body, for many other fluid bodies will do the same thing) which, breaking out of the lesser [pores], were collected into very large bubbles and so might make their way out of the sponge, leaving a round cavity in their passage. If the bubble were large, it might carry up the adjacent bubbles with it, which may be perceived on the outside of the sponge if it is first thoroughly wetted and allowed to plump itself into its natural form, or if it is then wrung dry and allowed to expand itself again—which it will freely do while moist. For when it has thus plumped itself into its natural shape and dimensions, it is obvious enough that the mouths of the larger holes have a kind of lip or rising around them, but the other smaller pores have little or none. It may further be found that each of these great pores has many other small pores below that are united unto it and help to constitute it, almost like so many rivulets or small streams that contribute to the maintenance of a large river. Nor from this *Hypothesis* would it have been difficult to explain how those little branches of coral, small stones, shells, and the like, come to be included by these frothy bodies. But this indeed was but a conjecture; and upon a more accurate inquiry into its form with the *Microscope*, it seems not to be their true origin; for whereas sponges have only three arms which join together at each knot, if they had been generated from bubbles they must have had four.

But that they are Animal Substances, the chemical examination of them seems to manifest; they afford a volatile salt and spirit, like *Harts-Horn* <note>The horn of a stag, historically used as a source of ammonia</note>, as does also their great strength and toughness, and their smell when burned in the fire or a candle, which has a kind of fleshy scent, not much unlike to hair. And having since examined several authors concerning them, among others, I find this account given by *Bellonius* <note>Pierre Belon, a 16th-century French naturalist</note>, in the 11th chapter of his second book, *De Aquatilibus*.

> "Fresh sponges," says he, "are far different from dry ones; they cling to the rocks of the sea at a depth of two or three cubits, sometimes only four inches, and like mushrooms on trees, they are filled with a certain foul juice or rather a mucous discharge, so fetid that it excites nausea even from a distance. This is contained in those cavities which we see empty in dry and washed sponges. They appear black, like a rotting lung, but those which grow in shallow water are suffused with a much more opaque blackness. Aristotle considers that sponges live by adhering, though not absolutely; and they are believed to have some sense, he says, by this argument: that they are very difficult to pull away unless it is done secretly. At the approach of the puller, they contract so much that it is difficult to tear them away, which they also do whenever winds and storms press upon them. I think that the foul juice we mentioned above was given to them by nature in place of flesh, and that they use the wider passages as intestines or internal organs. Furthermore, the part where the sponge adheres to the rocks is like the stalk of a leaf, from which a sort of slender neck begins, which then, spreading into a width, forms the globe of a head. In fresh ones, nothing is pipe-like, and they cling as if by roots. Above, almost all the passages lie hidden and closed; but below, four or five are open, through which..."

*eas fugere existimamus.* From which description, they seem to be a kind of plant-animal that adheres to a rock, and these small fibers or threads which we have described seem to have been the *vessels* which (it is very probable) were very much larger while the *interstitia* [interstitial spaces] were filled (as he affirms) with a mucous, pulpy, or fleshy substance; but upon drying, they shrank into the size they now appear.

The texture of it is such that I have not yet met with any other body in the world that has the like, except only one of a larger sort of sponge (which is preserved in the *Museum Harveanum* belonging to the most illustrious and most learned Society of the *Physicians* of *London*) which is of a horny, or rather of a petrified substance. And of this indeed, the texture and make is exactly the same as common sponges, except only that both the holes and the fibers, or texture of it, are exceedingly much larger; for some of the holes were over an inch and a half across, and the fibers and texture of it were large enough to be distinguished easily with one's eye, but conspicuously with an ordinary single *Microscope*. And these indeed seemed to have been the habitation of some animal; and examining *Aristotle*, I find a very consistent account regarding this, namely, that he had known a certain little animal, called *Pinnothera*, like a spider, to be bred in those caverns of a sponge, from within which, by opening and closing those holes, he ensnares and catches the little fishes; and in another place he says that it is very confidently reported that there are certain *moths or worms* that reside in the cavities of a sponge and are nourished there. Notwithstanding all these *histories*, I think it well worth investigating the *history* and nature of a sponge, as it seems to promise some information about the *vessels* in animal substances (which, because of the solidity of the inserted flesh that is not easily removed without also destroying those interspersed *vessels*, are hitherto undiscovered); whereas here in a sponge, the *parenchyma*, it seems, is but a kind of mucous jelly, which is very easily and clearly washed away.

The reason that makes me imagine that there may probably be some such texture in animal substances is that, examining the texture of the filaments of tanned leather, I find it to be much of the same nature and strength as a sponge; and with my *Microscope*, I have observed many such joints and knobs as I have described in sponges. The fibers also in the hollow of several sorts of *bones*, after the *marrow* has been removed, I have found somewhat to resemble this texture, though, I confess, I never yet found any texture exactly the same, nor any comparable to it for intricacy.

The filaments of it are much smaller than those of *silk*, and through the *Microscope* appear nearly as transparent; indeed, some parts of them I have observed to be much more so.

Having examined also several kinds of *mushrooms*, I find their texture to be somewhat of this kind; that is, to consist of an infinite company of small filaments, interwoven and woven together in every way so as to make a kind of cloth; and more particularly, examining a piece of *touch-wood* (which is a kind of *Jew's-ear*, or *mushroom*, growing here in *England* also,

The filaments I could plainly enough perceive to be even, round, cylindrical, transparent bodies, and to cross each other every way—that is, there were no more that seemed to lie horizontally than perpendicularly and across—so that it is somewhat difficult to conceive how they should grow in that manner. By tearing off a small piece of it and looking on the ragged edge, I could among several of those fibers perceive small joints—that is, one of those hairs split into two, each of the same bigness with the other out of which they seemed to grow—but having not lately had an opportunity of examining their manner of growth, I cannot positively affirm anything of them.

But to proceed, the swelling of sponges upon wetting and the rising of the water in it above the surface of the water that it touches are both from the same cause, of which an account is already given in the sixth observation.

The substance of them indeed has so many excellent properties, scarcely to be met with in any other body in the world, that I have often wondered that so little use is made of it, and those only vile and sordid; certainly, if it were well considered, it would afford much greater conveniences.

### Observ. XXIII. *Of the curious texture of Sea-weeds.*

**F**or curiosity and beauty, I have not among all the plants or vegetables I have yet observed seen any one comparable to this sea-weed I have here described, of which I am able to say very little more than what is represented by the second *Figure* of the ninth *Scheme*: namely, that it is a plant which grows upon the rocks under the water, and increases and spreads itself into a great tuft, which is not only handsomely branched into several leaves, but the whole surface of the plant is covered over with a most curious kind of carved work, which consists of a texture much resembling a honeycomb; for the whole surface on both sides is covered over with a multitude of very small holes, being no bigger than so many holes made with the point of a small pin, and ranged in the neatest and most delicate order imaginable, they being placed in the manner of a *Quincunx*, or very much like the rows of the eyes of a fly, the rows or orders being very regular, whichever way they are observed: what the texture was, as it appeared through a pretty big magnifying microscope, I have here adjoined in the first *Figure* of the 14th *Scheme*, which round Area A B C D represents a part of the surface about one-eighth part of an inch in diameter: those little holes, which to the eye looked round, like so many little spots, here appeared very regularly shaped holes, representing almost the shape of the sole of a round-toed shoe, the hinder part of which is, as it were, trod on or covered by the toe of that next below it; these holes seemed walled about with a very thin and transparent substance, looking of a pale straw color; from the edge of which, against the middle of each hole, were sprouted out four small transparent straw-colored thorns, which seemed to protect and cover those cavities, two from either side; near the root of this plant, were sprouted out several small branches of a kind of bastard <term>Coralline</term>, curiously branched, though small.

### Observation XXIV. *Of the surfaces of Rosemary, and other leaves.*

This, which is depicted within the circle of the second *figure* of the 14th *scheme*, is a small part of the back or underside of a leaf of rosemary. I did not choose it because it had anything unique which was not observable with a *microscope* in several other plants, but because it exhibits at one view:

First, a smooth and shining surface, namely, A B, which is a part of the upper side of the leaf that appears on this side by a kind of hem or doubling of the leaf. There are multitudes of leaves whose surfaces are smooth like this, and as if quilted, which look like a curious quilted bag of green silk, or like a bladder, or some such pliable transparent substance, fully stuffed with a green juice or liquor. The surface of *rue*, or *herb-grass*, is polished and indented or pitted all over, like the *silk-worm's egg*, which I shall describe shortly; the smooth surfaces of other plants are quilted in different ways, Nature in this, as it were, expressing her needlework or embroidery.

Next, a downy or bushy surface, such as is almost the entire underside, appearing through the *microscope* much like a thicket of bushes. The leaves and stalks of multitudes of *vegetables* are covered with this kind of down or hair; and there seems to be as great a variety in the shape, size, and manner of growth of these "secondary plants," as I may call them (they being, as it were, a plant growing out of a plant, or somewhat like the hairs of *animals*), as there is to be found among small shrubs that compose bushes. But for the most part, they consist of small transparent parts, some of which grow in the shape of small needles or bodkins, as on the *thistle*, *cowhage-pod* <note>The original "Cowag-ecod" refers to the stinging hairs of the cowhage plant.</note> and *nettle*; others in the form of *cat's claws*, as in *cleavers* <note>The original "Cliders" refers to the plant Galium aparine.</note>, the beards of *barley*, the edges of several sorts of *grass* and *reeds*, *etc.* In others, such as *coltsfoot*, *rose-campion*, *aspen* <note>The original "Aps" is an archaic term for the aspen tree.</note>, *poplar*, *willow*, and almost all other downy plants, they grow in the form of bushes, very diversified in each particular plant. But whatever their use may be, they afford a very pleasant object through the *microscope*, and may perhaps, upon further examination, prove very luciferous <note>enlightening or informative</note>.

## Observation XXV. *Of the stinging points and juice of nettles, and some other venomous plants.*

A nettle is a plant so well known to everyone, in terms of what its appearance is to the naked eye, that it needs no description; and there are very few who have not felt as well as seen it. Therefore, it will be no news to tell that a gentle and slight touch of the skin by a nettle often not only creates very sensible and acute pain, much like that of a burn or scald, but also often very angry and hard swellings and inflammations of the parts, such as will immediately rise and continue swollen for several hours. These observations, I say, are common enough; but how the pain is so suddenly created, and by what means it is continued, increased for a time, and afterwards diminished, and at length quite extinguished, has not, as far as I know, been explained by anyone.

And here we must have recourse to our *microscope*; and that will, if almost any part of the plant be looked upon, show us the whole surface of it set very thick with turnpikes <note>spikes or defensive barriers</note>, or sharp needles, of the shape of those represented in the 15th *scheme* and first *figure* by A B, which are visible also to the naked eye. Each of these consists of two parts, very distinct in shape and also differing in quality from one another. For the part A is shaped very much like a round bodkin <note>a sharp, slender tool for piercing</note>, tapering from B until it ends in a very sharp point; it is of a substance very hard and stiff, exceedingly transparent and clear, and, as I certainly found by many trials, is hollow from top to bottom.

This I found by this experiment: I had a very convenient *micro-*

But the base underneath these bodkins on which they were fixed, were made of a more pliable substance, and looked almost like a little bag of green leather, or rather resembled the shape and surface of a wild cucumber, or *cucumeris asinini*, and I could plainly perceive them to be certain little bags, or receptacles full of water, or as I guess, the liquid of the plant, which was poisonous, and those small bodkins were but the syringe-pipes, or clyster-pipes, which first made way into the skin, and then served to convey that poisonous juice, upon the pressing of those little bags, into the interior and sensitive parts of the skin, which being so discharged, does corrode, or, as it were, burn that part of the skin it touches; and this pain will sometimes last very long, according as the impression is made deeper or stronger.

The other parts of the leaf or surface of the nettle, have very little noteworthy, except what is common to most of these kinds of plants, as the ruggedness or indenting, and hairiness, and other roughness of the surface or outside of the plant, of which I may say more in another place. As I shall likewise of certain little pretty clear balls or apples which I have observed to stick to the sides of these leaves, both on the upper and under side, very much like the small apples which I have often observed to grow on the leaves of an oak called *oak-apples* which are nothing but the *matrices* of an insect, as I elsewhere show.

The chief thing therefore is, how this plant comes, by so slight a touch, to create so great a pain; and the reason of this seems to be nothing else, but the corrosive penetrant liquid contained in the small bags or bladders, upon which grow out those sharp syringe-pipes, as I before noted; and very consistent with this, is the reason of the pain created by the sting of a bee, wasp, etc., as I elsewhere show: For by the dart, which is likewise a pipe, a deep passage is made into the skin, and then by the anger of the fly, is his gall-like poisonous liquid injected; which being admitted among the sensitive parts, and so mixed with the humours or stagnating juices of that part, creates an ebullition perhaps, or *effervescence*, as is usually observed in the mingling of two different chemical saline liquids, by which means the parts become swelled, hard, and very painful; for thereby the nervous and sensitive parts are not only stretched and strained

beyond their natural state, but are also pricked, perhaps, or corroded by the pungent and incompatible particles of the intruded liquid.

And this seems to be the reason why *Aqua fortis* <note>nitric acid</note>, and other saline liquids, if they come to touch the sensitive parts, as in a cut of the skin or the like, do so violently and intolerably cause pain and torment the patient. And it is not unlikely that the inventors of that diabolical practice of poisoning the points of arrows and daggers might have received their first hint from some such instance in natural contrivances as this of the nettle. For the reason why such poisoned weapons kill so reliably as they do seems no different than this of our nettle's stinging; for the dagger or dart makes a passage or entrance into the sensitive or vital parts of the body, whereby the contagious substance comes to be dissolved by, and mixed with, the fluid parts or humors of the body, and by that means spreads itself by degrees into the whole liquid part of the body, in the same manner as a few grains of salt, put into a great quantity of water, will by degrees diffuse itself over the whole.

And this I take to be the reason for the killing of toads, frogs, efts <note>newts</note>, and several fishes by strewing salt on their backs (which experiment was shown to the *Royal Society* by a very ingenious gentleman and a worthy member of it); for those creatures always have a continual exudation, as it were, of slimy and watery parts sweating out of the pores of their skin, and the saline particles, by that means, obtain a *vehicle* <note>a medium for transmission</note> which conveys them into the internal and vital parts of the body.

This seems also to be the reason why bathing in mineral waters are such sovereign remedies for a multitude of distempers, especially chronic ones; for the liquid and warm vehicles of the mineral particles, which are known to be in very considerable quantities in those healing baths, do—by the body's long stay in them—gradually soak and insinuate themselves into the pores and parts of the skin. Thereby those mineral particles have their ways and passages opened to penetrate into the inner parts and mingle themselves with the stagnant juices of the several parts. Besides, many of those offensive parts which were united with those stagnant juices, and which were contrary to the natural constitution of the parts, and so became irksome and painful to the body but could not be discharged because Nature had made no provision for such accidental mischiefs, are—by means of this soaking and filling the pores of the skin with a liquid—afforded a passage through that liquid that fills the pores into the surrounding fluid, and thereby the body comes to be discharged of them.

So it is very evident that there may be a good as well as an evil application of this principle. And the ingenious invention of that excellent person, Doctor *Wren* <note>Christopher Wren</note>, of injecting liquids into the veins of an animal, seems to be reducible to this head. I cannot stay, nor is this a fit place, to mention the several experiments of this kind made by the most incomparable Mr. *Boyle*, or the many made by the lately mentioned physician Doctor *Clark* <note>Timothy Clarke</note>, the *history* of which, as he has been pleased to communicate to the *Royal Society*, so he may perhaps be prevailed upon to publish himself. But I shall rather hint that certainly, if this principle

If these matters were well considered, there might—besides the further improvement of bathing and syringing into the veins—be thought of several ways by which several obstinate diseases of a human body, such as the gout, dropsy, stone, etc., might be mastered and expelled; and good men might make as good a use of it as evil men have made a perverse and diabolical one.

And that the filling of the pores of the skin with some fluid *vehicle* <note>a medium for transmission</note> is of no small efficacy toward preparing a passage for several kinds of penetrating juices and other soluble bodies to insinuate themselves within the skin and into the sensitive parts of the body, may be, I think, proved by an instance given to us by *Bellonius* <note>Pierre Belon, a 16th-century French naturalist</note> in the 26th chapter of the second book of his *Observations*. This contains a very remarkable story which I have here transcribed: 

"When we were supervising the digging up of the roots of the black Chameleon thistle," he says, "near a village named Livadochorio, many Greeks and Turks came to watch what we were digging up. We were cutting them into small pieces and threading them on a string so they could be dried more easily. The Turks, seeing us busy with that task, likewise wanted to handle and cut those roots. But since the heat was extreme and everyone was dripping with sweat, whoever had handled that root and wiped away their sweat, or scratched their face with their fingers, afterward felt such a great itching in the places they had touched that they seemed to be burned. For the root of the black Chameleon is so powerful that, when applied to the skin, it inflames it so much that neither squill nor any nettle burns even a hundredth part as much. However, the itching does not show itself so quickly. After one or two hours, however, we each began to have the skin on various parts of our faces so inflamed that the whole appeared bloody; and the more we rubbed it, the more the itching was excited. We were sitting by a fountain under a plane tree, and at first we treated it as a joke and laughed; but eventually they became very indignant, and if we had not sworn that we had never known that plant to possess such power, they undoubtedly would have treated us badly. Yet our excuse was more easily accepted by them when they saw us affected by the same misfortune. It is indeed a marvel that we experienced such immense efficacy to our harm in such a small root."

By this observation of his, it seems manifest that their being all covered with sweat while they gathered and cut this root of the black Chameleon thistle was the great reason why they suffered that inconvenience; for it seems the like circumstance had not been noted before that, nor do I find any mention of such a property belonging to this vegetable in any of the herbals I have at present with me.

I could give very many observations which I have made of this kind, whereby I have found that the best way to get a substance to be insinuated into the material or insensible pores of another is, first, to find a fluid *vehicle* that has some congruity both to the substance to be insinuated and to the body into whose pores you would have the other conveyed. And in this principle lies the great mystery of staining several sorts of bodies, such as marble, woods, bones, *etc.* and of dyeing silks, cloths, wools, feathers, *etc.* But these being digressions, I shall proceed to:

> *Phaseolus siliqua hirsuta*; The hairy kidney bean, called in Surat <note>Historically Zurratte</note> where it grows, Cowhage: We have had (says he) another of this kind brought to us out of the East Indies, which being planted, was in appearance like the former, but did not come to perfection, the unfavorable season not allowing it to show the flower; but of the pods that were brought, some were smaller, shorter, and rounder than the garden variety; others much longer, and many growing together, as if in clusters, and covered all over with a brown short hairiness, so fine, that if any of it be rubbed, or fall on the back of one's hand, or other tender parts of the skin, it will cause a kind of itching, but not strong, nor long-enduring, but passing quickly away, without either danger or harm; the beans were smaller than ordinary, and of a black shining color.

Having one of these pods given to me by a sea captain, who had frequently visited those parts, I found it to be a small pod, about three inches long, much like a short pod of **French beans**, which had six beans in it; the whole surface of it was covered over with a very thick and shining brown down or hair, which was very fine, and for its size, stiff. Taking some of this down and rubbing it on the back of my hand, I experienced very little or no trouble; I was only sensible that several of these little downy parts, through rubbing, did penetrate and were sunk, or stuck pretty deep, into my skin. After I had rubbed it thus for a good while, I felt very little or no pain, insomuch that I doubted whether it were the true Cowhage; but while I was considering this, I found the down begin to make my hand itch, and in some places to smart, much like the stinging of a flea or gnat. This continued for a good while, so that by degrees I found my skin to be swelled with little red pustules, and to look as if it were itchy. But leaving it alone without rubbing or scratching, the itching, tickling pain quickly grew faint, and within an hour I felt nothing at all, and the little protuberances had vanished.

The cause of this odd phenomenon, I suppose, is much the same as that of the stinging of a nettle; for by the **microscope**, I discovered this down to consist of a multitude of small and slender conical bodies, much resembling needles or bodkins, such as are represented by A B, C D, and E F of the first figure of the 16th **Scheme**; their ends A A A were very sharp, and their substance was stiff and hard, much like the substance of several kinds of thorns and hooks growing on trees. And though they appeared very clear and transparent, yet I could not perceive whether they were hollow or not; to me they appeared like solid transparent bodies, without any cavity in them. Whether they might not be a kind of cane, filled with some transparent liquor which had hardened (because the pod I had was very dry), I was not able to examine.

Now, being such stiff, sharp bodies, it is easy to conceive how, with rubbing, they might easily be thrust into the tender parts of the skin, and there, by reason of their exceeding fineness and dryness, not create any considerable trouble or pain, until by remaining in those places moistened with the humors of the body, some caustic part sticking on them, or residing

## Observation XXVII. *Of the Beard of a wild Oat, and the use that may be made of it for exhibiting always to the eye the temperature of the air, as to dryness and moisture.*

This beard of a wild *oat* is a body of a very curious structure, though to the naked eye it appears very slight and inconsiderable, being only a small black or brown beard or bristle which grows out of the side of the inner husk that covers the grain of a wild *oat*. The whole length of it, when put in water so that it may extend itself to its full length, is not above an inch and a half, and for the most part somewhat shorter; but when the grain is ripe and very dry, which is usually in the months of *July* and *August*, this beard is bent somewhat below the middle—namely, about two-thirds from the bottom of it—almost to a right angle, and the under part of it is twisted like a withe; the substance of it is very brittle when dry, and it will very easily be broken from the husk on which it grows.

If you take one of these grains and wet the beard in water, you will presently see the small bent top turn and move round, as if it were sensitive; and by degrees, if it is kept wet enough, the joint or knee will straighten itself; and if it is allowed to dry again, it will by degrees move round another way, and at length bend again into its former posture.

If it is viewed with an ordinary single *microscope*, it will appear like a small twisted sprig with two clefts; and if wet as before, and then looked at with this *microscope*, it will appear to untwist itself, and by degrees to straighten its knee, and the two clefts will become straight and almost on opposite sides of the small cylindrical body.

If it continues to be looked at a little longer with a *microscope*, it will within a little while begin to twist itself again, and soon after return to its former posture, bending itself again near the middle into a kind of knee or angle.

Several of those bodies I examined with larger *microscopes*, and there found them much like the construction of those two long twisted cylinders delineated in the second figure of the 15th *scheme*, which two cylinders represent

This so oddly constituted vegetable substance was first (that I have encountered) noticed by *Baptista Porta* in his *Natural Magick* as a thing known to children and jugglers; it has been called by some of those last named persons, the better to cover their cheat, the "Leg of an *Arabian spider*" or the "Leg of an enchanted *Egyptian Fly*," and has been used by them to make a small index, cross, or the like, to move round upon the wetting of it with a drop of water and the muttering of certain words.

But the use that has been made of it for the discovery of the various conditions of the air regarding dryness and moistness is incomparably beyond any other, for this it does to admiration. The manner of contriving it so as to perform this great effect is only thus:

Provide a good large box of ivory, about four inches across, and of what depth you shall judge convenient (according to your intention of making use of one, two, three, or more of these small beards, ordered in the manner which I shall describe shortly). Let all the sides of this box be turned with basket-work (which here in *London* is easily enough procured) full of holes, in the manner almost of a lattice; the larger or more numerous the holes are, the better, so that the air may have the more free passage to the enclosed beard and may more easily pass through the instrument. ...presented in the 4th Figure of the 15th *Scheme*. Or, if you intend to use many of these small beards joined together, you may have a small, long case of ivory, whose sides are turned like basket-work and full of holes, which may be screwed onto the underside of a broad plate of ivory; on the other side of this is to be made the divided ring or circle. To these divisions, the pointing of the hand or index, which is moved by the joined beard, may show all the *minute* variations of the air.

There may be multitudes of other ways for designing this small instrument so as to produce this effect, which anyone may, according to his specific use and the requirements of his current occasion, easily enough devise and use, on which I shall not, therefore, dwell. The entire manner of making any one of them is as follows: Having your box or frame A A B B appropriately adapted for the free passage of the air through it, in the middle of the bottom B B B, you must have a very small hole C, into which the lower end of the beard is to be fixed; the upper end of this beard, a b, is to pass through a small hole of a plate or top A A, if you use only a single one, and on the top of it, e, is to be fixed a small and very light *index f g*, made of a very thin sliver of a reed or cane. But if you use two or more beards, they must be fixed and bound together, either with a very fine piece of silk, or with a very small dab of hard wax, or glue (which is better), and the *index f g* is to be fixed on the top of the second, third, or fourth in the same manner as on a single one.

Now, because in each of these designs the *index f g* will, with certain conditions of the air, move two, three, or more times around—which, without some mechanism other than this, will be difficult to distinguish—I therefore thought of this expedient: The *index* or *hand f g* being raised a fair distance above the surface of the plate A A, fix a small pin *h* at a little distance from its center, so as almost to touch the surface of the plate A A; and then in any convenient place on the surface of the plate, fix a small pin upon which you put a small piece of paper, thin pasteboard, vellum, or parchment, made of a convenient size and shaped in the manner of that shown in the figure as *i k*. So, having a suitable number of teeth, every turn or return of the pin *h* may move this small indented circle one tooth forward or backward; by which means, as the teeth of the circle are marked, it will be very easy to know certainly how much variation any change of weather will make upon the small twisted body. In the making of this secondary circle of vellum or the like, great care is to be had that it be made exceedingly light and to move very easily; otherwise, a small variation will ruin the entire operation. The box may be made of brass, silver, iron, or any other substance, if care is taken to make it open enough to let the air have a sufficiently free access to the beard. The *index* also may be designed in various ways so as to show both the number of the revolutions it makes and the *minute* divisions of each revolution.

to dryness and moisture, so that with one breath upon it, I have made it untwist a whole turn, and the *Index* or *Hand* has showed or pointed to various divisions on the upper Face or Ring of the instrument, according as it was carried nearer and nearer to the fire, or as the heat of the *Sun* increased upon it.

Other trials I have made with gut strings, but I find them nowhere near so sensitive, though they also may be so contrived as to exhibit the changes of the air, as to dryness and moisture, both by their stretching and shrinking in length, and also by their twisting and untwisting themselves; but these are nowhere near so exact or so responsive, for their varying property will in a little time change very much. But there are several other vegetable substances that are much more sensitive than even this beard of a wild oat; such I have found the beard of the seed of *Musk-grass*, or *Geranium moschatum*, and those of other kinds of *Crane's-bill* seeds, and the like. But always the smaller the twisting substance be, the more sensitive it is to the mutations of the air, a hypothesis for the reason of which I shall shortly add.

The lower end of this wreathed cylinder being stuck upright in a little soft wax, so that the bent part or *Index* of it lay *horizontal*, I have observed it always with moisture to untwist itself from the East (for instance) by the South to the West, and so by the North to the East again, moving with the sun (as we commonly say) and with heat and drought to re-twist and wreathe itself the contrary way, namely, from the East (for instance) by the North to the West, and so onwards.

The cause of all which *phenomena* seems to be the differing texture of the parts of these bodies, each of them (especially the beard of a wild oat and of *Musk-grass seed*) seeming to have two kinds of substances: one that is very porous, loose, and spongy, into which the watery vapors of the air may be very easily forced, which will be thereby swelled and extended in its dimensions, just as we may observe all kinds of vegetable substances upon steeping in water to swell and grow bigger and longer; and a second that is more hard and close, into which the water can very little, or not at all penetrate, this therefore retaining always very near the same dimensions, and the other stretching and shrinking, according as there is more or less moisture or water in its pores; by reason of the structure and shape of the parts, the whole body must necessarily untwist and twist itself.

And upon this principle, it is very easy to make several sorts of contrivances that should thus twist and untwist themselves, either by heat and cold, or by dryness and moisture, or by any greater or less force, from whatever cause it proceeds, whether from gravity or weight, or from wind which is motion of the air, or from some spring-like body, or the like.

This, had I time, I should enlarge much more upon; for it seems to me to be the very first footstep of *Sensation* and *animate* motion, the most plain, simple, and obvious contrivance that Nature has made use of to produce a motion, next to that of *rarefaction* and *condensation* by heat and

and cold. And if this principle were very well examined, I am very apt to think it would afford us great help in discovering the **mechanism** of the **muscles**, which indeed—as far as I have been able to examine them so far—seems to me not as complex as one might imagine, especially based on the examination I made of the **muscles** of **crabs**, **lobsters**, and several sorts of large **shellfish**, and by comparing my observations of them with the circumstances I observed in the muscles of terrestrial animals.

Now, as in this instance of the *beard* of a *wild oat*, we see there is nothing else required to make it wreathe and unwreathe itself, and to straighten and bend its knee, than only a little breath of moist or dry air, or a small atom, almost, of water or liquor, and a little heat to make it evaporate again. For by holding this beard—placed and fixed as I previously directed—near a fire, and dipping the tip of a small shred of paper in well-rectified spirit of wine, and then touching the wreathed *cylindrical part*, you may perceive it untwist itself; and immediately again, upon the *avolation* <note>evaporation</note> of the spirit caused by the great heat, it will re-twist itself. Thus it will move forward and backward as often as you repeat touching it with the spirit of wine; so, perhaps, the shrinking and relaxing of the muscles may be caused by the influx and evaporation of some kind of liquor or juice. But of this inquiry I shall add more elsewhere.

## Observation XXVIII. *Of the Seeds of* Venus's Looking-glass, *or* Corn Violet.

From the leaves, downs, and beards of plants, we come at last to the seeds; and here indeed seems to be the cabinet of Nature, wherein its jewels are stored. The providence of Nature regarding vegetables is manifested in no part more than in the various contrivances concerning the seed; nor indeed is there in any part of the vegetable such curious carvings and beautiful adornments as around the seed. This is most evident to the eye in the larger sorts of seeds; nor is it less manifest through the *microscope* in those seeds whose shape and structure, by reason of their smallness, the eye is hardly able to distinguish.

Of these there are multitudes, many of which I have observed through a *microscope*, and I find that for the most part, every one affords exceedingly pleasant and beautiful objects. For besides those that have various kinds of carved surfaces, there are others that have smooth and perfectly polished surfaces, and others a downy, hairy surface; some are covered only with a skin, others with a kind of shell, and others with both, as is also observable in larger seeds.

Of these seeds I have only described four sorts, which may serve as a *specimen* of what inquisitive observers are likely to find among the rest. The first of these seeds described in the 17th *scheme* <note>illustrated plate</note> are those of *Corn Violets*. The seed is very small, black, and shining, and to the naked eye looks almost like a very small *flea*; but through the

I therefore drew it so that I might thereby demonstrate how unable we are to judge of beautiful or less intricate *microscopical objects* by the naked eye; cutting some of them in half, I observed them to be filled with a greenish-yellow pulp and to have a very thick husk in proportion to the pulp.

## Observation XXIX. *Of the Seeds of Thyme.*

These pretty fruits represented here, in the 18th *Scheme*, are nothing else but nine several seeds of Thyme; they are all of them in different positions, both in relation to the eye and the light. Nor are they all exactly of the same shape, as there is a great variety in both the size and figure of each seed; but they all agreed in this: that when looked at with a *Microscope*, they each exactly resembled a lemon or orange dried, both in shape and color. Some of them are a little rounder, having the shape of an orange, such as A and B; they each have a very conspicuous part by which they were joined to their little stalk, and one of them had a small piece of stalk remaining on it. The opposite side of the seed, as you may perceive very plainly by the figure, is very peaked and prominent, as is very common in lemons; these prominences are expressed in D, E, and F.

They each seemed a little creased or wrinkled, but E was very conspicuously furrowed, as if the internal structure of this seed had also been somewhat like that of a lemon; but upon dividing several seeds with a very sharp penknife and examining them afterward, I found their structure to be differing in nothing but size from that of peas; that is, they have a pretty thick coat, and the rest is an unremarkable white pulp which seemed very dense. Thus, it seems Nature does not very much alter her method of enclosing and preserving the vital principle in the seed of these very small grains from that used for beans, peas, *etc.*

The grain affords a very pretty object for the *Microscope*, namely, a dish of lemons placed in a very small space; should a lemon or nut be proportionally magnified as much as this seed of Thyme is, it would appear as large as a great hay-rick, and it would be no great wonder to see *Homer’s Iliad*, and *Homer* and all, crammed into such a nutshell. We may perceive even in these small grains, as well as in larger ones, how meticulous and careful Nature is in preserving the seminal principle of vegetable bodies, and in what delicate, strong, and most convenient cabinets she

<meta>This page continues the philosophical reflection on the complexity of nature's designs, moving from the description of Thyme seeds to a hierarchical comparison of minerals, vegetables, and animals, before beginning a new observation on poppy seeds.</meta>

lays them and closes them in a pulp for their safer protection from outward dangers, and for the supply of convenient nutritional juice, when the heat of the Sun begins to animate and move these little *automatons* or engines; as if she would, from the ornaments wherewith she has decked these cabinets, hint to us that in them she has laid up her jewels and masterpieces. And this, if we are but diligent in observing, we shall find to be her method throughout. There is no curiosity in the elemental kingdom—if I may so call the bodies of air, water, and earth—that is comparable in form to those of minerals; air and water having no form at all, unless a potentiality to be formed into globules, and the clods and parcels of earth are all irregular; whereas in minerals she does begin to geometrize and practice, as it were, the first principles of *mechanics*, shaping them into plain regular figures, such as triangles, squares, etc., and *tetrahedrons*, cubes, etc. But none of their forms are comparable to the more complex ones of vegetables; for here she goes a step further, forming them both of more complicated shapes and adding also multitudes of curious mechanical contrivances in their structure. For whereas in vegetables there was no determinate number of leaves or branches, nor any exactly certain figure of leaves, or flowers, or seeds, in animals all those things are exactly defined and determined; and wherever there is either an excess or defect of those determinate parts or limbs, there has been some impediment that has spoiled the principle which was most regular. Here we shall find not only most curiously compounded shapes, but most stupendous mechanisms and contrivances; here the ornaments are in the highest perfection—nothing in all the vegetable kingdom is comparable to the deckings of a peacock; nay, to the curiosity of any feather, as I show elsewhere, nor to that of the smallest and most despicable fly. But I must not stay on these speculations, though perhaps it would be very well worth while for one who had leisure to see what information may be learned of the nature, or use, or virtues of bodies by their several forms and various excellencies and properties. Who knows but *Adam* might, from some such contemplation, give names to all creatures? If, at least, his names had any significance in them of the creature's nature on which he imposed it, as many (upon what grounds I know not) have supposed. And who knows but the Creator may, in those characters, have written and engraved many of his most mysterious designs and counsels, and given man a capacity which, assisted with diligence and industry, may be able to read and understand them. But not to multiply my digression more than I can the time, I will proceed to the next, which is:

<header>MICROGRAPHIA.</header>

...other *microscopic* seeds of vegetables: For first, though they grow in a case or hive often bigger than one of these pictures of the *microscopic* appearance, yet they are for the most part so very small that they do not exceed the size of a small nit, being no more than 1/32nd part of an inch in diameter. Whereas the diameter of their hive often exceeds two inches, so that it is capable of containing nearly two hundred thousand; and so, in all likelihood, it does contain a vast quantity, though perhaps not that exact number. Next, for their beauty, they may be compared to any *microscopic* seed I have yet seen; for they are of a dark brownish-red color, curiously honeycombed all over with a very pretty variety of network, or a small kind of embossing of very orderly raised ridges; the surface of them looks not unlike the inside of a beef's stomach. But that which makes it most significant of all is its medicinal virtues, which are such as are not provided to us by any mineral preparation; and that is for the procuring of sleep—a thing as necessary to the well-being of a creature as food, and that which refreshes both the voluntary and rational faculties, which, while this state has seized the body, are for the most part unmoved and at rest. And, I think, Nature does seem to hint at some very notable virtue or excellence in this plant from the intricate detail she has bestowed upon it. First, in its flower, it is of the highest scarlet dye, which is indeed the prime and chief color and has been in all ages of the world most highly esteemed. Next, it has as much intricacy shown also in the husk or case of the seed as any plant I have yet encountered; and thirdly, the very seeds themselves, the *microscope* discovers to be very curiously shaped bodies. And lastly, Nature has taken such abundant care for its propagation that one single seed grown into a plant is capable of producing some hundred thousands of seeds.

It would be very worthy of some capable person's inquiry whether the intention of Nature, regarding the secondary purpose of animal and vegetable substances, might not be found out by some such characters and notable impressions as these, or from various other circumstances—such as the shape, color, place, time of flourishing, springing and fading, duration, taste, smell, etc. For if such things exist (as a capable *physician* upon good grounds has given me cause to believe), we might then, instead of studying herbals (where so little is delivered of the virtues of a plant, and even less of truth), have recourse to the Book of Nature itself. There we could find the most natural, useful, and most effectual and specific medicines, of which we have among vegetables two very noble instances to encourage such a hope: one being the *Jesuit's powder* <note>Cinchona bark, used to treat malaria</note> for the cure of *intermitting fevers*, and the other being the juice of the *poppy* for curing the lack of sleep.

2. That the part which was next to the top was larger than that which was nearer the root.
3. That they were transparent all along from end to end, though not very clear; the end next to the root appearing like a black transparent piece of horn, and the end next to the top more brown, somewhat like transparent horn.
4. That the roots of the hairs were quite smooth, tapering inwards, almost like a parsnip; nor could I find that they had any filaments or any other vessels, such as the fibers of plants.
5. That the top, when split (which is common in long hair), appeared like the end of a stick that has been beaten until it is all shredded; there were not only two splinters, but sometimes half a score or more.
6. That they were all, as far as I was able to find, solid *cylindrical* bodies, not permeable like a cane or bulrush; nor could I find that they had any pith, or distinction of rind or the like, such as I had observed in horsehairs, the bristles of a cat, the *Indian* deer’s hair, etc.

### Observations on several other sorts of hair.

As for the bristles of a hog, I found them to be, first, a hard, transparent, horny substance, without the least appearance of pores or holes in it. I tested this with the greatest care I was able, cutting many of them with a very sharp razor, so that they appeared, even in the glass, to have a quite smooth surface, though somewhat waved by the sawing to and fro of the razor, as is visible in the end of the *prismatical* body *A* of the same figure. Then, making trials by causing the light to be cast on them in all the various ways I could think of that were likely to make the pores appear if there had been any, I was not able to discover any.

Next, the shape of the bristles was very varied, being neither perfectly round nor sharp-edged, but *prismatical*, with several sides and rounded angles, as appears in Figure *A*. Bending them in any part where they previously appeared clear would cause them all to flaw and make them look white.

The whiskers <note>Hooke uses the word "mustacheos."</note> of a cat (part of one of which is represented by the short *cylinder B* of the same figure) seemed to have, in all of those I observed, a large pith in the middle, like the pith of an elder tree, whose texture was so close that I was not able to discover the least sign of pores. Those parts which seemed to be pores, as they appeared in one position to the light, I found in another position to cast a manifest reflection.

I mention this as an instance to hint that it is not safe to conclude anything to be positively this or that—even though it appears ever so plain and likely when looked at with a *microscope* in one posture—before the same has been examined by placing it in several other positions.

And I take this to be the reason why many have believed and asserted the hairs of a man’s head to be hollow, and like so many small pipes perforated from end to end.

Now, though I grant that by an *analogy* one may suppose them to be so,

He cautions that microscopic objects must be viewed from multiple angles to avoid optical illusions, such as mistaking reflections for pores.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Robert Hooke's observations of various types of hair under the microscope, comparing human hair to that of other animals and discussing whether they contain pores or a pith.</meta>

and from the *Polonian* disease <note>Plica polonica, a condition where hair becomes matted and encrusted.</note> one may believe them to be so, yet I think we have not the least encouragement from the *Microscope* to believe either, much less to positively assert it. And perhaps the very essence of the *Plica Polonica* may be the hairs growing hollow and having an unnatural constitution.

And as for the *Analogie*, though I am apt enough to think that the hairs of several animals may be perforated somewhat like a cane, or at least have a kind of pith in them—first, because they seem to be a kind of vegetable growing on an animal, which growth, they say, remains a long while after the animal is dead, and therefore should like other vegetables have a pith; and secondly, because horns and feathers, and porcupine's quills, and cats' bristles, and the long hairs of horses, which come very near the nature of a man’s hair, seem all of them to have a kind of pith, and some of them to be porous—yet I think it not safe (in these cases, where we have such help for the senses as the *Microscope* affords) to conclude or build on more than we sensibly know. This is because we may find, upon examination, that Nature often varies her method in framing the same kind of substance. We may find enough instances to confirm this in the horns of several creatures: for example, what a vast difference is there in shape between the horns of an ox and those of some sorts of stags? And even in the hairs of several creatures, we find a vast difference; as the hair of a man's head seems, as I said before, long, *Cylindrical*, and sometimes a little *Prismatical*, solid or impervious, and very small. 

The hair of an *Indian Deer* (a part of the middle of which is described in the third Figure of the fifth *Scheme*, marked with F) is larger in circumference through the middle of it than the bristle of a hog, but the end of it is smaller than the hair of any kind of animal (as may be seen by the Figure G). The whole middle of it, which is about two or three inches long, looks to the eye like a thread of coarse canvas that has been newly unraveled, being all waved or bent to and fro much in that manner; but through the *Microscope*, it appears all perforated from side to side and spongy, like a small kind of spongy coral which is often found upon the *English* shores. However, although I cut it transversely, I could not perceive that it had any pores that ran the long way of the hair. The long hairs of horses, CC and D, seem *Cylindrical* and somewhat pithy; the bristles of a cat, B, are conical and pithy; the quills of porcupines and hedgehogs, being cut transversely, have a whitish pith in the shape of a star or spur-rowel; pig's hair (A) is somewhat *triagonal* and seems to have neither pith nor pore; and other kinds of hair have a quite different structure and form. And therefore I think it in no way agreeable to a true natural *Historian* to pretend to be so sharp-sighted as to see what a preconceived *Hypothesis* tells them should be there, when another man—though perhaps just as observant, but not biased—can discover no such matter.

But to proceed; I observed several kinds of hairs that had been dyed, and found them to be a kind of horny *Cylinder*, being of much the same transparency as a pretty clear piece of ox horn; these appeared quite through-

throughout tinged with the colors they exhibited. And it is likely that those hairs, being boiled or steeped in those very hot tinged liquors in the dye-vat, and the substance of the hair being much like that of an ox's horn, the penetrating liquor so far mollifies and softens the substance that it sinks into the very center of it; thus, the tinged parts come to be mixed and united with the very body of the hair, and do not (as some have thought) only stick upon the outward surface. And this, the boiling of horn will make more probable; for we shall find by that action that the water will insinuate itself to a considerable depth within its surface, especially if this penetration of the water is much helped by the salts that are usually mixed with the dyeing liquors. 

Now, whereas silk may be dyed or tinged into all kinds of colors without boiling or dipping into hot liquors, I guess the reason is twofold: First, because the filaments, or small cylinders of silk, are abundantly smaller and finer, and so have a much shorter depth to be penetrated than most kinds of hairs; and next, because the substance or matter of silk is much more like a glue than the substance of hair is. And I have reason to suppose this: First, because when it is spun or drawn out of the worm, it is a perfectly glutinous substance and very easily sticks and cleaves to any adjacent body, as I have several times observed, both in silkworms and spiders. Next, because I find that water easily dissolves and mollifies the substance again, which is evident from the manner of preparing those cocoons or pods of the silkworm before they are able to unwind them. It is no great wonder, therefore, if those dyes or tinged liquors very quickly mollify and tinge the surfaces of so small and so glutinous a body. 

And we need not wonder that the colors appear so lovely in the one and so dull in the other, if we simply view the tinged cylinders of both kinds with a good *microscope*; for whereas the substance of hair, at best, is but a dirty, dusky white and somewhat transparent, the filaments of silk have a most lovely transparency and clearness, the difference between those two being not much less than that between a piece of horn and a piece of crystal. The one yields a bright and vivid reflection from the concave side of the cylinder—that is, from the concave surface of the air that encompasses the back part of the cylinder—the other yielding a dull and distorted reflection from the several *heterogeneous* parts that compose it. And this difference will be manifest enough to the eye if you take a couple of small cylinders—the smaller of crystal glass, the other of horn—and then varnish them very thinly with some transparent color; this will represent to the naked eye much the same kind of object which is represented to it from the filaments of silk and hair by the help of the *microscope*. 

Now, since the threads of silk and serge <note>A type of durable twilled fabric, often made of wool.</note> are made up of a great number of these filaments, we may henceforth cease to wonder at the difference. From much the same reason proceeds the vivid and lovely colors of feathers, wherein they very far exceed the natural as well as artificial colors of hair, of which I shall say more in its proper place. The coverings indeed of creatures are all of them adapted to the peculiar use and convenience of that animal which they envelop; and very

Very much also for its ornament and beauty, as will be most evident to anyone who shall attentively consider the various kinds of clothing with which most creatures are invested and covered by Nature. Thus, I have observed that the hair or fur of those Northern white bears that inhabit the colder regions is exceedingly thick and warm; I have observed the same of the hair of a *Greenland* deer, which, having been brought alive to *London*, I had the opportunity of viewing. Its hair was so exceedingly thick, long, and soft, that I could hardly with my hand grasp or take hold of its skin, and it seemed so exceedingly warm that I had never encountered anything like it before. And as for their ornamental use, it is most evident in a multitude of creatures, not only for color, such as leopards, cats, reindeer, etc., but for shape, as in horses' manes, cats' beards, and several other of the larger sort of terrestrial animals; but it is much more conspicuous in the coverings of fishes, birds, and insects, of which I shall shortly give some instances.

As for the skin, the *Microscope* discovers as great a difference between the texture of those several kinds of animals as it does between their hairs; but all that I have yet noticed, when tanned or dressed, are of a spongy nature and seem to be made up of an infinite number of small long *fibers* or hairs, which look not unlike a heap of tow or oakum. Each of these fibers seems to have been some part of a muscle, and probably, while the animal was alive, might have had its distinct function and served for the contraction and relaxation of the skin, and for its stretching and shrinking in this or that direction.

And indeed, without such a kind of texture as this, which is very like that of *spunk* <note>Spunk: a type of touchwood or tinder made from fungi, known for its porous and fibrous structure.</note>, it would seem very strange how any body as strong as the skin of an animal usually is, and as dense as it seems while the animal is living, should be able to undergo such great extension in any direction without at all hurting or tearing any part of it. But since we are informed by the *Microscope* that it consists of a great many small filaments, which are intertwined or entangled one within another, almost no differently than the hairs in a lock of wool or the flakes in a heap of tow (though not quite so loose), but the filaments are here and there twisted, as it were, or interwoven, and here and there they join and unite with one another, so that indeed the whole skin seems to be but one piece, we need not wonder much. And though these fibers do not appear through a *Microscope* to be exactly jointed and woven as in a sponge, yet, as I formerly hinted, I am inclined to think that could we find some way of discovering its texture while it invests the living animal, or had some very easy way of separating the pulp or intervening juices (such as in all probability fill those *interstices* <note>Interstitia: the small spaces or gaps between tissues or fibers.</note>) without tearing, bruising, or otherwise spoiling its texture (as it seems to be very much by the ways of tanning and dressing now used), we might discover a much more intricate texture than I have hitherto been able to find—perhaps somewhat like that of sponges.

That of *Chamois* leather is indeed very much like that of *spunk*, save only that the *filaments* seem nowhere near so even and round, nor altogether so small, nor does it have such intricate joints as *spunk* has, some of which I have

I have lately discovered, like those of a sponge; and perhaps all three of these bodies may be of the same kind of substance, though two of them indeed are commonly considered vegetable (which, whether they are or not, I shall not now dispute). But this seems common to all three: that they undergo a tanning or dressing, whereby the interspersed juices are wasted and washed away before their texture can be discovered.

I confess I cannot learn what their method is for dressing or curing sponges; but the way of dressing *spunk* <note>tinder-wood or a type of fungus used for fuel</note> is by boiling it for a long time in a strong *lixivium* <note>a solution of alkaline salts, such as lye</note> and then beating it very well; and the manner of dressing leather is sufficiently known.

It would indeed be extremely desirable if a method could be found whereby the *parenchyma* <note>the functional tissue of an organ</note> or flesh of the *muscles*, and several other parts of the body, might be washed or wasted clean away without damaging the form of its fibrous parts or vessels; for by this means, the texture of those parts might be most accurately discovered with the help of a good *microscope*.

But to digress no further, we may, from this discovery of the *microscope*, clearly enough understand how the skin—though it appears as solid as it does—manages to provide passage for such a vast quantity of excrementitious <note>waste</note> substances, as the diligent *Sanctorius* has excellently observed in his *Medicina Statica*; for it seems very probable, from the texture after dressing, that there are an infinity of pores that pierce it in every direction, and that those pores are only filled with some kind of juice or some very pulpy, soft substance. Thereby, the vapors may almost as easily find a passage through such a fluid *vehicle* as the vaporous bubbles generated at the bottom of a kettle of hot water find a passage through that fluid *medium* into the surrounding air.

Nor is the skin of animals alone pervious in this way, but even those of vegetables also seem to be the same; for otherwise I cannot conceive why, if two sprigs of *rosemary* (for instance) are taken as exactly alike in all particulars as can be, and one is set with its bottom in a glass of water, and the other is set just outside the glass, but only in the air—though you stop the lower end of the one in the air very carefully with wax—it shall nevertheless wither almost immediately; whereas the other, which seems to have a supply from the underlying water through its small pipes or *microscopical* pores, preserves its greenness for many days, and sometimes weeks.

Now, this seems to me unlikely to proceed from any cause other than the *avolation* <note>evaporation or escaping</note> of the juice through the skin; for by the wax, all those other pores of the stem are very firmly and closely stopped up. And from the greater or lesser porosity of the skins or rinds of vegetables, perhaps some reason may be given for why they stay green longer or wither sooner; for we may observe by the blistering and cracking of the leaves of *bay*, *holly*, *laurel*, etc., that their skins are very tight and do not allow the juices within to pass through them so freely.

But I shall more fully consider this and the experiment of the *rosemary* elsewhere, as it seems to me an extremely *luciferous* <note>enlightening or informative</note> experiment—one that indeed seems very clearly to prove the *schematism* or structure of
