### Observ. XXXIII. Of the Scales of a Sole, and other Fish.

Having hinted somewhat at the skin and covering of terrestrial animals, I shall next add an observation I made on the skin and scales of a *sole*, a small fish commonly enough known. Here in fish, as well as other animals, Nature follows its usual method, framing all parts so that they are both useful and ornamental in all its compositions, mingling *utile* and *dulce* <note>the useful and the pleasant</note> together. It seems to follow both these designs, though our unassisted senses are not able to perceive them. This is not only manifest in the covering of this fish alone, but in multitudes of others which it would take too long to list; witness particularly that small sand shell which I mentioned in the eleventh observation, and infinite other small shells and scales, many of which I have viewed. This skin I viewed was flayed from a pretty large *sole*, and then expanded and dried. The inside of it, when dry, looked to the naked eye very like a piece of canvas, but the *microscope* discovered that texture to be nothing else but the inner ends of those curious scalloped scales I, I, I, in the second *figure* of the twenty-first *scheme*—namely, the part GGGG (of the larger representation of a single scale in the first *figure* of the same *scheme*)—which on the back side, through an ordinary single magnifying glass, looked not unlike the tiles on a house.

The outside of it, to the naked eye, exhibited nothing more of ornament except the usual order of arranging the scales into a *triagonal* form; only the edges seemed to shine a little. When a finger was rubbed from the tail toward the head, the scales seemed to catch and scrape it. But through an ordinary magnifying glass, it exhibited a most curiously carved and adorned surface, such as is visible in the second *figure*, each of those (formerly almost imperceptible) scales appearing much like the shape I, I, I; that is, they were round and protuberant, and shaped somewhat like a scallop, the whole scale being creased with curiously waved and indented ridges, with proportional furrows between. Each of these was terminated with a very sharp, transparent bony substance which, like so many small turnpikes <note>spiked defensive barriers</note>, seemed to arm the edges.

The back part KKK was the skin into which each of these scales was very deeply fixed, in the curious regular order visible in the second *figure*.

Having briefly mentioned the skin and covering of land animals, I shall next add an observation I made on the skin and scales of a *sole*, a small fish that is well enough known. Here in fish, as well as other animals, Nature follows its usual method, framing all parts so that they are both useful and ornamental in all its creations, mingling *utile* and *dulce* <note>the useful and the pleasant</note> together. Indeed, you can hardly look on the scales of any fish without discovering an abundance of curiosity and beauty; and this is true not only in these fish, but in the shells and crusts or armor of most sorts of *marine animals* so covered.

### Observation XXXIV. Of the *Sting of a Bee*.

The sting of a *bee*, delineated in the second *Figure* of the *XVI Scheme*, seems to be a weapon of offense, and is as great an instance that Nature did really intend revenge as any. This is true first because there seems to be no other use for it; secondly, by reason of its admirable shape, appearing to be purposely shaped for that very end; and thirdly, from the virulence of the liquor it ejects and the sad effects and symptoms that follow it.

But whatever its use may be, it is certain that its structure is very admirable. I need not describe what it appears like to the naked eye, the thing being known almost to everyone; but it appears through the *microscope* to consist of two parts. One is a sheath without a chape <note>the metal mounting or tip of a scabbard</note> or top, shaped almost like the holster of a pistol, beginning at *a* and ending at *b*. I could most plainly perceive this sheath to be hollow and to contain within it both a sword or dart and the poisonous liquor that causes the pain. The sheath or case seemed to have several joints or settings together, marked by *f, g, h, i, k, l, m, n, o*. It was armed, moreover, near the top with several crooks or forks (*p, q, r, s, t*) on one side and (*p, q, r, s, t, u*) on the other, each of which seemed like many thorns growing on a briar, or rather like many cat's claws; for the crooks themselves seemed to be little sharp transparent points or claws, growing out of little protuberances on the

The other part of the sting was the sword, as I may so call it, which is sheathed, as it were, in it, the top of which *ab* appears quite through at the smaller end, just as if the chape <note>the metal tip of a scabbard</note> of the sheath of a sword were lost, and the end of it appeared beyond the scabbard; the end of this dart (*a*) was very sharp, and it was armed likewise with the same tenterhooks or claws as those of the sheath, such as (*vxy, xyzz*); these crooks, I am very apt to think, can be closed up also, or laid flat to the sides of the sword when it is drawn into the scabbard, as I have several times observed it to be, and can be spread again or extended whenever the animal pleases.

The consideration of which very pretty structure has hinted to me that certainly the use of these claws seems to be very considerable as to the main end of this instrument, for the drawing in and holding the sting in the flesh; for the point being very sharp, the top of the sting or dagger (*ab*) is very easily thrust into an animal's body, which being once entered, the bee, by endeavoring to pull it into the sheath, draws (by reason of the crooks (*vxy*) and (*xyzz*) which lay hold of the skin on either side) the top of the sheath (*t s r v*) into the skin after it, and the crooks *t, s,* and *r, v,* being entered, when the bee endeavors to thrust out the top of the sting out of the sheath again, they lay hold of the skin on either side, and so not only keep the sheath from sliding back, but help the top inwards; and thus, by an alternate and successive retracting and emitting of the sting in and out of the sheath, the little enraged creature by degrees makes his revengeful weapon pierce the toughest and thickest hides of his enemies, insomuch that some few of these stout and resolute soldiers with these little engines, do often put to flight a huge masty <note>burly or massive</note> bear, one of their deadly enemies, and thereby show the world how much more considerable in war a few skillful engineers and resolute soldiers politically ordered, that know how to manage such engines, are, than a vast unwieldy rude force, that confides in, and acts only by, its strength. But (to proceed) that he thus gets his sting into the skin, I conjecture, because, when I have observed this creature living, I have found it to move the sting thus, to and fro, and thereby also, perhaps, does, as it were, pump or force out the poisonous liquor, and make it hang at the end of the sheath about *b* in a drop. The crooks, I suppose also to be the cause why these angry creatures, hastily removing themselves from their revenge, do often leave these weapons behind them, sheathed, as it were, in the flesh, and, by that means, cause the painful symptoms to be greater and more lasting, which are very probably caused, partly by the piercing and tearing of the skin by the sting, but chiefly by the corrosive and poisonous liquor that is by this syringe-pipe conveyed among the sensitive parts thereof and thereby more easily gnaws

## Observation XXXV. Of the texture and shape of the particles of Feathers.

Examining several sorts of *Feathers*, I took notice of these particulars in all sorts of wing-feathers, especially in those which served for the beating of the air in the action of flying.

That the outward surface of the Quill and Stem was of a very hard, stiff, and horny substance, which is obvious enough; and that the part above the Quill was filled with a very white and light pith. With the *Microscope*, I found this pith to be nothing else but a kind of natural *congeries* <note>a collection or mass</note> of small bubbles, the films of which seem to be of the same substance as the Quill—that is, of a stiff, transparent, horny substance.

This particular detail seems to me very worthy of more serious consideration; for here we may observe Nature, as it were, put to its shifts to make a substance that shall be both light enough and very stiff and strong, without varying from its own established principles. We may observe these principles to be such that very strong bodies are for the most part very heavy also—strength of the parts usually requiring density, and density requiring gravity <note>weight</note>. Therefore, had Nature made a body as broad and as strong as a feather in almost any other way than the one it has taken, its weight must necessarily have many times exceeded this. For this pith seems to be like so many stops or cross-pieces in a long optical tube, which contribute very much to the strength of the whole; its pores were such that they seemed to have no communication with one another, as I have elsewhere hinted.

But the Mechanism of Nature is usually so excellent that one and the same substance is adapted to serve many ends. For the chief use of this indeed seems to be for the supply of nourishment to the downy or feathery part of the stem; for it is obvious enough in all sorts of feathers that it is placed just under the roots of the branches that grow out of either side of the quill or stalk, and is exactly shaped according to the ranking of those branches, coming no lower into the quill than just the beginning of the downy branches, and growing only on the underside of the quill where those branches do so. Now, in a ripe feather (as one may call it), it seems difficult to conceive how the *succus nutritius* <note>nutritive juice</note> should be conveyed to this pith; for it cannot, I think, be well imagined to pass through the substance of the quill, since, having examined it with the greatest diligence I was able, I could not find the least appearance of pores. But he who shall examine an unripe or pinned feather <note>a developing feather still in its sheath</note> will plainly enough perceive the vessel for its conveyance to be the thin, filmy pith (as it is called) which passes through the middle of the quill.

As for the make and texture of the down itself, it is indeed very

rare and admirable, and such as I can hardly believe that the like is to be discovered in any other body in the world; for there is hardly a large feather in the wing of a bird but contains near a million distinct parts, and every one of them shaped in a most regular and admirable form, adapted to a particular design. For examining a middle-sized goose-quill, I easily enough found with my naked eye that the main stem of it contained about 300 longer and more downy branchings upon one side, and as many on the other of more stiff but somewhat shorter branchings. Examining many of these long and downy branchings with an ordinary *Microscope*, I found several of them to contain near 1200 small leaves (as I may call them, such as *EF* of the first Figure of the *23rd Scheme*) and as many stalks; on the other side, such as *IK* of the same Figure, each of the leaves or branchings, *EF*, seemed to be divided into about sixteen or eighteen small joints, as may be seen plainly enough in the Figure. Out of most of these there seem to grow small long *fibres*, such as are expressed in the Figure, each of them very proportionably shaped according to its position, or placed on the stalk *EF*; those on the underside of it, namely, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, *etc.*, being much longer than those directly opposite to them on the upper; and several of them, such as 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, *etc.*, were terminated with small hooks, much resembling those small hooks which are visible enough to the naked eye in the seed-buttons of burdocks. The transverse sections of the stems of these branchings manifested the shape or figure of it to be much like *INOE*, which consisted of a horny skin or covering and a white, seemingly frothy pith, much like the construction of the main stem of a feather.

The use of this strange kind of form is indeed more admirable than all the rest, and such as deserves to be much more seriously examined and considered than I have hitherto found time or ability to do; for certainly, it may very much instruct us in the nature of the air, especially as to some properties of it.

The stems of the downy branches *INOE* being ranged in the order visible enough to the naked eye, at the distance of *IF*, or somewhat more, the *collateral* stalks and leaves (if I may so call those bodies I newly described) are so ranged that the leaves or hairy stalks of the one side lie at the top, or are resting on the stalks of the other, and cross each other much after the manner expressed in the second Figure of the *23rd Scheme*. By this means, every one of those little hooked *fibres* of the leaved stalk gets between the naked stalks; and the stalks being full of knots and a pretty way disjointed, so that the fibers can easily get between them, the two parts are so closely and admirably woven together that they are able to impede, for the greatest part, the passage of the air; and though they are so exceedingly small that the thickness of one of

these stalks do not amount to a 500th part of an inch, yet they compose so strong a texture that, notwithstanding the exceedingly quick and violent beating of them against the air by the strength of the bird's wing, they firmly hold together. And it demonstrates an admirable providence of Nature in their contrivance and fabric; for their texture is such that, even if their parts are violently disjointed by any external injury, so that the leaves and stalks do not touch one another, and consequently several of these rents would impede the bird's flying; yet, for the most part, they readily rejoin and re-weave themselves on their own, and are easily settled and woven into their former and natural posture by the bird stroking the feather or drawing it through its bill; for there is such an infinite company of those small fibers on the underside of the leaves, and most of them have such little hooks at their ends, that they readily catch and hold the stalks they touch.

From this strange structure, it seems rational to suppose that there is a certain kind of mesh or hole so small that the air will not very easily pass through it, as I also hinted in the sixth observation about small glass canes; for otherwise it seems probable that Nature would have drawn over some kind of thin film which should have covered all those almost square meshes or holes, as there appears through the *Microscope* to be more than half of the surface of the feather which is open and visibly pervious; which conjecture will seem even more probable from the texture of the brushy wings of the *Tinea argentea*, or white feather-winged moth, which I shall describe shortly. But Nature, which knows its own laws best and the various properties of bodies, also knows best how to adapt and fit them to her designed ends; and whoever would know those properties must endeavor to trace Nature in its working and see what course she observes. And I suppose this will be no inconsiderable advantage which the *schematisms* and structures of animate bodies will afford the diligent inquirer, namely, most sure and excellent instructions, both as to the practical part of *Mechanics* and to the *theory* and knowledge of the nature of bodies and motions.

multitude of bright reflecting parts, whose figure it is no easy matter to determine, as anyone who examines it shall find; for every new position of it to the light makes it seem to be of a perfectly different form and shape, and nothing like what it appeared a little before; indeed, it often appeared very different from such a seemingly inconsiderable circumstance as the interposing of one's hand between the light and it, which makes a very great change, just as the opening or shutting of a casement window and the like very much diversifies the appearance. And though, by examining its form in many different ways, which would be tedious to enumerate here, I suppose I have discovered its true figure, yet oftentimes, upon looking at it in another posture, I have almost thought my former observations deficient; though indeed, upon further examination, I have found even those also to confirm them.

These threads, therefore, I find to be a collection of small *Laminæ* or plates, as *eeee*, etc., each of them shaped much like that of *abcd* in the fourth *Figure*. The part *ac* is a ridge, prominence, or stem, and *b* and *d* are the corners of two small thin plates that grow onto the small stalk in the middle, so that they make a kind of little feather. Each of these plates lies close to another, almost like a set of sloping ridge or gutter tiles; they grow on each side of the stalk opposite to one another, two by two, from top to bottom, in the manner expressed in the fifth Figure, the tops of the lower ones covering the roots of the next above them. The underside of each of these laminated bodies is of a very dark and opaque substance, and allows very few rays to be transmitted, but reflects them all toward the side from which they come, much like the foil of a looking-glass. But their upper sides seem to me to consist of a multitude of thin plated bodies, which are exceedingly thin and lie very close together, and thereby, like mother-of-pearl shells, do not only reflect a very bright light, but tint that light in a most curious manner; and by means of various positions in respect to the light, they reflect back now one color, and then another, and those most vividly.

Now, that these colors are only optical ones—that is, such as arise immediately from the refractions of the light—I found by this: that water wetting these colored parts destroyed their colors, which seemed to proceed from the alteration of the reflection and refraction. Now, though I was not able to see those hairs at all transparent by a common light, yet by looking at them against the sun, I found them to be tinted with a darkish red color, nothing akin to the curious and lovely greens and blues they exhibited.

What the reason for color seems to be in such thin plated bodies, I have shown elsewhere. But how water cast upon those threads destroys their colors, I suppose to be performed thus: the water falling upon these plated bodies, having a greater affinity to feathers than the air does, insinuates itself between those plates and so pushes out the strong reflecting air. From this, both these parts grow more transparent, as the *Microscope* informs us, and colorless also, at best retaining a very faint and

dull color. But once this moisture has evaporated through the continuous vapors and steams that pass through them from the peacock while the bird is still alive, the colors appear again in their former luster, the spaces between these plates being filled with the strongly reflecting air.

The beautiful and vivid colors of the feathers of this bird are found to result from the curious and exceeding smallness and fineness of the reflecting parts. Thus, we are given the reason for all those vivid ornaments in the plumage of other birds as well, and why they surpass the colors of all other kinds of animals, except *insects*. For since (as we show here and elsewhere) the vividness of a color depends upon the fineness and transparency of the reflecting and refracting parts; and since our *microscope* reveals to us that the component parts of feathers are made this way, while the hairs of animals are not; and since we also find by the experiment of that noble and most excellent person <note>Likely referring to Robert Boyle</note> I named earlier that the difference between silk and flax regarding color is nothing else (for flax reduced to a very great fineness of parts, both white and colored, appears as white and as vivid as any silk, but loses that brightness and its silken appearance as soon as it is twisted into thread, because the component parts, though very small and fine, are pliable flakes rather than cylinders, and therefore, by twisting, become united into one opaque body; whereas the threads of silk and feathers retain their luster by preserving their cylindrical form entirely without mixing, so that each reflected and refracted beam that composes the gloss of silk preserves its own property of modulating the light entirely); and since we find the same confirmed by many other experiments mentioned elsewhere, I think we may safely conclude this as an axiom: that wherever we find transparent bodies spun out into very fine parts, whether clear or tinted in any way, the colors resulting from such a composition must necessarily be very glorious, vivid, and clear, like those of silk and feathers. This may perhaps suggest some useful way of making other bodies besides silk susceptible to bright dyes, but I mention this only in passing.

I have also found, by examination with my *microscope*, that the iridescent feathers of ducks and several other birds result from much the same causes and textures.

...contain themselves in that posture as long as they please; indeed, they can walk and hang themselves against the under surface of many bodies, such as the ceiling of a room or the like. They do this with as much apparent ease and firmness as if they were a kind of *Antipodes* and had a *tendency* upward, though we are certain they have the opposite tendency [gravity]. This they also clearly demonstrate by the fact that they cannot make themselves light enough to stick to or hang from the under surface of a glass that is well polished and cleaned. Their hanging, therefore, is entirely to be attributed to some mechanical contrivance in their feet. We shall briefly explain what this is by showing that its mechanism consists principally of two parts: first, its two claws or talons, and second, two palms, pattens, or soles.

The two talons are very large in proportion to the foot and handsomely shaped in the manner described in the figures by AB and AC. The larger part of them, from A to *dd*, is entirely hairy or bristly, but toward the tips at C and B, they are smooth. The tips or points, which seem very sharp and turn downward and inward, are each moved by a joint at A, which allows the fly to open or shut them at will. Thus, when the points B and C enter any pores and the fly attempts to shut them, the claws not only pull against each other to fasten themselves, but they also pull the whole foot, GADD, forward. Consequently, on a soft surface, the tenters or points G G G G (of which a fly has about ten in each foot—namely, two in every joint) run into the pores if they find any, or at least push into the surface. This is visible to the naked eye in the feet of a *Chafer* <note>A type of beetle, such as a cockchafer or scarab</note>, which, if allowed to crawl over the hand or any other part of the skin of one's body, makes its steps as perceptible to the touch as they are to the sight.

But just as this mechanism often fails the *Chafer* when it walks on hard and dense bodies, it would also fail our fly, even though it is a much smaller and nimbler creature. Therefore, Nature has furnished its foot with another *addition* [*additament*] that is much more curious and admirable: a pair of palms, pattens, or soles, marked D D. The structure of these is as follows: from the bottom or underside of the last joint of its foot, K, arise two small, thin, plated, horny substances, each consisting of two flat pieces, D D. These seem to be flexible, like the covers of a book, at F F. Because of this, the surfaces of the two sides E E do not always lie in the same plane but may sometimes be shut closer together, allowing each of them to take some grip on an object.

But that is not all, for the undersides of these soles are entirely covered with small bristles or tenters, like the wire teeth of a card used for combing wool. The points of all these bristles face forward. Thus, when the two talons pull the feet forward, as I mentioned before, and these soles are pressed against the surface of a body with all the points facing the opposite way—that is, forward and outward—the fly hangs itself very firmly and easily if there is any irregularity or softness in the surface. This happens without the need for any sponges filled with an imaginary *glue* [*gluten*], as many people have supposed, perhaps due to a lack of good magnifying glasses or a lack of careful and diligent examination. Now, the fact that the fly is able to walk on glass arises partly from some roughness...

This structure I surveyed somewhat more diligently because I could not well comprehend how, if there were such a glutinous matter in those supposed sponges, as most (who have observed that object in a *microscope*) have previously believed—how, I say, the fly could so readily un-glue and loosen its feet: and, because I have not found any other creature to have a contrivance any ways like it; and chiefly, so that we might not be cast upon unintelligible explanations of the *phenomena* of nature—at least others than the true ones—where our senses were able to furnish us with an intelligible, rational, and true one.

Somewhat a similar contrivance to this of flies shall we find in most other animals, such as all kinds of flies and case-winged creatures; nay, in a flea, an animal abundantly smaller than this fly. Other creatures, as mites, the land-crab, etc., have only one small, very sharp talon at the end of each of their legs, which, all drawing towards the center or middle of their body, enable these exceedingly light bodies to suspend and fasten themselves to almost any surface.

How they are able to do this will not seem strange if we consider, first, how little body there is in one of these creatures compared to their surface area, or outside—their thickness, perhaps, often not amounting to the hundredth part of an inch. Next, the strength and agility of these creatures compared to their bulk; being, proportional to their bulk, perhaps a hundred times stronger than a horse or man. And thirdly, if we consider that Nature always appropriates the instruments so as they are the most fit and convenient to perform their offices, and the most simple and plain that possibly can be; this we may see further verified also in the foot of a louse, which is very much different from those I have been describing, but more convenient and necessary for the place of its habitation. Each of its legs is footed with a couple of small claws which it can open or shut at pleasure, shaped almost like the claws of a lobster or crab, but with appropriated contrivances for its peculiar use; which being to move its body to and fro upon the hairs of the creature it inhabits, Nature has furnished one of its claws with joints, almost like the joints of a man’s fingers, so as thereby it is able to encompass or grasp a hair as firmly as a man can a stick or rope.

Nor is there a less admirable and wonderful *mechanism* in the foot of a spider, whereby he is able to spin, weave, and climb, or run on his curious transparent thread, of which I shall say more in the description of that animal.

And to conclude, we shall in all things find that Nature does not only work mechanically, but by such excellent and most compendious, as well as stupendous contrivances, that it would be impossible for all the reason in the world to find out any contrivance to do the same thing that would have more convenient properties. And can any be so foolish,

### Observ. XXXVIII. *Of the structure and motion of the wings of flies.*

The wings of all kinds of insects are, for the most part, very beautiful objects, and afford no less pleasing an object for the mind to speculate upon than for the eye to behold. This of the blue fly, among the rest, does not lack its peculiar ornaments and contrivances; it grows out of the <term>Thorax</term>, or middle part of the body of a fly, and is seated a little beyond the center of gravity in the body towards the head, but that eccentricity is skillfully balanced; first, by the expanded area of the wings which lies further backward than the root, and by their motion, whereby the center of their vibration is much further back toward the tail of the fly than the root of the wing is. What the vibratory motion of the wings is, and in what manner they are moved, I have endeavored through many trials to find out. And for the first manner of their motion, I endeavored to observe several of those kind of small spinning flies, which will naturally suspend themselves, as it were, poised and steady in one place in the air, without rising or falling, or moving forwards or backwards; for by looking down on those, I could, by a kind of faint shadow, perceive the utmost extremes of the vibratory motion of their wings. This shadow, while they so endeavored to suspend themselves, was not very long, but when they endeavored to fly forwards, it was somewhat longer. Next, I tried it by fixing the legs of a fly upon the top of the stalk of a feather with glue, wax, etc., and then making it endeavor to fly away; for being thereby able to view it in any posture, I concluded that the motion of the wing was in this manner. The extreme limits of the vibrations were usually about the length of the body distant from one another, often shorter, and sometimes also longer; the foremost limit was usually a little above the back, and the hinder somewhat beneath the belly. Between these two limits, if one may guess by the sound, the wing seemed to be moved forwards and backwards with an equal velocity. And if one may (from the shadow or faint representation the wings afforded, and from the consideration of the nature of the thing) guess at the posture or manner of the wings moving between them, it seemed to be this: the wing, being supposed placed in the uppermost limit, seems to be positioned so that its plane lies almost horizontal, but only the forepart dips a little, or is somewhat more depressed; in this position the wing is vibrated or moved to the lower limit. Being almost arrived at the lower limit, the hinder part of the wing moving somewhat faster than the former,

And these vibrations or motions to and fro between the two limits seem so swift, that it is very probable (judging from the sound it makes, if it is compared with the vibration of a musical string tuned in unison with it) that it makes many hundreds, if not some thousands, of vibrations in a second <note>Hooke uses the phrase "second minute" to refer to what we now call a second</note> of time: And, if we may be allowed to guess by the sound, the wing of a bee is yet more swift, for the tone is much more high-pitched, and that, in all likelihood, proceeds from the exceedingly swift beating of the air by the *small* wing. And it seems even more likely too, because the wing of a bee is smaller in proportion to its body than the other wing is to the body of a fly; so that for all I know, it may be one of the quickest vibrating *spontaneous* motions of any in the world; and though perhaps there may be many flies in other places that produce an even more shrill noise with their wings, yet it is most probable that the quickest vibrating *spontaneous* motion is to be found in the wing of some creature. Now, if we consider the exceeding quickness of these animal spirits that must cause these motions, we cannot help but admire the exceeding vividness of the governing faculty or *Anima* of the insect, which is able to dispose and regulate the motive faculties so as to cause every specific organ, not only to move or act so quickly, but also to do so regularly.

While I was examining and considering the curious *mechanism* of the wings, I observed that under the wings of most kinds of flies, bees, etc., there were placed certain *pendulums* or extended *drops* (as I may call them from their resembling motion and figure); for they much resembled a long hanging drop of some transparent viscous liquid; and I observed them constantly moving just before the wings of the fly began to move, so that at first sight I could not help but guess that there was some excellent use for the regulation of the motion of the wing. I did imagine that it might be something like the handle of a cock <note>A "cock" here refers to a tap or valve</note>, which by vibrating to and fro, might, as it were, open and shut the valve, and thereby give passage to the specific influences into the muscles. Afterwards, upon some other trials, I supposed that they might be for some use in respiration, which for many reasons I suppose those animals use; and it seemed to me not very improbable that they might have convenient passages under the wings for emitting, at least, if not admitting, air, as is most evident in the gills of fishes. Or, perhaps, this *pendulum* might be somewhat like the handle of a pump, by which these creatures might exercise their *analogous* lungs, and not only draw in, but force out, the air they live by; but these were only conjectures, and upon further examination seemed less probable.

The structure of the wing, as it appears through a moderately magnifying *microscope*, seems to be a body consisting of two parts, as is visible in the 4th *figure* of the 23rd *scheme* <note>Hooke uses the word "scheme" to refer to his illustrated plates</note>; and by the 2nd *figure* of the 26th *scheme*; the one is

...a quilly or finny substance, consisting of several long, slender and variously bent quills or wires, somewhat resembling the veins of leaves; these are, as it were, the fins or quills which stiffen the whole *area*, and keep the other part distended, which is a very thin transparent skin or membrane variously folded and pleated, but not very regularly; it is, besides, exceedingly thickly covered with innumerable small bristles, which are only perceptible through the larger magnifying *microscope*, and not even with that, unless with a very convenient augmentation of skylight projected on the object with a burning glass, as I have elsewhere shown, or by looking through it against the light.

Instead of these small hairs, in several other *flies*, there are an infinite number of small *feathers* that cover both the under and upper sides of this thin film, as in almost all types of *butterflies* and *moths*. These small parts are not only shaped very much like the feathers of *birds*, but are also variegated with all the variety of curious, bright, and vivid colors imaginable. These feathers are likewise so admirably and delicately arranged as to compose very fine flourishes and ornamental paintings, like *Turkish* and *Persian carpets*, but of far more surpassing beauty, as is evident enough to the naked eye in the painted wings of *butterflies*, but much more so through an ordinary *microscope*.

Intermingled likewise with these hairs, one may perceive multitudes of little pits or black spots in the extended membrane, which seem to be the roots of the hairs that grow on the other side; these two bodies seem dispersed over the whole surface of the wing.

The hairs are best perceived by looking through it against the light, or by laying the wing upon a very white piece of paper in a convenient light, for by this means every little hair most clearly appears. A specimen of this you may observe drawn in the fourth figure of the 23rd *Scheme*, where AB, CD, and EF represent some parts of the bones or quills of the wing. You may perceive each of these to be covered over with a multitude of scales or bristles; the first, AB, is the largest stem of the entire wing and may be properly enough called the *cut-air*, as it is that which terminates and stiffens the foremost edge of the wing. The front edge of this is armed with a multitude of little bristles or *tenter-hooks*, standing regularly and in order in some, and not in others. All their points are directed from the body towards the tip of the wing; nor is only this edge thus fringed, but the entire edge of the wing is covered with a small fringe consisting of short and more slender bristles.

This subject, had I time, would afford excellent material for the contemplation of the nature of wings and of flying; but because I may, perhaps, find a more convenient time to pursue that investigation and collect several observations that I have made on that particular, I shall at present proceed to

MICROGRAPHIA.

## Observation XXXIX. *Of the Eyes and Head of a Grey Drone-Fly, and of several other creatures.*

<margin>*or dragonfly*</margin>
**I** took a large grey *Drone-Fly* that had a large head but a small and slender body in proportion to it, and cutting off its head, I fixed it with the front or face upwards upon my *Object Plate* (I chose this rather than the head of a great blue *fly*, because my inquiry being now about the eyes, I found this *fly* to have, first, the biggest clusters of eyes in proportion to its head of any small kind of *fly* that I have yet seen, it being somewhat inclined toward the build of the large *dragonflies*. Next, because there is a greater variety in the knobs or balls of each cluster than in any small *fly*). Then examining it according to my usual manner, by varying the degrees of light and altering its position to each kind of light, I drew that representation of it which is shown in the 24th *Scheme*, and found these things to be as plain and evident as they were notable and pleasant.

First, that the greatest part of the face—nay, of the head—was nothing else but two large and *protuberant* bunches, or prominent parts, A B C D E A, the surface of each of which was entirely covered over or shaped into a multitude of small *hemispheres*, placed in a triagonal order, that being the closest and most compact arrangement; and in that order, they were ranged over the whole surface of the eye in very lovely rows. Between each of these, as is necessary, were left long and regular trenches, the bottoms of every one of which were perfectly entire and not at all perforated or drilled through, which I was most certainly assured of by the regularly reflected image of certain objects which I moved to and fro between the head and the light, and by examining the *cornea* or outward skin after I had stripped it off from the various substances that lay within it, and by looking both upon the inside and against the light.

Next, that among those multitudes of *hemispheres*, there were observable two degrees of size: the half of them that were lowermost and looked toward the ground or their own legs—namely, CDE, CDE—being quite a bit smaller than the others—namely, ABCE, ABCE—that looked upward, sideways, forward, and backward; this variety I have not found in any other small *fly*.

Thirdly, that every one of these *hemispheres*, as they seemed to be quite near the true shape of a *hemisphere*, had a surface that was exceedingly smooth and regular, reflecting as exact, regular, and perfect an image of any object from its surface as a small ball of *quicksilver* of that size would do, but not nearly so vivid; the reflection from these was very faint, much like the reflection from the surface of water, glass, crystal, etc. So much so that in each of these *hemispheres*, I have been able to discover a landscape of those things which lay before my window,

window, one thing of which was a large tree, whose trunk and top I could plainly discover, as I could also the parts of my window, and my hand and fingers, if I held it between the window and the object; a small drawing of nineteen of which, as they appeared in the larger magnifying glass to reflect the image of the two windows of my chamber, are depicted in the third figure of the 23rd *Scheme*.

*Fourthly*, that these rows were so arranged, that there was no direction visible from its head that some of these *hemispheres* were not directed against; so that a fly may be truly said to have an *eye every way*, and to be *really circumspect*. And it was further observable, that in the direction where the trunk of its body hindered its prospect backward, these protuberances were elevated, as it were, above the plane of its shoulders and back, so that it was able to see backward also over its back.

*Fifthly*, in living flies, I have observed that when any small speck or dust, which flies up and down the air, chances to land upon any part of these knobs, it is sure to stick firmly to it and not fall, though through the *Microscope* it appears like a large stone or stick (which one would wonder at, especially since it is in no way probable that there is any wet or sticky matter upon these *hemispheres*, but I hope I shall explain the reason in another place). Thus the fly presently makes use of its two fore-feet instead of eyelids, with which—as with two *brooms* or *brushes*, they being all covered with *bristles*—it often sweeps or brushes off whatever hinders the view of any of its *hemispheres*. Then, to free its legs from that dirt, it rubs them one against another; the pointed bristles or <term>tenters</term> <note>hook-like bristles</note> of which, looking both the same way, the rubbing of them to and fro one against another cleanses them in the same manner as I have observed those that *comb wool* to cleanse their *cards* <note>tools for combing wool</note>, by placing their cards so that the teeth of both look the same way, and then rubbing them one against another. In the very same manner do they brush and cleanse their bodies and wings, as I shall shortly show; other creatures have other contrivances for the cleansing and clearing of their eyes.

*Sixthly*, that the number of the *pearls* or *hemispheres* in the clusters of this fly was near 14,000, which I judged by numbering certain rows of them several ways and calculating the whole content, accounting each cluster to contain about seven thousand pearls. Three thousand of these were of one size, and consequently the rows were not as thick, and the four thousand I accounted to be the number of the smaller pearls next to the feet and *proboscis*. Other animals I observed to have a still greater number, such as the *Dragon-fly* or *Adderbolt*; and others to have a much smaller company, such as an *Ant*, etc., and several other small flies and *insects*.

*Seventhly*, that the order of these eyes or *hemispheres* was altogether intricate and admirable, they being placed in all kinds of flies and aerial animals in a most curious and regular arrangement of triangular rows. In this order they are ranged as near together as they possibly can be, and consequently leave the smallest pits or trenches between them. But in *shrimps*, *crayfish*, *lobsters*, and such kinds of *crustaceous* water animals, I have

yet I observed them arranged in a quadrangular order, the rows intersecting each other at right angles. While this allows for a smaller number of pearls <note>facets of the compound eye</note> on equal surfaces, those creatures are compensated by having their eyes slightly movable in their heads, which the others completely lack. We find all the dispensations in nature so infinitely wise and provident that certainly *Epicurus* and his followers must have considered them very little; they ascribed to chance those things that will appear to a more attentive observer as the products of the highest wisdom and providence.

Upon the anatomy or dissection of the head, I observed these particulars:

First, that this outward skin, like the *cornea* of the eyes of the larger animals, was both flexible and transparent, and seemed, through the *microscope*, perfectly to resemble the very substance of the *cornea* of a man's eye; for having cut out the cluster and removed the dark and *mucous* stuff that is situated beneath it, I could see it was transparent like a thin piece of skin, having as many cavities on the inside as it had *protuberances* on the outside, and arranged in the same order. This property I found to be the same in all the animals that had it, whether flies or shellfish.

Secondly, I found that all animals that I have observed with these kinds of eyes have within this *cornea* a certain clear liquor or juice, though in a very small quantity.

I observed thirdly, that within that clear liquor, they had a kind of dark *mucous* lining, which was spread all around within the cavity of the cluster and seemed very nearly adjoining to it. The color of this lining in some flies was grey; in others, black; in others, red; in others, of a mixed color; and in others, spotted. The whole clusters, when looked at while the animal was living or only newly killed, appeared to be the same color as this coat (as I may call it) appeared when that outward skin, or *cornea*, was removed.

Fourthly, I observed that the rest of the capacity of the clusters was in some—as in dragonflies, etc.—hollow or empty; in others, it was filled with some kind of substance. In blue flies, it was filled with a reddish muscular substance with fibers extending from the center or bottom outwards; and in various others, it was filled with different kinds of substances.

That this curious contrivance is the organ of sight to all those various *crustaceous* animals which are furnished with it, I think we need not doubt, if we consider the several similarities it has with the eyes of larger creatures.

First, that it is furnished with a *cornea*, with a transparent humor, and with a *uvea* or *retina*. The figure of each of the small *hemispheres* is very spherical, exactly polished, and most vivid, lively, and plump when the animal is living—as in larger animals—and in like manner, they are dull, flaccid, and irregular or shrunk when the animal is dead.

Next, those creatures that are furnished with it have no other organs that have any resemblance to the known eyes of other creatures.

<sig>B b</sig>
<meta>catchword: Thirdly,</meta>

# MICROGRAPHIA.

Thirdly, those which are called the eyes of crabs, lobsters, shrimps, and the like—and truly are eyes—are <term>Hemispher'd</term>, almost in the same manner as those of flies are. And that they really are so, I have very often tested by cutting off these little movable knobs and putting the creature back into the water; it would swim to and fro and move up and down as well as before, but would often hit itself against the rocks or stones. And though I put my hand just in front of its head, it would not startle or flee back at all until I touched it, whereas while those eyes remained, it would start back and avoid my hand or a stick at a good distance before it was touched. And if this is true in <term>crustaceous</term> sea animals, then it seems very probable also that these knobs are the eyes in <term>crustaceous</term> insects, which are also of the same kind, only in a higher and more active element [the air]; this is strongly argued by the conformity or consistency of many other parts common to both: their <term>crustaceous</term> armor; their number of legs, which are six <note>Hooke likely refers to the hexapod nature of insects compared to the many legs of crustaceans</note>, besides the two great claws (which correspond to the wings in insects); and in all kinds of spiders, as well as in many other insects that lack wings, we shall find the complete number of them. We find not only the number, but the very shape, figure, joints, and claws of lobsters and crabs, as is evident in scorpions and spiders, and visible in the second <term>Figure</term> of the 31. <term>Scheme</term>, and in the little mite-worm (which I call a land-crab) described in the second Figure of the 33. <term>Scheme</term>, as well as in their manner of reproduction, being <term>oviparous</term>, etc. And it would be very worthy of observation to see whether there are some kinds of transformation and <term>metamorphosis</term> in the various states of <term>crustaceous</term> water animals, as there are in several sorts of insects; for if such could be found, the progress of the variations would be much more conspicuous in those larger animals than they can be in any kind of insects our colder climate provides.

Since these are their eyes, it provides us with a very pleasing speculation to contemplate their manner of vision, which—as it is very different from that of <term>biocular</term> animals—is no less admirable.

That each of these pearls or <term>Hemispheres</term> is a perfect eye, I think we need not doubt, if we consider only the outside or shape of any one of them; for as each of them is covered with a transparent, protruding <term>Cornea</term> and contains a liquid within them resembling the watery or glassy humors of the eye, they must necessarily refract all the parallel rays that fall on them out of the air into a point not far distant within them. It is there (in all probability) that the <term>Retina</term> of the eye is placed; and that opaque, dark, and mucous inward coat that (as I formerly showed) I found to line the concave part of the cluster is very likely to be that tunicle or coat, as it appears through the <term>Microscope</term> to be placed a little more than a diameter of those pearls below or within the <term>tunica cornea</term>. And if so, then there is in all probability a little picture or image of the objects outside painted or made at the bottom of the <term>Retina</term> against every one of those pearls, so that there are as many impressions on the <term>Retina</term> or opaque skin as there are pearls or <term>Hemispheres</term> on the cluster. But because it is impossible for any protruding surface whatsoever, whether spherical or otherwise, to so refract the rays that come from far remote

lateral points of any object as to collect them again, and unite each of them into a distinct point, and that only those rays which come from some point that lies in the *Axis* of the *Figure* produced, are so accurately refracted to one and the same point again, and that the *lateral Rays*, the further they are removed, the more imperfect is their refracted confluence; It follows therefore, that only the *Picture* of those parts of the external objects that lie in, or near, the *Axis* of each *Hemisphere*, are discernibly painted or made on the *Retina* of each *Hemisphere*, and that therefore each of them can distinctly sense or see only those parts which are very near perpendicularly opposed to it, or lie in or near its optical *Axis*. Now, though there may be by each of these eye-pearls, a representation to the animal of a whole *Hemisphere* in the same manner as in a man's eye there is a picture or sensation in the *Retina* of all the objects lying almost in an *Hemisphere*; yet, as in a man's eye also, there are but some very few points which lying in, or near, the optical *Axis* are distinctly discerned: So there may be multitudes of *Pictures* made of an object in the several pearls, and yet but one, or some very few that are distinct; The representation of any object that is made in any other pearl, but that which is directly, or very near directly, opposed, being altogether confused and unable to produce a distinct vision.

So that we see, that though it has pleased the All-wise Creator, to endow this creature with such multitudes of eyes, yet has he not endowed it with the faculty of seeing more than another creature; for whereas this cannot move his head, at least can move it very little, without moving his whole body, *biocular* creatures can in an instant (or the *twinkling of an eye*, which, being very quick, is commonly used in the same signification) move their eyes so as to direct the optical *Axis* to any point; nor is it probable, that they are able to see attentively at one time more than one physical point; for though there be a distinct image made in every eye, yet it is very likely, that the observing faculty is only employed about some one object for which they have most concern.

Now, as we accurately distinguish the site or position of an object by the motion of the muscles of the eye requisite to put the optical line in a direct position, and confusedly by the position of the imperfect picture of the object at the bottom of the eye; so are these *crustaceous* creatures able to judge confusedly of the position of objects by the picture or impression made at the bottom of the opposite pearl, and distinctly by the removal of the attentive or observing faculty, from one pearl to another; but what this faculty is, as it requires another place, so a much deeper speculation. Now, because it were impossible, even with this multitude of eye-balls, to see any object distinct (for as I hinted before, only those parts that lay in, or very near, the optical lines could be so) the Infinitely wise Creator has not left the creature without a power of moving the head a little in *aerial crustaceous animals*, and the very eyes also in *crustaceous sea-animals*; so that by these means they are enabled to direct some optical line or other against any object, and by that means they have the visual faculty as complete as any animal that can move its eyes.

<sig>Bb 2</sig>
<meta>catchword: Distances</meta>

<summary>Hooke explains that each lens in a compound eye only produces a clear image for objects aligned with its central axis, mirroring the way human vision is sharpest at the center. He concludes that these multiple fixed eyes compensate for an insect's limited head movement, providing a functional visual field equivalent to that of animals with movable eyes.</summary>

<keywords>compound eyes, optical axis, refraction, retina, crustaceous animals, biocular, visual faculty, Robert Hooke</keywords>

--- Page 268 ---
<meta>This page continues Hooke's discussion on the mechanics of insect vision, specifically focusing on how the "pearls" (individual lenses) of compound eyes might perceive distance and the extreme minuteness of biological and physical structures.</meta>

MICROGRAPHIA.

It is also very likely that they distinguish the distances of objects, partly by the consistent impressions made in two suitable pearls, one in each cluster; for, depending on how those matching impressions affect them, the closer together the two pearls are, the nearer the object is, and the further apart they are, the more distant the object is. This is also achieved partly by the alteration of each pearl required to make the sensation or *picture* perfect; for it is impossible that the *pictures* of two objects at different distances can be perfectly painted or made on the same *retina* or bottom of the eye without it being altered, as will be very evident to anyone who shall attentively consider the nature of refraction. Now, whether this alteration occurs in the shape of the *cornea*, in the movement of the *retina* toward or away from the *cornea*, or in the alteration of a crystalline humor (if such a thing exists), I do not claim to determine. However, I think we need not doubt that there may be as much ingenuity in the design and structure of every one of these pearls as in the eye of a whale or elephant. The Almighty's *fiat* could just as easily cause the existence of the one as the other; and as one day and a thousand years are the same to Him, so may one eye and ten thousand be.

We may be sure of this: that the filaments or sensitive parts of the *retina* must be exceedingly intricate and minute, since the entire *picture* itself is so. What must the component parts be of that *retina* which distinguishes a part of an object's *picture* that must be many millions of millions of times smaller than those in a man's eye? And how exceedingly intricate and subtle must the component parts of the *medium* that conveys light be, when we find the instrument made for its reception or refraction to be so exceedingly small? I think we may, from this speculation, be sufficiently discouraged from hoping to discover—by any optical or other instrument—the specific size of the parts of the *medium* that conveys the pulse of light, since we find no less accuracy shown in the shape and polish of those exceedingly minute lens-like surfaces than in the larger and more conspicuous surfaces of our own eyes. And yet I cannot doubt that there is a specific size to those parts, since I find them unable to enter between the parts of mercury, which, being in motion, must necessarily have pores (as I shall show elsewhere, and skip here as it is a digression).

As for the horns FF, the feelers or smellers GG, the *proboscis* HH, and I, the hairs and bristles KK, I shall endeavor to describe them in the 42nd *Observation*.

### **Observ. XLI.** 
## *Of the Eggs of Silk-worms, and other Insects.*

The eggs of silk-worms (one of which I have described in the second figure of Scheme 25) provide a beautiful object for a <term>Microscope</term> that magnifies significantly, especially in bright weather when the light from a window is cast or collected upon it by a deep convex glass or water-ball. For then the entire surface of the shell may be perceived as being covered with exceedingly small pits or cavities with interposed edges, almost like the surface of a poppy seed, except that these holes are scarcely a hundredth part of that size. When the young ones were hatched (which I found easy to do if the eggs were kept in a warm place), the shell appeared no thicker in proportion to its size than that of a hen's or goose's egg is to its size. The entire shell appeared very white (which seemed to result from its transparency), causing all those pits to almost vanish so that they could not be discerned without great difficulty. The inside of the shell also seemed to be lined with a kind of thin film, not unlike (keeping the proportion to its shell) the film with which the shell of a hen's egg is lined. The shell itself seemed like common eggshells, very brittle and cracked. In various others of these eggs, I could plainly enough perceive the small insect lying coiled around the edges of the shell through the casing. The shape of the egg itself is represented well enough by the figure (though, through the fault of the engraver, it does

<meta>This page continues the discussion of insect eggs, specifically comparing those of silk-worms and other insects, and begins an observation on the blue fly.</meta>

...did not appear as rounded, or as if they were raised from the paper, as they should have. That is, they were mostly quite oval lengthwise, somewhat like an egg, but the other way they were a little flattened on two opposite sides. Many of these eggs, as is common with most others, I found to be barren or addled, for they never produced any young. I usually found those to be much whiter than the others that were prolific. I have found the eggs of other kinds of <term>oviparous</term> insects to be perfectly round in every way, like so many globules; I have observed some sorts of spiders' eggs of this type. By chance last summer, I enclosed a very large and beautifully patterned butterfly in a box, intending to examine its finery with my *Microscope*. I found within a day or two after I enclosed her that almost the entire inner surface of the box was covered with an infinite number of exactly round eggs. These were stuck very firmly to the sides of it in such an exactly regular and close order that it reminded me of my *hypothesis*, which I had previously considered, for explaining all the regular shapes of salt (which I have hinted at elsewhere). Here I found all of them arranged in a most precise triangular order, much like the way the *hemispheres* are placed on the eye of a fly. After a short time, I found all these eggs had hatched, and out of them came a multitude of small worms, very much resembling young *silk-worms*. They left all their thin hollow shells behind them, sticking to the box in their *triangular* arrangement. Using the *Microscope*, I found these to have much the same substance as *silk-worms'* eggs, but I could not see them as being pitted. Indeed, there is as great a variety in the shape of the eggs of egg-laying insects as there is among those of birds.

A large and vigorous fly will lay nearly four or five hundred of these eggs at one time, so the increase of these kinds of insects would certainly be enormous if they were not preyed upon by many birds and destroyed by frosts and rains. This is why those hotter climates between the *Tropics* are infested with such multitudes of locusts and other such pests.

### Observ. XLII. Of a blue fly.

This kind of fly, of which a *microscopic* picture is drawn in the first figure of the 26th *Scheme*, is a very beautiful creature and has many notable features. I have already partially described several of these, namely the feet, wings, eyes, and head, in the preceding observations.

And although the head described before belongs to a gray *drone-fly*, it is mostly very similar to this one. The things in which they differ most will be easily found by the following details:

First, the clusters of eyes on this fly are much smaller than those of the *drone-fly* in proportion to its head.

And next, all the eyes of each cluster seemed much the same size as one another, not differing like the others, but arranged in the same *tri-*agonal order.

Thirdly, between these two clusters, there was a scaly prominent front B, which was armed and adorned with large tapering sharp black bristles. Growing out in rows on either side, these were so bent toward each other near the top as to make a kind of arched arbor of bristles, which almost covered the front.

Fourthly, at the end of this arch, about the middle of the face, on a prominent part C, grew two small oblong bodies, DD, which through a *microscope* looked not unlike the pendants in *lilies*. These seemed to be jointed onto two small parts at C, each of which seemed again jointed into the front.

Fifthly, out of the upper part and outsides of these horns (as I may call them, from their shape in the 24th *Scheme*, where they are marked with FF), there grows a single feather or brushy bristle, EE, somewhat of the same kind as the tufts of a gnat, which I have previously described.

I cannot well imagine what the use of these kinds of horned and tufted bodies might be, unless they serve for smelling or hearing. However, it seems very difficult to describe how they are adapted for either, as they are of such various shapes in almost every different kind of fly. Yet certainly they are some very essential part of the head and have some very notable office assigned to them by Nature, since they are found in one form or another in all insects.

Sixthly, at the lower part of the face FF, were several of the previously mentioned bent bristles; and below all was the mouth, out of the middle of which grew the *proboscis* GHI. By means of several joints, of which it seemed to consist, the fly was able to move it to and fro and thrust it in and out as it pleased. The end of this hollow body (which was covered all over with small short hairs or bristles) was, as it were, bent at H, and the outer or foremost side of the bent part HI was slit, as it were, into two jaws, HI, HI. All the outside of these was covered with hairs and fairly large bristles; these it could, like two jaws, very readily open and shut. When it seemed to suck anything from the surface of a body, it would spread those jaws wide and apply the hollow part of them very close to it.

From either side of the *proboscis*, within the mouth, grew two other small horns or fingers, KK, which were hairy but small in this figure; however, they are of another shape and larger in proportion in the 24th *Scheme*, where they are marked GG. These two indeed seemed to be a kind of smellers, but whether they are so or not, I cannot positively determine.

The *thorax* or middle part of this fly was encased, both above and beneath, with a very firm crust of armor; the upper part was more rounded and covered over with long conical bristles, all of whose ends pointed backward. Out of the rear and lower part of this grew a cluster of six legs, three of which are apparent in the figure, while the other three were hidden by the body

The legs were all much of the same make, being all of them covered with a strong hairy scale or shell, just like the legs of a crab or lobster, and the contrivance of the joints seemed much the same; each leg seemed made up of eight parts, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, to the eighth or last of which, grew the soles and claws, described before in the 38th *Observation*.

These films, in many flies, were so thin, that, like several other plated bodies (mentioned in the ninth *Observation*) they afforded all varieties of fantastical or transient colors (the reason of which I have here endeavored to explain); they seemed to receive their nourishment from the stalks or wires, which seemed to be hollow, and near the upper part of the wing **LL** several of them seemed jointed, the shape of which will sufficiently appear by the black lines in the second Figure of the 26th *Scheme*, which is a delineation of one of those wings expanded directly to the eyes.

All the hinder part of its body is covered with a most exquisite blue shining armor, looking exactly like a polished piece of steel brought to that blue color by annealing, all of which armor is very thickly stuck with an abundance of tapering bristles, such as grow on its back, as is visible enough by the Figure.

Nor was the inside of this creature less beautiful than its outside; for cutting off a part of the belly, and then viewing it, to see if I could discover any vessels, such as are to be found in larger animals, and even in snails exceedingly clearly, I found, much beyond my expectation, that there were abundance of branchings of milk-white vessels, no less intricate than the branchings of veins and arteries in bigger terrestrial animals; in one of which, I found two notable branches, joining their two main stocks, as it were, into one common <term>ductus</term>; now, to what veins or arteries these vessels were <term>analogous</term>, whether to the <term>vena porta</term>, or the <term>meseraic</term> vessels, or the like, or indeed, whether they were veins and arteries, or <term>vasa lactea</term>, properly so called, I am not hitherto able to determine, having not yet made sufficient inquiry; but in all particulars, there seems not to be any thing less of intricate contricance in these <term>Insects</term>, than in those larger terrestrial animals, for I had never seen any more intricate branchings of vessels, than those I observed in two or three of these flies thus opened.

It is a creature active and nimble, so that there are very few creatures like it, whether bigger or smaller, in so much, that it will escape and avoid a small body, though coming on it exceedingly swiftly, and if it sees anything approaching it, which it fears, it presently squats down, as it were, that it may be the more ready for its rise.

Nor is it less hardy in the winter, than active in the summer, enduring all the frosts, and surviving until the next summer, notwithstanding the bitter

This kind of fly seems, by the vapors or taste of fermenting and rotting meat (which it often kisses, as it were, with its *proboscis* as it trips over it), to be stimulated or excited to eject its eggs or seed on it, perhaps for the same reason as dogs, cats, and many other brute creatures are excited to their particular lusts by the smell of their females when prepared by nature for generation; the males seeming, by those kinds of smells or other incitements, to be as much compelled to it as *Aqua Regis* <note>A highly corrosive mixture of acids</note> strongly impregnated with a solution of gold is forced to precipitate it by the pouring on of spirit of *urine* <note>An ammonia-rich solution</note>, or a solution of *salt of tartar* <note>Potassium carbonate</note>.

One of these, placed in spirit of *wine* <note>Ethanol</note>, was very quickly seemingly killed, and both its eyes and mouth began to look very red; but upon taking it out and letting it lie for three or four hours, and heating it with the sunbeams cast through a burning-glass, it revived again, appearing, as it were, to have been all the intermediate time merely dead drunk, and after certain hours it grew fresh again and sober.

### Observ. XLIII. *Of the Water-Insect or Gnat.*

This little creature, described in the first *figure* of the 27th *scheme*, was a small scaled or crusted animal, which I have often observed to be generated in rainwater; I have also observed it both in pond and river water. It is supposed by some to derive its first origin from the putrefaction of rainwater, in which—if it has stood any time open to the air—you shall seldom fail to find, all summer long, a store of them frisking to and fro.

It is a creature wholly differing in shape from any I ever observed; nor is its motion less strange. It has a very large head in proportion to its body, all covered with a shell, like other *testaceous* <note>Shelled</note> animals, but it differs in this: that it has, on several parts of it, several tufts of hair or bristles placed in the order expressed in the figure. It has two horns, which seemed almost like the horns of an ox inverted and, as near as I could guess, were hollow, with tufts of bristles likewise at the top; these horns they could move easily this way or that, and might, perhaps, be their nostrils. It has a fairly large mouth, which seemed constructed much like those of crabs and lobsters, by which I have often observed them to feed on water or some imperceptible nutritive substance in it.

I could perceive through the transparent shell, while the animal lived, several motions in the head, thorax, and belly, very distinctly,

of different kinds which I may, perhaps, elsewhere endeavor more accurately to examine, and to show how great a benefit the use of a *Microscope* may be for the discovery of Nature's course in the operations performed in animal bodies. By this, we have the opportunity of observing her through these delicate and transparent skins of the bodies of insects acting according to her usual course and way, undisturbed; whereas, when we endeavor to pry into her secrets by breaking open the doors upon her, and dissecting and mangling creatures while there is life yet within them, we find her indeed at work, but put into such disorder by the violence offered, as it may easily be imagined. How different a thing we should find if we could, as we can with a *Microscope* in these smaller creatures, quietly peep in at the windows without frightening her out of her usual behavior.

The form of the whole creature, as it appeared in the *Microscope*, may—without troubling you with more descriptions—be plainly enough perceived by the diagram. The hinder part or belly consists of eight separate jointed parts, namely, A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H, of the first *Figure*. From the middle of each of these, on either side, issued three or four small bristles or hairs, I, I, I, I, I, I. The tail was divided into two parts of very different make; one of them, namely K, having many tufts of hair or bristles, which seemed to serve both for the fins and tail, and for the oars and rudder of this little creature. With these it was able, by frisking and bending its body nimbly to and fro, to move itself anywhere, and to scull and steer itself as it pleased. The other part, L, seemed to be, as it were, the ninth division of his belly, and had many single bristles on either side. From the end V of this, through the whole belly, there was a kind of gut of a darker color, M M M, wherein, by certain *peristaltic* motions, there was a kind of black substance moved upwards and downwards through it, from the orbicular part of it, N (which seemed to be the ventricle or stomach), to the tail V, and so back again. I have observed this *peristaltic* motion also in a louse, a gnat, and several other kinds of transparent-bodied flies. The *thorax* or chest of this creature, O O O O, was thick and short, and quite transparent, for through it I could see the white heart (which is the color also of the blood in these and most other insects) beating, and several other kinds of motions. It was stuck and adorned here and there with several tufts of bristles, such as are pointed out by P, P, P, P. The head Q was likewise covered with several of those tufts, S S S; it was broad and short, and had two black eyes, T T, which I could not perceive to be at all "pearled" <note>Faceted, like a compound eye</note> as they afterwards appeared, and two small horns, R R, such as I formerly described.

Both its motion and rest are very strange, pleasant, and different from those of most other creatures I have observed. For, when it ceases from moving its body, its tail—seeming much lighter than the rest of its body, and a little lighter than the water it swims in—presently buoys it up to the top of the water, where it hangs suspended with the head always downward. And like our *Antipodes* <note>People on the opposite side of the globe, imagined to be upside down</note>, if they do by a frisk get below that surface, they presently ascend again to it if they cease moving.

The way they hung in this posture reminded me of a certain creature I have seen in *London* that was brought from *America*, which would very firmly suspend itself by the tail with its head downwards, and was said to sleep in that position with her young ones in her "false belly." This is a pouch provided by Nature for the production, nutrition, and preservation of her young ones, which is described by *Piso* in the 24th Chapter of the fifth Book of his *Natural History of Brazil*.

Its motion was with the tail forward, drawing itself backward by the frisking to and fro of that tuft which grew out of one of the stumps of its tail. It had another motion, which was more similar to that of other creatures, and that is with the head forward; for by the moving of its jaws (if I may call the parts of its mouth that) it was able to move itself downward very gently toward the bottom, and did, as it were, eat its way through the water.

But what was most remarkable in this creature was its *metamorphosis* or change; for having kept several of these *animals* in a glass of rainwater in which they were produced, I found, after keeping them for about a fortnight or three weeks, that several of them flew away as *gnats*, leaving their husks behind them in the water floating under the surface—the place where these *animals* used to reside while they were inhabitants of the water. This made me watch them more diligently to see if I could find them at the time of their transformation; and not long after, I observed several of them change into an unusual shape, wholly differing from what they were before. Their head and body had grown much larger and deeper, but not broader, and their abdomen, or hinder part, was smaller and coiled around this large body, much like the fashion represented by the dotted line in the second *Figure* of the 27th *Scheme*. The head and horns now swam uppermost, and the whole bulk of the body seemed to have grown much lighter; for when I frightened it, it would sink itself below the surface toward the bottom by flicking its tail (in the manner expressed in the *Figure* by B C), but the body would re-ascend more swiftly than when it was in its former shape.

I continued to mark its progress from time to time and found its body still growing larger and larger, as if Nature were fitting and equipping it for the lighter element [air], of which it was now going to be an inhabitant. For, by observing one of these with my *microscope*, I found its eyes to be altogether different from what they seemed before, appearing now all over "pearled" or knobbed, like the eyes of *gnats*, as is visible in the second *Figure* at A. At length, I saw part of this creature swimming above and part beneath the surface of the water, below which it would quickly plunge itself if I frightened it by any means, and immediately re-ascend into its former posture. After a little longer expectation, I found that the head and body of a *gnat* began to appear and stand clear above the surface, and by degrees it drew out its legs—first the two foremost, then the others—at length its whole body appeared perfect and entire out of the husk (which it left in the water), standing on its legs upon
