the top of the water, and by degrees it began to move, and afterward flew about the glass, a perfect gnat.

I have been more detailed and extensive in the account of the transformation of various little animals which I observed, because I have not found that any author has observed the same; and because the thing itself is so strange and different from the usual development of other animals, I judge it may not only be pleasant, but very useful and necessary toward completing Natural History.

There is indeed in *Piso* a very odd story, which this account may make more probable; and that is in the 2nd Chapter of the 4th Book of his *Natural History of Brazil*, where he says: "Furthermore, besides so many proofs of fertility regarding the marine plants and creatures that rival the land, this also happened: a few miles from Pernambuco, a fisherman's hook accidentally caught in the stony shallows, and instead of a fish, sponges, corals, and other marine shrubs were caught. Among these emerged a spongy shrub of unusual form, a foot and a half long, with short roots, shining in the stony shallows and fixed to the rocks. It rises into a spongy, soft, oblong, round, cone-shaped body; inside it is constructed with wonderful lattices and channels, but outside it is covered everywhere with a tenacious glue like the propolis of bees, with a sufficiently wide and deep opening left at the top, as can be seen well-depicted in one of the illustrations (see the third and fourth figures of the 27th Scheme). Thus, you might truly call it a marine beehive; for at first glance, when brought from the sea to the land, it teemed with small blue worms, which were soon transformed by the heat of the sun into flies—or rather bees, and those small and black—and flying about they vanished. Thus, nothing certain could be observed regarding their honey-making, although the waxy matter, the propolis, and the bees' cells clearly appeared; and the substance of the honey itself, whatever it may be, will no doubt be revealed to divers when they investigate these beehives more curiously and examine them more thoroughly at different times in their native soil and sea."

This story contains things strange enough to be considered: such as whether the husk was a plant growing by itself at the bottom of the sea, from whose decay these strange kinds of maggots might be generated; or whether the seeds of certain bees, sinking to the bottom, might naturally form that vegetable hive there and take root; or whether it might have been placed there by some diving fly; or whether it might be some peculiar property of that plant by which it might ripen or form its vegetable juice into an animal substance; or whether it may be of the nature of a sponge, or rather a sponge of the nature of this—according to some of those accounts and conjectures I formerly made of that body—is a matter very difficult to be determined. But indeed, in this description, the excellent *Piso* has not been detailed enough in setting down the whole process, as one would wish. There are indeed very odd developments in the production of several kinds of insects, which are no less instructive than pleasant; several of these the diligent *Goedartius* has carefully observed and recorded, but among all his observations, he has none like this, though that of the *Hemerobius* is somewhat of this kind, which is added as an appendix by *Johannes Mey*.

# MICROGRAPHIA.

I have, for my own part, besides several of those mentioned by him, observed various other circumstances—perhaps not much noticed, though very common—which indeed provide us with a very compelling argument to admire the goodness and providence of the infinitely wise Creator in his most excellent designs and arrangements. I have observed, at several times during the summer, that many of the leaves of various plants have been spotted, or, as it were, scabbed; and looking on the undersides of those that were only a little irregular, I have perceived them to be sprinkled with various sorts of little eggs. Leaving them alone, I have found them to grow bigger by degrees and become little worms with legs, but they still kept their former places. Those parts of the leaves, of their own accord, grew very protuberant upwards and very hollow and arched underneath, whereby those young creatures are, as it were, sheltered and housed from external injury. I have observed various leaves to grow and swell so far as at length to perfectly enclose the animal, which, by other observations I have made, I guess contains it and becomes, as it were, a womb to it, until it is fit and prepared to be transformed into another state. At which time, like (what they say of) vipers, they gnaw their way through the womb that bred them; I have met with various kinds of these on gooseberry leaves, rose-tree leaves, willow leaves, and many other kinds.

There are often to be found upon rose trees and briar bushes little red tufts, which are certain knobs or excrescences growing out from the rind or bark of those kinds of plants. They are covered with strange kinds of threads or red hairs, which feel very soft and do not look unpleasant. In most of these, if there is no hole in it, you shall find certain little worms, which I suppose to be the cause of their production; for when that worm has eaten its way through, they, having performed what they were designed by Nature to do, gradually die and wither away.

Now, I suppose the manner of their production to be thus: that the All-wise Creator has implanted in every creature a faculty of knowing what place is convenient for the hatching, nutrition, and preservation of their eggs and offspring, whereby they are stimulated and directed to convenient places, which become, as it were, the wombs that perform those offices. He has also suited and adapted a property to those places whereby they grow and enclose those seeds, and having enclosed them, provide a convenient nourishment for them; but as soon as they have performed the office of a womb, they die and wither.

The progress of enclosure I have often observed in leaves, which, in those places where those seeds have been cast, have gradually swelled and enclosed them, so perfectly round as not to leave any perceptible passage out.

From this same cause, I suppose that galls, oak-apples, and several other productions of that kind upon the branches and leaves of trees have their origin; for if you open any of them when almost ripe, you shall find a little worm in them. Thus, if you open any number of dry galls, you shall find either a hole whereby the worm has eaten its passage out,

...out, or if you find no passage, you may, by breaking or cutting the gall, find in the middle of it a small cavity, and in it a small body, which still plainly enough retains a shape to show that it was once a worm, though it died by too early a separation from the oak on which it grew—its navel-string, as it were, being broken off from the leaf or branch by which the globular body that enveloped it received its nourishment from the oak.

And indeed, if we consider the great care of the Creator in the dispensations of his providence for the propagation and increase of the race, not only of all kinds of animals, but even of vegetables, we cannot help but admire and adore him for his excellencies. However, we shall stop admiring the creature itself or wondering at the strange behaviors of several animals that seem to suggest so much reason. It seems most manifest to me that these are merely actions according to their structures—operations that such bodies, so composed, must necessarily perform when certain circumstances occur. Thus, when we find flies swarming about any piece of flesh that begins to ferment; butterflies around coleworts <note>Cabbage-like plants of the genus Brassica.</note> and several other leaves that will serve to hatch and nourish their young; gnats and several other flies around waters and marshy places; or any other creatures seeking and placing their seeds in convenient repositories—we may, if we attentively consider and examine it, find that there are sufficient circumstances (assuming the excellent design of their <term>machine</term>) to excite and force them to act in such a manner. Those vapors that rise from these various places may, perhaps, set several parts of these little animals at work, just as in the device for killing a fox or wolf with a gun, the moving of a string results in the death of the animal. For the beast, by moving the flesh laid to entrap him, pulls the string that moves the trigger, which releases the cock, which strikes the steel to create sparks of fire that kindle the powder in the pan, and that immediately enters the barrel, where the powder catching fire expands and drives out the bullet that kills the animal. In all these actions, there is nothing of intention or <term>ratiocination</term> to be ascribed either to the animal or the engine, but everything to the ingenuity of the designer.

But to return to the more immediate consideration of our gnat: we have in it an instance, unusual and uncommon, of a very strange amphibious creature; for being a creature that inhabits the air, it yet produces a creature that for some time lives in the water like a fish, though afterward (which is just as strange) it becomes an inhabitant of the air like its sire, in the form of a fly. And this, I think, prompts me to propose certain conjectures as queries, as I have not yet had sufficient opportunity or leisure to answer them myself through my own experiments or observations.

And the first is, whether all those things that we suppose to be bred from corruption and putrefaction might not be rationally supposed to have an origin as natural as these gnats, which, it is very probable, were first dropped into this water in the form of eggs. Those seeds or eggs

Eggs must certainly be very small, which so small a creature as a gnat yields, and therefore we need not wonder that we do not find the eggs themselves; some of the younger ones, which I have observed, have not exceeded a tenth part of the bulk they afterwards reached. Next, I have observed some of those little ones which must have been generated after the water was enclosed in the bottle, and therefore most probably from eggs, whereas those creatures have been supposed to be bred from the corruption of the water, there being no previously known probable way for them to be generated.

A second question is whether these eggs are immediately dropped into the water by the gnats themselves, or indirectly brought down by the falling rain; for it seems not very improbable that those small seeds of gnats might (being, perhaps, of such a light nature, and having so great a proportion of surface to such a small bulk of body) be ejected into the air, and so, perhaps, carried for a good while back and forth in it, until they are washed out of it by falling drops of rain.

A third question is whether multitudes of those other little creatures that are found to inhabit the water for some time do not, at certain times, take wing and fly into the air, while others dive and hide themselves in the earth, and so contribute to the increase of life in both the one and the other element.

### *Postscript.*

A good while after the writing of this description, I was presented by *Doctor Peter Ball*, an ingenious member of the *Royal Society*, with a little paper of nuts, which he told me was sent to him by a brother of his from the country, from *Mamhead* in *Devonshire*. Some of them were loose, having been, I suppose, broken off; others were still growing firmly onto the sides of a stick, which seemed by the bark, its flexibility, and certain strings that grew out of it, to be some piece of the root of a tree. They were all dried and a little shriveled; others were more round and of a brown color. Their shape was much like a fig, but very much smaller, some being about the size of a bayberry, and others, the largest, about the size of a hazelnut. Some of these that had no hole in them, I carefully opened with my knife and found in them a good large, round, white maggot, almost as big as a small pea, which seemed shaped like other maggots, but shorter. I could not find them to move, though I guessed them to be alive, because upon pricking them with a pin, there would issue out a great deal of white *mucous* matter, which seemed to result from a voluntary contraction of their skin. Their husk or <term>matrix</term> consisted of three coats, like the bark of trees: the outermost being more rough and spongy, and the thickest; the middlemost more dense, hard, white, and thin; the innermost very thin, appearing almost like the skin inside an eggshell. The two outermost had roots in the branch or stick, but the innermost had no stem or connection, but was only a skin that covered the cavity of the nut. All the nuts that had no holes eaten in them, I found to contain these maggots, but all that had holes, I found empty, the maggots,

Four or five of these were then opened; some were found to contain live insects that had reached maturity, very much like flying ants, if not the same. In others, the insects were still imperfect, having only the head and wings formed, with the rest remaining a soft, white, pulpy substance.

Now, as this provides us with one more unusual account, very consistent with what I suggested before, I do not doubt that if men were diligent observers, they might encounter multitudes of the same kind in the earth, the water, and the air, and on trees, plants, and other vegetables—all places and things being, as it were, *animarum plena* <note>Full of life or souls.</note>. And I have often, with wonder and pleasure during the spring and summer, looked closely and diligently at common garden soil; in a very small portion of it, I found such multitudes and varieties of little crawling creatures—some in husks, others only creepers, many winged and ready for the air, and various husks or habitations left behind empty. Now, if the earth of our cold climate is so fertile with living bodies, what might we think of the rich soil of hotter climates? Certainly, the sun there may, by its activity, cause as large a portion of earth to take wing in the air as it does water in the form of steam and vapor. And what swarms must we imagine are sent out from those plentiful floods of water that are poured down by the sluices of rain in such vast quantities? Thus, we need not wonder much at those innumerable clouds of locusts with which *Africa* and other hot countries are so pestered, since in those places all the necessary causes for their production are found: namely, progenitors or parents, suitable receptacles or <term>matrices</term>, and a sufficient degree of natural heat and moisture.

I was going to include a small drawing of the shape of those nuts sent from *Devonshire*, but while I happened to be examining Mr. *Parkinson’s* Herbal for something else—specifically regarding galls and oak-apples—I found no fewer than 24 different kinds of excrescences of the oak. I do not doubt that, upon examination, all will be found to be the <term>matrices</term> of as many different kinds of insects; I myself have observed many of them to be so. Among those 24 different kinds, I say, I found one described and illustrated exactly like the one I had with me. <margin>Observ. XLIV.</margin>

### Of the tufted or Brush-horned Gnat.

This little creature was one of those multitudes that fill our *English* air all the time that warm weather lasts, and is exactly of the shape of that which I observed to be generated and hatched out of those little *insects* that wriggle up and down in rain-water. But, though many were of this form, yet I observed others to be of quite other kinds; nor were all of this or the other kind generated out of water *insects*; for whereas I observed that those that proceeded from those *insects* were at their full growth, I have also found multitudes of the same shape, but much smaller and tenderer, seeming to be very young ones, creeping up and down upon the leaves of trees, and flying up and down in small clusters, in places very remote from water; and this spring, I observed one day, when the wind was very calm, and the afternoon very fair, and pretty warm, though it had for a long time been very cold weather, and the wind continued still in the east, several small swarms of them playing to and fro in little clouds in the sun, each of which was not a tenth part of the bigness of one of these I have here delineated, though very much of the same shape, which makes me guess that each of these swarms might be the offspring of only one gnat, which had been hoarded up in some safe repository all this winter by some provident parent, and were now, by the warmth of the spring air, hatched into little flies.

And indeed, so various and seemingly irregular are the generations or productions of *insects*, that he who shall carefully and diligently observe the several methods of nature therein, will have infinite cause further to admire the wisdom and providence of the Creator; for not only may the same kind of creature be produced in several kinds of ways, but the very same creature may produce several kinds: For, as diverse watches may be made out of several materials, which may yet have all the same appearance, and move after the same manner—that is, show the hour equally true, the one as the other—and out of the same kind of matter, like watches, may be wrought in differing ways; and, as one and the same watch may,

### Observation XLV. Of the great-bellied gnat, or female gnat.

The second gnat, illustrated in the twenty-ninth Scheme, is of a very different shape from the former; but yet of this sort also, I found several of the gnats that were generated out of the water insect: the wings of this one were much larger than those of the other, and the belly much bigger, shorter, and of another shape; and, from several details, I guessed it to be the female gnat, and the former to be the male.

The *thorax* of this was much like that of the other, having a very strong and ridged back-piece, which also extended on either side of its legs; around the wings there were several jointed pieces of armor, which seemed curiously and conveniently contrived for promoting and strengthening the motion of the wings. Its head was very different from the other, being much bigger and more neatly shaped, and the horns that grew out between its eyes on two little balls were of a very different shape from the tufts of the other gnat—these having but a few knots or joints, and each of those having but a few short and strong bristles. The foremost horns, or feelers, were like those of the former gnat.

One of these gnats I have allowed to pierce the skin of my hand with its *proboscis*, and from there to draw out as much blood as to fill its belly as full as it could hold, making it appear very red and transparent; and this occurred without any further pain than while it was sinking in its *proboscis*, as is also the case with the stinging of fleas. This is a good argument that these creatures do not wound the skin and suck the blood out of enmity and revenge, but for mere necessity and to satisfy their hunger. By what means this creature is able to suck, we shall show in another place.

Wings, the two foremost somewhat longer than the two hindermost, and the two shorter about half an inch long, each of which four wings seemed to consist of two small long feathers, very exquisitely tufted, or haired on each side, with purely white and exceedingly fine and small hairs, proportioned to the stalks or stems out of which they grew, much like the tufts of a long wing-feather of some bird, and their stalks or stems were, like those, bent backwards and downwards, as may be plainly seen by the drawings of them in the figure.

Observing one of these in my *Microscope*, I found, in the first place, that all the body, legs, horns and the stalks of the wings, were covered over with various kinds of exquisite white feathers, which did, with handling or touching, easily rub off and fly about, so much that looking on my fingers, with which I had handled this moth, and perceiving little white specks on them, I found by my *Microscope* that they were several of the small feathers of this little creature, that stuck here and there in the *rugosities* of my skin.

Next, I found that underneath these feathers, the pretty insect was covered all over with a crusted shell, like other of those animals, but with one much thinner and more tender.

Thirdly, I found, as is also notable in birds, it had different and appropriate kinds of feathers that covered several parts of its body.

Fourthly, surveying the parts of its body with a more accurate and better magnifying *Microscope*, I found that the tufts or hairs of its wings were nothing else but a congeries, or thick-set cluster of small *vimina* or twigs, resembling a small twig of birch, stripped or whitened, with which brushes are usually made to beat out or brush off the dust from cloth and hangings. Every one of the twigs or branches that composed the brush of the feathers appeared in this larger magnifying glass (of which E F, which represents <gloss>1/24</gloss> part of an inch, is the scale, as G is of the lesser, which is only <gloss>1/3</gloss>) like the figure D. The feathers also that covered a part of his body, and were interspersed among the brush of his wings, I found, in the larger magnifying glass, to be of the shape A, consisting of a stalk or stem in the middle, and a seeming tuftedness or brushy part on each side. The feathers that covered most part of his body and the stalk of his wings were, in the same *Microscope*, much like the figure B, appearing in the shape of a small feather, and seemed tufted; those which covered the horns and small parts of the legs, through the same *Microscope*, appeared as the shape C. Whether the tufts of any or all of these small feathers consisted of such component particles as the feathers of birds, I doubt very much, because I find that nature does not always keep or operate according to the same method in smaller and larger creatures. And of this, we have particular instances in the wings of several creatures. For whereas, in birds of all kinds, it composes each of the feathers of which its wing consists of such an exceedingly exquisite and most admirable and stupendous texture, as I elsewhere show in the observations on a feather, we find it alters its method quite in the fabric of the wings of these minute creatures, composing some of thin extended membranes

or skins, such as the wings of dragonflies; in others, those skins are all overgrown, or quite thickly stuck, with short bristles, as in flesh-flies; in others, those films are covered, both on the upper and under side, with small feathers, placed almost like the tiles on a house, and are curiously arranged and adorned with most lively colors, as is observable in butterflies and several kinds of moths. In others, instead of their films, Nature has provided nothing but about ten stalks (if I remember the number correctly; for I have not lately met with any of these flies, and did not, when I first observed them, take sufficient notice of various details) and each of these stalks, with a few single branches on each side, greatly resembles the branched backbone of a herring or similar fish, or a thin-haired peacock's feather with the top or the eye being broken off. Other insects have their wings encased, or covered over, with certain hollow shells, shaped almost like those hollow trays in which butchers carry meat, whose hollow sides being turned downwards do not only secure their folded wings from injury from the earth, in which most of those creatures reside, but while they fly, serve as a help to sustain and bear them up. And these are observable in *scarabees* <note>beetles</note> and a multitude of other *terrestrial crustaceous insects*; in which we may yet further observe a particular providence of Nature.

Now in all these kinds of wings, we observe this particular detail as something most worthy of remark: that wherever a wing consists of disconnected parts, the pores or *interstitia* <note>intervals or gaps</note> between those parts are very seldom either much bigger or much smaller than those which we find here between the particles of these brushes. This seems to suggest that the parts of the air are such that they will not easily or readily, if at all, pass through these pores; thus they seem to be strainers fine enough to hinder the particles of the air (whether hindered by their bulk or by their *agitation, circulation, rotation*, or *undulation*, I shall not here determine) from getting through them, and, by that means, serve the animal as well as, if not better than, if they were little films. I say, if not better, because I have observed that all those creatures that have filmed wings, such as all kinds of flies, *scarabees*, and bats, move them much more quickly and strongly than those that have their wings covered with feathers, such as butterflies and birds, or "twigs," as in moths, which each have a much slower motion of their wings. That little roughness perhaps of their wings helps them somewhat by taking a better hold of the parts of the air, or by not allowing them to pass by so easily in any direction but one.

But whatever the reason for it, it is most evident that the smooth-winged insects have the strongest muscles or moving parts in their wings, and the others much weaker ones; and this very insect we are now describing,

And this last property we also find observed in larger kinds of flying creatures, birds; so that we see that the wisdom and providence of the all-wise Creator is no less shown in these small, despicable creatures—flies and moths, which we have branded with a name of ignominy, calling them vermin—than in those larger and more remarkable animate bodies, birds.

I cannot stop here to add anything about the nature of flight, though, perhaps, on another occasion, I may say something on that subject, as it deserves a much more accurate examination and scrutiny than it has hitherto met with. For to me there seems nothing wanting to make a man able to fly, except what may be easily enough supplied from the mechanics known until now, save only the lack of strength, of which the muscles of a man seem utterly incapable, by reason of their smallness and structure; but how even strength also may be mechanically made—an artificial muscle so contrived that a man shall be able to exert whatever strength he pleases, and to regulate it also to his own mind—I may elsewhere endeavor to demonstrate.

***

### Observ. XLVII. Of the Shepherd Spider, or long-legged Spider.

The Carter, Shepherd Spider, or long-legged Spider, has, for two peculiarities, very few similar creatures that I have met with. The first, which is discoverable only by the *microscope*, and is plainly described in the first and second *figures* of the 31st *scheme*, is the curious contrivance of its eyes. Of these (differing from most other spiders) it has only two, and those placed upon the top of a small pillar or hillock, rising out of the middle of the top of its back, or rather the crown of its head; for they were fixed on the very top of this pillar (which is about the height of one of the transverse diameters of the eye, and looked at in another posture, appeared much like the shape BCD). The two eyes, BB, were placed back to back, with the transparent parts, or the pupils, looking toward either side, but somewhat more forward than backward. C was the column or neck on which they stood, and D the crown of the head out of which that neck sprung.

These eyes, to all appearance, seemed to be of the very same structure as those of larger binocular creatures, appearing to have a very smooth and very protuberant *cornea*, and in the midst of it to have a very black pupil, encompassed by a kind of gray *iris*, as appears by the *figure*. Whether it was able to move these eyes to and fro, I have not observed, but it is not very likely it should, as the pillar or neck, C, seemed to be covered and stiffened with a crusty shell; but Nature, in probability, has supplied

This creature, as do all other spiders I have yet examined, differs very much from most other *Insects* in the shape of its eyes; for I cannot, with my best *Microscope*, discover its eyes to be in any way knobbed or pearled like those of other *Insects*.

The second peculiarity which is obvious to the eye is also very remarkable, and that is the prodigious length of its legs in proportion to its small round body—each leg of this one I drew being over sixteen times the length of its whole body; and there are some which have them even longer, and others that seem to be of the same kind that have them a great deal shorter. The eight legs are each of them jointed just like those of a *crab*, but every part is spun out prodigiously longer in proportion. Each of these legs ends in a small case or shell, shaped almost like that of a *mussel shell*, as is evident in the third *Figure* of the same *Scheme* (which represents the appearance of the under part or belly of the creature) by the shape of the protuberant *conical body*, I I I I, etc. These are, as it were, placed or fastened onto the protuberant body of the *insect*, which is to be supposed very high at M, making a kind of blunt cone of which M is to be supposed the *Apex*; around this larger cone of the body, the smaller cones of the legs are placed, each of them almost reaching to the top in such an admirable manner that it clearly manifests the wisdom of Nature in the design. For these long levers (as I may call them) of the legs, not having the advantage of a long end on the other side of the <term>hypomochlion</term> <note>the fulcrum or center of motion for a lever</note> or centers on which the parts of the legs move, must necessarily require vast strength to move them and keep the body balanced and suspended; so much so that if we were to suppose a man's body suspended by such a mechanism, one hundred and fifty times the strength of a man would not keep the body from falling on its breast. To supply each of these legs with its proper strength, therefore, Nature has allowed each one a large chest or cell in which a very large and strong *muscle* is included; thereby this little animal is not only able to suspend its body upon fewer than these eight legs, but also to move very swiftly over the tops of grass and leaves.

Nor are these eight legs so prodigiously long without contrast, for the ninth and tenth appendages, which are the two claws, K K, are as short and serve instead of a <term>proboscis</term>, for those seemed very little longer than its mouth. Each of them had three parts, but very short ones, the joints K K, which represented the third part, being longer than both the others. This creature seems (as I have several times observed with pleasure) to throw its body upon its prey instead of using its hands, not unlike a hunting *spider*, which leaps like a cat at a *mouse*. The whole fabric was a very beautiful one, and could I have dissected it, I do not doubt that I would have found as many singularities within it as without—perhaps, for the most part, not unlike

## Observ. XLVIII. *Of the hunting Spider, and several other sorts of Spiders.*

The hunting spider is a small grey spider, prettily speckled with black spots all over its body, which the *microscope* discovers to be a kind of feathers like those on *butterflies'* wings, or the body of the white *moth* I lately described. Its gait is very nimble by fits—sometimes running, and sometimes leaping, almost like a *grasshopper*—then standing still and setting itself on its hinder legs, it will very nimbly turn its body and look all around itself. It has six very conspicuous eyes: two looking directly forward, placed just in front; two others on either side of those, looking forward and sideways; and two others about the middle of the top of its back or head, which look backward and sideward; these seemed to be the largest. The surface of them all was very black, spherical, and purely polished, reflecting a very clear and distinct image of all the surrounding objects, such as a window, a man’s hand, a white paper, or the like. Some other properties of this spider, observed by the most accomplished *Mr. Evelyn* in his travels in *Italy*, are most emphatically set forth in the history annexed hereunto, which he was pleased, upon my request, to send me in writing.

Of all the sorts of insects, there are none that have afforded me more entertainment than the *Venatores* <note>Hunters</note>, which are a sort of *Lupi* <note>Wolves</note> that have their dens in the rugged walls and crevices of our houses; a small brown and delicately spotted kind of spiders, whose hinder legs are longer than the rest.

Such I did frequently observe at *Rome*, which, spying a *fly* at three or four yards distance upon the balcony (where I stood)

There are multitudes of other sorts of spiders, whose eyes, and most other parts and properties, are so exceedingly different both from those I have described and from one another, that it would be almost endless, or at least too long for my present essay, to describe them; such as some with six eyes, placed in quite another order; others with eight eyes; others with fewer, and some with more. They all seem to be creatures of prey and to feed on other small insects, but their ways of catching them seem very different: the shepherd spider by running upon its prey; the hunting spider by leaping on it; other sorts weave nets, or cobwebs, by which they ensnare them. Nature has both fitted them with materials and tools, and taught them how to work and weave their nets, and to lie in wait <note>originally "lie perdue," meaning to stay hidden in ambush</note>, and to watch diligently to run upon any fly as soon as it is entangled.

Their thread or web seems to be spun out of some sticky kind of excrement lying in their belly, which, though soft when drawn out, is presently hardened and dried by the surrounding air because of its thinness. Examining several of these with my *microscope*, I found them to appear much like white horsehair, or some similar transparent horny substance, and to be of very different sizes; some appeared as big as a pig's bristle, others equal to a horsehair, others no bigger than a human hair, and others even smaller and finer. I observed further that the radiating cords of the web were much larger and smoother than those that were woven in circles, which seemed smaller and were all over knotted or pearled with small transparent globules, not unlike small crystal beads or seed pearls thinly strung on a ball of silk; whether these were so spun by the spider, or caused by the external moisture of a fog (which I have observed to cover all these filaments with such crystalline beads), I will not now dispute.

These threads were some of them so small that I could very plainly, with the *microscope*, discover the same sequences of colors as in a *prism*, and they seemed to proceed from the same cause as those colors which I have already described in thin plated bodies.

<margin>They are only clouds of ice which will be so thinned as soon as the sun shines out, as might easily be proved by the author by touching them with a finger or anything else, or breathing toward them when they are frozen, and they will then be dissolved.</margin>
Much resembling a cobweb, or a confused lock of these cylinders, is a certain white substance which, after a fog, may be observed to fly up and down the air; catching several of these and examining them with my *microscope*, I found them to be much of the same form, looking most like a flake of wool prepared to be spun, though by what means they should be generated or produced is not easily imagined: they were of the same weight, or very little heavier than the air; and it is not unlikely that those great white clouds that appear all through the summertime may be of the same substance.

### Observation XLIX. *Of an Ant or Pismire.*

This was a creature more troublesome to be drawn than any of the rest, for I could not, for a good while, think of a way to make it allow its body to lie quiet in a natural posture. While it was alive, if its feet were fettered in wax or glue, it would so twist and wind its body that I could not in any way get a good view of it; and if I killed it, its body was so small that I often spoiled its shape before I could thoroughly view it. For this is the nature of these minute bodies: as soon, almost, as ever their life is destroyed, their parts immediately shrivel and lose their beauty. It is the same with small plants, as I mentioned before in the description of moss. And from this also comes the reason for the variations in the beards of wild oats, and in those of musk-grass seed; because their bodies are exceedingly small, those small variations which are made on the surfaces of all bodies upon almost every change of air—especially if the body is porous—become noticeable here, where the whole body is so small that it is almost nothing but surface. For as in vegetable substances, I see no great reason to think that the moisture of the air (which, sticking to a wreathed beard, makes it untwist) should evaporate or exhale away any faster than the moisture of other bodies; rather, the evaporation from or access of moisture to the surfaces of bodies being much the same, those bodies become most sensitive to it which have the least proportion of body compared to their surface. So it is also with animal substances; the dead body of an ant, or such a little creature, shrivels and dries almost instantly, and your object shall be quite another thing before you can half describe it. This proceeds not from extraordinary evaporation, but from the small proportion of body and juices compared to the usual drying of bodies in the air, especially if warm. For this inconvenience, where I could not otherwise remove it, I thought of this expedient.

I took the creature I had designed to describe and put it into a drop of very well rectified <term>spirit of wine</term> <note>High-proof alcohol or ethanol</note>; I found this would presently dispatch the animal, so to speak. Being taken out of it and laid on a paper, the spirit of wine would immediately fly away and leave the animal dry in its natural posture—or at least in a condition where it might easily be placed with a pin in whatever posture you desired to draw it—and the limbs would remain that way without either moving or shriveling. And thus I dealt with this ant, which I have depicted here. It was one of many of a very large kind that inhabited under the roots of a tree, from which they would sally out in great parties and make most grievous havoc of the flowers and fruits in the surrounding garden, and return back again very expertly by the same ways and paths they went.

It was more than half the size of an earwig, of a dark brown or reddish color, with long legs, on the hindmost of which it would stand

->Observation 50. *Of the wandering Mite.*<-

In September and *October* 1661, I observed in *Oxford* several of these pretty little creatures wandering to and fro, often traveling over the surface of my window. And in *September* and *October* 1663, I likewise observed several of these very same creatures traversing a window in *London*; looking outside the window upon the wall below, I found whole flocks of the same kind running to and fro among the small groves and thickets of green moss, and upon the curiously spreading vegetable blue or yellow moss, which is a kind of mushroom or Jew's-ear <note>A type of jelly fungus, Auricularia auricula-judae</note>.

To the naked eye, these creatures seemed to be a kind of black mite, but much nimbler and stronger than the ordinary cheese mites; but examining them in a *microscope*, I found them to be a very finely crusted or shelled insect, much like that represented in the first figure of the thirty-third *Scheme* <note>A plate or set of illustrations</note>, with a protruding oval shell, A, indented or pitted with an abundance of small pits, all covered over with little white bristles whose points were all directed backwards.

It had eight legs, each of them provided with a very sharp talon or claw at the end, which this little animal fastened into the pores of the surface over which it walked as it moved. Each of these legs was stuck at every joint with a multitude of small hairs or (if we consider the proportion they bore to the size of the leg) spikes, all pointing toward the claws.

The *thorax*, or middle part of this creature's body, was exceedingly small in comparison to both the head and belly, being nothing but that part covered by the two shells, BB, though it seemed to grow thicker underneath. And indeed, if we consider the great variety Nature uses in proportioning the three parts of the body (the *head*, *thorax*, and *belly*), we shall not wonder at the small proportion of this *thorax*, nor at the larger bulk of the belly; for if we could exactly anatomize this little creature and observe the particular designs of each part, we should doubtless, as we do in all her more manageable

The head of this little insect was shaped somewhat like a mite's; that is, it had a long snout, in the manner of a hog's, with a knobbed ridge running along the middle of it, which was set on either side with many small bristles, all pointing forward, and two very large pikes or horns, which rose from the top of the head, just over each eye, and pointed forward also. At the same time and place, and several times since, I have observed with my *microscope* another little insect, which, though I have not included a picture of it, may be worth noting for its exceeding nimbleness as well as smallness; it was as small as a mite, with a body deep and ridged, almost like a flea; it had eight blood-red legs, not very long but slender; and two horns or feelers in front. Its motion was so exceedingly quick that I have often lost sight of one I have observed with my naked eye; and though, when it was not frightened, I was able to follow the motions of some with my *microscope*, yet if it were ever so slightly startled, it hurried away with such speed, and turned and wound itself so quickly, that I would presently lose sight of it.

When I first observed the former of these insects, or mites, I began to conjecture that I had certainly found out the vagabond parents of those mites we find in cheeses, meal, corn, seeds, musty barrels, musty leather, etc. These little creatures, wandering to and fro everywhere, might perhaps, as they were invited hither and thither by the musty steams of several putrefying bodies, make their invasions upon those new and pleasing territories; and there, spending the remainder of their life (which might perhaps be a day or thereabouts) in very plentiful and riotous living, might leave their offspring behind them, which by the change of the soil and country they now inhabit might be quite

But on the other side, if it should be found that these, or any other animate body, have no immediate similar parent, I have in another place set down a conjectural hypothesis whereby those *phenomena* may likely enough be solved, wherein the infinite wisdom and providence of the Creator is no less rare and wonderful.

### Observation LI. *Of the Crab-like Insect.*

Reading one day in *September*, I chanced to observe a very small creature creep very slowly over the book I was reading; having a *microscope* by me, I observed it to be a creature of a very unusual form, and no less notable, such as is described in the second figure of the 33rd *Scheme*. It was about the size of a large mite, or somewhat longer; it had ten legs, eight of which, A A A A, were topped with very sharp claws, and were those upon which he walked, appearing shaped much like those of a crab, which in many other things also this little creature resembled; for the two other claws, B B, which were the foremost of all the ten and seemed to grow out of his head like the horns of other animals, were exactly formed in the manner of crab or lobster claws, for they were shaped and jointed much like those represented in the *Scheme*, and the ends of them were furnished with a pair of claws or pincers, C C, which this little animal did open and shut at pleasure. It seemed to make use of those two horns or claws both for feelers and holders; for in its motion it carried these aloft, extended in front, moving them to and fro, just as a man blindfolded would do with his hands when he is fearful of running against a wall; and if I put a hair to it, it would readily take hold of it with these claws and seem to hold it fast. Now, though these horns seemed to serve him for two uses, namely, for feeling and holding, yet he did not seem to be blind, having two small black spots, D D, which by their makeup and the bright reflection from them seemed to be his eyes; nor did it lack other hands, having another pair of claws, E E, placed very near to its mouth and appearing adjoining to it.

The whole body was encased in armor-shells, as is usual in all

Each leg has as many parts, and as many joints as a crab’s, nay, and as many hairs or bristles, and the like may be in all the other visible parts; and it is very likely that the internal curiosities are not less excellent: it being a general rule in Nature’s proceedings, that where she begins to display any excellency, if the subject be further searched into, it will manifest that there is no less curiosity in those parts which our single eye cannot reach, than in those which are more obvious.

## Observation LII. Of the small Silver-colored Book-worm.

As among greater animals there are many that are scaled, both for ornament and defense, so there are not wanting such also among the lesser bodies of insects, of which this little creature gives us an instance. It is a small white silver-shining worm or moth, which I found much conversant among books and papers, and is supposed to be that which corrodes and eats holes through the leaves and covers; it appears to the naked eye as a small glistening pearl-colored moth, which upon the removing of books and papers in the summer, is often observed very nimbly to scud and pack away to some lurking cranny, where it may the better protect itself from any appearing dangers. Its head appears big and blunt, and its body tapers from it towards the tail, smaller and smaller, being shaped almost like a carrot.

This the *microscopical* appearance will more plainly manifest, which exhibits, in the third *figure* of the 33rd *scheme*, a conical body, divided into fourteen several partitions, being the appearance of so many several shells or shields that cover the whole body; every one of these shells is again covered or tiled over with a multitude of thin transparent scales, which, from the multiplicity of their reflecting surfaces, make the whole animal appear of a perfect pearl-color.

MICROGRAPHIA.

Which, by the way, may suggest to us the reason for that so much admired appearance of those so highly esteemed bodies, as also of the like in mother-of-pearl shells, and in multitudes of other shelly sea-substances; for each of them, consisting of an infinite number of very thin shells, or laminated orbiculations, cause such multitudes of reflections that the compositions of them—together with the reflections of others that are so thin as to afford colors (for which I give the reason elsewhere)—gives a very pleasant reflection of light. And that this is the true cause seems likely, first, because all those appearing bodies are compounded of multitudes of plated substances. And next, that by ordering any transparent substance in this manner, similar *phenomena* may be produced; this will be made very obvious by the blowing of glass into exceedingly thin shells, and then breaking them into scales, which any lamp-worker will presently do; for a good quantity of these scales, laid in a heap together, have much the same resemblance to pearls. Another way, no less instructive and pleasant, is a method which I have several times performed, which is by working and tossing, as it were, a parcel of pure crystalline glass while it is kept glowing hot in the blown flame of a lamp; for, by that means, that purely transparent body will be so divided into an infinite number of plates, or small strings, with interposed aerial plates and fibers, that from the multiplicity of the reflections from each of those internal surfaces, it may be drawn out into beautiful pearl-like or silver wire, which though small, will yet be opaque; the same thing I have done with a composition of red colophon and turpentine, and a little bee’s wax, and it may be done likewise with birdlime, and such like glutinous and transparent bodies: But to return to our description.

The small blunt head of this insect was furnished on either side of it with a cluster of eyes, each of which seemed to contain but a very few, in comparison of what I had observed the clusters of other insects to abound with; each of these clusters was beset with a row of small bristles, much like the *cilia* or hairs on the eyelids, and, perhaps, they served for the same purpose. It had two long horns before, which were straight, and tapering towards the top, curiously ringed or knobbed, and bristled much like the marsh weed, called Horse-tail, or Cat-tail, having at each knot a fringed girdle, as I may so call it, of smaller hairs, and several bigger and larger bristles, here and there dispersed among them: besides these, it had two shorter horns, or feelers, which were knotted and fringed, just as the former, but lacked bristles, and were blunt at the ends; the hinder part of the creature was terminated with three tails, in every particular resembling the two longer horns that grew out of the head: The legs of it were scaled and haired much like the rest, but are not shown in this *figure*, the moth being entangled all in glue, and so the legs of this appeared not through the glass which looked perpendicularly upon the back.

### Observation LIII. *Of a Flea.*

The strength and beauty of this small creature, even if it had no other relation at all to man, would deserve a description. 

Regarding its strength, the <term>Microscope</term> cannot reveal any more about it than the naked eye can, but only the curious design of its legs and joints for exerting that strength is very plainly manifested—a design unlike anything I have yet observed in any other creature. For its joints are so adapted that it can, as it were, fold them short one within another and suddenly stretch or spring them out to their full length. That is, for the forelegs, the part **A** of the 34th <term>Scheme</term> lies within **B**, and **B** within **C**, parallel to or side by side with each other; but the parts of the next two legs lie quite the opposite way, that is, **D** outside **E**, and **E** outside **F**, though also parallel; but the parts of the hind legs—**G**, **H**, and **I**—bend one within another like the parts of a double-jointed ruler, or like the foot, leg, and thigh of a man. These six legs it clutches up all together, and when it leaps, it springs them all out, thereby exerting its whole strength at once.

But as for its beauty, the <term>Microscope</term> reveals it to be adorned all over with a curiously polished suit of sable armor, neatly jointed and beset with multitudes of sharp pins, shaped almost like porcupine quills or bright, conical steel bodkins. The head is beautified on either side with a sharp and round black eye **K**, behind each of which there also appears a small cavity, **L**, in which it seems to move to and fro a certain thin film covered with many small transparent hairs, which may probably be its ears. In the front part of its head, between the two forelegs, it has two small, long, jointed feelers, or rather "smellers," **M M**, which have four joints and are hairy, like those of several other creatures; between these, it has a small <term>proboscis</term> or probe, **N N O**, that seems to consist of a tube,

## Observation LIV. Of a Louse.

This is a creature so intrusive that it will be known to everyone at one time or another; so busy and so impudent that it will intrude itself into everyone's company; and so proud and ambitious as well that it does not fear to trample on the best of people, and desires nothing so much as a crown. It feeds and lives very high, and that makes it so insolent as to pull anyone by the ears that comes in its way, and it will never be quiet until it has drawn blood. It is troubled by nothing so much as a man scratching his head, as it knows that man is plotting and contriving some mischief against it; this often makes it skulk into some lowlier and lower place and run behind a man's back, even though it goes very much against the hair. These bad qualities, having made it better known than trusted, would excuse me from providing any further description of it, if my faithful *Mercury*, my *Microscope*, did not bring me other information about it.

For this has revealed to me, by means of a very bright light cast upon it, that it is a creature of a very odd shape. It has a head shaped like the one shown in *Scheme* 35, marked with A, which seems almost conical but is a little flattened on the top and bottom sides. At the widest part of this, on either side behind the head (being the place where other creatures' ears are located), are placed its two black, shining, goggle eyes BB, looking backward and protected by several small *cilia* or hairs that encompass them; so it seems this creature has no very good foresight. It does not seem to have any eyelids, and therefore perhaps its eyes were so placed that it might better clean them with its front legs. Perhaps this may also be the reason why they so much avoid and run from the light behind them; for being designed to live in the shady and dark recesses of the hair, and because their eyes probably have a large aperture, the open and clear light, especially that of the sun, must certainly bother them. To protect these eyes from receiving any injury from the hairs through which the creature moves, it has

The digestion of this creature must certainly be very quick, for though I perceived the blood thicker and blacker when sucked, yet when in the guts, it was of a very lovely ruby color, and that part of it which was digested into the veins seemed white. From this it appears that a further digestion of blood may turn it into milk, or at least a similar color. Whatever else is observable in the figure of this creature may be seen in the 35th *Scheme*.

### Observ. LV. Of Mites.

<margin>
Their eggs are not nearly as small in proportion to their bodies as I have often observed, but are proportioned like the eggs of all birds.

They are in size generally one-third of common white sand.
</margin>

The smallest of <term>Reptiles</term> I have met with so far is a mite, a creature of which some are so very small that the sharpest sight, unaided by glasses, is not able to discern them, though, being white themselves, they move on a black and smooth surface. The eggs from which these creatures seem to be hatched are even smaller, usually being no more than a four or five-hundredth part of a well-grown mite, and those well-grown mites are not much more than one-hundredth of an inch in thickness. So, according to this reckoning, there may be no fewer than a million well-grown mites contained in a cubic inch, and five hundred times as many eggs.

Notwithstanding this minuteness, a good microscope discovers those small movable specks to be very prettily shaped insects, each of them furnished

The body, as in other larger insects, consists of three regions or parts. The hind part or belly, A, seems covered with one entire shell; the middle, or chest, seems divided into two shells, B and C, which, by sliding one within the other, allow the mite to shrink in and thrust out as it finds occasion, just as it can also do with the snout, D. The whole body is quite transparent, so that when looked at against the light, various motions within its body may be perceived; also, all the parts are much more plainly defined than in other positions relative to the light. The shell, especially that which covers the back, is curiously polished, so that it is easy to see—as in a *convex* looking-glass or a silvered glass ball—the image of all the objects round about. Up and down, in several parts of its body, it has several small long white hairs growing out of its shell, which are often longer than the whole body and are represented too short in the first and second figures. They seem all quite straight and flexible, except only two upon the fore-part of its body, which seem to be the horns, as may be seen in the figures. The first of these is a view of a smaller sort of mite (which are usually more plump) as it was *moving* to and fro; the second is the view of one fixed on its tail (by means of a little mouth-glue rubbed on the object plate), showing the manner of the legs' growth, together with their several joints.

This creature is very much diversified in shape, color, and various other properties, according to the nature of the substance out of which it seems to be engendered and nourished: being in one substance longer, in another rounder; in some more hairy, in others smoother; in this one nimble, in that one slow; here pale and whiter, there browner, blacker, more transparent, and so forth. I have observed it to be resident on almost all kinds of substances that are moldy or rotting, and have seen it very nimbly moving through the thickets of mold, and sometimes lying *dormant* underneath them; and it is not unlikely that it may feed on that growing substance, as spontaneous vegetables seem a food proper enough for spontaneous animals.

But whether indeed this creature, or any other, be such or not, I cannot positively determine from any experiment or observation I have yet made. prime parent might be of a shape very different from what the offspring, after a little while, by reason of the substance they feed on, or the region (as it were) they inhabit; yet perhaps even one of these altered progeny, wandering again from its native soil, and happening by chance upon the same place from which its prime parent came, and there settling and planting, may produce a generation of mites of the same shapes and properties as the first wandering mite: And from some such accidents as these, I am very inclined to think, most sorts of animals, generally accounted *spontaneous*, have their origin; and all those various sorts of mites that are to be met with here and there in various putrefying substances, may perhaps be all of the same kind, and have sprung from one and the same sort of mites at the first.

### Observ. LVI. *Of a small creature hatched on a vine.*

There is, almost all the spring and summer time, a certain small, round, white cobweb, as it were, about the size of a pea, which sticks very close and fast to the stocks of vines nailed against a warm wall: being attentively viewed, they seem covered, upon the upper side of them, with a small husk, not unlike the scale, or shell of a wood-louse, or hog-louse, a small insect usually found about rotten wood, which upon touching immediately rolls itself into the form of a peppercorn: Separating several of these from the stock, I found them, with my *microscope*, to consist of a shell, which now seemed more likely to be the husk of one of these insects: And the fur seemed a kind of cobweb, consisting of an abundance of small filaments, or strands of cobwebs. In the midst of this, if they were not hatched and run away before—the time of which hatching was usually about the latter end of *June*, or beginning of *July*—I have often found an abundance of small brown eggs, such as **A** and **B** in the second figure of the 36th *scheme*, much about the size of mites' eggs; and at other times, multitudes of small insects, shaped exactly like that in the third figure marked with **X**. Its head is large, almost half the size of its body, which is usual in the fetus of most creatures. It had two small black eyes *a a*, and two small long jointed and bristled horns *b b*. The hinder part of its body seemed to consist of nine scales, and the last ended in a forked tail, much like that of a *cutio* <note>A regional or archaic term for a wood-louse or similar wood-dwelling insect</note>, or wood-louse, out of which grew two long hairs; they ran to and fro very swiftly, and were much of the size of a common mite, but some of them less: The longest of them seemed not the hundredth part of an inch, and the eggs usually not above half as much. They seemed to have six legs, which were not visible in this I have here depicted, because they were drawn under its body.

If these minute creatures were *wood-lice* (as indeed from their own shape and frame, the skin, or shell, that grows on them, one may with great pro-

(probably guess), it affords us an instance of which perhaps there are not many like in Nature, and that is the prodigious increase of these creatures after they are hatched and run about; for a common wood-louse, about half an inch long, is no less than a hundred and twenty-five thousand times bigger than one of these, which though it indeed seems very strange, yet I have observed that the young ones of some spiders have almost kept the same proportion to their parent.

This, it seems to me, if it be so, next suggests a query, which may perhaps deserve a little further examination: and that is, whether there are not many of those minute creatures, such as mites and the like, which, though they are commonly thought of otherwise, are only the *pully* <note>likely "pulli," a Latin term for the young of animals</note>, or young ones, of much bigger insects, and not the generating or parent insect that has laid those eggs; for having many times observed those eggs, which usually are found in great abundance where mites are found, it seems something strange that so small an animal should have an egg so big in proportion to its body. Though on the other side, I must confess that having kept several of those mites enclosed in a box for a good while, I did not find them very much increased beyond their usual size.

What the husk and cobweb of this little white substance should be, I cannot imagine, unless it is that the parent, when impregnated with eggs, stays there and fixes itself on the vine, and dies, and the entire body by degrees rots, except for the husk and the eggs inside the body: and the heat, or fire, as it were, of the approaching sunbeams vivifies those relics of the corrupted parent, and out of the ashes, as it were (as is fabled of the *Phoenix*), raises a new offspring for the perpetuation of the species. Nor will the cobweb, as it were, in which these eggs are enclosed, count much against this conjecture; for we may learn from those cobwebs that are carried up and down the air after a fog (which with my <term>Microscope</term> I have discovered to be made up of an infinite number of small filaments or threads), that such a texture of body may be made otherwise than by the spinning of a worm.

### Observ. LVII. *Of the Eels in Vinegar.*

Of these small eels, which are to be found in various sorts of vinegar, I have little to add besides their picture, which you may find drawn in the third figure of the *25. Scheme*: that is, they were shaped much like an eel, except that their nose A (which was a little more opaque than the rest of their body) was a little sharper and longer in proportion to their body, and the wriggling motion of their body seemed to be only upwards and downwards, whereas that of eels is only sideways: They seemed to have a more opaque part about

<summary>Hooke discusses the massive growth scale of insects from birth and hypothesizes that mites may be the larvae of larger creatures. He also introduces a microscopic study of "eels" found in vinegar, noting their unique vertical swimming motion.</summary>
<keywords>wood-louse, insect growth, mites, spontaneous generation, Phoenix, vinegar eels, microscopy, Robert Hooke</keywords>

--- Page 331 ---
<meta>This page continues the observation of microscopic "eels" found in vinegar, concluding the study of their movement and physical properties before beginning a new observation on atmospheric refraction.</meta>

around B, which might, perhaps, be their gills; it seemed always to be at the same proportionate distance from their nose, from which, to the tip of their tail, C, their body seemed to taper.

Taking several of these out of their pond of vinegar with a net made of a small piece of filtering paper, and laying them on a smooth black glass plate, I found that they could wriggle and wind their body almost as much as a snake, which made me wonder whether they were a kind of eel or leech.

I shall add no other observations made on this minute animal, as I have been preceded in this by many excellent ones already published by the ingenious Doctor Power among his *Microscopical Observations*, except only that when a quantity of vinegar replete with them was enclosed in a small vial and stopped very closely from the ambient air, all the trapped worms died in a very short time, as if they had been stifled.

And their motion seems (contrary to what we may observe in the motion of all other insects) exceedingly slow. But the reason for it seems plain: for since they must move to and fro in the manner they do, only by waving or wriggling their body, the tenacity or stickiness, and the density or resistance of the fluid <term>medium</term> becomes so exceedingly sensible to their extremely minute bodies that it is indeed a greater wonder to me that they move as fast as they do than that they move no faster. For what a vastly greater proportion do they have of their surface area to their bulk than eels or other larger fish? And next, since the tenacity and density of the liquid to be moved through is much the same for both the small and the large, the resistance or impediment arising from it to the motions made through it must be almost infinitely greater to the small one than to the great. We find this experimentally verified in the air, which—though a medium a thousand times more rarefied than water—still offers a resistance to motions made through it that is so perceptible to very minute bodies that a down feather (the smallest parts of which still seem larger than these eels, and many parts of which are almost incomparably larger, such as the quill and stalk) is suspended by it and carried to and fro as if it had no weight.

## Observ. LVIII. *Of a new* Property *in the* Air, *and several other transparent* Mediums *named* Inflection, *whereby very many considerable* Phenomena *are attempted to be solved, and various other uses are hinted.*

Since the invention (and perfecting in some measure) of telescopes, it has been observed by several people that the Sun and Moon near the horizon are disfigured (losing that exactly smooth, terminating circular edge which they are observed to have when situated nearer the zenith) and are bounded with an edge every way (especially on the right and left

<meta>catchword: sides)</meta>

<summary>This page concludes the study of "vinegar eels," explaining how fluid resistance significantly impacts their movement due to their small size. It then introduces the concept of atmospheric "inflection" (refraction) and its role in distorting the appearance of celestial bodies near the horizon.</summary>

<keywords>vinegar eels, nematodes, fluid resistance, surface area to volume ratio, Henry Power, atmospheric refraction, inflection, telescopes, horizon distortion</keywords>

--- Page 332 ---
<meta>This page transitions from the microscopic study of vinegar "eels" (concluding on the previous page) to a detailed astronomical observation regarding atmospheric refraction and the visual distortion of celestial bodies near the horizon.</meta>

surfaces) ragged and indented like a saw. I have further observed that this inequality of their edges does not always remain the same but is continually changed by a kind of fluctuating motion, much like that of the waves of the sea. Thus, the part of the edge that was just now notched or indented is now bulging, and will soon be sinking again. Nor is this all; the entire body of the celestial luminaries seems, in the *Telescope*, to be compressed and flattened, with the upper and especially the lower sides appearing closer to the middle than they really are, while the right and left appear further away. Consequently, the whole *Area* seems to be shaped like an oval. It is further observed that the body, for the most part, appears red, or some color close to it, such as a kind of yellow. I have always noted that the more the edge is flattened or oval-shaped, the redder the body appears, though the reverse is not always true. It is further observable that both fixed stars and planets look redder and duller the closer they appear to the horizon, and they are observed to twinkle more; so much so that I have seen the Dog-star vibrate with such a strong and bright radiation of light that it almost dazzled my eyes, only to almost disappear immediately after. It is also observable that those bright scintillations near the horizon do not follow one another nearly as quickly or suddenly as the nimbler twinklings of stars nearer the zenith. It is also notable that stars near the horizon twinkle with several colors, appearing sometimes red, sometimes more yellow, and sometimes blue, even when the star is quite a distance above the horizon. Furthermore, I have very often seen some of the small stars of the fifth or sixth magnitude occasionally disappear for a brief moment and then reappear more conspicuously and with a greater luster. Several times, with my naked eye, I have seen many smaller stars—which might be called the seventh or eighth magnitude—appear for a short time and then vanish. By directing a small *Telescope* toward the area where they appeared and disappeared, I could immediately find that they were indeed small stars situated just as I had seen them with my naked eye, and they appeared to twinkle like the ordinary visible stars. Moreover, while examining some very notable parts of the heavens with a three-foot tube, I thought I could now and then perceive little twinklings of stars in various parts of the constellation, appearing very briefly and then vanishing. After diligently noting the places where they seemed to play peek-a-boo, I used a very good twelve-foot tube. With that, it was not difficult to see those and several other levels of smaller stars, and some smaller still that seemed to appear and disappear again. By giving that same object-glass a much larger aperture, I could plainly and constantly see them appear in their former places. Thus, I have observed some twelve different magnitudes of stars smaller than the six magnitudes commonly recorded on globes.

It has been observed and confirmed by the most accurate observations of our best modern astronomers that all luminous bodies appear above the horizon when they are actually below it. So that the

<header>MICROGRAPHIA.</header>
219

The Sun and Moon have both been seen above the horizon while the Moon has been eclipsed. I will not here cite the examples of the great refractions that the tops of high mountains, seen at a distance, have been found to have; all of which seem to argue that horizontal refraction is much greater than it is generally believed to be until now.

I have further noticed that not only the Sun, Moon, and stars, and high tops of mountains have suffered these kinds of refraction, but trees and several bright objects on the ground: I have often noticed the twinkling of the reflections of the Sun from a glass window at a great distance, and of a candle in the night, but that is not so conspicuous; and in observing the setting Sun, I have often noticed the shimmering of the trees and bushes, as well as of the edges of the Sun. Several of these *phenomena* have been noticed by many, who have given various reasons for them, but I have not yet met with any that are altogether satisfactory, though some of their conjectures have been partly true, but partly also false. Therefore, setting myself to the inquiry of these *phenomena*, I first endeavored to be very diligent in taking notice of the several particulars and circumstances observable in them; and next, in making various particular experiments that might clear some doubts, and serve to determine, confirm, and illustrate the true and adequate cause of each; and upon the whole, I find much reason to think that the true cause of all these *phenomena* is from the <term>inflection</term>, or <term>multiplicate refraction</term> of those rays of light within the body of the *atmosphere*, and that it does not proceed from a refraction caused by any terminating surface of the air above, nor from any such exactly defined surface within the body of the *atmosphere*.

This conclusion is grounded upon these two propositions:

First, that a *medium* whose parts are unequally dense, and moved by various motions and transpositions relative to one another, will produce all these visible effects upon the rays of light, without any other contributing cause.

Secondly, that there is in the air or *atmosphere* such a variety in its constituent parts, both as to their density and rarity, and as to their diverse changes and positions to one another.

By <term>density</term> and <term>rarity</term>, I mean a property of a transparent body that refracts a ray of light (coming obliquely upon its surface out of a third *medium*) either more or less toward its perpendicular: as I call glass a more dense body than water, and water a more rare body than glass, because of the refractions (deflecting more or less toward the perpendicular) that are made in them by a ray of light coming out of the air that has the same inclination upon either of their surfaces.

So as to the matter of refraction, <term>spirit of wine</term> is a more dense body than water, it having been found by an accurate instrument that measures the angles of refractions to minutes that for the same refracted angle of 30° 00' in both those mediums, the angle of incidence in water was only 41° 3' 5", but the angle of incidence in the trial with *spirit of wine* was 42° 45'. But as to gravity, water is a more dense body than

So as to refraction, water is more dense than ice; for I have found by a most certain experiment, which I exhibited before various illustrious persons of the *Royal Society*, that the refraction of water was greater than that of ice, though some considerable authors have affirmed the contrary, and though ice is a very hard body and water a very fluid one.

That the former of the two preceding propositions is true may be shown by several experiments: First, if you take any two liquids differing from one another in density, but yet such as will readily mix—such as salt water (or brine) and fresh; almost any kind of salt dissolved in water and filtered so that it is clear; spirit of wine and water; or even spirit of wine and spirit of wine, one more highly rectified than the other, and many other liquids—if (I say) you take any two of these liquids and mix them in a glass vial, against one side of which you have fixed or glued a small round piece of paper, and shaking them well together (so that their parts may be somewhat disturbed and move up and down), you endeavor to see that round piece of paper through the body of the liquids, you shall plainly perceive the figure to wave and to be indented much in the same manner as the edge (limb) of the Sun seems to be through a *Telescope*, except only that the changes here are much faster. And if, instead of this larger circle, you take a very small spot and fasten and view it as before, you will find it to appear much like the twinkling of the stars, though much faster. These two *phenomena* (for I shall take notice of no more at present, though I could instance many others) must necessarily be caused by an *inflection* of the rays within the bounding surfaces of the compounded *medium*, since the surfaces of the transparent body through which the rays pass to the eye are not at all altered or changed.

This *inflection* (if I may so call it) I imagine to be nothing else but a <term>multiplicate refraction</term> caused by the unequal density of the constituent parts of the *medium*, whereby the motion, action, or progress of the *ray* of light is hindered from proceeding in a straight line and *inflected* or *deflected* in a *curve*. Now, that it is a *curve* line is manifest by this experiment: I took a box, such as ADGE in the first *figure* of the 37th *scheme*, whose sides ABCD and EFGH were made of two smooth flat plates of glass; then filling it half full with a very strong solution of salt, I filled the other half with very clear fresh water. Then, exposing the opaque side, DHGC, to the Sun, I observed both the *refraction* and *inflection* of the sunbeams, ID and KH; and marking as exactly as I could the points P, N, O, M, by which the ray KH passed through the compounded *medium*, I found them to be in a *curve* line; for the parts of the *medium* being continually more dense the nearer they were to the bottom, the ray *pf* was continually more and more deflected downwards from the straight line.
