M I C R O G R A P H I A.

Descartes' principles, by conceiving that the globules of the third element find less and less resistance against the side of them which is downwards—or by a way which I have further explained in the inquiry about colors, as being from a slanting of the pulse of light, by which the coarser part is continually pushed forward and consequently refracted toward the perpendicular, which intersects the orbs at right angles. I shall not examine now what the particular figure of the *curve line* described by this path of light is, especially since there may be as many types of it as there may be variations in the positions of the *intermediate degrees of density and rarity* between the bottom and the top of the *inflecting medium*.

I could produce many more examples and experiments to illustrate and prove this first proposition: namely, that there is such a constitution of some bodies that will cause inflection. I will not mention those I have observed in *horn, tortoise shell, transparent gums, and resinous substances*; the *veins of glass*, and even of melted *crystal*—found and much complained about by glass-grinders and others—might sufficiently demonstrate the truth of it to any diligent observer.

But I presume that with this example I have given sufficient proof (*namely, visual demonstration*) to show that there is such a modulation or bending of the rays of light, which I have called *inflection*. This differs from both *reflection* and *refraction* (since they are both produced at the surface, while this occurs only in the middle); and likewise, that this is capable or sufficient to produce the effects I have ascribed to it.

It remains, therefore, to show that there is such a property in the air, and that it is sufficient to produce all the above-mentioned *phenomena*, and therefore may be the principal, if not the only, cause of them.

First, it may be proved that such a property exists because some parts of the air are more *condensed* and others more *rarefied*, either by the differing heat or differing pressure it sustains, or by the somewhat diverse vapors scattered through it. For as the air is more or less rarefied, it refracts a ray of light (coming out of a denser medium) more or less from the perpendicular. You may find this to be true if you attempt this experiment.

Take a small glass bubble, made in the form of that in the second figure of the 37th *Scheme*, and by heating the glass until it is very hot and thereby greatly rarefying the contained air—or, which is better, by rarefying a small quantity of water included in it into vapors, which will expel most, if not all, the air—and then sealing up the small neck of it and letting it cool, you may find, if you place it in a convenient instrument, that there will be a manifest difference regarding the refraction.

As if in this second figure you suppose A to represent a small sight or hole through which the eye looks upon an object, such as C, through the glass bubble B and the second sight L; all of which remain exactly fixed in their several places, the object C being so sized and placed that it may just seem to touch the upper and under edge of the hole L, and so all of it be seen through the small glass ball of rarefied air; then by

# M I C R O G R A P H I A.

By breaking off the small sealed neck of the bubble (without moving the sights, object, or glass at all) and admitting the external air, you will find yourself unable to see the furthest ends of the object. Instead, the boundary rays A E and A D (which were previously refracted to G and F by the rarified air) will proceed almost directly to I and H. This alteration of the rays (seeing as there is no other change made in the apparatus by which the experiment is tried, except only the admission or exclusion of the condensed air) must necessarily be caused by the variation of the *medium* contained in the glass B. The greatest difficulty in conducting this experiment arises from the uneven surfaces of the bubble, which will represent a distorted image of the object.

Now, that there is such a difference between the upper and lower parts of the air is clearly enough evidenced from the recent improvement of the *Torricellian* experiment <note>The mercury barometer experiment</note>, which has been tried at the summits and bases of mountains. It may be further illustrated and investigated by a method which I thought of and used some time ago to find by what degrees the air passes from one degree of density to a certain degree of rarity. And another method was used for finding what pressure was required to make it pass from a certain degree of rarefaction to a specific density. Because these experiments may be useful to illustrate the present inquiry, I shall briefly describe them.

I then took a small glass pipe A B, about the size of a swan's quill and about four feet long, which was very evenly drawn so that, as far as I could perceive, no one part was larger than another. This tube (being open at both ends) I fitted into another small tube D E that had a small bore just large enough to contain the small pipe; this was sealed at one end and open at the other. Around this open end, I fastened a small wooden box C with cement, so that by filling the larger tube and part of the box with *quicksilver*, I could thrust the smaller tube into it until it was entirely covered with the *quicksilver*. Having done this, I fastened my larger tube against the side of a wall so that it might stand more steadily; and plunging the small tube entirely under the *mercury* in the box, I stopped its upper end very securely with cement. Then, lifting the small tube, I drew it up by a small pulley and a string that I had fastened to the ceiling, and found the height of the *mercurial cylinder* to be about twenty-nine inches.

Then letting the tube down again, I opened the top and thrust down the small tube until I perceived the *quicksilver* rise within it to a mark that I had placed exactly one inch from the top. Immediately applying a small piece of cement that I had kept warm, I sealed up the top very securely with a hot iron. Then, letting it cool (so that the cement might grow hard, and more especially so that the air might reach its natural temperature for the day I tried the experiment), I observed diligently and found the trapped air to be exactly one inch.

And therefore, having the expansion in the second column, the height of the subjacent *cylinder* of *mercury* in the first, and the greatest height of the *cylinder* of *mercury* (which of itself counterbalances the whole pressure of the *atmosphere*), by subtracting the numbers of the first column from the numbers of the third, you will have the measure of the cylinders so depressed, and consequently the force of the air in the several expansions registered.

I had several other tables of my observations and calculations which I made at that time. However, since it has been over a twelvemonth since I made them, and I have consequently forgotten many circumstances and particulars, I was resolved to perform them once again. I did this on *August the second, 1661*, with the very same tube which I used the year before when I first made the experiment (for since it was a very good one, I had carefully preserved it). After having tried it over and over again, and not being well satisfied with some particulars, I finally put everything in very good order. Being as attentive and observant as I possibly could be of every circumstance necessary to be noted, I recorded my several observations in the following table. In making this, I did not exactly follow the method that I had used at first; but, having lately heard of *Mr. Townly's Hypothesis*, I shaped my course in such a way as would be most convenient for the examination of that *hypothesis*; the result of which you have in the latter part of the last table.

The other experiment was to find what degrees of force were required to compress, or condense, the air into such and such a volume.

The manner of proceeding in this was as follows: I took a tube about five feet long, one end of which was sealed and bent in the form of a *siphon*, much like that represented in the fourth figure of the 37th *scheme*. One side, *AD*, which was open at *A*, was about fifty inches long; the other side, *BC*, closed at *B*, was not much more than seven inches long. Then, placing it exactly perpendicular, I poured in a little *quicksilver* and found that the air in *BC* was 6 7/8 inches, or very near to seven. Then, pouring *quicksilver* into the longer tube, I continued filling it until the air in the shorter part of it was contracted into half its former dimensions, and found the height to be exactly twenty-nine inches. By making several other trials at various other degrees of condensation of the air, I found them to exactly match the former *hypothesis*.

But because it was a long time since I first conducted it, and I had forgotten many particulars and was much unsatisfied with others, I made the experiment over again. From these several trials, I collected the first part of the following table: where in the row next to the left hand, 24 signifies the dimensions of the air sustaining only the pressure of the *atmosphere*, which at that time was equal to a cylinder of *mercury* of twenty-nine inches. The next figure above it (20) was the dimensions of the air during the first compression, made by a cylinder of *mercury* 5 13/16 high; when the *atmospheric* pressure of twenty-nine inches is added to this, the elastic strength of the air so compressed will be found to be 34 13/16, etc.

# MICROGRAPHIA.

From these experiments, I think we may safely conclude that the elasticity (*Elater*) of the air is inversely proportional to its expansion, or at least very nearly so. So, to apply it to our present purpose (which was indeed the chief cause of inventing these ways of testing), we will imagine a *cylinder* extended indefinitely upwards. [I say a *cylinder*, not a piece of a *cone*, because—as I may show elsewhere in the explanation of *gravity*—I suppose that the cubed proportion of the shells of a sphere to their respective diameters is balanced out in this case by the decrease in the power of gravity.] We will also suppose the pressure of the air at the bottom of this *cylinder* to be strong enough to support a *cylinder* of *mercury* of thirty inches. Now, because by the most accurate trials of the most illustrious and incomparable Mr. *Boyle*, published in his deservedly famous *Pneumatic Book*, the weight of *quicksilver* compared to that of the air here below is found to be about fourteen thousand to one: if we suppose the parts of the *cylinder* of the *atmosphere* to be everywhere of an equal density, we shall (*as he there deduces*) find it extended to the height of thirty-five thousand feet, or seven miles.

But because by these experiments we have somewhat confirmed the hypothesis of the reciprocal proportion of the *elasticities* to the *expansions*, we shall find that by supposing this *cylinder* of the *atmosphere* divided into a thousand parts, each of which is equivalent to thirty-five feet, or seven geometrical paces—that is, each of these divisions containing as much air as is supposed in a *cylinder* near the earth of equal diameter and thirty-five feet high—we shall find the bottom-most part to press against the surface of the Earth with the whole weight of the above-mentioned thousand parts. The pressure of the bottom of the second against the top of the first would be 1000 — 1 = 999; of the third against the second to be 1000 — 2 = 998; of the fourth against the third to be 1000 — 3 = 997; of the uppermost against the 999th, or that next below it, to be 1000 — 999 = 1. 

So the expansion of the bottom-most layer next to the Earth will be to the expansion of the layer next below the uppermost as 1 is to 999. For as the pressure sustained by the 999th layer is to the pressure sustained by the first, so is the expansion of the first to the expansion of the 999th. Thus, from this hypothetical calculation, we shall find the air to be indefinitely extended. For if we suppose the whole thickness of the air to be divided, as I just now cited, into a thousand parts, and each of those under differing *dimensions* or *altitudes* to contain an equal quantity of air, we shall find that the first *cylinder*, whose base is supposed to rest on the Earth, will be found to be extended 35 35/999 feet; the second equal division, or *cylinder*, whose base is supposed to rest on the top of the first, shall have its top extended higher by 35 70/998; the third 35 105/997; the fourth 35 140/996; and so onward, each equal quantity of air having its dimensions measured by 35 and some additional number always expressed in the manner of a fraction, whose numerator is always the number of the layer's place multiplied by 35, and whose denominator is always the pressure of the *atmosphere* sustained by that part. By this means, we may easily calculate the height of 999 divisions of those 1,000 divisions I supposed; whereas the uppermost

...may extend itself more than twice as high—indeed, perhaps indefinitely, or beyond the Moon. Since the elasticities (*elaters*) and expansions are in reciprocal proportions, and because we cannot yet find a limit (*plus ultra*) beyond which the air will not expand itself, we cannot determine the height of the air. For since, as we have shown, the proportion will always be as the pressure sustained by any part is to 35, so 1000 is to the expansion of that part; the multiplication or product, therefore, of the pressure and expansion (that is, of the two extreme proportionals) being always equal to the product of the means, or 35,000, it follows—since that product (*rectangle*) may be composed of the multiplication of an infinite variety of numbers—that the height of the air is also indefinite. For since (as far as I have yet been able to test) the air seems capable of an indefinite expansion, the pressure may be decreased *to infinity* (*in infinitum*), and consequently its expansion upwards is indefinite also.

Since there is therefore such a difference of density, and no experiment is yet known to prove a jump (*saltus*) or skipping from one degree of thinness (*rarity*) to another significantly different from it—that is, that an upper part of the air should differ so much from the part immediately below (*subjacent*) it as to create a distinct surface (*superficies*), such as we observe between the air and water, etc.—but it being more likely that there is a continual increase of thinness in the parts of the air the further they are removed from the surface of the Earth: it will therefore necessarily follow (as in the experiment of the salt and fresh water) that a ray of light passing obliquely through the air, which is of very different density, will also be continually and infinitely inflected, or bent, away from a straight or direct motion.

This granted, the reason for all the above-mentioned phenomena (*phænomena*) concerning the appearance of the celestial bodies will very easily be deduced.

As,

First, the redness of the Sun, Moon, and stars will be found to be caused by the inflection of the rays within the *atmosphere*. I suppose it will be very easily granted that this color is not actually in or near the luminous bodies, seeing that this redness is observed to be different at the same time in several places differing in longitude, as the setting and rising Sun in all parts is for the most part red.

And secondly, I suppose it will be accepted without much more difficulty that it is not merely the color of the intervening air, seeing that we may observe that a very large gap (*interstitium*) of air between the object and the eye makes it appear a dull blue, which is different enough from red or yellow.

But thirdly, I suppose the following experiment will sufficiently show that it proceeds from the refraction or inflection of the rays by the *atmosphere*.

Take a spherical glass vial (*crystalline viol*), such as the one described in the fifth figure **ABCD**, and, having filled it with pure clear water, expose it to the sunbeams. From this, according to the laws of refraction made in a triangular *prism*, and the generation of color set down in the description of *Muscovy glass*, there must necessarily appear a red color in the *transitus* or passage of those tangent rays. To make this more plain, we will suppose (in the sixth figure) A B C D to represent the globe of the *atmosphere*, and E F G H to represent the opaque globe of the Earth lying in the midst of it. Near the Earth, the parts of the air, sustaining a very great pressure, are thereby very much condensed; from which those rays that are by inflection made tangents to the globe of the Earth—and those outside them that pass through the more condensed part of the *atmosphere*, as, suppose, between A and E—are, by reason of the inequality of the *medium*, inflected toward the center, whereby a red color must necessarily be generated, as is more plainly shown in the previously cited place. Hence, whatever opaque bodies (such as vapors or the like) happen to be elevated into those parts will reflect a red toward the eye; and therefore those evenings and mornings appear reddest that have the greatest store of vapors and <term>halituous</term> substances exhaled to a suitable distance from the Earth. For by that the inflection is made greater, and the color also more intense; and since several of those exhalations are opaque, they reflect several of those rays which, through a *homogeneous* transparent *medium*, would pass unseen; and therefore we see that when there happen to be any clouds situated in those regions, they reflect a strong and vivid red. Now, though one great cause of the redness may be this inflection, yet I cannot wholly exclude the color of the vapors themselves, which may have something of redness in them, being partly nitrous and partly <term>fuliginous</term>; both of these vapors tinge the rays that pass through them, as is made evident by looking at bodies through the fumes of *aqua fortis*, or spirit of nitre <note>as the newly mentioned illustrious person has demonstrated</note> and also through the smoke of a fire or chimney.

Therefore, the semi-diameter I L will be shorter than L G, and consequently the underside of the appearing sun will be flatter than the upper.

Now, because the rays from the right and left sides of the sun, etc., have been observed by *Ricciolo* and *Grimaldi* to appear more distant from one another than they really are—though I could never perceive any great alteration through very many observations that I have made for that purpose with a very good *telescope* fitted with a divided ruler—there being some actual change, it will not be amiss to show that this also proceeds from the refraction or inflection of the *atmosphere*. This will be manifest if we consider the *atmosphere* as a transparent globe, or at least a transparent shell, encompassing an opaque globe. This shell, being more dense than the *medium* encompassing it, refracts or inflects all the entering parallel rays into a point or focus. Thus, wherever the observer is placed within the *atmosphere* between the focus and the luminous body, the *lateral* rays must necessarily be more converged toward his eye by the refraction or inflection than they would have been without it; and therefore the horizontal diameter of the luminous body must necessarily be augmented.

Taking a short *telescope* that I had then with me, I observed the body of the Sun—though it had only just peeked above the horizon—to have its underside not only flattened and pressed inward, as it usually is when near the Earth, but to appear more protuberant downwards than if it had suffered no refraction at all. Besides all this, the whole body of the Sun appeared to tremble or dance, and the edges or limb appeared very ragged or indented, undulating or waving, much like a flag in the wind.

I have likewise often observed this on a hot, sunny summer day: that looking at an object over a hot stone or dry, hot earth, I have found the object to be undulating or shaken in much the same manner. And if you look at any remote object through a *telescope* (especially on a hot summer day), you shall likewise find it to appear tremulous. Furthermore, if a wind happens to blow, or if the air between you and the object is in a motion or current—whereby its parts, both rarefied and condensed, are swiftly moved toward the right or left—and you then observe the horizontal ridge of a far distant hill through a very good *telescope*, you shall find it to wave much like the sea, and those waves will appear to pass in the same direction as the wind.

From these and many other experiments, it is clear that the lower region of the air, especially that part of it which lies closest to the Earth, has, for the most part, its constituent parts variously agitated, either by heat or winds. By the first of these, some of them are made more rare and so suffer less refraction; others are interwoven with either ascending or descending vapors. The former of these, being lighter and so more rarefied, likewise have less refraction; the latter, being heavier and consequently more dense, have a greater refraction.

Now, because heat and cold are equally diffused in every direction, and grow weaker the further they spread, it follows that most of the lower region of the air will be made up of several kinds of *lenses*, some of which will have the properties of *convex*, others of *concave glasses*. To explain this more intelligibly, we will suppose in the eighth figure of the 37th *Scheme* that A represents an ascending vapor. Because it is somewhat *heterogeneous* to the surrounding air, it is thrust into a kind of globular form, not sharply terminated anywhere but finished gradually. That is, it is most rarefied in the middle around A, somewhat more condensed around B B, more so around C C, even more around D D (almost of the same density as the surrounding air near E E), and lastly enclosed by the more dense air F F, so that from A to F F there is a continual increase of density. Therefore, by the intervention of this descending vapor, the visible body of the star, or other object, is greatly enlarged, as by the former it was diminished.

From the rapid succession of these two, one after another, between the object and your eye—caused by their motion upward or downward (proceeding from their lightness or weight) or to the right or left (proceeding from the wind)—a star may appear now larger, now smaller, than it really would be otherwise without them; and this is that property of a star which is commonly called twinkling, or scintillation.

The reason why a star will appear now of one color, now of another—which for the most part happens when it is near the horizon—may very easily be deduced from its appearing now in the middle of the vapor, at other times near the edge; for if you look at the body of a star with a *telescope* that has a fairly powerful *convex eyepiece*, and so order it that the star may appear sometimes in one place and sometimes in another part of it, you may perceive this or that particular color to be predominant in the apparent shape of the star, according to whether it is more or less remote from the middle of the *lens*. I would have explained this further here, but it more properly belongs to another place.

6. Whether the expansion and contraction of water are not produced in the same way as those effects are produced in the air by heat; for I once balanced a sealed glass bubble so exactly that the slightest addition would make it sink, and the slightest subtraction would make it float. Leaving it to rest in that vessel of water for some time, I always found it at the bottom of the water around noon, and at the top at night and in the morning. Imagining this to result from the expansion of the water caused by heat, I tested it and found it most true; for I was able at any time to either lower or raise it using heat and cold. For if I let the tube stand for some time in cold water, I could easily raise the bubble from the bottom, where I had recently pushed it down by putting the same tube into warm water. And in this way, I have been able for a very considerable time to keep a bubble so balanced in the water that it would remain in the middle, neither sinking nor floating. For by gently heating the upper part of the tube with a candle, coal, or hot iron until I perceived the bubble begin to descend, and then stopping, I observed it descend to a certain position and remain suspended there for several hours until the heat vanished by degrees, at which point it would again ascend to its former place. This I have also often observed naturally performed by the heat of the air, which—being able to expand the upper parts of the water sooner than the lower because of its direct contact—the heat of the air

...has sometimes increased so slowly that I have observed the bubble taking several hours to pass between the top and the bottom.

7. Whether the appearance of the *Peak of Tenerife* and several other high mountains at a much greater distance than seems to agree with their respective heights should not be attributed to the curvature of the visual ray. This curvature is caused by the ray passing obliquely through a medium of such differently dense parts from the mountain top to an eye located very far away on the horizon. For since I have already, I hope, made it very probable that there is such an inflection of the rays caused by the differing density of the parts of the air; and since I have found, by several experiments made in places that are not very high by comparison, that the pressure sustained by those parts of the air at the top and bottom, as well as their differing expansions, is very considerable. For example, I have found the pressure of the *atmosphere* at the top of St. Paul’s Steeple in *London* (which is about two hundred feet high) to be lighter than at the bottom by a sixtieth or fiftieth part, and the expansion at the top was greater than at the bottom by nearly as much. The *mercurial cylinder* <note>A barometer</note> at the bottom was about 29 inches, and at the top it was half an inch lower. The air included in the *weather-glass* <note>An instrument used to measure the expansion of air, acting here as a thermo-baroscope</note>, which at the bottom filled only 155 spaces, filled 158 at the top, even though the heat at the top and bottom was found to be exactly the same with a sealed *thermometer*. I think it very rational to suppose that the greatest curvature of the rays occurs nearest the Earth, and that the inflection of the rays more than 3 or 4 miles upward is very insignificant. Therefore, calculations of the height of mountains made from the distance they are visible on the horizon—based on the assumption that the ray is a straight line (treating the ray from the top of the mountain as if it were a tangent to the horizon from which it is seen) when it is really a curve—are very erroneous. This, I suppose, is the reason for the greatly differing opinions and assertions of various authors regarding the height of several very high hills.

8. Whether this inflection of the air will not significantly alter the assumed distances of the planets, which seem to depend heavily upon the hypothetical refraction or inflection of the air, and that refraction, in turn, depends upon the hypothetical height and density of the air. Since I have shown here (as I hope) that the air is quite different from what has been previously supposed—by demonstrating it to be of a vast, or at least uncertain, height, and of an inconstant and irregular density—it must necessarily follow that its inflection must vary accordingly. Therefore, we may learn from this upon what shaky foundations all astronomers have built who have calculated the distance of the planets using their *horizontal parallax*. Since refraction and parallax are so closely related that one cannot be known without the other—especially by any ways that have been attempted so far—how uncertain must the parallax be when the refraction is unknown? And how easy it is for astronomers to assign whatever distance they please to the planets and defend them, since they have such a clever subterfuge as refraction; a very slight variation in it gives them enough freedom to place the celestial bodies at whatever distance they wish.

# M I C R O G R A P H I A.

If therefore we would come to any certainty in this point, we must work in other ways; and as I have here examined the height and refractive property of the air by other ways than are usual, so must we find the parallax of the planets by ways not yet practiced. To this end, I cannot imagine any better way than the observations of them by two persons at very far distant parts of the Earth, who lie as near as may be under the same meridian, or degree of longitude, but differing as much in latitude as there can be places conveniently found. These two persons, at certain appointed times, should (as near as could be) both at the same time observe the path of the *Moon*, *Mars*, *Venus*, *Jupiter*, and *Saturn* among the fixed stars with a good large *telescope*. They should make little *iconisms* <note>Diagrams or sketches</note>, or pictures, of the small fixed stars that appear to each of them to lie in or near the path of the center of the planet, and the exact measure of the apparent diameter. From the comparison of such observations together, we might certainly know the true distance, or parallax, of the planet. And having any one true parallax of these planets, we might very easily have the others by their apparent diameters, which the *telescope* likewise affords us very accurately. And from there, their motions might be much better known, and their theories more exactly regulated. And for this purpose, I know not any one place more convenient for such an observation to be made in than in the island of *St. Helena*, upon the coast of *Africa*, which lies about sixteen degrees to the southwards of the Line <note>The Equator</note>, and is very near, according to the latest geographical maps, in the same meridian with *London*. For though they may not perhaps lie exactly in the same one, yet their observations, being ordered according to what I shall shortly show, it will not be difficult to find the true distance of the planet. But were they both under the same meridian, it would be much better.

And because observations may be much easier and more accurately made with good *telescopes* than with any other instruments, it will not, I suppose, seem irrelevant to explain a little what ways I judge most fit and convenient for that particular. Such therefore as shall be the observers for this purpose should be furnished with the best *telescopes* that can be had; the longer they are, the better and more exact will their observations be, though they are somewhat more difficultly managed. These should be fitted with a *rete* <note>A reticle or divided grid</note>, or divided scale, placed at such a distance within the eyepiece that they may be distinctly seen, which should be the measures of minutes and seconds. By this instrument, each observer should, at certain prefixed times, observe the Moon, or other planet, in, or very near, the meridian. And because it may be very difficult to find two convenient stations that will happen to be just under the same meridian, they shall, each of them, observe the path of the planet both for an hour before and an hour after it arrives at the meridian. And by a line, or stroke, among the small fixed stars, they shall mark out the path that each of them observed the center of the planet to be moved in for those two hours. These observations each of them shall repeat for many days together, so that it may happen that both of them

And because many of the stars which may happen to come within the compass of such an *iconism* <note>diagram or map</note>, or map, may be such as are only visible through a good *telescope*, whose positions perhaps have not been noted, nor their longitudes or latitudes anywhere remarked; therefore each observer should endeavor to insert some fixed star whose longitude and latitude is known; or with his *telescope* he shall find the position of some notable telescopic star, inserted in his map, relative to some known fixed star whose place in the *Zodiac* is well defined.

Having by this means found the true distance of the Moon, and having observed well its apparent *diameter* at that time with a good *telescope*, it is easy enough, by one single observation of the apparent diameter of the Moon with a good glass, to determine her distances in any other part of her *orbit*, or *Dragon* <note>the lunar orbit path</note>, and consequently, a few observations will tell us whether she moves in an *ellipsis* <note>ellipse</note> (which, by the way, may also be found even now, though I think we are yet ignorant of her true distance). Next (which without such observations, I think, we shall not be sure of), we may know exactly the size of that *ellipsis*, or circle, and her true velocity in each part, and thereby be much the better enabled to find out the true cause of all her motions. And though even now we may, by such observations in one station, as here at *London*, observe the apparent *diameter* and motion of the Moon in her *Dragon*, and consequently be enabled to make a better guess at the *species* or kind of curve in which she moves—that is, whether it be spherical, or elliptical, or neither, and with what proportional velocities she is carried in that curve—yet until her true *parallax* is known, we cannot determine either.

Next, for the true distance of the Sun, the best way will be by accurate observations, made in both these aforementioned stations, of some convenient eclipse of the Sun, many of which may happen to be seen by both; for the *penumbra* of the Moon may, if she is sixty semidiameters distant from the Earth and the Sun above seven thousand, extend to about seventy degrees on the Earth, and consequently be seen by observers as far distant as *London* and *St. Helena*, which are not full sixty-nine degrees apart. And this would much more accurately than any way that has been yet used determine the *parallax* and distance of the Sun. For as for the horizontal parallax, I have already shown it to be sufficiently uncertain; nor is the way of finding it by the eclipse of the Moon anything other than hypothetical; and that by the difference of the true and apparent quadrature of the Moon is no less uncertain, as witnessed by the deductions of those who have used it. For *Vendeline* puts that difference to be but 4' 30", from which he deduces a vast distance for the Sun, as I have shown before. *Ricciolo* makes it a full 30' 00", but *Reinoldus* and *Kircher* no less than three degrees. And it is no wonder, for if we examine the theory, we shall find it so complicated with uncertainties.

First, from the irregular surface of the Moon and from several parallaxes, unless the *dichotomy* <note>the phase where the Moon appears exactly half-illuminated</note> happens in the *nonagesimus* <note>the 90th degree of the ecliptic from the horizon</note> of the *ecliptic*, and that on the *meridian*, etc.—all of which happen so very seldom that it is almost impossible to perform them without uncertainty. Besides, we are not yet certain whether there might be something about the Moon *analogous* to the air around the Earth, which may cause a refraction of the light of the Sun, and consequently make a great difference in the apparent *dichotomy* of the Moon. Their method indeed is very rational and ingenious, and one that is much to be preferred over the method using the horizontal parallax, if all the uncertainties could be removed and the true distance of the Moon were known.

But because we find by the experiments of *Vendiline* <note>Godefroy Wendelin</note>, *Reinoldus* <note>Erasmus Reinhold</note>, etc., that observations of this kind are also very uncertain; it were to be wished that such kinds of observations, made at two very distant stations, were promoted. And it is so much the more desirable because, from what I have now shown of the nature of the *air*, it is evident that the refraction may be very much greater than all the *astronomers* hitherto have imagined it. Consequently, the distance of the Moon and other *planets* may be much less than what they have hitherto estimated.

For first, this *inflection* I have proposed here will allow the shadow of the *Earth* to be much shorter than it can be made by the other *hypothesis* of refraction; consequently, the Moon will not suffer an eclipse unless it comes very much nearer the Earth than the *astronomers* hitherto have supposed.

Secondly, there will not be in this *hypothesis* any other shadow of the *Earth*, such as *Kepler* supposes and calls the *penumbra*, which is the shadow of the refracting *atmosphere*. For the bending of the rays being altogether caused by *inflection*, as I have already shown, all that part which is ascribed by *Kepler* and others after him to the *penumbra*, or dark part, which is outside the *umbra terræ* <note>the shadow of the Earth</note>, clearly vanishes. In this *hypothesis*, there is no refracting surface of the air, and consequently there can be no shadows such as appear in the ninth figure of the 37th *Scheme*. In that figure, let *ABCD* represent the Earth, and *EFGH* the *atmosphere*, which according to *Kepler's* supposition is like a *sphere* of water terminated with an exact surface *EFGH*. Let the lines *MF*, *LB*, *ID*, and *KH* represent the rays of the Sun; it is manifest that all the rays between *LB* and *ID* will be reflected by the surface of the Earth *BAD*, and consequently the conical space *BOD* would be dark and obscure. But, say the followers of *Kepler*, the rays between *MF* and *LB*, and between *ID* and *KH*, falling on the *atmosphere*, are refracted both at their entry and exit out of the *atmosphere*, nearer towards the axis of the spherical shadow *CO*, and consequently enlighten a great part of that formerly dark cone and shorten and contract its top to *N*. And because of this reflection of these rays, they say, there is superinduced another shell of a dark cone, *FPH*, whose *apex*, *P*, is yet further distant from the Earth. By this *penumbra*, they say, the Moon

To which I say, that if the air be such as I have recently shown it to be, and consequently causes such an inflection of the rays that fall into it, those dark *penumbras FYZQ, HXVT*, and *ORPS* will all vanish. For if we suppose the air indefinitely extended, and to be nowhere bounded with a determinate refracting surface (as I have shown it is incapable of having, from its very nature), it follows that the Moon will nowhere be totally obscured except when it is below the apex *N* of the dark blunt cone of the Earth’s shadow. Now, from the supposition that the Sun is distant about seven thousand diameters, the point *N*, according to calculation, is not above twenty-five terrestrial semidiameters from the center of the Earth. It follows that whenever the eclipsed Moon is totally darkened, without affording any kind of light, it must be within twenty-five semidiameters of the Earth, and consequently much lower than any astronomers have hitherto placed it.

This will seem much more consistent with the rest of the secondary planets; for the highest of *Jupiter*’s moons is between twenty and thirty *Jovial* <note>pertaining to the planet Jupiter</note> semidiameters distant from the center of *Jupiter*; and the moon of *Saturn* is about the same number of *Saturnial* <note>pertaining to the planet Saturn</note> semidiameters from the center of that planet.

But these are only conjectures as well, and must be determined by the kind of observations I have recently mentioned.

Nor will it be difficult, by this *hypothesis*, to explain all the appearances of eclipses of the Moon; for in this *hypothesis* also, there will be a *penumbra* on each side of the shadow of the Earth, not caused by the refraction of the air as in the *hypothesis* of *Kepler*, but by the faint enlightening of it by the Sun. For if, in the sixth figure, we suppose *ESQ* and *GSR* to be the rays that terminate the shadow from either side of the Earth—*ESQ* coming from the upper limb of the Sun, and *GSR* from the lower—it follows that the shadow of the Earth within those rays (that is, the cone *GSE*) will be totally dark. But the Sun being not a point but a large area of light, there will be a secondary dark cone of shadow *EPG*, which will be caused by the Earth’s hindering part of the rays of the Sun from falling on the parts *GPR* and *EPQ*. In this halved shadow, or *penumbra*, that part will appear brightest which lies nearest the terminating rays *GP* and *EP*, and those darker that lie nearest to *GS* and *ES*. When, therefore, the Moon appears quite dark in the middle of the eclipse, she must be below *S*—that is, between *S* and *F*; when she appears lighter near the middle of the eclipse, she must pass somewhere between *RQ* and *S*; and when she is equally light through the whole eclipse, she must pass between *RQ* and *P*.

### Observation LIX. *Of multitudes of small stars discoverable by the* Telescope.

Having, in the last observation, introduced some details observable in the *medium* through which we must look at *celestial objects*, I shall here add one observation of the *bodies themselves*; and as a *specimen*, I have made choice of the *Pleiades*, or seven stars, commonly so called (though in our time and climate no more than six appear to the naked eye). I did this primarily because the deservedly famous *Galileo*, having published a picture of this *asterism*, was able, it seems, with his glass to discover no more than thirty-six; whereas with a quite good twelve-foot *telescope*, with which I drew this 38th *illustration*, I could very plainly discover seventy-eight, placed in the order they are ranged in the figure, and of as many different magnitudes as the *asterisks* marking them specify. There are no fewer than fourteen several magnitudes of those stars comprised within the drawing, the largest of which is not accounted greater than one of the third magnitude; and indeed that assessment is much too large if it is compared with other stars of the third magnitude, especially with the help of a *telescope*. For then it may be perceived that its splendor to the naked eye may be somewhat increased by the three little stars immediately above it, which are closely adjoining it.

The *telescope* also discovers a great variety even in the size of those commonly reckoned of the first, second, third, fourth, fifth, and sixth magnitude; so that if they were distinguished by it, those six magnitudes would afford at least three times that number of magnitudes, plainly enough distinguishable by their size and brightness. Thus, a good twelve-foot glass would provide us with no fewer than twenty-five different magnitudes. Nor are these all; a longer glass goes even further, both more precisely distinguishing the magnitudes of those already noted and also discovering several others of smaller magnitudes not discernible by the twelve-foot glass. Thus I have been able, with a good thirty-six-foot glass, to discover many more stars in the *Pleiades* than are depicted here, and those of three or four distinct magnitudes smaller than any of those spots of the fourteenth magnitude. And by the twinkling of various other places in this *asterism*, when the sky was very clear, I am inclined to think that with longer glasses, or those that would support a larger aperture, multitudes of other small stars, yet invisible, might be discovered. And indeed, for the discovery of small stars, the larger the aperture is, the better adapted the glass is; for though it perhaps makes the various specks more radiant and glaring, yet by that means—uniting more rays very near to one point—it makes many of those radiant points conspicuous,

So that it is not unlikely, but that the improving of *telescopes* will afford as great a variety of new discoveries in the heavens as better *microscopes* would among small terrestrial bodies, and both would give us infinite cause, more and more, to admire the omnipotence of the Creator.

## Observation LX. Of the Moon.

Having a pretty large corner of the plate for the seven stars void, for the filling it up, I have added one small *specimen* of the appearance of the parts of the Moon, by describing a small spot of it, which, though taken notice of both by the excellent *Hevelius* and called *Mons Olympus* (though I think somewhat improperly, being rather a vale) and represented by the Figure X of the 38th *scheme*, and also by the learned *Ricciolus*, who calls it *Hipparchus* and describes it by the Figure Y, yet how far short both of them come of the truth may be somewhat perceived by the drawing which I have here added of it in the Figure Z (which I drew by a thirty-foot glass in *October* 1664, just before the Moon was half illuminated), but much better by the reader's diligently observing it himself, at a convenient time, with a glass of that length, and much better yet with one of sixty foot long; for through these it appears a very spacious vale, encompassed with a ridge of hills, not very high in comparison of many others in the Moon, nor yet very steep. The vale itself A B C D is much of the figure of a pear, and from several appearances of it, seems to be some very fruitful place—that is, to have its surface all covered over with some kinds of vegetable substances; for in all positions of the light on it, it seems to give a much fainter reflection than the more barren tops of the encompassing hills, and those a much fainter than various other cragged, chalky, or rocky mountains of the Moon. So that I am not unapt to think that the vale may have

Vegetables *analogous* to our grass, shrubs, and trees; and most of these surrounding hills may be covered with such a thin vegetable coat as we may observe our own hills to be, such as the short sheep pasture which covers the hills of Salisbury Plain.

Up and down in several parts of this place described here (as there are multitudes in other places all over the surface of the Moon) several kinds of pits may be perceived which are shaped almost like a dish—some bigger, some smaller, some shallower, some deeper. That is, they seem to be a hollow *hemisphere*, encompassed by a round rising bank, as if the substance in the middle had been dug up and thrown on either side. These seem to me to have been the effects of some motions within the body of the Moon, *analogous* to our earthquakes. By the eruption of these, as it has thrown up a brim or ridge all around, higher than the surrounding surface of the Moon, so has it left a hole or depression in the middle, proportionally lower. I have observed various places resembling some of these here in *England* on the tops of some hills, which might have been caused by some earthquake in the younger days of the world. But that which most inclines me to this belief is, first, the prevalence and diversity of the size of these pits all over the body of the Moon. Next, the two experimental ways by which I have made a representation of them.

The first was with a very soft and well-tempered mixture of tobacco-pipe clay and water, into which, if I let fall any heavy body, such as a bullet, it would throw up the mixture around the place, which for a while would create a representation not unlike those of the Moon. But considering the state and condition of the Moon, there seems to be no probability of imagining that it should proceed from any cause *analogous* to this; for it would be difficult to imagine where those bodies would come from, and next, how the substance of the Moon could be so soft. But if a bubble is blown under the surface of it and allowed to rise and break, or if a bullet or other body sunk in it is pulled out from it, these departing bodies leave an impression on the surface of the mixture exactly like those of the Moon, except that these also quickly subside and vanish. But the second, and most notable, representation was what I observed in a pot of boiling alabaster; for there that powder, being reduced to a kind of fluid consistency by the eruption of vapors, if, while it boils, it is gently removed from the fire, the alabaster presently ceases to boil, and the whole surface—especially where some of the last bubbles have risen—will appear covered all over with small pits exactly shaped like those of the Moon. By holding a lighted candle in a large dark room in various positions relative to this surface, you may exactly represent all the *phenomena* of these pits in the Moon, according to how they are more or less enlightened by the Sun.

And that there may have been in the Moon some such motion as this, which may have made these pits, will seem the more probable if we suppose it is like our Earth; for the earthquakes here with us seem to proceed from some such cause as the boiling of the pot of alabaster,

# MICROGRAPHIA.

Because after, there seeming to be generated in the Earth from some subterranean fires, or heat, great quantities of vapors—that is, of expanded aerial substances—which, not immediately finding a passage through the surrounding parts of the Earth, do (as they are increased by the supplying and generating principles, and thereby, not having sufficient room to expand themselves, are extremely condensed) at last overpower, with their elastic properties, the resistance of the encompassing Earth. Lifting it up, or cleaving it, and so shattering the parts of the Earth above it, they at length, where they find the parts of the Earth above them more loose, make their way upwards; and carrying a great part of the Earth before them, they not only raise a small brim around the place out of which they break, but for the most part considerably high hills and mountains. And when they break from under the sea, several times, they form mountainous islands. This seems confirmed by the *volcanoes* in several places of the Earth, the mouths of which, for the most part, are encompassed with a hill of a considerable height, and the tops of those hills, or mountains, are usually shaped very much like these pits, or basins, of the Moon. Instances of this we have in the descriptions of *Etna* in *Sicily*, of *Hecla* in *Iceland*, of *Tenerife* in the *Canaries*, of the several *volcanoes* in *New Spain*, described by *Gage*, and more especially in the eruption of late years in one of the *Canary Islands*. In all of which there is not only a considerable high hill raised about the mouth of the *volcano*, but, like the spots of the Moon, the top of those hills are like a dish or basin. And indeed, if one attentively considers the nature of the thing, one may find sufficient reason to judge that it cannot be otherwise; for these eruptions, whether of fire or smoke, always raising great quantities of Earth before them, must necessarily, by the fall of those parts on either side, raise very considerable heaps.

Now, both from the figures of them and from several other circumstances, these pits in the Moon seem to have been generated much in the same manner that the holes in *alabaster* and the *volcanoes* of the Earth are made. For first, it is not improbable that the substance of the Moon may be very much like that of our Earth—that is, may consist of an earthy, sandy, or rocky substance in several of its superficial parts—which parts being agitated, undermined, or heaved up by eruptions of vapors, may naturally be thrown into the same kind of figured holes as the small dust or powder of *alabaster*. Next, it is not improbable that there may be generated within the body of the Moon various such kinds of internal fires and heats as may produce such exhalations; for since we can plainly enough discover with a *telescope* that there are multitudes of such kinds of eruptions in the body of the Sun itself, which is accounted the most noble ethereal body, certainly we need not be much scandalized at such kinds of alterations or corruptions in the body of this lower and less considerable part of the universe, the Moon, which is only secondary, or an attendant, on the bigger and more considerable body of the Earth. Thirdly, it is not unlikely, but that supposing such a sandy or moldering substance to

<summary>Hooke proposes that lunar craters are formed by internal heat and expanding vapors, drawing parallels to volcanic activity on Earth and observed eruptions on the Sun. He suggests the Moon's composition is similar to Earth's, consisting of earthy or rocky material capable of being shaped by these geological forces.</summary>

<page-num>245</page-num>
<header>MICROGRAPHIA.</header>
<meta>catchword: Ebullitions,</meta>

be there found, and supposing also a possibility of the generation of the internal elastic body (whether you will call it air or vapors), it is not unlikely, I say, but that there is in the Moon a principle of gravitation, such as in the Earth. And to make this probable, I think we need no better argument than the roundness, or globular figure of the body of the Moon itself, which we may perceive very plainly by the *telescope* to be (excepting the small inequality of the hills and valleys in it, which are all of them likewise shaped, or leveled, as it were, to correspond to the center of the Moon’s body) perfectly of a spherical figure; that is, all the parts of it are so arranged (excepting the comparatively small ruggedness of the hills and dales) that their outermost bounds are equally distant from the center of the Moon, and consequently, it is exceedingly probable also that they are equidistant from the center of gravitation. And indeed, the figure of the superficial parts of the Moon are so exactly shaped, just as they should be assuming it had a gravitating principle as the Earth has, that even the figure of those parts themselves is of sufficient efficacy to make the gravitation and the other two suppositions probable; so that the other suppositions may be rather proven by this significant circumstance or observation, than this supposed explanation can be proven by them. For he that shall attentively observe with an excellent *telescope* how all the circumstances notable in the shape of the superficial parts are, as it were, exactly adapted to suit with such a principle, will—if he well considers the usual method of Nature in its other proceedings—find abundant argument to believe it to have really there also such a principle; for I could never observe, among all the mountainous or prominent parts of the Moon (of which there is a huge variety), that any one part of it was placed in such a manner that, if there should be a gravitating or attracting principle in the body of the Moon, it would make that part to fall, or be moved out of its visible posture. Next, the shape and position of the parts is such that they all seem put into those very shapes they are in by a gravitating power: For first, there are but very few cliffs, or very steep declivities in the ascent of these mountains; for besides those mountains which are by *Hevelius* called the *Apennine Mountains*, and some others which seem to border on the *Seas* of the Moon, and those only upon one side (as is common also in those hills that are here on the Earth), there are very few that seem to have very steep ascents; but, for the most part, they are made very round, and much resemble the make of the hills and mountains also of the Earth. This may be partly perceived by the hills encompassing this vale, which I have described here; and as on the Earth also, the middlemost of these hills seems the highest, so is it obvious also, through a good *telescope*, in those of the Moon. The valleys also in many are much shaped like those of the Earth, and I am apt to think that, could we look upon the Earth from the Moon with a good *telescope*, we might easily enough perceive its surface to be very much like that of the Moon.

Now whereas in this small drawing (as there would be multitudes if the whole Moon were drawn after this manner) there are several little *ebullitions*,

<summary>Hooke argues that the Moon's spherical shape and the arrangement of its mountains and valleys provide strong evidence that it possesses a principle of gravitation similar to the Earth's. He notes that lunar topography closely resembles terrestrial features, suggesting the two bodies share similar physical processes.</summary>

Bubbles, or pits, even in the valleys themselves, and in the surrounding hills as well; this will, from this hypothesis (which I have, I think, adopted for very good reason), be very easily explained. For, as I have several times also observed on the surface of alabaster prepared as I previously described, the later eruptions of vapors may be even in the middle, or on the edges, of the former ones; and others succeeding these in time may be in the middle or edges of these, etc. There are enough examples of this in various parts of the body of the Moon, and it will be sufficiently demonstrated by a boiling pot of alabaster.

To conclude, therefore, it being very probable that the Moon has a principle of gravitation, it provides an excellent distinguishing example in the search for the cause of gravitation, or attraction, to suggest that it does not depend upon the daily or rotating motion of the Earth, as some have somewhat thoughtlessly supposed and affirmed it to do. For if the Moon has an attractive principle, by which it is not only shaped roundly, but does firmly contain and hold all its parts united—though many of them seem as loose as the sand on the Earth—and given that the Moon does not rotate about its center, then certainly rotation cannot be the cause of the attraction of the Earth. Therefore, some other principle must be thought of that will agree with all the secondary as well as primary planets. But this, I confess, is only a probability, and not a demonstration, of which (from any observation yet made) it seems hardly capable, though how successful future endeavors (promoted by the improvement of telescopes, and observing particular circumstances) may be in this, or any other kind, must be waited for with patience.

### Obs. 59. Of the *fixed stars.*
<margin>241</margin>
Of the multitudes of stars disco-
verable by the *telescope*, and the
variety of their magnitudes: 78 stars
distinguished in the *Pleiades*: that there
are degrees of bigness even in the *stars*
accounted of the same magnitude: the
longer the *lenses* are, and the larger
apertures they will allow, the more
fit they are for these discoveries: that
it is probable longer *lenses* would yet
make greater discoveries. Five stars <margin>242</margin>

### Obs. 60. Of the *Moon.*

A description of a *vale* in the
*Moon*; what it is called by *Hevelius* and
*Ricciolus*, and how described by them.
With what substances the hills of the <margin>243</margin>

of the pits of the *Moon*, and a conje-
cture as to their cause: two experiments
that make it probable, with the sur-
face of boiled *alabaster* dust appearing <margin>244</margin>
the most likely to be resembled by eru-
ptions of vapors out of the body of the
*Moon*: that *earthquakes* seem to be
generated much the same way, and
their effects seem very similar. An ar-
gument that there may be such varia-
tions in the *Moon*, because greater
have been observed in the *Sun*: because <margin>245</margin>
the substance of the *Moon* and *Earth*
seem much alike: and because it is pro-
bable the *Moon* has a gravitating
principle: this is argued from several
particulars. The reason why several <margin>246</margin>
pits are one within another. The use
that may be made of this instance of
gravity in the *Moon*.
